en: Nyāyaratnamālā by Pārthasārathi Miśra:
[Salutation to] the Lord, who is bliss, immortal, consciousness, unborn, and the witness.
I bow to Lord Hari, the Sovereign, who is both the Brahman that is all and the Brahman that is not all. 1.
With the jewels of logic produced from the ocean of Mīmāṃsā and composed by Kumārasvāmin, I string together this beautiful garland. (2)
First, the purpose of the injunction for private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) is stated, following the view of the Teacher (*ācārya*), by means of the refutation of opposing views. (3)
In this regard, first they set forth the following prima facie argument:
"The purpose of Vedic study is the injunction to become a teacher, because that is the context. (4)
For that purpose is appropriate which is understood first;
in this case, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is what is subsequently cognized. (5)
Therefore, because the Veda has no intended meaning, an investigation into its meaning should not be undertaken;
consequently, the treatise on Mīmāṃsā is purposeless.

For when the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*), which is enjoined by the rule for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), stands in need of a purpose, its very accomplishment is the appropriate purpose; this is because it is the first thing understood, even though it is an external factor (*bahiraṅga*) insofar as it pertains to another person [the teacher]. Knowledge of the meaning, however, is not the purpose, because it occurs later. Since the study of the Veda thus serves another end, the meaning is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). And that which is not intended to be expressed need not be determined, as there is no purpose for doing so.

Furthermore, since there would be no deliberation (*vicāra*) regarding a determination that ought not to be made, the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra—which consists of such [deliberation]—would be purposeless and thus should not be commenced. How is it that study is impelled by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) and not by its own injunction? It is said in reply: "In the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*);
and in the absence of that, it is not logical for it to have the status of an impeller (*prayojaka*), as is the case with the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. (Verse 7)

For it is not possible for an injunction lacking a qualified subject to impel the performance of its object, as is the case with the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Furthermore, no qualified subject is heard in the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*); therefore, it is not possible for this [injunction] to function as an impeller.
And it cannot be conceived as something to be enjoined, like the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);
for even when that [injunction] is not conceived, the performance is nonetheless accomplished. ||8||

It is argued that even if not explicitly heard in the text, an *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is to be postulated, as in the case of the *pitṛyajña* and other rites; but this is not so. For the performance of the rite is established even without a postulated *niyojya*. Once that [performance] is established, the *niyojya* cannot be postulated, because there is no logical necessity for it. An *niyoga* (an injunction), whose establishment depends upon performance, requires a performer for the sake of its own fulfillment. Since it is impossible for one who is not an *adhikārin* (one entitled to the rite) to be a performer, and since it is impossible for one who is not an *niyojya* to be an *adhikārin*, the *niyoga* does not necessitate the postulation of an *niyojya*.

But when one perceives that its own self-acquisition occurs through an object already established by the performance of another injunction, then, due to the absence of any logical inconsistency, it does not postulate a separate person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), as is the case with the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. And here, since the fulfillment of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-niyoga*) is possible precisely through the object of the self which is established by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), there is no possibility of postulating a separate person to be enjoined. How, then, does the injunction to become a teacher impel one toward the act of studying? This is explained:
the status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*) arises from teaching after having initiated a pupil (*upanīya*); and teaching is not possible without [the pupil] studying.

This [objection] is refuted: since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is understood through the suffix *ktvā* to have the same agent as the teaching (*adhyāpana*), it is recognized as being a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of that very act. When its means (*dvāra*) is required, the presence of the one to be initiated (*upaneyasattā*) is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) to be that very means. Furthermore, since the one to be initiated cannot be a subsidiary without performing some function, when its activity is required, study (*adhyayana*)—which is taught in the context of the initiation—is determined to be that activity by virtue of its being helpful to the teaching.

And thus, since it is understood that the student, while performing the study of the Veda, assists the act of teaching, the act of teaching itself—having that [study] as its object—is the means for attaining the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*). Consequently, through that [teaching], the performance of all the ancillaries of study, such as the vows (*vrata*) and so forth, is established by that very [act of teaching]. Therefore, because the purpose of study is the accomplishment of the injunction for becoming a teacher, and because the meaning of the Veda is not intended to be expressed [by the student], the Mīmāṃsā system has not been commenced for the sake of determining the meaning of that [Veda].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is true that the study [of the Veda] is prompted by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), yet the attainment of that status is not its primary purpose, because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Since knowledge of the meaning is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*)—as it accrues to the agent—it is accepted as the purpose by virtue of being the actual goal. Objection: Because it is first understood, the study, which requires a purpose, accepts the status of being a teacher itself; and once that has been accepted, there is no further need for anything else. Therefore, knowledge of the meaning, though understood later and being intrinsic, cannot be the purpose.

It is not so; for it is not postulated that the first act of teaching (*ācāryaka*) is the purpose [of study]. If it were the case that the performance of study could not be established unless that [purpose] were postulated, then it might be postulated; however, this is not the case, because even when that is not postulated, the performance [of study] is nonetheless achieved. Once study has been performed, when there arises a requirement for a purpose, the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) alone is accepted as such, because it is more intimately related (*antaraṅga*). But surely, the mandate (*niyoga*) itself, as understood from the words, should be the purpose, and not the knowledge of the meaning?

No; for it is impossible to abandon even the knowledge of the meaning when it is being apprehended. Therefore, it is logical that both are purposes, since both the knowledge of the meaning and the injunction (*niyoga*) are understood [to be so]. Among these, the purpose consisting of the knowledge of the meaning cannot be accomplished through study without inquiry; thus, the injunction of study itself implies inquiry for the sake of achieving that [knowledge], and consequently, this treatise (*śāstra*), which consists of such inquiry, must be commenced. To this, it is replied: This inquiry is not tenable, because the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is prompted by the injunction to teach (*adhyāpana*). (Verse 9)
It is appropriate to perform an investigation; it is not employed by that [investigation], because it can be employed only by its own method. || 10 ||

For if study were indeed impelled by the injunction for teaching, then the inquiry as to whether its purpose is merely the accomplishment of that [teaching] or the knowledge of the meaning would have been appropriate; however, it is not so impelled, since its performance is possible through its own independent injunction.

As for the refutation of the status of being an instigator on the grounds of the absence of one to be enjoined, that applies equally to the act of teaching; for even there, such a person is not explicitly heard [in the Veda].

As for the argument that the injunction to study cannot serve as the motivator for study because there is no person to be enjoined, that same objection applies equally to the injunction to teach. For in the rule "one should initiate a Brahmin boy of eight years and teach him," and in the rule "that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, is called an Ācārya," no person to be enjoined is explicitly mentioned. Therefore, since there is no motivator even in the act of teaching, how much less could there be one for the act of studying?
If, for one who desires the status of a teacher, the state of being enjoined is postulated, why is it not likewise postulated for one who desires knowledge in other instances as well? (12)

For if, in the injunction for teaching, one who desires the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) is postulated as the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) even though it is not explicitly heard [in the text], then the same applies to the injunction for study: one who desires knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) must likewise be postulated. But surely such a person desiring knowledge of the meaning cannot be the one who is enjoined? For if the meaning is already known, it cannot be desired to be known simply because it is already known; nor can a desire for knowledge arise regarding a meaning that is unknown—how indeed could one, whose mind has not grasped it, hope to know it, thinking, "I wish to know this"?

Therefore, it is impossible for one who desires the knowledge of the meaning [of a Vedic injunction] to be a *niyojya* (the person to be directed). To this, it is replied: Oh, how you have set out to deceive yourself, your disciples, and the entire world!

For how could he—disregarding all people who, like himself, are traveling along a difficult path and casting their gaze here and there with the desire to discern the presence or absence of robbers, serpents, thorns, beasts of prey, tigers, lions, and so forth; or those who pursue him out of a desire to know the meaning of the Vedas while looking toward this or that inner chamber and such places with the desire to discern the presence or absence of beloved ones and the like; or those who are striving in the hearing of scriptures, the examination of books, and so on, for the sake of knowing the truth of those matters?

It is possible to deny knowledge and desire; however, such a denial by him is not a cause for wonder. For he denies that which is well-known to everyone, even down to cowherds—the cognition of two moons and so forth—and the fact that the performance of dharma and adharma is the cause of benefit and harm. But we pity those very people who, seeking to understand the meaning of the Vedas, do not abandon one who speaks what is contrary to the whole world, asserting that "the desire to know" does not exist. And the author of the Sūtras [states]: [The text continues: ...and the author of the Sūtras... [The provided text ends here].

For how could the author of the Bhāṣya, having set aside an inquiry similar to that of Sumanas, present it as something to be undertaken? Moreover, this [inquiry] is not well-known; yet, having raised it as if it were well-known, he has resolved it. How, then, is it resolved? It is said: although an object is not desired to be known when it is entirely unknown, nor when it is known in its entirety, nevertheless, it is desired to be known in some respect when it is already known in another respect, for such is observed in experience.

Just as a word such as "udbhid," once understood as denoting either a quality or an action, is further investigated in its specific form; and just as in common worldly experience, [the presence of] a place obstructed by a wall or the like is inferred by means of the movement of shadows and so forth.

Having understood the mere fact of existence, one desires to know specific particulars such as "cow" or "horse. Likewise, having learned from elders such as one's father that dharma and adharma are merely the causes of benefit and harm respectively, it is entirely logical that a desire to know them arises because one is unable to perform their avoidance or adoption without knowing them in their specific forms. Thus, for one who desires knowledge, there is the status of being a person to be enjoined, as expressed in the injunction: "One who desires to know dharma and adharma should study the Veda."

As for the one who says, "We do not deny the desire for knowledge, because it is impossible to deny it given that it is well-known to all the world; for everyone seeks the knowledge of the means for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired—who would disagree on that point? It is only said that there is no desire for the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda"—if indeed the entire meaning of the Veda were the cause for attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired, then that knowledge would be sought by a person.

But this is not so, because both the occasioned prohibition (*naimitika-niṣedha*) and the qualification for entitlement (*adhikāra*) are fully established merely through the performance of the injunction. Therefore, one who desires knowledge of the meaning [of the text] does not possess the status of a person entitled to the action (*niyojyatva*). To this, he should be asked: "In that case, is the knowledge of the meaning of the occasioned statement then entirely disregarded?"

If this were so, then would there be activity toward the entire capacity or only toward a portion of it—just like the deliberation regarding whether a cuckoo has been eaten or a crow? Furthermore, would one perform the sacrifice disregarding time altogether, thinking "one must simply sacrifice," or only at the [proper] time? And in the absence of the primary substance, should another substance be substituted or not—and if so, should it be similar or dissimilar? Such questions would not need to be raised, because deliberation exists for the sake of reaching a conclusion, and its purpose would not be something intended to be concluded.

Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that even in the absence of a [visible] fruit, the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences must be required solely for the sake of accomplishing the performance of the injunction's purpose; thus, one who desires the knowledge of the meaning is the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined). If this is so, then the statement "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) would be untenable, since the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) would have already arisen prior to the study of the Veda. No, for there is a distinction between the inquiries, as it has been said: "The first [inquiry] belongs to one who has been initiated (*upanīta*); the second to one who has studied the revealed scripture (*śruti*); another belongs to one who has mastered the Vedāṅgas; and yet another is that which is preceded by Mīmāṃsā. (Verse 13)

First, having heard from the elders that dharma and adharma must be known, and desiring to know them, he studies the Veda after determining—through the elders themselves—the study prescribed for that purpose according to the rules for Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*). Then, because knowledge of the meaning does not arise even from the studied Veda for one who is unlearned, he exerts himself in hearing the *Nigama*, *Nirukta*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and so forth; and subsequently, although the meaning of the sentence is perceived through knowledge of the word-meanings, it becomes subject to doubt due to a lack of ascertainment regarding the principles of reasoning (*nyāya*).

Then, there arises a further desire to know the specific meaning of the sentence; this subsequent inquiry is mentioned here with the intention of referring to mere curiosity in general. Furthermore, the Teacher employed the word "atha" (now/thereafter) with reference to that specific inquiry into Dharma which is not possible without the study of the Veda. Although the inquiry into validity and invalidity could indeed occur even prior to the study of the Veda, it will nevertheless be undertaken only afterwards, for fear of not fixing the time for such study.

Therefore, enough of going too far. It is established, then, that for one who desires the knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda], there is the status of being enjoined to study. On the contrary, it will be explained immediately hereafter that a person cannot be enjoined to teaching at all, because the status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*) is not understood even in a general sense prior to this very statement.

Now, if it is argued that the qualification of the person enjoined (*niyojya*) does not arise from the injunction itself—[and thus the desire for knowledge is a qualification]—that is not tenable; for the cognition of the meaning is equally present in the case of being a teacher as well. (14)

For only that which is the fruit of the injunction (niyoga) is capable of defining the person to be enjoined (niyojya) by way of being desired, as in the case of the removal of husks and so forth. If it is argued that knowledge, however, is the fruit of the study which constitutes its object and is not produced by the injunction, and therefore it is impossible for one who desires that [knowledge] to be the person to be enjoined—then, for this very reason, even "the status of being a teacher" (ācāryakatva) could not be a qualification of the person to be enjoined, since that too is the fruit of the object [of the injunction]. Furthermore, desire arises toward a beloved thing when it is known through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But the status of being a teacher was not recognized by him through pride or by any other means. ||15||

It is your view that the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*)—which is non-worldly (*alaukika*) like the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth, and not known through any other means of knowledge—is understood only by the very injunction that ordains the act of leading [the pupil] to completion (*adhyāpana*). Furthermore, since desire is impossible toward what is unknown, it is not possible for one who desires that [status] to be the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). However, if it is maintained that one knows [it] through this very injunction and then desires it, the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) arises:
"This injunction proceeds having as its objective one who desires that [status]; and once this injunction has proceeded, there is the determination of one who desires that. (Verse 16)
It might be argued: "Performance exists due to the qualification (adhikāra), and that [qualification] exists here as well;
even though there is no status of being one who is to be enjoined (niyojyatva), for that [qualification] is not directly the means [to the result]. (17)

Regarding the mandate (*niyoga*), there is no state of being "one to be enjoined" (*niyojyatā*) that is directly a means for the performance of the object [of the injunction]; rather, the mandate becomes something to be performed by a person who is connected to it through the status of being "one to be enjoined. For he alone is "one to be enjoined" who understands the mandate as "this is my duty. And for him to whom the mandate is to be performed, there arises an entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the action that is the means to that mandate, because it is the means to accomplish his own duty; and from that entitlement comes the performance. Even where [the connection] exists without [explicitly] being one to be enjoined...

Furthermore, there exists an entitlement (*adhikāra*) for teaching, because it is a means to becoming an *ācārya*. Since teaching is established by scriptural injunction as a means to the status of an *ācārya*, its performance is accomplished for one who desires that status, just as the performance of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) is accomplished for one who desires the sacred fires. Because the injunction to study (*adhyayana-niyoga*) derives its existence from the very act of studying—which is itself prompted by that [teaching]—it does not posit a separate person entitled to perform it. If this is so, then since the performance [of study] is established through entitlement, the claim that study is prompted by teaching is purposeless. (Verse 18)

If it is argued that even without being subject to an injunction (*viniyojyatva*), the performance of study—which is a means to the knowledge of meaning—is established for one who desires that result simply by virtue of one's own entitlement (*svādhikāra*), then it follows that study cannot be said to be prompted by the teacher’s instruction (*adhyāpanaprayuktatva*). Indeed, you yourselves accept that there is an entitlement to study; yet you do not accept mere subjection to an injunction. However, the performance of an act does not depend on being prompted by another merely because of that entitlement, since the performance is obtained from one's own entitlement alone. Furthermore, even when there is a person subject to an injunction regarding an action that is a means to a fruit, the performance proceeds from that very entitlement, and not otherwise.

By virtue of the injunction, it is like the case of the qualification for desire (*kāma-adhikāra*). Furthermore, even in the absence of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the performance of the means is capable of impelling the agent; thus, why should study be understood as having the knowledge of meaning as its purpose? Since the performance [of study] is established from that very [purpose], it is impossible for study to be prompted by teaching. Consequently: "Because of the absence of a person to be enjoined, the lack of a motivating factor is equal for both.
Because of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the status of being the prompter is the same for both. (Verse 19)

If the injunction to study lacks a motivating force because of the absence of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then the injunction to teach would likewise lack a motivating force for the same reason. If, however, the injunction to teach possesses a motivating force due to the existence of an entitlement (*adhikāra*), then it is logical that the injunction to study also possesses a motivating force because that [entitlement] exists for it as well; thus, since both are equal, it is possible that the study is motivated by the injunction to teach. Furthermore, the motivation for inquiry does not arise from the injunction regarding the status of a teacher;
rather, its motivation is through its own entitlement, just as that of the study is. (Verse 20)

The status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*), which is accomplished through teaching, may imply mere study (*adhyayana*) alone, but not inquiry (*vicāra*), since [the status of a teacher] can be attained even without inquiry. Therefore, it must be accepted that the impulsion toward inquiry is prompted by the very entitlement (*adhikāra*) produced by study, which would otherwise be unaccountable without inquiry. In the same way, the impulsion toward study itself is possible through that [entitlement] alone; thus, no other motivating factor need be sought.

For by that result called "knowledge of the meaning" (arthajñāna), for which reflection constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the study—which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is indeed employed; it is employed all the more so by this [result]. Now, it might be argued: "The injunction to teach (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) itself is the motivator of reflection; for, enjoining teaching directed toward a study that has a specific purpose, it employs such a study for the sake of accomplishing that [teaching]; and since such a nature of the study is untenable without reflection, reflection is implied (*ākṣipta*) by that [injunction].
This is incorrect, even if that [injunction] pertains to a specific study.
It impels the performance [of action], because knowledge is not a subordinate factor [in that regard]. ||21||

Although the injunction to teach (adhyāpana-vidhi), by employing study through the medium of initiation (upanayana), prompts the performance of that very study which is enjoined by the sentence "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) studied during the course of initiation must be recited"—and which is for the purpose of knowing the meaning—nevertheless, it prompts only the mere form of that study because it is an auxiliary; it does not, however, prompt the performance of the knowledge of the meaning, as that is not an auxiliary to it.

If, however, the knowledge of the meaning were a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study, then it would be prompted by the injunction that enjoins study through that medium—just as the restriction of speech is prompted by the injunction for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice through the medium of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. But that knowledge is not a subsidiary of study; rather, study itself is the subsidiary of that [knowledge]. Furthermore, a primary act cannot be prompted by means of its subsidiary. And one who does not prompt the knowledge is not entitled to prompt the inquiry for the sake of accomplishing that knowledge.

Now, one might object: "Even if knowledge is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), inquiry (*vicāra*) certainly is. True; however, it is possible for that which is an auxiliary of study (*adhyayana*) to be prompted by teaching (*adhyāpana*) through that [study] as a medium.
For if the principal [teaching] could not come into being without it, and if the prompter [the teacher] were not established [without it], then it would be prompted by that. (22)
However, when that [word] is obtained otherwise, its own self-acquisition is established;
therefore, the employment of what is a subordinate part of another purpose is not thereby established. (23)

For teaching, being impossible without study, directly enjoins only the essential nature of that [study] itself and not its subsidiaries; however, if the primary act of study were not possible without the subsidiary, then it would enjoin the subsidiary by way of that [primary], just as the cutting and other acts are enjoined by way of the sacrificial post for the sake of the animal-apūrva.

Furthermore, if teaching were not accomplished by a study devoid of its subsidiary parts (aṅgas), such that only a study endowed with at least some of its own subsidiaries could assist in teaching, then the subsidiary part of study would be employed solely by virtue of the injunction for teaching—just as the restraint of speech is employed by virtue of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

However, neither of these two [conditions] exists here; for the very nature of study is established even without its auxiliary parts. Since the observances (*vrata*) and other such elements, which are useful for the nature of study, are employed by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryaka-vidhi*)—which pertains to the teaching of the entire Veda and seeks the completion of the task without obstacles—it is possible for them to be applied. Nevertheless, inquiry (*vicāra*) is not implied by that [injunction], because it is an auxiliary to a different purpose. For inquiry is an auxiliary to study when that study is accomplishing a different purpose called the "knowledge of meaning" (*arthajñāna*), but not when it is serving as an aid to teaching.
Therefore, it is not enjoined by that injunction for teaching, but rather by the very entitlement produced by study. And thus:
"In the same way, since study is also prompted by that [entitlement] alone, its prompting by the injunction for teaching is not tenable. (24)

Now, if you think that although there is indeed eligibility for study, it is not understood at that time because of one's childhood while studying, and its application is not possible when it is not understood; [then we reply: 25.
When his study is completed, he is understood by one who is proficient;
and when that [proficiency] is known, investigation is also undertaken. (26)
For an entitlement (*adhikāra*) that is being known serves as the motivator (*prayojaka*), yet at the stage of study, it cannot be understood by the young student (*māṇavaka*).

Therefore, study is not motivated by one's own entitlement; rather, when study is performed for the sake of teaching—which has the learned as its entitled subject—the student, having become proficient in the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*), comes to understand the meaning of the Veda. However, it is impossible for the student to understand his own entitlement during the act of studying itself; rather, one's entitlement to study is understood through the power of understanding the Vedic meaning, and once that is understood, it motivates the inquiry (*vicāra*). Thus, [the opponent's position] is incorrect.
This [agent] is an instigator only when known by those who act for his benefit;
even if unknown by the actual doer, he would certainly not be a non-motivator. (27)

Just as, for the sake of a patient, those who act for his benefit—knowing the fruits of taking medicine—cause him to undertake the medicine through gentle means or by demonstrating its results by pointing out other desired fruits needed by the patient, because the patient’s own qualification is the actual motivator since he proceeds with the intention of that [qualification], and the physicians, acting for his benefit, cause him to undertake it while intending only the fruit of the medicine, which is health; even so, by those acting for one's benefit who understand the qualification to be accomplished through study...

The study being performed under the direction of the father and others is logically established as being prompted by that [study itself]. Furthermore, if it were necessarily required that only one who is performing the action must be known as the prompter, then the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*), being unknown to the child, would not be its prompter. Therefore, just as that [injunction] which is understood through the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) serves as the prompter, so too will the qualification (*adhikāra*) to be accomplished by the study serve as the prompter; thus, study is not prompted by the injunction for teaching.

And if it were impelled by that [the injunction to study], then its purpose would not be established as the knowledge of meaning. For one who has already obtained the performance [of the act] has no further need for a purpose, such that the knowledge of meaning—being internal to it—could be its purpose. [Objection: But surely all injunctions culminate in a qualification (adhikāra); therefore, the injunction to study must also be so. [Response: No, because the purpose is obtained through the performance itself; for a qualification is required for the sake of performing an act. But once that [performance] has been obtained, there is no basis for requiring that qualification.

It might be argued: "The injunction for study culminates in a qualification for performance (adhikāra), because it is an injunction, like the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites. This is incorrect. The injunction for study is devoid of a qualification for performance, because it attains its own existence even in the absence of such a qualification. For when an injunction attains its own existence despite the absence of something else, it is devoid of that thing—just as an occasional injunction (naimittika-vidhi) is devoid of a [specific] result; thus, there exists a counter-reason (pratihetu).

If, even in the absence of a logical inconsistency, an entitlement (*adhikāra*) were to be postulated on the grounds that [the procedure] has been observed elsewhere, then—since it is observed that optional rites (*kāmya*) extend up to the attainment of their fruit—an entitlement extending up to that same fruit would also have to apply to occasional (*naimittika*) and prohibitive (*niṣedha*) injunctions. This is not accepted by you; therefore, no entitlement is established for the study [of the Veda].

Now, even if it is granted that the knowledge of the meaning is the purpose because it is observed [to occur] despite the injunction not being intent upon it—alas! Since study is perceived as being intent upon teaching rather than the meaning, and since what is not intended to be expressed is unfit for investigation, the treatise would simply not be commenced. Even if, somehow, the meaning were intended to be expressed, nevertheless, because the injunction is not intent upon it, the necessity of the investigation as a mandatory duty (vaidhatva) is not established.

Furthermore, that which is non-authoritative (avaidha) cannot override what is authoritative (vaidha). For if the injunction for study itself were to enjoin that study must terminate with the knowledge of the meaning, then—inasmuch as the meaning cannot be known without inquiry—the inquiry would be implied by the sense of that injunction and would thus override the bathing, which is contrary to it. However, [the injunction] implies only the performance [of the rite].

If, on the other hand, a person, for the sake of performing subsequent ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), by his own will engages in means of knowing the purpose—such as instructions and so forth—in a worldly manner, he might at some point also perform an inquiry (*vicāra*). That being the case, once the performance of the rite has commenced and an instructor is found, he would then carry it out; therefore, it would not necessarily follow that the performance is established immediately after study. [Objection: But inquiry is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study, and a ritual injunction (*vidhi*) is not accomplished by means of something that is not an auxiliary. Thus, the injunction itself...

How can it be said that inquiry is not a mandatory duty (*avaśyakartavya*), given that one undertakes inquiry for the sake of establishing [the truth] for oneself? It is true that inquiry is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study; nevertheless, it is not employed for the fulfillment of the injunction [of study itself], because it is useful for the result known as the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*). Furthermore, a subsidiary element useful for one effect cannot be [subsumed] under another effect, even if both effects share the same instrument, just as the *apūrva* resulting from the desire for rain [is not subsumed by another].

The *mūrchanidhana* (the *mūrcha* finale) is employed as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the *saubhara* chant—which is intended for one desiring food and serves as a means to produce a transcendental result (*apūrva*)—by virtue of its being the cause of the *saubhara*. Now, if it is argued that the injunction itself implies the investigation (*vicāra*), because study is accomplished for the sake of knowing the meaning and thus requires such an inquiry to achieve its objective, we have already refuted that by demonstrating that the investigation is not prompted by the injunction to teach. Even if study is for the sake of knowing the meaning, nevertheless, it does not function as a means to the injunction in that specific form; rather, it serves as a means to it in its own essential nature alone.

An injunction (vidhi) implies the performance of that very thing without which it cannot be accomplished, and not anything else. Even if an injunction could not be established without inquiry, it does not imply the performance of inquiry because there is no person to be enjoined (niyojya). For such an injunction is not perceived by any person as "this is my duty"; therefore, it would not impel even a person toward its own realization, much less toward the means for its accomplishment. For this very reason, its status as an impeller of performance is not established even in the case of Vedic study.

For how could that which possesses the capacity to impel performance even when there is no person to be enjoined in its own case possibly have such capacity regarding the subsidiaries? Therefore, it is not established that the inquiry is mandatory by scriptural injunction.

It might be argued that the injunction for study itself, having recognized the knowledge of meaning—which is understood from the context—as the purpose of study, implies the necessity of inquiry for the sake of achieving that purpose. That is incorrect. What is the meaning of the claim that the injunction for study recognizes the knowledge of meaning, understood from the context, as its motivator? It cannot mean that it enjoins [the inquiry] therein, because the means to that [knowledge] is already understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because, unlike the case of threshing and so forth, no restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is perceived.

If it is argued that the purpose [of study] is intended [by the injunction], that is not so, because that purpose is attained even without being intended. To say that whatever is obtained even in the absence of an intention is what is intended is laughable. Furthermore, the fact that study has the purpose of understanding the meaning is obtained even without the intention of an injunction; therefore, what is the use of an intention? Consequently, the mandatory nature of inquiry cannot be established in any way, and thus one cannot effect a postponement of the bath on its strength.

If the purpose of the injunction were fulfilled by mere study alone, then—after one has studied the Veda according to the force of the Smṛti rule "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe"—and when the performance of rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma presents itself, it might be that the inquiry [into the meaning] is sometimes performed and sometimes not, since no other means for its determination is available. In that case, the Sūtra *athāto dharmajijñāsā* would not be appropriately established as having the purpose of indicating immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). Therefore, study is not prompted by the injunction to teach.

And what is this injunction for teaching, prompted by which study [is undertaken]? It is said: "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya. This statement, inferred from Smṛti, takes the form: "One should effect the status of an Ācārya by means of initiating and teaching. That is incorrect, because this sentence is not capable of enjoining the act of teaching;
for it is already established as a means for acquiring wealth, and it is connected with the word *yat* (which indicates a known cause). (Verse 28)

Just as in the case of the injunction "one should cause one who desires food to sacrifice," where the word *yājayet* (should cause to sacrifice), although heard subsequent [to the primary injunction], remains a prescription for the sacrifice itself—being a term referring to the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and thus a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the officiating priest’s activity already established as a means of acquiring wealth—so too, the expression "one should teach" (*adhyāpayet*) is intended solely as a prescription for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and not as a prescription for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*), because [teaching] is already established as a means of acquiring wealth. Furthermore, initiation (*upanayana*) is also an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study, since it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the student.

By this very [principle], the statement "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa of eight years and teach him" is explained. Now, one might object: since the Ātmanepada ending is heard in that [passage] regarding initiation (*upanayana*), it is understood that the purpose is the status of an *ācārya* (teacher). This is not so; for the Ātmanepada affix is prescribed for the root *nī* because it does not intend to benefit the agent. Otherwise, since the Ātmanepada would already be established for the root *nī* even when it functions toward the accomplishment of the status of an *ācārya* by the rule *svaritajitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*, the sūtra *sammānana-śāthana-kāraṇa-mitrīkaraṇa-pathiṣu nayati* would be redundant. Thus, they say: "The purpose [of the sūtra] is to indicate cases where the result does not intend to benefit the agent."

Regarding the phrase "a renewed undertaking": therefore, initiation (*upanayana*) is indeed a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study by way of purifying the student; like the bringing of curd for the sake of the *āmikṣā* offering, it accomplishes the status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*) as a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅga*), but not for its own sake. Consequently, there is no scriptural injunction that prescribes teaching with the aim of attaining the status of a teacher. Furthermore, the word "teacher" (*ācārya*) does not denote something transcendental (*alaukika*), unlike words such as "reader" (*pāṭhaka*) and the like.

However, the statement "having initiated the pupil... is solely intent upon explaining the meaning of the word *upanaya* (initiation); therefore, since the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana*) is not established therein, study is not prompted by that injunction. Even if, on the other hand, teaching were enjoined as being subordinate to another result—on the grounds that it consists in the gift of knowledge, as in such passages as "the wise man is honored in the world of Brahman through the gift of knowledge"—nevertheless, because no person to be directed (*niyojya*) is heard of in all those instances, and because the qualification (*adhikāra*) [for the act] exists even in the case of study; [therefore, study is not subordinate to teaching].

Because the existence of such inquiry would lead to the undesirable consequence that [the study] is not sanctioned by the Veda, study is not prompted by the injunction to teach. However, someone else says: "Even though it is possible for study to be prompted by its own specific entitlement (*svādhikāra*), nevertheless, that [entitlement] is not fit to be accepted.
For instance: Knowledge would not, by its own power, be the prompter of study;
rather, the Agnihotra and other rites, which are accomplished through that [knowledge], are the prompters by means of it. (29)

For the knowledge of the meaning cannot itself be the motivator for study, as it is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). However, the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the Agnihotra and other rites, which are accomplished through that knowledge, become motivators by means of it; yet knowledge is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of those rites, but merely an auxiliary (*upakāraka*). On the other hand, the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) has instruction as its very constituent part; therefore, it attains the status of a motivator for study by way of that constituent part. The *apūrva* of the Agnihotra and other rites, however, acts as a motivator by way of being an auxiliary.

Furthermore, even if the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) were obtained through the medium of its being a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—as in the case of curd (*āmikṣā*)—it would not be proper to accept its status as a motivator through the medium of being a benefactor (*upakāraka*), as in the case of whey (*vājina*). Therefore, the claim that "study is motivated by the injunction to teach" is incorrect.
For it has been said: "Knowledge is not a subsidiary of ritual acts; study is considered a subsidiary of knowledge.
This [study] is not a subsidiary of teaching; therefore, it is not motivated by it. (Verse 30)

Although knowledge is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, whereas study is indeed an auxiliary part of knowledge, the study performed for that purpose becomes prompted by the principal act (*śeṣin*) itself; it does not mean that study is an auxiliary part [of the principal]. Therefore, study prompted by that [knowledge] would be prompted merely by what is to be assisted (*upakārya*), and not prompted by the principal act; thus, study is certainly prompted by its own specific qualification (*svādhikāra*), and not prompted by the teaching of others (*adhyāpana*).

Although knowledge is not sought for its own sake, it is nevertheless desired by persons because it is instrumental to the performance of ritual acts; thus, since it serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), it is possible for knowledge to be the motivator (*prayojaka*) of study, just like the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*). For that [status of being a teacher] also, though not desired in its own form, is sought by a person solely for the sake of obtaining the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); therefore, just as that [status] is a motivator, so too is knowledge. Indeed, there is no rule that only that which is desired for its own sake can be a motivator.

This is because there is no contradiction in [the Veda] being the motivator for one who desires it as a means to another result, just as cattle, sons, and so forth are means to happiness. Even though it is the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *agnihotra* and other rites alone that is the motivator by way of knowledge, nevertheless, that alone is logical; teaching is not, because it belongs to another person, whereas knowledge—or its result—which resides in the student, is rightly the motivator for study.

As for the distinction that was stated—that the injunction to teach functions as the motivator (*prayojaka*) by way of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*), whereas the Agnihotra and other rites do so by way of providing assistance (*upakāra*)—that too does not exist. For both possess the status of being a subsidiary and the status of providing assistance; these are merely the means (*dvāra*). To explain: since the knowledge [of the Veda] provides assistance to the Agnihotra and other rites, and since the study [of the Veda] is a subsidiary to that knowledge, it motivates the study. This is merely a difference in sequence. It is not on this account that any real distinction arises, because the Agnihotra and other rites themselves are the motivators, as they reside in the same person [as the study].

Regarding the phrase "not from the injunction for [becoming] a teacher": it has been stated that the Agnihotra and other such rites are not the motivators, but rather knowledge alone is the motivator; this will be explained in detail later. Furthermore, how could an injunction regarding the status of a teacher, which pertains to one person, impel the study performed by another person?

For injunctions such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are understood as tasks to be accomplished by a person of common status, it is logical that they impel that very person to perform the prayāja and other subsidiaries as their own means for the sake of their own accomplishment. But how could a task to be accomplished by one person impel another to its performance? Indeed, a conscious being does not engage in anything other than the means for accomplishing its own task. Even if the teacher himself were the impeller there by demonstrating the student's own entitlement, the impulsion would still be based on the student's own entitlement. (31)

If it is argued that the teacher himself, for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, instigates the student to study by pointing out the student's own obligation (*svādhikāra*), this is indeed true; however, even so, it is the student's own obligation that would be the motivator in that case, not the injunction to teach (*adhyāpanavidhi*). Just as in the *Sthapati-isti*, where the obligation belongs to the Niṣāda, yet the sacrifice is performed by the Niṣāda—who is prompted by officiating priests engaged in acquiring wealth—by pointing out his obligation, it is motivated solely by his own obligation and not by the acquisition of wealth; so too is the act of studying.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it would not be possible to demonstrate one's own qualification; nor can the status of being enjoined to teach be established there [in that view]. (32)

Or let it be granted that the act of the student being made to perform [the study] is prompted by the teaching, through the teacher’s demonstration of his own entitlement (*adhikāra*). Yet even this is not possible under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). For in that view, there is no entitlement whatsoever on the part of the student by the demonstration of which he would be made to study; because, according to the prima facie view, the purpose of study is solely the accomplishment of the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*). [Objection: But surely, through the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*), an entitlement is possible even under the prima facie view. [Reply: No, because it is not something to be performed (*akāryatvāt*).

For an injunction cannot be directed toward a mere youth (*māṇavaka*), such that through its fulfillment there would be an entitlement (*adhikāra*), because he is not one to whom an injunction applies. Indeed, an injunction cannot be directed toward one who is not subject to it; therefore, an entitlement is impossible through its fulfillment.

Now, even if one were to somehow achieve [the goal] by other means such as *sāman*-chants despite lacking one's own entitlement, if that were the case, then even in the Viśvajit and other sacrifices, performance could be accomplished by the sacrificer simply through the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have somehow been engaged in the priestly duties. Consequently, it is not possible to postulate a person subject to the injunction (*niyojya*) for the sake of establishing entitlement in order to ensure the accomplishment of the performance.

Furthermore, because it would be purposeless, the officiating priests do not summon the sacrificer; for he does not give them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) since he has no entitlement to the ritual. This is the same here as well: a boy (*māṇavaka*) being entitled to study does not perform the giving of a fee and so forth for the sake of his teacher; rather, the teacher’s status as a teacher is desired through that [fee]. For the status of a teacher is not desired by a person in its own right. Moreover, on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), study does not entitle the boy [to anything], and thus an impulsion toward teaching is not possible.

The application of that [study] is accepted by you as being common to both sides. Even the statement, "By the gift of knowledge one becomes wise," and so forth, intends the giving of knowledge regarding the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Otherwise, even the giving of knowledge regarding the meaning of the Lokāyata treatises would lead to the world of Brahmā. Furthermore, since study does not have the goals of human life as its purpose according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), its application cannot possibly be established even by virtue of an injunction for the gift of knowledge whose fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahmā. Thus it is established.

Study is not prompted by the injunction for teaching; therefore, the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and final position (*uttarapakṣa*) arguments as [previously] stated are not tenable. As for the inquiry—whether the purpose of study is the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) or the knowledge of meaning, or whether it concerns that which is accessible through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): first, that which is merely accessible through other means of knowledge should not be the subject of deliberation in this treatise. Furthermore, since both [purposes] are already understood through other means of knowledge, there is no occasion for such inquiry. Nor is an inquiry into what is accessible through an injunction (*vidhi*) possible, for an injunction does not have "command" (*niyoga*) as its primary meaning.
Therefore, the profound explanation set forth by the author of the *Vārttika* is in accord with the *Bhāṣya*.
The inquiry into the meaning of the injunction for Vedic study is called *nīti*. (33)

Regarding the injunction "one's own Veda should be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) delimited by the act of study is expressed by the suffix *-tavya* as being impelled by a mandate. When that *bhāvanā* requires an end to be realized (*bhāvya*), it sets aside even the act of study—which, though mentioned in the same word, is not a human goal—and remains awaiting some end that constitutes a human goal. In this regard, there is a doubt:

should heaven be postulated as its end according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, or should the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences (*vākyārtha-jñāna*), which is accomplished through the sequence beginning with the grasping of syllables, be accepted as the end? Therein lies the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
It is not logical that its purpose is the cognition of the object, because that [cognition] is established by other means of valid cognition;
rather, according to the principle "it shall be heaven," its purpose must be heaven. (34)

And although it is observed that after study, the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence arises through the sequence of grasping the syllables, determining the words, and understanding the word-meanings—and since this [knowledge] is desired by a person because it is useful for the performance of fruitful rituals—it is certainly capable of becoming the objective to be attained (bhāvya).

Furthermore, since it is not possible to postulate an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) when a seen result is possible, the notion arises that it is logical for [the study] to have the knowledge of meaning as its purpose. Nevertheless, because the scripture is purposeful only with respect to what has not yet been attained, and because the fact that the knowledge of meaning is produced by the cultivation of study is established through other means of knowledge, it would follow that the injunction would be purposeless if it were merely for that purpose; therefore, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, it is logical that its purpose is heaven (svarga). If it be argued:
"Even though it is established by other means of knowledge, the injunction serves to establish a restrictive rule (niyama), like the threshing [of grain]," [we reply:
such an injunction is not tenable, because that [knowledge of meaning] does not exist without [the Veda] serving the purpose of the ritual (kratvartha). (Verse 35)

If it is argued that even though the purpose of knowing the meaning [of the Veda] is established through other means of knowledge, the injunction is not purposeless because it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—just like the act of husking (*avaghāta*) and so forth—that is not correct, because study does not serve the purpose of the sacrifice. For acts such as husking are restricted specifically within the context of the sacrifice; since rice grains are prepared only by husking, they accomplish the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice. Thus, there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge regarding the essential nature of the rice grains, for we observe their preparation through other methods such as measuring out a *prastha*, grinding on a flat surface, or tearing them out with the nails.

Likewise here too, since the arising of knowledge is possible even without formal study—through means such as examining books and so forth—a restriction regarding its very nature is not possible. At most, [one might argue] that it must come from study; however, because study is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), such a restriction is improper. Since a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is untenable in this case, it is better to hold that its purpose is simply heaven (*svarga*). Therefore...

It is logical that the fruit [of study] is merely that which is stated in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), for if it were not heard [in the text], one would have to infer a fruit. However, in this case, the attainment of the fruits of the sacrifices is seen in such statements as: "Whatever sacrifice he studies, by that very act his desired object is accomplished"; and regarding the Rigveda: "When he studies the Ṛg-verses, streams of milk flow for his ancestors; they offer the *svadhā* oblations, and thus he satisfies the gods with offerings of milk. Those ancestors and gods, being satisfied, in turn satisfy the student with longevity and other blessings"—thus there is the attainment of longevity and so forth.

"But the twice-born who studies his own Veda daily according to his ability—he indeed performs the highest austerity from the tips of his nails. Thus, the attainment of the fruit of austerity is indeed heard [in scripture]. Therefore, it is not logical that [the study] has heaven as its purpose. To this we reply: "In the primary act of study, there is no mention of any fruit at all; for where is this mention of a fruit found, except in the context of retention and the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña)? (Verse 36)

The attainment of the fruits of ritual action, such as longevity and so forth, pertains to the sphere of recitation (*japa*), sacrifice (*yajña*), and study (*adhyayana*); however, the attainment of the fruits of austerity (*tapas*) pertains to the sphere of retention (*dhāraṇā*). Regarding the first two—acceptance (*svīkaraṇa*) and study—there is no mention of any fruit whatsoever, so that one would not perform an inference of what is unmentioned based on a specific indication (*nirdeśa*). Even from the *codaka* (the general injunction), only the excellence (*prāśastya*) which constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the verbal efficient force (*śabdabhāvanā*) is obtained, but not the actual nature of longevity and so forth.

Therefore, since the study [of the Veda] is for the sake of heaven (*svarga*), the purpose of the scriptural injunction characterized by the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) is fulfilled by the mere recitation itself, even without investigation. Consequently, it cannot be asserted that the postponement of the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) is necessitated by that [study]. Thus, by the force of the Vedic text inferred from the Smṛti rule—"Having studied the Veda, one should bathe immediately thereafter"—one may either investigate the meaning after bathing according to the requirements of the purpose, or not; however, it is not the case that the meaning perceived from the study, which serves another purpose, is not intended (*avivakṣita*). How so?

[Objection: This is not a fault; for even that which conveys a meaning can be studied for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Just as, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) itself, it is prescribed that "having officiated at a sacrifice or having accepted a gift, one should study the Veda—that is, the sacred text—three times while fasting" for the purpose of expiation, yet this does not entail that the meaning of the Veda is not intended to be conveyed; so too should it be understood regarding study for the sake of heaven (*svarga*).

For the mere fact that a sentence capable of conveying meaning has never been uttered for an unseen purpose does not, by itself, cause its inherent orientation toward meaning to be lost. Thus it is established that the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) should not be undertaken immediately after Vedic study.
To this, it is replied: "An unseen purpose is indeed postulated only when a visible purpose is absent;
but here, since the visible purpose—namely knowledge—is present, the injunction serves the purpose of a restrictive rule (niyama). (37)

For if the restriction were indeed upon the meaning of the sentence itself, then, because a restriction would be impossible regarding the nature of the knowledge of that meaning, and because it would not be restricted for a sacrifice that does not have that as its purpose, the status of being for the sake of restriction would not be tenable; however, this is not the case. This is simply an injunction of what was previously unestablished (*aprāptavidhi*). For as long as the performance of study and so forth has not been conceived as a means to the knowledge required for the performance of fruitful rituals, then—by the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), which is recited at the beginning of that [section] for initiated twice-born men—the study is enjoined, since the direct scripture (*śruti*) is swifter than the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Regarding the *pravatas* (the downward-sloping paths): once that [knowledge] has been established, since the subsequent rites are obtained through performance by those who possess the knowledge of the means (*tapādi-jñāna*), they do not imply any other means for the sake of accomplishing that knowledge—because they are not mandatory (*avaidhatvāt*)—according to the maxim, "there would be an absence of action" (*abhāvaḥ karmaṇi syāt*). Thus, these [rites], having proceeded with reference to the knower, result effectively in a statement of restriction (*niyamabhāṣā*). For example, although the fact that the mantra for taking the girth-rope is an auxiliary to the horse's rope is established by its indicative power (*liṅga*) alone, the application (*viniyoga*) based on direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) results in an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).

For in that case, the meaning of the sentence is not a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), because that would entail the abandonment of its own primary meaning and other such faults. Furthermore, since the application [of the mantra] to the donkey-rein was not previously established by indicative power (*liṅga*), it is simply an injunction of what was not previously established (*aprāptavidhi*); the term "restrictive injunction" is used only figuratively, based on its result. In the same way, the term "rule" (*niyama*) should be understood in the context of the injunction for Vedic study as well. However, the study itself does not thereby become a subordinate element of the ritual; rather, it is the knowledge of the meaning produced by that study which is a subordinate element of the ritual, while the study itself is merely a subordinate element of that knowledge.

Just as, by the principle that although the fires produced by the *ādhāna* rite serve the purpose of the sacrifice, the *ādhāna* itself—because it produces a substance at a time other than that of the ritual performance—is not for the sake of that [sacrifice], so too should it be understood here. Even by the *ekadeśins*, it must be admitted that knowledge, which is accomplished through study prompted by the injunction to teach (*adhyāpana-vidhi*)—the very object of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*)—is a constituent part of the subsequent rituals.

Otherwise, any Śūdra whatsoever, through audacity, might acquire knowledge for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) either by means of study or by some other method; his entitlement [to perform those rites] would thus be unavoidable. Therefore, eligibility for subsequent rituals belongs only to those who possess knowledge acquired through study accompanied by the procedural requirements (itikartavyatā), such as the observances and restrictions (vrata-niyama) performed by an initiated agent (upanīta-kartṛka) as enjoined by the injunction of study. Even so, this does not mean that study itself has the sacrifice as its purpose. This much is indeed common to both us and the proponents of the "Partial" view (ekadeśins).

There is a dispute as to whether study is prompted by its own injunction (*svavidhi*) or by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*). Consequently, because it is not studied within the context of a specific ritual, the injunction for study is not for the sake of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) consisting of knowledge for the purpose of a sacrifice—which would make it a subsidiary element of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); rather, the knowledge acquired through study is what serves the purpose of the sacrifice.
Thus it is established that, because the injunction has a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*), it is not purposeless;
therefore, since a visible purpose is obtained, it remains established that study is for the sake of understanding the meaning. (39)

Now, how can the study of meaningless syllables such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ* be for the sake of understanding their meaning? And how can the portion of the Veda that prescribes the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites for which Kṣatriyas and others are the authorized performers be studied by Brāhmaṇas and others for the sake of understanding its meaning? Even if it might somehow be possible for a Brāhmaṇa to study it for the sake of knowledge useful for his own ritual duties, nevertheless, the study of the Vaiśyastoma and the horse sacrifice by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas would be entirely useless or intended merely for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

And how can there be a description of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) in prohibitive injunctions such as "one should not threaten" or "one should not kill"? If it were assumed that only one who possesses knowledge acquired through Vedic study incurs demerit (*pratyavāya*) by performing an act of threatening—and no one else—then, in that case, the study [of the Vedas] would result in an undesirable consequence. For who indeed would desire knowledge of the meaning of a prohibitive injunction that has demerit as its fruit, such that they would undertake the study for that purpose?

Now, if it is argued that since non-performance is the meaning of the scripture regarding prohibitions, this rule applies specifically to that subject—namely, that only one who possesses knowledge preceded by Vedic study performs [the rite] for the sake of avoiding sin, whereas for others, even if they perform it, that sin is not avoided—then, because sin would be inevitable for those who have not studied the Vedas even when they perform the rite, they might perform prohibited acts at will, since the degree of sin remains the same regardless of performance. And this is not desired.

Because non-violence and the other [virtues] are common to all social classes (*varṇa*), no restrictive rule (*niyama*) can apply there. Furthermore, how could there be a restrictive rule regarding the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*)? For it is not possible for the performance of its meaning to be preceded by that study, since the very act of study is the meaning of the sentence itself. Moreover, how could study be preceded by study? This would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If, on the other hand, study in such cases were for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), then, to avoid inconsistency, it would follow that this must be the case everywhere. Therefore, study is not for the purpose of knowing the meaning. To this, it is replied: [The following passage follows: "But it is not so; for we see that the knowledge of the meaning is the purpose of the study, because it is seen that when the meaning is known, there is the performance of the prescribed acts, and when it is not known, there is no performance. Furthermore, the knowledge of the meaning is not the purpose of the study merely because it is seen, as in the case of the study of spells for warding off poison and the like, where the purpose is seen to be something else. Rather, it is because it is not seen otherwise; for the knowledge of the meaning is not seen to be the result of anything other than the study of the Veda. Nor is it reasonable to assume another purpose when the purpose of the knowledge of the meaning is already established by perception. And even if it were assumed, it would lead to a lack of uniformity, as it would imply that the study of the Veda has multiple purposes. Therefore, the study of the Veda is for the purpose of knowing the meaning."*1* *1. Śabara-bhāṣya on Jaimini-sūtra 1.1.1.*
The accomplishment of the cognition of the mere object is not its sole purpose;
rather, whatever is observed to be required is accepted as its fruit. (40)

For if the purpose of study were held by us to be solely the knowledge of the meaning, then a censure would be appropriate on the grounds that such [knowledge] is impossible in the cases cited; however, that is not its sole purpose. Indeed, whatever is seen to be required for the application of other injunctions and is accomplished through study—all that constitutes its purpose.

Therefore, just as that knowledge is required by the injunctions for sacrifices (kratuvihiti), making it their purpose, so too is the determination of the very nature of the Veda required by the injunctions for daily study, such as "one should study one's own portion of the Veda every day," "having officiated at a sacrifice or having accepted a gift, one who has not eaten should recite the Veda three times," and so forth; thus, that [determination] is also a purpose.

Therefore, since a purpose is postulated for the Veda acquired through study according to its fitness, and since restrictive rules (niyama) are described in accordance with that [purpose], there is a restriction such that in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, the rite brings about its fruit only when known by means of the Veda acquired through study. Regarding mantras, the recollection produced specifically by the mantra acquired through study is a constituent part of the performance. Regarding the *hum* and other [interjections], the indication of the timing of the chant occurs only by means of those [sounds] acquired through study.

And in the case of those [texts] useful solely for the chanting (*stotra*) and recitation (*śastra*) of mantras (*japa*), the measurement of the duration of the singing is accomplished by means of those very [mantras]. And in the case of those useful solely for the chanting and recitation of mantras, the *stotra* and other rites must be performed by means of those very [mantras]. Furthermore, regarding prohibitive statements concerning Brāhmaṇas and others, even when they are engaged solely in the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) and so forth within the Aśvamedha and other rituals, the sacrifice of recitation and the like must be performed by means of the methods of Vedic study (*adhyayana*).

And it has been said: "Insofar as there is deliberation regarding study from the presence of a teacher, since that [study] is independent of the accomplishment of common recitation (*japa*), sacrifice (*yajña*), and ritual (*kratu*) knowledge, there is no occasion for postulating any other fruit. But in the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), regarding that study which is enjoined by it..."

Since it is impossible for the act of study to be preceded by itself—due to the fallacy of self-dependence—it follows that the rule of being preceded by that [study] applies only to the inquiry (*vicāra*) which is enjoined by it and serves as its procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*). Having understood through the injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*)—which is undertaken by means of study—that the inquiry must be performed, the inquiry is then to be carried out.

For this very reason, before the performance of inquiry, the inquiry into the meaning of the injunction for study is conducted at the beginning of the treatise, so that one may understand through that very injunction for study the necessity of performing such inquiry. Regarding the *arthavādas*, it is held that ritual acts should be performed in accordance with the renown [of the texts] by means of those very *arthavādas* acquired through study.

Regarding the *Upaniṣads*, those statements which establish the nature of the Self as the agent and enjoyer employed in sacrifices, it is held that the sacrifice should be performed after knowing—by means of those very [texts] acquired through study—that the Self is distinct from the aggregate of the elements and their products, and is capable of experiencing results both already come into being and yet to be produced.

However, regarding those [Upanishadic passages] which establish the nature of the Self as neither agent nor enjoyer—such as "This Self is free from evil, stainless, deathless," and so forth—the rule is that the knowledge of the Self, having been accomplished through the Upanishads acquired by study, results in both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), because their fruits are shown to be such in statements like "He obtains all desires by his very self" and "He does not return again. Thus, there is a necessary connection between the Upanishads studied and the attainment of the fruits of prosperity and liberation.

It should be understood that this entire restriction is accomplished solely by way of its result (*phala*), and not as the primary meaning of the sentence itself. Furthermore, one should not consider the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) to be inconsistent (*vairūpya*) due to the acceptance of multiple purposes; for since all purposes are attained through a single mode of expression—namely, "one should accomplish whatever is required and possible by means of study which serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Veda"—there is no inconsistency.

For if study were sometimes a primary action (*pradhāna-karma*) having the Veda as its material object (*dravya*), and sometimes a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Veda, then there would be a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) between the meanings of the two words in the injunction "the Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), due to their relationship as subordinate and primary. But this is not the case, because in every respect study has the Veda as its primary object. Someone, however, says: "The status of study as a refinement is not tenable, because the Veda lacks both past and future utility."

For there is nothing whatsoever that enjoins it toward the knowledge of meaning. Nor is it correct to say that the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) itself is its enjoiner, because it is an injunction for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*). Just as the injunction for the oblation of groats (*saktu-homa*) enjoins the groats after they have been purified, [the injunction for study] enjoins [the Veda] after it has been purified; therefore, it is impossible for [the Veda] to have the purpose of being a purificatory rite for study. This is merely the prattle of one who is devoid of the labor of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika*, whose discrimination is obscured by the darkness of instruction in improper methods, who is ignorant of the subtleties of Mīmāṃsā logic, and who, having failed to serve a teacher, is merely "dear to his mother. To illustrate:
This defect would occur if the application [of the Veda] were limited to mere recitation; but when it extends to the knowledge of the meaning, it would be like the Sāman and other [Vedic texts]. (41)

For if the application of study were limited solely to the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedic text (*svādhyāya*), then this defect would indeed arise. However, since the application of study extends precisely to that [knowledge of meaning]—in accordance with its visible capacity as a means to the knowledge of meaning through the successive stages beginning with the grasping of syllables—then by this very injunction, the application of the Vedic text itself to the knowledge of meaning is obtained.

Since that [knowledge] possesses the capacity to generate the cognition of the meaning only by means of its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), why would it terminate in that alone? Even that [refinement], having been made a medium, does not lead to anything other than the performance of the sacrifice or its fruit; for since knowledge is established through other means, its status as an auxiliary to the performance of the fruitful sacrifice is established by implication (*sāmarthya*) itself as a rule. Thus, the injunction regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyavidhi*) has no mandatory function in that regard.

However, since the process beginning with study and ending with knowledge is not necessarily established [by other means], an injunction (*vidhi*) remains necessary in that regard. Therefore, study is prompted by knowledge, and not prompted by the ritual sacrifice (*kratu*). Thus, when it is said, "One should produce knowledge of the meaning through study by means of its observed capacity," the following sense is achieved: "One should know the meaning by means of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) once it has been studied."

For this very reason, in the section concerning other Vedic branches (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), it is shown that the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is intended to be something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) because it is to be adopted for the sake of knowing the meaning. For example, although a *sāman* is employed in a hymn of praise (*stuti*), its inherent nature as a refinement of syllables (*akṣarasaṃskāra*) is not lost, precisely because it serves as a means to the praise through those very syllables. Indeed, in that case, there is no application of the *ṛc* verses to the praise by means of another sentence; nevertheless, the *sāman* functions solely as a refinement of them.

Similarly, although the *caru* (sacrificial porridge) is not explicitly enjoined for the production of the *sthala* (elevated mound), by the injunction "he places the *caru*" (*carum upadadhāti*), the placing of the *caru* is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *sthala*. Since the *caru* itself does not effect the production of the *sthala*, but rather its production is observed through the *caru* once it has been placed, and since it is impossible to assume a purely transcendental benefit (*ārādupakāraka*) when a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is possible, the *caru* becomes a subordinate element of the *sthala*, and the act of placing (*upadhāna*) becomes a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for it.

Therefore, even though such a thing is by its very nature a *saṃskāra* (consecration), because it is not enjoined with reference to a previously specified object of consecration, it sometimes receives the designation of an *arthakarman* (a primary act for a purpose). With this very intention it was said: "Even in the case of an *arthakarman*, there is indeed primacy with respect to the act of placing (*upadhāna*)," yet in the ultimate sense it is not an *arthakarman* like the *sāman*; rather, it is a *saṃskārakarman*. And that which is to be consecrated is enjoined by this very [text] as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the ritual action.
