Therefore, those who assert that the *ṛc*s lack the status of being auxiliary members because they are not enjoined for recitation in praise (*stuti*) should be disregarded. Thus, it is established that there is no inconsistency (*vairūpya*) in the injunction for Vedic study. Now, even if such inconsistency does not exist, the postulation of multiple purposes is improper, according to the principle: "Or rather, [there is] one [purpose], because the injunction is one. This might be so if [the purpose] were something to be postulated; however, it is already established.

As it has been stated, the accomplishment of many purposes is inherent to the act of study (*adhyayana*). Therefore, by means of study, one should accomplish whatever is required and possible through the medium of the *svādhyāya* (the Vedic text); thus, since all purposes are attained with a single effort, there is neither any complexity nor any inconsistency. For this very reason, even the injunctive sentences concerning the *samidh* and other such offerings are accepted as being merely reminders (*smāraka*), provided that no mantra exists to serve as a reminder; for it is indeed possible for injunctive sentences themselves [to function as reminders].

This [study] is intended to bring about the recollection of the relationship [between words and their meanings]. In this regard, the sequence of sentences prescribed by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) dictates that the word-meanings must be recollected through sentences arranged in that very same order. For there is no functional requirement for them to follow that sequence within the injunction itself;

however, for those performing the recollection, this sequence establishes an order within the act of remembering, which in turn results in the sequential performance of the word-meanings to be remembered. Thus, it becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
This has been clearly stated by the author of the Sūtras in the fifth book.
Because it serves another purpose, the author of the commentary himself has explained that [work] as being for the sake of ritual action and unity. ||42||

While explaining this sūtra—"Because [words] serve another purpose, [they are subordinate] to the ritual act" (*kratvekatve parārthatvāt*)—the author of the Bhāṣya will state: "The Veda indeed serves another purpose; it is designated as such because of that which can be accomplished by it. And by means of it, the word-meanings (*padārtha*) can be expressed, and they can be understood at the time of the performance of the action. Therefore, the Veda and the word-meanings are to be acquired for the sake of knowing them and for understanding them at the time of the action. Furthermore, no distinction is perceived such that 'this [Veda] is recited for the sake of enjoining [something], not for the sake of understanding'; since no such distinction is apprehended..."

It is understood that [the mantra] is to be employed for both purposes; furthermore, it is possible to perform the ritual action by means of this [mantra] in this specific sequence, and not by any other. However, where a mantra exists, since it serves no other purpose and the injunctive statement has already fulfilled its function through its own injunction, the mantra itself performs the act of recollection (*smārakatva*).

For this very reason, in that context, the performance of ritual acts follows the sequence of the *mantras* alone, not the sequence of the injunctions; in that regard, the sequence of the *brāhmaṇas* is utilized for recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*) and the like, as it is for those passages that establish other sacrifices. Enough of this excessive detail. Thus it is established that even if the injunction for study has a visible purpose, since there is no necessity for a restrictive rule (*niyama*), study is for the sake of understanding the meaning.

Nor is there this restriction that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) applies only to matters pertaining to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), for it is accepted that restrictive injunctions apply even to matters pertaining to the person (*puruṣārtha*), such as the acquisition of wealth and so forth. Therefore, like those cases, the restrictive injunction here is indeed purposeful. However, the experts in logic speak of "restriction" (*niyama*) only in its result, according to the principle previously stated. Consequently, study has as its purposes the recitation-sacrifice (*japayajña*), the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), sacrifices, and the attainment of knowledge. For this very reason, it is obligatory (*nitya*), because the entitlement to perform ritual acts—which is the fruit of that study—is indispensable.

In its absence, there would be sin (*pratyavāya*) due to the non-performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. Furthermore, the study of the entire Veda is indeed necessary, as it is required for purposes such as the compulsory recitation (*pārāyaṇa*). Likewise, because one who has not studied the Veda lacks the qualification [for rites], the legal authorities (*smṛti*) record that he becomes like a *śūdra*, stating: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself elsewhere, quickly attains the state of a *śūdra* while still living, along with his lineage; he is equal to a *śūdra* as long as he is not born [into the Vedic knowledge]. And so forth.

Therefore, since the purpose of Vedic study is the knowledge of its meaning, and since that knowledge is impossible without inquiry, it is established that the desire to know Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) must be undertaken immediately thereafter.
Relying upon the opinion of the Teacher, this *Prayuktitilaka* has been composed by Pārthasārathi Miśra, the son of the illustrious Yajñātman. (43)
Thus ends the discussion on the rule for Vedic study in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* composed by the Great Professor Pārthasārathi Miśra.
Just as the validity of cognition is determined intrinsically, so too is the principle stated regarding its invalidity being extrinsic. (1)

Beginning with the words "of all means of valid cognition, [the validity] is from themselves," the Teacher has established that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). Regarding this, commentators disagree as to whether the word "self" (*sva*) signifies the self (*ātman*) or what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). For instance, does validity arise from itself, or does it manifest from itself? Likewise, what is called "validity"? Is it the correspondence of the object with reality, or is it the determination of an object as it truly exists? And in that regard: "The word 'self' here signifies the self; validity manifests from itself."
And the existence of the object in that very way is designated as its validity. ||2||

Regarding this, some say that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in non-deviation from the object—that is to say, having as its object an object that exists exactly as it is. And this [validity] arises for cognitions *intrinsically* (*svataḥ*). This word "own" (*sva*) signifies "one's own"; thus, the characteristic of having an object that exists exactly as it is arises from nothing other than one's own cause. However, it is said to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*) because it does not arise from one's own cause alone, but rather from a defect residing therein. For if the state of having a true object were caused by excellence (*guṇa*), then the state of having a false object would result from a defect in its own cause.

If that were the case, then in cognitions such as that of a yellow conch arising from sense organs and so forth which are defective and devoid of excellence, nothing real would be apprehended; yet even there, the actual nature of the conch and so forth is indeed apprehended as real.

However, when its non-correspondence [to reality] (ayathārthatva) is dependent on defects, and its having an object is dependent on its own causes, it becomes established that what arises from both combined factors has as its object both true and false things. Therefore, validity—characterized by correspondence to reality—is produced from its own causes, but it does not manifest itself. For cognition does not make known either itself or its own validity, because it is exhausted solely in the illumination of the object.

According to the other view, however, invalidity—characterized by non-correspondence with reality—is due to defects in the cause; thus, because of the absence of defects, the Veda possesses correspondence with reality. But in this position, the refutation of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) based on the consequence of infinite regress (starting from the phrase "if, even when [the cognition] has arisen... would not be applicable. For an infinite regress would occur only if the validity of a cognition depended upon the knowledge of its excellence (*guṇajñāna*), just as it does for the senses. However, since the excellences function as the very nature of the cause, they produce the validity of the cognition even when unperceived, just like the senses; therefore, there is no occurrence of an infinite regress.

Likewise, by refuting the objection, "If the absence of defects arises from the excellences, then surely that same instability would occur," he demonstrates that according to the opponent's position, validity arises solely from the cognition of excellences and not from the nature of the excellences themselves. Thus: "Therefore, the validity of cognition, which is obtained by virtue of its being of the nature of consciousness, is sublated by the cognitions of defects arising from causes that produce a discrepancy in the object."

By saying this, he makes it perfectly clear that, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), invalidity arises solely from the cognition of defects (*doṣajñāna*) and not from the intrinsic nature of the defects themselves. Furthermore, many other verses in this position—such as "from the ascertainment of qualities and defects produced in the causes" and so forth—are inconsistent; therefore, this position is not intended by the author of the *Vārttika*.

Others, however, say that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in the capacity to determine an object as it truly is (*tathābhūtārtha*), and that this arises for cognitions intrinsically (*svataḥ*). This word "self" (*sva*) refers to the cognition itself; thus, the determination of the object as it truly is arises from the very nature of the cognition, and not from the cognition of its qualities, from a corroborating cognition, or from the cognition of the object being otherwise. Therefore, it is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Even in this view, validity is produced intrinsically, but it is not known intrinsically.

In this regard, the following must be said: if invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) were produced in the arising [of a cognition] by the knowledge of a defect, the knowledge of a sublation, or a sublating cognition, it would not be so; for the invalidity of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not produced by a sublating cognition or the like. This is because that cognition is already invalid at the very moment of its arising. For invalidity is the ascertainment of an object as being other than it actually is, and since such an invalid cognition arises *svalataḥ* (intrinsically), it does not depend on a sublating cognition or the like. Indeed, a cognition is not first valid at the time of its arising and subsequently rendered invalid by a sublating cognition; rather, such invalidity exists at the very moment of its arising, [which is merely] revealed by the sublating cognition.

It is explained that it is not the case that the certainty regarding the absence of the object’s being otherwise is produced by the sublater (*bādhaka*) alone; this is true, yet that [certainty] itself is not invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). For the certainty that the object is otherwise is not the invalidity of the prior cognition, but rather the actual state of the object being otherwise. Alternatively, the fact that [the prior cognition] determines something to be as it was when it is actually otherwise—neither of these two is produced by the sublater. This is because the object’s being otherwise exists *per se* (inherently), and because the determination of its being so [as it was] occurs with respect to an object that is actually otherwise through the knowledge of invalidity *per se*.
Thus, invalidity also arises *per se*.
Therefore, the status of being a valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇya),
which is initially attained by virtue of its dual nature, is sublated by cognitions that perceive either a discrepancy in the object or defects arising from the causes [of cognition].

Thus, this verse must also be explained by you in the following manner: "The validity that arises from the cognition itself is subsequently sublated"—but this is incorrect, because invalidity exists at the very moment of its arising. If, on the other hand, your view is that validity consists in being determinative (*niścāyakatva*) and invalidity is the absence thereof, and that the latter is removed by a sublating cognition (*bādhaka*), that too is incorrect. For a sublating cognition does not effect the destruction of the determination, since that determination is perishable by its own nature. Therefore, it should be stated thus: the cognition's own status as valid is understood intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
And its lack of authority is extrinsic, arising from the cognition of defects and sublation. ||3||

But surely, even here, there would be a contradiction with the texts and a contradiction with logic; for instance: consciousness does not grasp itself, much less its own validity (*prāmāṇya*), since it is exhausted by the grasping of the object. And thus, perception and the other means of knowledge are not apprehended as "this is a valid means of knowledge. If they are not apprehended in this manner, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is not possible; having thus raised the objection regarding the non-apprehension of validity, [the author] states: "The means of knowledge exists in its own form prior to its apprehension."

By asserting that [the cognition] is apprehended by other conditions while being independent regarding its own effects, one resolves the consequence of a fault only by accepting the non-apprehension of its validity; however, this is contradicted if validity is apprehended by itself.

Likewise, since validity is produced by excellences (*guṇa*) because it is an object that is ascertained, the production of validity—which consists of ascertainment—is determined to be the effect of the knowledge of excellences that are the causes of correspondence, due to its being the very nature of the thing itself. Thus, while the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) asserts that excellences are the cause only in the *origination* (*janman*) of validity, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) shows that even in this [view], origination alone is "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*). Therefore, this position—that validity manifests intrinsically (*svato bhāti*)—is also untenable.

To this it is replied: as for what was said—that cognition does not apprehend itself because it illuminates its object, and that validity cannot be apprehended as belonging to it when the cognition itself is not apprehended—[that is now addressed].

If we were to say that [the cognition] apprehends "this cognition is valid" and likewise "my [other] cognition is invalid," then we would indeed be subject to such a reproach. However, we do not say this. Rather, it is said that the validity of a cognition—which consists in that by virtue of which a cognition becomes a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)—is apprehended by the cognition itself as the very basis for the application of the terms and cognitions "valid" (pramāṇa), having thereby acquired the designation "valid."

What is this "truthfulness of the object"? Indeed, this alone is the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition, namely that the object exists as it is; for a cognition whose object is not as it is lacks validity. And this alone constitutes invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), namely that the object is otherwise than it appears. Therefore, the validity of a cognition—consisting in the truthfulness of its object—is determined by the cognition itself (*svataḥ*), and is not to be understood through the cognition of causal qualities (*guṇa*), the cognition of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), or the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Invalidity, however, which consists in the object being otherwise than it appears, is [determined] intrinsically.

It is not understood [as false] directly through the cognition of a defect in the cause, nor is it understood through the cognition that "this is not so"; rather, this is what is being established here. And it has been said:
"For by him, it was not known that 'all this cognition is false';
for by him, the object was determined to be exactly as it is, in accordance with the means of valid cognition."
"How can there be alteration in that [cognition] without another cognition, given that it is already established?
Likewise:
"Furthermore, an invalid cognition appears on its own as if it were valid with respect to its object."
Its falsity cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition.
For the non-existence of the object as it was previously stated is not like its existence;
for if it were so [existent], it would have been perceived, and thus further cognition would be fruitless.

"But if there were otherwise [i.e., if validity were extrinsic], then because it would be unestablished, another means of knowledge (pramāṇa) would have scope; therefore, one resorts to a single thesis that is independent of others and free from doubt. By saying this, he clearly states that the very investigation of whether validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*) is what is being considered. As for that which...

Because there is no apprehension in the form "this is a commentary (vārtika), it is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)," and likewise, perception and the other [means of knowledge] are not apprehended as being "means of valid knowledge," he says this. Now, if validity is understood at the very time of the arising of the cognition—such that what does not appear as a means of valid knowledge upon its arising is [thereby known to be] invalid—then invalidity too would follow as being intrinsic (svataḥ), since it could be determined by elimination at the very moment of arising even without [the presence of] defects in the causes or a subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya).

Do not speak thus; for this word "sva" (self) is not employed here with the sense of "validity," as in the claim that "validity shines forth from validity itself. Nor does it mean "by way of being a means of valid cognition," for if it were so, then since invalid cognitions would appear as having the manifestation of validity, invalidity would be established by elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Rather, the word "sva" refers to "cognition" (*vijñāna*), meaning that "validity shines forth from cognition itself."

Furthermore, even from the knowledge of invalidity, it is understood that validity itself exists in the self, though it was previously non-existent; thus, there is no establishment of invalidity by way of elimination (pariśeṣa). Rather, invalidity is understood subsequently in the form of a sublation of the perceived validity, as it has been said: "Since self-validity is established everywhere as the general rule, it is set aside by the cognition of a sublating factor and by the cognition of a defect in the cause."

The meaning is that it is "established," "attained," and "realized" in all cases; that is to say, not only in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but in the case of mere cognition (*jñāna*) as well. Likewise, even an invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*) is indeed intrinsically a means of valid cognition with respect to its own object.

Furthermore, this inquiry as to whether the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*) is not undertaken with reference to those cognitions that are themselves the means of valid cognition; rather, it is undertaken with reference to all those cognitions of the form "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," which are distinct from cognitions that touch upon multiple mutually exclusive alternatives—such as "is this a post or a person?"—and from recollective cognitions (*smṛti*).
Let this examination first be conducted regarding the domain of all cognitions whatsoever.

Thus the argument proceeds: if one were to consider only those [means of knowledge] that are accepted as valid by both parties, then—since the object [of cognition] is established for both disputants—one might conclude that the validity of those things well-known to both as being means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Consequently, because the Veda lacks validity established by both parties, it would not be a subject for inquiry; thus, its intrinsic validity would not be proven. In that case, an investigation into the validity of the Veda would be useless and unnecessary, like an examination of a crow’s teeth.

However, when intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) and extrinsic invalidity (*parataścāprāmāṇya*) are being established with respect to cognition (*jñāna*) alone, then even in the case of the Veda, its validity—consisting in the correspondence of its object (*viṣayatathātvarūpa*)—would be understood as intrinsic; for [if it were otherwise], invalidity would consist merely in the non-correspondence of the object due to the knowledge of defects in the causes and so forth, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even memory (*smṛti*) would possess such validity. True, it is not merely that much; however, in this particular context, it is precisely that much—whether [validity] is intrinsic or extrinsic—that is being investigated.

The word *pramāṇa* (valid means of knowledge) denotes that which ascertains an object as it truly is, provided that it is not already apprehended by another [means of knowledge] and is not being subsequently recollected. Its state (*bhāva*) is *prāmāṇya* (validity). What is its state? It is a triad combined: (1) the fact of not being apprehended by another cognition, (2) the existence of the object as it truly is, and (3) the capacity of the cognition to produce the ascertainment of that [object]. This triad combined is what is expressed by the concepts and words *pramāṇa* and *prāmāṇya*.

In this regard, that non-connection [of the object] due to its being already cognized is not apprehended from the nature of the cognition itself, because it is apprehended through the appropriate non-perception (*yogyānupalabdhi*). For the cognition of a jar does not establish the jar's state of not being cognized by any other means; nor is that established through the cognition of its qualities and so forth.

Therefore, there is no need to consider whether [validity] arises from itself or from another; rather, that which was suspected to be invalid—characterized by being non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārthatva*)—by the phrase "but surely it is not thus," is refuted by establishing that validity, characterized by correspondence with reality (*arthatathātva*), is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*). As for the passage stating "the production of validity consisting of ascertainment," that too is not contradictory.

For that very thing which ascertains the correspondence of an object is precisely what produces the ascertainment regarding that object; for that which is a communicator (*jñāpaka*) in relation to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is precisely what is a producer (*janaka*) in relation to the cognition (*jñāna*).

Furthermore, since certainty (*niścaya*) is the very ground for the application of the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), it is itself validity; thus, for the proponent who maintains that validity—defined as the correspondence with the object—is ascertained through the knowledge of excellence (*guṇajñāna*), the objection is not irrelevant. However, the production of validity consisting of certainty occurs because it is the very nature of the thing itself; rather, it is determined by its being the effect of the knowledge of excellence and of corroboration (*saṃvāda*). This is the meaning of the text.

If, on the other hand, it were stated directly that this very validity, being of the nature of certainty, arises intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then it must likewise be said that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises extrinsically (*parataḥ*); otherwise, it would not even constitute its opposite. [The correct position is: "Validity arises intrinsically, while invalidity is understood extrinsically. Therefore, the meaning of the section is precisely that both validity and invalidity are understood both intrinsically and extrinsically. For in this way, both the logic and the text become consistent.

Thus, this is the summary of the preceding and following positions here: Since the cognition of a jar is observed both when there is a jar and when there is no jar, the jar cannot be ascertained by that [cognition] alone. Therefore, it is only through the observation of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) that the production of the prior cognition of the jar from the jar must be ascertained, preceded by the ascertainment of the jar which is its cause. Because the knowledge of purposeful action is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*), it can ascertain the validity of the prior cognition by ascertaining its own validity regarding the purposeful action.

Likewise, the corroboration by another cognition (*jñānāntara-saṃvāda*) is not possible in the absence of the reality of the object; therefore, from that too, there is the ascertainment of the reality of the object. Similarly, since a cognition produced by a cause possessing excellence (*guṇavat-kāraṇa-janya*) is necessarily in accordance with the object, the reality of the object can be ascertained even through the determination of the excellence of its causes.

Therefore, the ascertainment of the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition occurs only extrinsically (*parataḥ*); it is not possible to ascertain its validity—characterized as the conformity of the object—with reference to itself, because that would be inconclusive (*anaikāntikatvāt*). Furthermore, the prior non-existence of the ascertainment cannot be [removed] by the cognition of defects (*doṣa-jñāna*).

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: since it is possible to produce certainty through the knowledge of qualities (*guṇa-jñāna*) and so forth because [the object] is a real entity (*vastutva*), therefore the validity (*prāmāṇya*) consisting in the "suchness" of the object is determined solely from external sources.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: cognition does not determine an object solely by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), but rather intrinsically (*svataḥ*). For if it were not capable of being determined intrinsically, there would be an absolute absence of determination, and the entire world would fall into blindness. Indeed, an object that is not determined intrinsically cannot be determined extrinsically (*parataḥ*), because the other [external factor] likewise lacks the capacity to do so.

For just as the cognition of a jar is seen even when the jar is non-existent and is therefore not determinative, so too the cognition of causal efficiency is seen even when causal efficiency is non-existent, as in the state of dreaming; thus, it cannot be determined by that [cognition] either, and certainly not can the jar be determined by it—consequently, total blindness would result for the entire world.

Now, if by the term "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) one does not mean the fetching of water and so forth, but rather knowledge itself consisting of pleasure—and it is asserted that all pleasurable knowledge is intrinsically valid (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own nature because it is non-erroneous—then let there indeed be a certainty regarding purposeful action; nevertheless, the correspondence (*yāthārthya*) of the preceding cognition cannot be known through that [subsequent pleasure]. For even from what is non-correspondent, such as the application of sandalwood paste in a dream, pleasure arises.

Furthermore, the ascertainment of the object of a prior cognition by means of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) whose invariable concomitance has been grasped is indeed an inference, for this [inference] has the cause as its domain based on the effect. And it is not possible to grasp a relation when the related term has not been grasped. Therefore, at the time of grasping the relation, the ascertainment of the jar must necessarily be admitted to arise from the cognition of the jar itself. The same should be said regarding the cognition of a quality and the cognition of its correspondence.

For even a quality cannot be ascertained through the non-cognition of a quality, much less the validity of a prior cognition; the same applies to corroboration (*saṃvāda*). Corroboration means that what was not ascertained by a prior cognition is ascertained by this [subsequent one]. Although, by virtue of being a real entity, an ascertainment is produced, it is nevertheless produced by a cognition alone and not by anything else. Therefore, validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), whereas invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) and must be ascertained either from the cognition of a defect (*doṣajñāna*) or from a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*).

Now, since it is not a real entity, invalidity cannot be produced by defects; and that which is not produced by them cannot be determined from them. It is replied: we do not say that validity, in the form of the prior absence of certainty, is apprehended by defects; rather, we mean that validity in the form of the object being otherwise (i.e., incorrectness) is what is apprehended. For that [invalidity] can indeed be ascertained through the cognition of defects, because incorrectness is observed in defective causes due to its being caused by those defects. In the case of the Veda as well, validity is established as intrinsic (*svataḥ*), remaining unrefuted due to the absence of defects.

How is it understood that inaccuracy is caused by defects (*doṣa*) and not by the absence of excellences (*guṇa*)? For in all cases, inaccuracy is known to occur when the causes are either devoid of excellences or are defective; in such instances, how is this distinction made—that the cause is the defect alone and not the deficiency of excellences? Therefore, even if [it is argued] that [the validity] is extrinsic (*parataḥ*)...

Even so, although this serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for invalidity, since that indication is possible simply through the absence of excellences (*guṇa*), and because the Veda lacks the excellence of being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), the Veda—despite its validity being established by its own inherent nature (*svarasaprāpta*)—would consequently incur invalidity due to the very absence of excellences, which is extrinsic (*parataḥ*). To this it is replied: postulation (*kalpanā*) must indeed follow what is observed (*dṛṣṭa*), and not in contradiction to what is observed.

Therefore, if it is possible to conceive of this [the Veda's authority] in such a way that the inherent validity of the Veda is not contradicted, then it is not right to conceive of anything contradictory. Thus, although in well-known cases of erroneous cognition the absence of excellence (*guṇa*) and the presence of defects (*doṣa*) are observed, nevertheless, since validity is seen in the Veda even in the absence of excellence, one must not subvert that; hence, for cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the unreality [of the object] is postulated as being caused solely by defects.

Otherwise, one might even postulate that being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is the cause of inaccuracy, since cognition is observed in all invalid cognitions; yet, because cognition is also observed in valid ones such as perception, inaccuracy cannot have that [cognition-ness] as its cause. Similarly, the absence of excellences (*guṇābhāva*) is not the cause of inaccuracy in the Veda, because it is observed to be accurate there. If it is argued that its accuracy is unestablished, then from what is the accuracy of perception and the other means of knowledge established?

If it is argued that [validity] arises from itself (*svataḥ*), this is equally true for the Veda as well, except for the obsession with nihilism (*nāstikya*). Therefore, validity is not based on that [the Veda]. Furthermore, in the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl and the like, even in the absence of excellences (*guṇa*), qualities such as whiteness and brilliance are perceived exactly as they are; thus, [validity] does not depend upon excellences.

The validity of knowledge consists in its correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*). However, if it were the case that validity arises solely from its own cause while invalidity arises from defects, then it would follow that cognitions such as "this is silver" in the case of mother-of-pearl arise—by virtue of their own causes and through defects—taking as their objects both the white color (*śuklatva*) and so forth which exist as they are, and the "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) and so forth which do not exist as they are; thus [the theory] becomes logically consistent. Therefore, it is established that the validity of all cognitions is self-evident (*svataḥ-siddha*), and this remains unrefuted in the case of the Veda.
This determination of self-evident validity has been composed by Pārthasārathi Miśra for the purpose of dispelling the delusion born of conflicting interpretations and debates. (Verse 4)
Since disputants disagree in many ways regarding the nature of injunction, a definitive resolution on this matter is now provided by the author of the Vārttika. (1)

What, then, is this injunction (*vidhi*)? Some say: An injunction is a mandate (*niyoga*) that is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, which has as its sole basis words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), whose nature is that of a task (*kārya*), which has as its object the meaning of the verbal root such as "sacrifice" (*yāga*), and which impels the person—such as one desiring heaven—to act. But how can there be a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) for the optative suffixes and so forth regarding such an injunction? To this they reply:

In the world, first of all, a person seeking to acquire linguistic knowledge (vyutpitsu), observing an elder (prayojyavṛddha) who sets about acting immediately after hearing words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), thinks: "Surely a cognition of an action (*kārya*) has arisen in him; otherwise, how could he act independently? For my own activity has always been seen to be preceded by a cognition of an action; since this person is not different from me, his activity must likewise be preceded by that same cognition."

And since that cognition of the task (*kārya*) follows immediately after words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), one determines that it is caused by those very words; thus, one concludes that words like the optative denote the task. In this regard, although—because the activity and the cognition [of the task] have the same object, and because activity has action (*kriyā*) as its object—the cognition of the task produced by the optative and other suffixes must also have that [action] as its object, leading to the thought that action itself, in its nature as a task, is the meaning of words like the optative, and not some "unseen potency" (*apūrva*) distinct from it; nevertheless, according to the established conclusion of the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], the task [is indeed something distinct].

It is established that those such as the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) are connected [to the Vedic injunction] by way of being the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined). And a *niyojya* is defined as one who understands, "This task is to be performed by me. Furthermore, a person desiring an object cannot understand as a task something that is not a means to that desired object. Moreover, for a desirer who seeks the enjoyment of a fruit, an impermanent action is not a suitable [object of desire]; therefore, it is determined that there must be a stable task, distinct from the mere action, which is denoted by words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and which is fit for connection with that desirer. Because it is not known through any other means of knowledge, it is called *apūrva* (the unprecedented); and because it enjoins the person toward itself, it is designated as *niyoga* (the mandate).

And regarding that effect which is expressed as a surplus of action (*kriyātireka*), the use of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth in reference to an action in common worldly usage is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), because it is improper for a word to have multiple primary meanings. Thus, even though there is no possession of a fruit (*phala*) in the case of occasional prohibitions (*naimitika-niṣedha*) and restrictive injunctions (*adhikāra*), the *apūrva* alone shall be the meaning of the sentence, since it is precisely that which is denoted by the word. This [view] is a delusion of the ignorant, resembling a great magician’s trick; it does not serve to delude those whose minds are refined by the medicine of sound logic. For instance:
"The comprehension of an action (*kārya*) is nowhere considered the cause of engagement (*pravṛtti*)."
For that [volition] always arises from the cognition that [the action] is a means to what is desired by the agent. ||2||

If it is held that the cognition of an end (*kārya*) is the cause of activity, then it must be stated what that end is and what the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it is. It is said that the end is that which is to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛti*). In that regard, the state of being accomplishable by effort is understood through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because [the end] exists when effort is present and does not exist when effort is absent; for effort is human exertion, and that is known through mental perception. If it is argued that the end is precisely that which is qualified by the object toward which one acts, and which is established by the means of valid knowledge—namely perception and inference—is the nature of being an end (*kāryatva*) then merely the state of being the object of effort?

If this is so, then whatever object of desire, aversion, greed, and so forth—whether it be a harmful thing or a beneficial thing—a person pursues by regarding it as an object, all that is an effect (*kārya*).

[Objection: It has been established that [the cognition of] the task (*kārya*) is [the motivator]. What is the fault in this? [Reply: A cognition of such a task cannot be the cause of activity (*pravṛtti*), because even when such a cognition exists, activity is not observed. For instance, one who proceeds out of delusion with the intent of placing a finger on a snake, upon realizing midway that it is harmful, desists from it; yet in that case, the agency (*kāryatā*) was already produced by the very act of proceeding with that intent, since the nature of being a task consists merely in that [intent].

And even when that [activity] is subsequently understood to be harmful, it is not sublated. For one does not determine, "Even though I knew it was harmful, my activity did not arise"; rather, one realizes, "I was impelled toward the harmful object due to delusion. Therefore, it is established that this "task-ness" (*kāryatā*), which consists merely in being the intended object of an action and is based on the means of valid cognition of perception, is not what causes activity. Its mere apprehension is not the cause of activity.

Now, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this "task-ness" (*kāryatā*), which consists in being fit for the designation of a task, cognized? It is certainly not by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because even at the time of engagement there remains a doubt regarding the task-ness of the action; for engagement sometimes occurs even from doubt. In that case, one who engages in a certain activity while still doubting its task-ness does not ascertain that task-ness even at the moment of engagement, prior to the attainment of the result.

For they say: "We do not know whether it is something to be done or not to be done; we shall proceed only because of doubt. If it is argued that while at the time of action the state of being a task (*kāryatva*) is not perceived, it will become so at the time of the result—then whose state of being a task is perceptible at that time? It cannot be that of the action, because it has already perished; nor can it be that of the result, because what is apprehended there is merely the nature of pleasure (*sukha*). Indeed, no such thing as "task-ness" is understood here.

For one who experiences the pleasure produced by the shade of a cloud created by fate, and another who experiences the pleasure produced by the shade of a parasol generated through effort—the perception of pleasure in both cases is equally direct; indeed, no additional quality called "being an effect" (kāryatva) is perceived in a pleasure produced by an action.

Or, even if the effect-nature of pleasure were accessible through perception, the effect-nature of its means—the activity—is never apprehended through perception, nor through inference; for the observed effect-nature of pleasure cannot be inferred to apply to its means.

It might be argued as follows: "Worthiness of being acted upon" (kṛtyarhatā) is indeed "action-ness" (kāryatā), and it is that form of an object toward which, having apprehended it, a person's eagerness for activity arises with respect to that goal. Furthermore, the [result] to be attained is twofold: pleasure and the absence of suffering.

In this regard, pleasure is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the absence of pain is accessible through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); and the fact that [certain things] are the means to these is accessible through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, it is not logically tenable that "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) is an object of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). However, if this were the case, one would have to admit that for all things other than pleasure and the avoidance of pain, the very fact of being a means to those two is the cause of activity. Consequently, in the command "Bring the cow," since bringing the cow is neither the attainment of pleasure nor the avoidance of pain, the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*), in denoting "being an effect" as the cause of activity, [would be referring to something other than the actual motive].

It would express the state of being a means to achieve what is desired; therefore, the meaning is that the act of bringing the cow is something to be done, and human effort proceeds toward such a thing as is fit for action according to the injunction.

Since such a state [of being a goal] cannot occur by itself as something desired, it follows by process of elimination that the word expressing the "task" (kārya) denotes precisely its means; thus, even in the Veda, since the *apūrva* itself lacks the nature of pleasure or the avoidance of pain, it is only as a means to these that it is fit for action. Therefore, a *liṅ* suffix denoting the *apūrva* in the form of a task must denote its status as a means to what is desired. Consequently, in the case of both occasional (*naimittika*) and prohibitory (*niṣedha*) injunctions as well, because they denote the *apūrva* in the form of a means, it is through that very form that [the connection with the result is established].

Furthermore, a result [of action] would have to be postulated. Now, it might be argued: "Pleasure-ness (*sukhatva*) is not the object of the notion of 'to be produced' (*kāryatva*), because that [notion] exists even with respect to the means of attaining it; nor is the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) the object, because that exists even with respect to pleasure itself. Therefore, there must be some common factor underlying both, which serves as the objective basis for the notion of 'to be produced' and acts as the cause of engagement. This is not so; for [the notion does not apply] to the means...

It has been stated that what is called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is apprehended through perception either at the time of its initial activity or at a subsequent time. Therefore, there is no distinct category of reality called "being an effect" that is common to both [the action and the object]. However, the word *kartavya* (to be done) applies to both cases by virtue of a single limiting condition (*upādhi*): namely, that both of these, while being accomplished, impel a person toward them for their own sake. It is precisely by this limiting condition that the word *kārya* (effect/task) is employed.

Therefore, the cognition of "task-ness" (*kāryatā*) is not the cause of engagement in action; rather, it is the knowledge that something is a means to what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatva*). Or, let it be granted that "task-ness" is indeed constituted by being a means to what is desired, yet it is precisely this [quality] that must be expressed regarding the action itself, because engagement is observed only with respect to that. If it is argued: "True, in common worldly usage (*loka*), it is the action alone that is conveyed by the word as a task; however, in the Veda, because of its compatibility with the connection to the agent who desires the fruit, the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. express a stable task," we say: not so.

Even in the case of an action, there is no contradiction in understanding it as something to be performed by one who desires [the result]. If it is argued that the action is incapable of becoming the means to the fruit because of its perishability, we say no; for this is possible through the mediation of the *apūrva*. It is not possible for one thing to be the means to another through some other intermediary, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Neither an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) nor a power (*śakti*) establishes the status of being a means, but rather the *apūrva* does.

If it is argued that this is because, once the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) or the possessor of activity (*vyāpāravat*) has passed away, the persistence of the power or the activity is untenable—then [we ask]: does firewood (*kāṣṭha*) no longer possess the status of being a means for cooking? For even in that case, fiery atoms (*taijasa-paramāṇu*) have emerged from the firewood and, entering the interior of the pot, soften the rice grains. Yet, those [atoms], being of the nature of substances (*dravya-rūpa*), cannot be the intermediate activity of the firewood, nor can they be its power; thus, by that route, the firewood and so forth would not have the status of being a means.

If it is argued that this should not be so, we say no, because it would contradict what is well-established in the world; for there is undisputed usage such as "the wood cooks. Therefore, whatever is accomplished as an intermediate means by something that has been set in motion toward a desired result is designated as its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). Consequently, it is indeed possible for the *apūrva* to be the intermediate operation of the ritual action.

If this were not accepted, then the action would not possess the status of being a means even with respect to the *apūrva* (the unseen potency); for that too does not arise immediately after the action, since it awaits the performance of subsequent rites such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. In that case, the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-potencies) must necessarily be posited as intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*). If it is argued that the *utpattyapūrvas* alone are the causes of the *paramāpūrva* (the final potency) and not the sacrifices and so forth, we say no; because that is unestablished and because it is not the meaning of the scriptural words.

Since it is established that in the *adhikāra*-sentence (the injunction of qualification) the verbal root denotes the *apūrva* in accordance with its connection to the enjoined person who desires the fruit, the denotation of the *apūrva* in the subsequent sentences concerning the *āgneya* and other offerings is subsequently proven. However, prior to that, it is possible for those [sentences] to denote only actions as understood from common worldly usage; thus, because the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-*apūrvas*) are not yet established, their connection as means to the *paramāpūrva* (final *apūrva*) is impossible. Furthermore, the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice) does not denote the *apūrva*, such that the intermediate *apūrvas* could serve as causes toward the final *apūrva*, which is the meaning of the suffix.

Therefore, the sacrifice alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, it is not even logically possible for the *apūrva* to be an effect (*kārya*), for an effect is defined as that which is to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛti*). And volitional effort is human exertion; yet it is impossible for the *apūrva* to be accomplished by exertion, because it arises only after the exertion has long since perished.

For indeed, from effort comes the sacrifice, from that comes the intermediate apūrva (unseen potency), and subsequently from that comes the apūrva of entitlement; therefore, since its status as an effect is established in this way, it is not possible for the apūrva to be denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as something to be accomplished. In that case, one must necessarily resort to the fact that the apūrva is to be achieved through effort by means of the sacrifice and the intermediate apūrva.

In the same way, why is it not accepted that the sacrifice itself is the means to the fruit by way of the *apūrva*? Or, even if it were not the direct means to the fruit, the action would certainly still be a means to the *apūrva*. To that extent, a person is indeed capable of understanding it as something to be performed (*kārya*). That which, when unperformed, the desired end is not attained, and when performed, it is attained—whether directly or through an intermediary—is precisely what is understood as "to be done" (*kārya*); however, a specific mode of existence (*sākṣādbhāva-viśeṣa*) is not useful in that regard.

Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that even for one who desires [a result], there is an understanding of the action as something to be accomplished (*kārya*); otherwise, how could he engage in it independently? It is true that such an understanding of the action as something to be accomplished exists there too, but it is not verbal; rather, it is implied (*ārthī*), because the action is a means to the *apūrva* (unseen potency) which accords with the desire. If it is argued that the desirer perceives even that [implied understanding] as something to be accomplished, we say no, because this cannot withstand analysis. Does the understanding of the action as something to be accomplished arise from the fruit, or does it arise from the *apūrva*? It is neither.

Thus, [the Veda] has never produced anything unprecedented in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), because it is not admitted that the injunction (*vidhi*) possesses the capacity to impel their performance. For if the cognition of the action as something to be accomplished (*kārya*) were dependent solely upon the injunction, then, by virtue of being prompted for performance by the injunction, it would follow that even the instrumental factor (*karaṇāṃśa*) must be enjoined. Furthermore, the production of the fruit is not established by the principle you have stated; for a person desiring a fruit is not capable of cognizing a momentary action as something to be accomplished.

Since it is impossible for that [action] to be a direct means [to the result], and since the *apūrva* lacks the status of an intermediate operation such that it could not serve as a means even by way of that [action], and because for one who desires the result, the comprehension of what is to be done (*kārya*) would be untenable if it were directed toward a means of a means; therefore, the comprehension of the action as something to be performed (*kāryatva*) could arise neither from the perspective of the result nor from the perspective of the injunction (*vidhi*), and thus its non-performance would necessarily follow.

Therefore, for one who desires the attainment of a fruit from the performance of a rite prompted by desire (kāmyānuṣṭhāna), which is not produced by [the Vedic] injunction, one must necessarily recognize either that the action is the means to the fruit, or—whether it be a means to a means—that there is a comprehension of what is to be done (kārya) by the seeker of the goal. Consequently, even through the word [of the Veda], it is indeed possible to convey the action as something to be performed (kāryatayā) to one who desires the fruit; thus, the proof of the denotation of the "unprecedented" (apūrva) is not established. And whatever else remains to be said, all of that we shall discuss in the very section on the determination of subsidiaries (aṅganirṇaya).

According to another view, it is precisely the state of being a means to achieve what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatva*) that is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). This is because it is observed within oneself that the very cognition of this [state] is the cause of activity. Now, one might object: "Desire itself is the cause of activity. True; however, it is desire when it has already arisen that is the cause of activity, not desire when it is merely cognized. Since the word is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it functions as the cause of activity by way of generating a cognition; therefore, it is impossible for it to denote desire.

For desire arises with reference to either the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain, as well as to the means for those two; therefore, immediately after hearing an optative suffix (*liṅ*), the learner (*vyutpitsu*) postulates that the cognition of the action being a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatva*) is what produces the desire that serves as the cause of activity in the elder who is being prompted to act. And because this [cognition] follows immediately upon the word, it is determined that the word itself denotes it. But [one might object]: would there not then be an undertaking of the tasting of wine, since it is a means to a desired end?

It is not [undertaken] due to a powerful aversion, because it is obstructed; for just as desire is the cause for engagement, so too is aversion the cause for withdrawal. Furthermore, since aversion operates with respect to suffering, the avoidance of pleasure, and the means to those two, and since drinking liquor has been established by prohibition as a means to achieve great misfortune, it ought not to be practiced as an object of aversion.

However, one whose mind is overcome by even a slight, immediate pleasure does not perceive or respect a great calamity; with his consciousness being repelled by a powerful passion, he indeed proceeds to drink liquor. Therefore, it is established in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* that an injunction, having generally made known through its productive force (*bhāvanā*) that [an action] is a means to a desired end, becomes free of expectancy once [that end] is supplied by another word, such as "heaven" (*svarga*).

In cases where there is no other word within the same sentence that bestows a specific fruit, a fruit must be inferred through context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth; this is established in the *Prakaraṇādhikaraṇa*. In the absence of even context and the rest, the connection is made with a fruit arising from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); this is settled in the *Rātrisatrādhikaraṇa*. In the absence of even that, the connection is made with an implied fruit; this is proven in the *Viśvajidadhikaraṇa*.

The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), although expressed by the same word in all cases, is displaced from its status as the objective element (sādhya) by the more powerful injunctive hearing (vidhiśruti); it then enters into the instrumental element (karaṇa) due to proximity. This is the conclusion of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*. Thus it has been said: "Likewise, while the performance of the verbal root's meaning is indicated by the word-hearing (*padaśruti*), the fact that it is the objective to be accomplished for the person is established by the injunctive hearing."

For it is understood from the Veda that these [sacrifices] are eternally the means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Therefore, the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and others denote nothing other than being the means to a desired end; thus, in that [context], the result itself is the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), while the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, for the Teacher (Maṇḍana Miśra), who says, "The injunctive suffixes and others express a different [force], namely the denotative efficient force (*abhidhābhāvanā*)," it is otherwise.

The nature of injunction (*vidhitattva*) is intended to be defined. What, then, is it said to be? First, this is established: that the independent activity of a conscious being is not possible without the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatva*). Therefore, one must conclude that for a person who proceeds to act immediately after hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the cognition of its being a means to a desired end has arisen from the word itself. Now, is that status of being a means to a desired end conveyed by the word through its own denotation (*abhidhāna*), or is it conveyed by the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*) which denotes a different meaning altogether?

Thinking that it must be understood through the impossibility of that [other meaning], [the opponent] argues: "In that case, denotative power (abhidhāyakatā) is not appropriate, because it contradicts our consciousness. For the cognition derived from the word 'yajeta' is not identical to the cognition that 'an activity conjoined with a sacrifice is the cause of a desired object.'"

Furthermore, because they are used together: in common worldly usage, the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*) and the word expressing the means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhana-tā*) are seen to be employed simultaneously, as in: "O boy, prosperity will be yours who performs the twilight worship; therefore, perform the twilight worship. Now, simultaneous employment does not occur between synonyms. Since the understanding of the meaning of words is based on worldly usage, the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. do not denote the state of being a means to a desired end. Therefore, it is better to resort to their denoting a task to be accomplished (*kārya*).

Now, if it is asserted that "this is to be done" (kārya) refers to that which is intended as the goal with respect to an effort (kṛti), then such a state of being a task (kāryatā) must be stated without distinction for all things, for the cognition of that [state] is indeed the cause of engagement.

By process of elimination, it must be stated that "being fit for action" (*kṛtyarhatā*) is what constitutes "being an effect" (*kāryatā*); for the cognition of that [fitness] is the cause of engagement. Furthermore, this fitness for action is nothing other than being a means to pleasure or the avoidance of pain. Therefore, since actions such as bringing [an object] do not consist in themselves of pleasure or the avoidance of pain, their fitness for action consists solely in being a means to those ends. Thus, the cognition of an effect regarding objects such as actions—which serves as the cause of engagement—has "being a means to a desired end" (*samīhitasādhanatva*) as its sole basis. As it has been said: "For the worldly understanding is that 'what is to be done' (*kartavya*) is a means to what is desired by the agent."
And because the impure is not accepted as a means [to liberation], there is another motivator for actions.

In that case, since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would also denote the effect in the form of fitness for action (*kṛtyarhatā*), it would necessarily denote the state of being a means to what is desired; thus, there would be no distinction between this view and that [previous] one. It is replied: there is indeed this distinction, namely, that the state of being a means to what is desired is not denoted in its own essential form; rather, the optative suffix denotes fitness for action in a manner common to both pleasure and the avoidance of pain, as well as to their respective means.

When that [the action] is denoted, since the action itself lacks inherent pleasure or the like, its status as a means [to such pleasure] is determined by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Thus, the injunction expressing "what is to be done" impels the person toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); this is the prevailing usage in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*. This view, however, is inconsistent with [the definition] beginning with "they call it the denotative productive operation" (*abhidhābhāvanām āhuḥ*). Furthermore, the word "injunction" (*vidhi*) is used together with the word "task" (*kārya*), as in: "The twilight worship is your task; therefore, perform it."

Although this application [of the optative suffix] is possible because it is not at all synonymous with the expression of the number of the agent or the object due to their distinctness, nevertheless, it is not logical for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) to have the "task" (*kārya*) as its denotation. For instance, even regarding an object that is not a task, one observes the use of the optative suffix and so forth in the context of a request, having accepted the status of a task [for that object]. For example, someone requests another in this way: "Even though this is indeed not a task for you because it is prohibited, nevertheless, do it for my sake."

If, however, it were for the sake of an action (*kārya*), there would be a contradiction; for one does not say, "Even though this is not an action, nevertheless it is an action. One who speaks thus becomes an object of ridicule. Therefore, the fitness for being performed (*kṛtyarhatā*) and the injunction (*vidhi*) are two distinct meanings. What, then, is this that was called the "denotative productive operation" (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*)? Every word indeed possesses a denotative function (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*) that is inferred from the cognition of its meaning. However, the function of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others is called "productive" (*bhāvanā*) and "instigating" (*pravartanā*), because its fruit is the arising of a person's activity.

Someone says: "No operation of sound is possible, because it is a quality; and even if it were a substance, it would be impossible because it is all-pervading. For all-pervading things such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, an operation such as cognition is indeed possible. However, the inherence of motion (*spanda*) is not possible, nor is that [motion] desired by us for sound. What then is its operation? It is simply its own cognition, or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by it; for sound, when conjoined with that, generates the comprehension of meaning. Thus it has been said: "Scripture is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of the word."

And [it has been said]: "The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes, is the signifier. When this [final phoneme], having acquired an adventitious property (*āgantukadharma*), becomes capable of producing the effect, that very adventitious property is called its "operation" (*vyāpāra*). By this, it is established that cognition and the impression possess the status of being the operation of the word.

Now, it is argued that it is improper for cognition to possess the nature of an expression (*abhidhātva*); for with respect to cognition, sound is accepted as being its object (*karman*), while its agency (*kartṛtva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is accepted with respect to expression. How then could it simultaneously assume the state of being an object, as well as either agency or instrumentality, within a single operation?

We say it is like an axe (*paraśu*). For an axe, although it is an object (*karman*) with respect to the acts of raising and lowering, becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of those very same acts when delimited by the result characterized as the splitting of the tree; for every instrument is indeed within the scope of the agent's operation. Likewise, even though knowledge has a word as its object, its object is the referent (*artha*) itself, once it has acquired the designation "denotation" (*abhidhā*) through being delimited by the result characterized as the comprehension of that referent.

The word, however, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in that state because it is pervaded by an operation whose activity culminates in the result; and when independence is intended to be expressed, its status as the agent (*kartṛ*) is likewise faultless. By this very same principle, the status of the object of activity (*pravṛtti-karmatva*) and the status of the object of the person (*puruṣa-karmatva*) have been explained for the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), which has the meaning as its object and whose designation as "instigation" (*pravartanā*) is obtained through the delimitation of the result of the person's activity.

When that single operation is denoted by the verb *jñā* (to know) as having the manifestation of the object as its inseparable result, then the word itself—which has become the object—is the *karman* (object), as in "he knows the word" (*śabdaṃ jānāti*). In that case, the meaning [of the verb] is that which possesses the result consisting of comprehension; thus, one says "the word expresses the meaning" (*artham abhidadhāti śabdaḥ*). However, when that same operation is denoted by the verb *bhāvayati* (to bring about) as having human activity as its inseparable result, then the activity—which possesses the result of coming into being—is the *karman*, as in "he brings about the activity" (*pravṛttiṃ bhāvayati*).

When, however, [the verb] *pravartayati* ("he causes to act")—which denotes an operation delimited by the fruit of a person's activity—is expressed by means of a word, then the person who possesses that fruit of activity becomes the object (*karman*), as in the expression "he causes the person to act. This same principle should be applied, as far as possible, even to the case of the operation of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) regarding the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). For the status of being an object does not depend on the essential nature of the operation; were it so, an action denoted by the verb *calati* ("he moves") would also be transitive, just like one denoted by *gacchati* ("he goes").

Likewise, effort (*prayatna*)—just as it is expressed by the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*—would also be transitive when expressed by *yat*. Similarly, the operation of the cutter (*chetṛvyāpāra*)—just as it is expressed by the roots *udyacchati* and *niyacchati*—would also have the axe (*paraśu*) as its object when expressed by *chinatti*. Therefore, there is only one single operation which, being defined according to different results, assumes those various distinctions of objects; however, when it is defined by its own nature independently of the result, [it remains unitary].

By such rules as *pūyati-ta-te-cali* and others, it becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*). However, when it is defined by a form whose determination is dependent upon a result (*phala*), then it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). In this regard, some who deny that the self (*ātman*) can be the object of cognition have stated that the definition of an object (*karman*) is "being the recipient of the fruit of an action residing in another. This, however, is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), because in cases such as "Devadatta purifies himself with the *Pāvamānī* verses," Devadatta is the object of the verb *punāti* even by virtue of being the recipient of the fruit of an action residing in himself (*svasamavāyin*).

And likewise, in the Veda, the usage "Agni purifies" (punāti) and "Purify yourselves" (punīta) is observed. Therefore, the definition of an object (*karman*) is exactly as stated before. Nor does it follow that the goer (*gantṛ*) would be the object in the act of going; for in the case of "he goes to the village," the object is the village and so forth, not the goer. And thus, in the action of knowing expressed by such terms as "knows" (*jānāti*) or "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), which is defined by the result consisting in the manifestation of the object of knowledge, the self's status as an object is established, since it appears in the cognition of "I."

[The opponent] says: Let it be that there is an operation consisting of denotation; however, it is not possible for this [denotation] to be the motivator of a person's activity (*puruṣapravartakatva*) nor to be the object denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*). For no prudent person engages in action merely from the comprehension of a denotation, since engagement depends upon the comprehension of something being a means to achieve a desired end (*samīhitasādhanatva*). Nor can this [denotation] be inferred from the result characterized by the understanding of the meaning, for even though it is denotable like the denotation of other words, it ought not to be so [in this context]. It is replied: True.

It has been stated that being a means to a result (*phalasādhanatva*)—which is the state of being an instigator—is not the direct denotation (*abhidheya*) of the word. Therefore, a child desiring to learn the meaning of words, observing an elder who is engaged in activity, determines that the understanding of "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), which serves as the cause of that activity, is produced by the word. Then, by the previously mentioned reasoning, since it is impossible for the word to be the direct producer [of that understanding], he concludes: "The *liṅ* suffix is a word that denotes that [property] by whose expression it is possible to infer its status as a means to a result."

Consequently, the denotation by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers is postulated as being of the nature of an instigation (*pravartanā*), which is itself imagined through the very cognition of the object of one's own activity. And this nature of instigation consists in having activity as its fruit. Since such a nature cannot be postulated through the mere cognition of the object, and because it is not obtainable through any other means, one postulates a power of the optative suffix that is distinct from other types of denotation. Furthermore, the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) thus constrained by the injunction is determined to be a means for achieving the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

For it is impossible for an activity whose fruit is not a human goal (puruṣārtha) to be connected with an injunction (vidhi) in the form of an instigation (pravartanā). Since those who act with foresight cannot be incited toward what is fruitless, words [such as *svargakāma*] convey the status of being a means to a fruit solely by virtue of the force of the injunction itself. [Objection: But on this view, since an injunction in the form of an instigation requires someone to be instigated (*pravartya*), words such as *svargakāma* would be connected only as providers of the person to be instigated, and not as providers of the fruit. [Response: "Let it be so," say some.

Nor does this lead to the consequence of fruitlessness, because the status of something as a "fruit" is postulated precisely because it must be something desired in order for [the injunction] to be operative. In both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, however, the words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) are observed to have the fruit as their primary meaning, and this is indeed appropriate. For instance, even if in this view—unlike the view where the injunction consists of a "task to be done" (*kārya*)—there were the contingency of non-difference between the agent (*kartṛ*) and the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), since agency pertains to the action to be performed while the state of being enjoined pertains to the injunction (and thus there is a difference in object), nevertheless, the [words] do not have that [agency] as their primary meaning.

It is appropriate that words denoting desire (*kāma*) refer to an object not yet attained, for a scripture here is intended to bring about what has not been previously established. By the force of the injunction (*vidhi*), it is understood that there exists someone to be enjoined (*niyojya*); and he is the one who is the "residual beneficiary" (*śeṣin*) of this operation connected with the injunction and is capable of performing it, for no one can be impelled toward an operation that does not serve their own interest. Nor can one who is incapable be so impelled. Furthermore, he alone is the residual beneficiary for whom this operation is the means to achieve a desired fruit. Since this much is understood even without words of desire—namely, that the operation is a means to a fruit—but the specific nature of that fruit remains unascertained, it is logical that words of desire are directed toward that specific fruit.

Thus, by expressing the injunction in the form of an instigation (*pravartanā*) through the injunctive word itself, the necessity of performing the enjoined act (*kartavyatā*) and its status as a means to achieve a result (*phala-sādhanatā*) are understood by implication. With this intention, there is the linguistic usage: "the suffix expresses the necessity of performance" (*kartavyatā-vacanaḥ pratyayaḥ*), and "for their status as a means to the good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*) is always cognized from the Veda. Now, an objection might be raised: "If one's own operation (*vyāpāra*) is being denoted, does it not follow that the [suffix's] own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is being denoted? For it is impossible to denote a qualified object (*viśiṣṭa*) without denoting its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Do not say so. For it has been stated: "The apprehension of a qualified object is not possible without the apprehension of its qualifier."
But no one here relies upon the relationship between the designator and the designated.

This is equally applicable even under the view that the injunction consists in being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). For there too, the injunction is not merely the state of being a means to a desired end; rather, because it is impossible [for the suffix] to denote the agent, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*), it must be accepted that what is expressed is the state of being a means to a desired end as qualified by an agent who is understood through the implication of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—since the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) does not denote the agent.

Thus, on this view, since the instigation (*pravartanā*) is understood from the directly perceived word "liṅ" and so forth, there is no fault such as the denotation of the nature of the word itself or the denotation of its expressive function.

For those who know the Nyāya, however, it is only the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that is intended, and there is no contradiction with experience, because [the word] does not denote [the action] in that form; rather, the word denotes it in the form of an instigation (*pravartanā*). And the property that is the cause of activity is the instigation. Since injunctions and so forth are impossible in the impersonal Veda, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is determined to be precisely the state of being a means to a desired end. Therefore, just as the verbal operation of denotation denotes the instigation, the word denotes the state of being a means to a desired end in the form of an instigation, and not in its own intrinsic form; thus, there is no contradiction with experience. This very point is also the view of the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra.
Since men are not motivated by the mere means itself, there is nothing else that impels them toward actions;
they declare that the "incitement" (pravartanā) is the property (dharma) which serves as the cause of engagement.

This is the intended meaning of one who says that the word *evaṃ-kāra* (the expression "so be it") is the causal factor for instigation (*pravartanā-pratyaya*), and so forth. In this way, the assumption of multiple meanings does not occur; otherwise, many meanings would have to be postulated for the word, such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*), entreating (*adhyeṣaṇa*), permitting (*abhyanujñāna*), and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭa-sādhanatva*). However, if it denotes the general category of instigation (*pravartanā-sāmānya*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*).

Even in that case, since the causes of activity—namely passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth—are not denotable, it must be stated thus: the optative (*liṅ*) word is that which denotes that which, by being cognized, is the cause of activity. Nor is it correct to maintain that the meaning of a word is a single entity common to all [instances], such as "command" (*praiṣa*) and the like, which is designated as "the task" (*kārya*) when it is presented by those who are superior, equal, or inferior; for it has already been stated that the optative is used in the sense of a request precisely because it is not accepted as a mere task. Therefore, the meaning of the word is the general property of incitement (*pravartanā-sāmānya*). And thus: "The meaning of the word is indeed the particular itself, for even the observed form is connected [to it]."
Nor is the subversion of the incitement [to action] desired, for it would be purposeless without the capacity [of the injunction].

In this verse, it should be explained that having presented the opponent's view in the first half, he presents his own position in the second half. Since the optative suffix (*liṅ*), by expressing the general property of "instigation" (*pravartanā-sāmānya*), would result in a useless cognition of a featureless generality, and since in the impersonal Veda the specific qualities of human agency—such as commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth—are impossible, it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that only the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is what is conveyed. This is precisely the meaning of the Vārttika passage: "They call it the *abhidhā-bhāvanā*."

It is called *abhidhā* because it is denoted (*abhidhīyate*); it is the instigation (*pravartanā*) or the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*).
