"For the nature of a word-meaning (*padārtha*) is common to all its states, whereas its connection with a particular state is a specific feature (*viśeṣa*); thus, the word-meaning itself is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This is not logical. For even if a general property implies a particular, it can only imply that "some particular exists"; however, an implication directed toward one specific, determined particular is impossible due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). Consequently, in the command "Bring the cow," the act of bringing is not understood as being connected specifically with a cow.

In my view, however, it is logical that the denotation of a word is that which is connected with another object characterized by expectancy and so forth; thus, when "bringing" is understood as being connected with a "cow," the cow—being proximate through its own word—is not [merely] another object, and thereby the attainment of a determinate cognition is established.
And if it depended upon proximity, there would be a mutual dependence;
for that [proximity] would exist even through mere denotation or through memory. (9)

Nor should it be said that if a word expresses its own meaning as connected with another proximate object, then—in the case of "gām ānaya"—the word *go* [expresses] its own meaning first; [and so on].

It need not be expressed; for as long as it is not expressed by the word *ānayan* (bringing), its own meaning cannot be denoted. For if it were so, then even though the word *go* (cow) had not itself expressed its own meaning, that meaning would still have to be denoted—thus, mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) is quite evident. Indeed, a word’s denotable object need not necessarily be connected with a meaning that is present through being expressed, such that this fault would arise; for mere proximity (*sannidhi*) serves as the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of that [connection], and proximity is possible even without expression, through memory (*smṛti*).

For all words indeed recall the nature of the object, which serves as the cause for the proximity of their respective counter-correlates; thereafter, having their syntactical relations determined by logic, they express their own meanings. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Now, it might be argued that even with a non-proximate enjoined agent (*niyojya*), the expression of a related meaning is observed in cases such as the *Viśvajit* sacrifice; however, even there, proximity is obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

For proximity (*sannidhi*) is not necessarily verbal; it is merely an indicator or a means, since in expressions such as "the door, the door," we observe in common worldly usage that the denotation of the related [action] occurs through non-verbal factors such as closing and so forth. If this were the case, then when a horse is present before one's eyes, in the command "Let the cow be brought," the act of bringing would denote a relation with the cow alone, because both the cow and the horse are equally proximate through both verbal testimony and direct perception, and there is no difference between them regarding proximity, expectancy, and compatibility. This is not a fault.

Because the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the verb *ānayati* is satisfied by its connection with "cow" alone, there is no evidence for its connection with "horse. How is it that, even though both are in proximity, the connection with "cow" cannot occur because of the satisfaction of expectancy by "cow" alone? It is not possible for the opposite to be the case; for if it were connected with "horse," the expectancy of the word "cow" would not be satisfied.

[Objection: Surely, in that case as well, the expectancy would cease through the very actions such as standing which are already apprehended by perception and other means; it would not require another means of knowledge. For instance, when it is said, "Let the cow be brought," while both a standing cow and a horse are present, one might perceive two distinct sentences: "The cow stands" and "Let the horse be brought. [Reply: That is not so, because they are understood to constitute a single sentence.

For it is observed in the world that when as many words as possible are employed in combination, they are intended to convey a single qualified meaning through that combination; and this is accomplished only when the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) exists between those very words heard [in the sentence]. Otherwise, it would be contradicted. Furthermore, since the cessation of expectancy for both [the word and its meaning] is possible through a single connection, it is improper to postulate multiple connections due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it is the words themselves that denote the connected meanings and constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sentence-meaning. To this, it is replied: even this view is not tenable, for in this position there would be a more extensive assumption of the unobserved (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*).
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of contradicting what is perceived; therefore, the theory of "the connection of the expressed" (abhihitānvaya) is correct. ||10||
In that case, there would be conformity with observed facts, and the conceptualization would be simpler.

For if words denote what is already related (*anvitābhidhāna*), then the relation (*anvaya*), even though it serves as a qualifier, must necessarily be denoted; otherwise, the cognition of the related object could not arise. Consequently, by postulating two powers—one for the relation and one for the related—the postulation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) would be much more cumbersome. Now, it might be argued: "We do not postulate a separate power for the relation; rather, that single power is postulated as culminating in the related. This is incorrect.
How, indeed, could both [the relation and the related] be the denotable objects through a single power?
The qualified object is indeed one; everything else is merely a qualification. (11)

For although the qualified object (*viśiṣṭarūpa*) is indeed one, nevertheless the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is distinct from the qualified; if that [qualifier] is not apprehended, it is impossible to apprehend the qualified object as qualified by it. And since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to grasp it, the qualified must be denoted by the word itself preceded by the denotation of that [qualifier]. Thus, because of the assumption of two capacities, there would be the same fault [of infinite regress]. Therefore, it is logical that only the essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) should be denoted.
Nor does this lead to the impossibility of the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), because:
"Even when the essential nature is denoted, the cognition may have the qualified object as its domain."
For a cognition of a particular is established without effort from a cognition of a universal. ||12||

Since the essential nature of a word-meaning (*padārtha-svarūpa*), which consists of all its states in common, is denoted by the word, the cognition of the specific state characterized by syntactic connection (*anvita-rūpa*) is established from that very [denotation]; therefore, it is not possible to postulate a further power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*). As for the objection that, this being the case, in the sentence "Let the cow be brought," since the action is implied merely by the factor (*kāraka*) and the factor is implied merely by the action, the act of bringing would not necessarily obtain its connection with the cow through the bringing; to that it is replied:
"That same defect regarding the scope of the word exists equally even on the theory of direct denotation (*abhidhā-pakṣa*).
And as for the unity of the sentence (*ekavākyatva*) in that case, it is the same even with respect to the word-meanings. (Verse 13)

This same fault applies even to one who maintains that the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is denotative by the words themselves. When another action such as standing, or another agent such as a horse, is present through other means of knowledge, and the two words "cow" and "let it be brought" are uttered, there would be no certainty regarding the connection between the cow and the act of bringing; for, since proximity, expectancy, and semantic competency (*yogyatva*) are equally present, the word "cow" might denote a cow connected with standing, and the act of bringing might denote bringing connected with a horse. To this, the opponent replies: "If that were so, the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) would be subverted."

This is the same even regarding the word-meanings (padārtha). Although the word *go* implies a connection with action in general, and the meaning of *ānaya* implies a connection with a factor of action (kāraka) in general, nevertheless, because one perceives that the two words expressing those meanings possess the single characteristic of being a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*)—defined by their intent toward the cognition of a single qualified object—one must not subvert that [unity]; thus, there is a mutual restriction between the two words as they are heard. And since this restriction is established solely from the sentence consisting of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the other words, and not merely from the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the word-meanings, for this very reason...

Otherwise, verbal testimony would be nothing other than inference. Therefore, even when there is an indeterminate overflow of multiple sentence-meanings based solely on the capacities of the word-meanings—and whether or not there is a pervasion (vyāpti) with a specific sentence-meaning—the comprehension of the specific sentence-meaning is established through the mutual co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) [of the words] alone. As it has been said: "When there is an influx of many non-exclusive sentence-meanings, the cognition is fixed upon one [meaning] through the mutual exclusion of their natures."

Therefore, regarding what is desired in inference through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, the exclusivity of a single meaning—it is established here in a different manner.

The meaning is this: that result of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in inference, characterized by the determination of a single object, is accomplished here through another means, namely, a sentence characterized by the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of other words. By this, the following is stated: for both disputants, the capacity of multiple common constituent words to convey a single unified meaning is mutually restricted by their forming a single sentence; this much must necessarily be postulated.

When another action is present through another means of knowledge and the cow is brought by another word, then—since there is no difference in the expectancy and other factors—the word "cow" must be understood as being capable of conveying the cow as connected to both [the action and the bringing]; thus, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), it is to be assumed that it denotes its own meaning precisely as connected to that [other element].

As for me, however, it must be assumed that the word-meaning, by its very nature, is incapable of conveying its own self as connected with just anything; rather, through syntactic unity with another word, it conveys its own self as connected specifically with that [other] meaning. This much is common to both of us. You, moreover, postulate the capacity of the word to reside in a qualified entity, whereas we [postulate it] in the mere intrinsic form alone.

Thus, there is a great distinction. If it is argued that there is no fault because of the absence of mutual requirement (*apekṣā*), we say no; for [the word's function] is not observed even when such a requirement exists. It might be argued as follows: "We do not assume that the common power of the word is restricted by its being part of a single sentence. Rather, why does the expression of what is connected with another meaning not occur? Because of the absence of requirement. For that [requirement] is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the expression of what is connected."

Furthermore, there is no mutual dependence between an action and its factors when they are already cognized through other means of knowledge; however, such dependence does exist when they are both heard [in a sentence], and that dependence is removed by their mutual connection, so there is no contingency of their being connected with some other meaning. This is not so, because even when such dependence exists, no actual connection is observed. For there occurs occasionally this situation: having inferred a horse in a certain place by the sound of neighing and the like, one desires to know its specific action, asking, "Is the horse going or standing still?"

And in another instance, having inferred the movement by means of the sound of footsteps, one desires to know the specific agent, wondering, "Is it a cow or a horse that is going there? At that moment, someone utters the two words, "A cow stands here."

In that case, if syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) were not accepted as the restrictive factor, then there would be a mutual connection between the horse inferred from the sound of neighing and the action understood from the word "stands" (*tiṣṭhati*), because the specific action requires a particular agent, and the action understood from the word "stands" requires a particular instrument; thus, [the sentence] would be "the horse stands. Similarly, there would be a mutual connection between the movement inferred from the sound of the footstep and the cow understood from the word "cow," because the movement requires an agent and the cow requires an action.

In the case of the expression "the cow goes" (*gaur gacchati*), the connection "the cow stands" (*gauḥ tiṣṭhati*) would not be ruled out as a necessary consequence, because proximity, expectancy, and semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) are equally present in both cases. Yet, such a thing is not observed. Nor should it be said that the inherent power of a word itself serves as the regulator for the cognition of its own meaning as connected with the meanings recalled by other words; for even those who do not accept verbal testimony (non-linguists) admit that the denotation of the connected meaning is desired. Therefore, the restriction [of meaning] is not established through the power of the word.

Therefore, unity of sentence alone must be sought as a refuge for the sake of producing a cognition of a necessary relation, even by words that denote things already related (the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*). And since that [unity] is naturally established even by word-meanings through their inherent capacity to produce a cognition of relation, it is permissible to rely on them for that restriction; thus, enough with this obsession with the postulation of *anvitābhidhāna*.

Furthermore, in cases such as "the *dhava* and the *khadira*," since it is accepted that a *dvandva* compound denotes a simultaneous substratum (*yugapadadhikaraṇa*), and since its denotative function (*vācakatva*) is not accepted [in this regard], the *khadira* necessarily indicates itself as being accompanied by another in order to connect with the dual number; it does not denote this. For if the connection with the dual number could be established by its being accompanied by just anyone, why would it indicate itself as being accompanied specifically by the *dhava*?

If it is argued that this is because of their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), then that very [unity] would be the cause for the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of word-meanings everywhere as being connected with something else; thus, there would never be the postulation of an unestablished [cause]. Even so, it is more reasonable to accept that the word-meanings themselves are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the sentence-meaning, rather than the words themselves, due to [their varying] proximity or intervention.

For even in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related), once the word-meanings have been understood through the words, the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises subsequently; otherwise, due to the difficulty of establishing proximity (*sannidhi*), it would not be possible. There is indeed a dispute as to whether those meanings are denoted by the words or merely recalled by them; however, in every respect, there is no disagreement that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs after the words have been apprehended and the word-meanings have been cognized.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that words separated by the skipping over of objects experienced immediately prior can be the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; nor is there a subsequent recollection of those words. Moreover, there is no evidence for such a thing. Furthermore, in extremely long sentences, such a recollection would simply be impossible. And even if it were possible, [the meaning would still not be grasped].

It is well known to all people that the meaning of a sentence is understood merely through the consideration of the meanings of its constituent words. Therefore, because it conforms to what is observed, the meaning of a sentence is caused by the word-meanings alone, and not by the words themselves; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting what is observed. As it has been said: "The capacity of word-meanings, which is being perceived, cannot be denied; and since the meaning of a sentence follows immediately [from them], it does not abandon its status as having those [meanings] as its cause."

By this, it should be understood that the reason previously stated—that words alone possess the capacity for [denoting] the related [meaning] because of their primacy—is actually a proof of the opposite. As for the claim that it is more reasonable for words themselves to directly convey the related meaning on account of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), that would lead to the absurd conclusion that firewood which does not depend on flames is the means of cooking, or that the Āgneya and other sacrifices are the means of achieving the ultimate result without depending on their respective intermediate operations.

Now, it is argued that when the forms of the Agneya and other constituent sacrifices have vanished, the supreme apūrva (transcendental result) arising therefrom cannot be produced by them directly; yet, this does not contradict the fact that they accomplish the intended purpose even through the mediation of intermediate operations. This point applies equally here as well. For in this case too, while the words themselves have vanished, the sentence-meaning—which is understood subsequent to the recollection of the word-meanings—is accomplished directly by the word-meanings alone, whereas the words are the means only through those [meanings] and not directly.

"Surely, in this way, words would not possess the capacity to denote (abhidhāyakatva), because the cognition of the nature of word-meanings would be no different from mere recollection (smaraṇa). Let it be that they are merely reminders (smāraka) and not denoters; let it be so, some say. And thus, [the suffix] expressing the efficient force (bhāvanā) reminds one of so many [meanings], as is seen in common worldly usage. A word also does not differ from a reminder, since there is no additional element [in its function]."
Since even those [words], when not remembered, do not lead us to understand the meaning of the sentence,
it is therefore only when their remembrances are combined that they possess the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Thus they say. Others, however, say: "The status of being a reminder (smārakatva) is based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*); yet there is no proximity characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like between a word and its object, from which [the word] could function as a reminder. If it is argued that this is 'like the status of being a denoter (*vācakatva*),' we say no, because that [status of being a denoter] is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). This may be so: just as the status of being a denoter exists even in the absence of another relation, so too will the status of being a reminder exist. That is not so.

Since denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is innate, being a denoter is indeed the state of conveying meaning; and that is established by means of an inherent power (*svabhāva-śakti*), just as in the case of the eyes and other senses regarding color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. [Objection: But even there, a relation characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), or inherence therein (*tatsamavāya*) certainly exists. [Reply: True; however, that [relation] is common to taste and the other objects of sense. It is power alone that is the unique cause for the capacity to convey meaning.

In the same way, a word will also possess the capacity to convey meaning through its own inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), whereas its function as a reminder (*smārakatva*) occurs through the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Nor can this [power] be awakened by the observation of another related object, because such a thing is never observed anywhere. [Objection: But even the capacity to cause comprehension is never seen in that which lacks a relation. For even the eyes and other senses, though endowed with inherent power, function as conveyors only through a relation; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving objects even when they are at a great distance.

But for a word, there is no connection whatsoever with its meaning. How, then, can it be a conveyor of meaning? If you argue that even though this [conveying power] is not observed elsewhere, it must be postulated here alone, then why not postulate instead that it is merely a reminder? Or rather, the distinction [between the two] must be stated. That is now explained: in any case, since it is not observed elsewhere, one must postulate either that a word is a reminder or that it is a conveyor of meaning. Between these two, the postulation of its being a conveyor of meaning is indeed superior.

Since the cognition of meaning is observed immediately following the word, it is logical to postulate that the word itself is the cause in that regard, rather than the view that the word first awakens a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and from that, the cognition of meaning arises; for there is no evidence for such an indirect process. Therefore, the word is indeed expressive (*abhidhāyaka*) and not merely a reminder (*smāraka*). If it is argued that the cognition produced by a word is merely remembrance because it apprehends what has already been grasped, that is incorrect, as it does not possess the defining characteristics of remembrance.

Furthermore, the defining characteristic of recollection (*smṛti*) is not the grasping of what has already been grasped, but rather being produced solely by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). On the contrary, that cognition which grasps what has already been grasped and is generated by a presently existing cause is called a restatement (*anuvāda*), not recollection. How then is the formulation in the *Vārttika* to be understood? It is indeed consistent; for even a restatement, by virtue of grasping what has already been grasped, is not distinct from recollection. In such cases as "the word denoting the mental impression causes those [objects] to be remembered," the conventional usage of "recollection" is figurative. And thus he shows that it is a reminder, even in the case of the mere nature of the object itself.

It is logical that a word possesses denotative power (*abhidhāyakatva*) with respect to its expressed meaning (*vācya*). As for the argument that primacy is the cause [of this], it serves to establish the opposite [of what is intended].
Furthermore, those who claim that the capacity to convey intention (*tātparya*) constitutes denotative power have their position rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (14)

This is the summary verse. Furthermore, if the cognition of the related meaning (*anvita*) arises solely through denotation (*abhidhāna*), how then is there the comprehension of the bank and so forth—which are indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—as being related to the hamlet in such expressions as “a hamlet on the Gaṅgā” (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*)? For even its own form (*svarūpa*) is not the denoted object of the word *gaṅgā*, much less its being related [to something else]. Now, if it should be argued: once the actual form of the object (*arthasvarūpa*) has been recalled by the word *gaṅgā* acting as a cause (*nimitta*), the word *ghoṣa* denotes its own object (*svārtha*) as related to that form of the bank which is recalled by virtue of its connection with that [recalled] form; whereas the word *gaṅgā*...

[The opponent objects: "It is useful merely for the recollection of the word-meanings. [The proponent asks: "In that case, where all the words have only metaphorical meanings and no word has a primary meaning at all, how can there be a comprehension of the related [sentence-meaning]?
Or does such a sentence even exist? Indeed, it exists—such as 'The king goes,' where there is neither a [purely] abstract action nor anything related to it. (Verse 15)

The denotable meaning (*abhidheya*) of all words is either the action (*kārya*) itself or that which is associated with it (*tadanvita*). The action belongs to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, while for other words it is that which is associated with the action. However, in common worldly usage, one observes the employment of words concerning established facts (*siddhārtha*) that are devoid of a [prescriptive] action, taking the form of curious questions and answers, such as "Who is this going? or "The king is going. Or there is the description of specific objects by poets, such as:
"Today, moving among the petals of blue lotuses with beautiful cries, these women, clothed in silk, are as lovely as *kādamba* swans."

This and other such [cognitions] are, according to your own tenet, "derived" (lākṣaṇika). Yet, even in those cases, there is indeed a cognition of the related [meaning]. And this [related meaning] cannot possibly arise from the words themselves, because they do not denote that [relation]; for the word *bhūmipa* (king), although its own meaning is denoted as related to an action, does not denote its own meaning as related to the act of "going" (*gacchati*), even when that act possesses the triad of expectancy and so forth; likewise, the act of "going" also does not denote its own meaning as related to that [king]. Thus, the cognition of the relation would not be caused by the words.

Therefore, even against one’s will, it must be admitted that this cognition of the related [meaning] arises solely from the nature of the objects themselves—which are recalled by the words as its causes—when accompanied by expectancy, semantic competency, and syntactic unity. Consequently, let it be so in all cases; what is the use of postulating the expression of the related [meaning] (*anvitābhidhāna*)?
Or, perhaps you think that in those cases the cognition whose object is the related [meaning] arises through inference, and not from words nor from word-meanings. (16)

Just as in the case of established meanings (*siddhārtha*), the cognition of the sentence-meaning is not based on the word-meanings, nor is it based on the words themselves; rather, it is based on inference. For the composition of a sentence is human and preceded by a desire to express a specific meaning; it thus leads to the inference of that [desire]. And since that [desire] establishes the inference of the object which is its cause—namely, the specific cognition—it is not possible to assume that all word-meanings possess the capacity to convey mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*). If this is so, then the same consequence follows even in cases where there is a cognition of something to be accomplished (*kārya*).
Therefore, the capacity of words is not established as residing in the related [object]. ||17||

Even in cases such as "Bring the cow," according to the very principle you have stated, the understanding of a qualified effect is established through a series of inferences; therefore, it is not easy to maintain that words possess the power to denote a meaning as already connected (anvitābhidhāna). To this, it is replied:

That object which is the subject matter of a sentence is inferred by means of that [sentence]; the determination of the power of words regarding a connected meaning cannot be established otherwise. (18)

For, by observing the linguistic usage directed toward a qualified object, one who engages in such usage must necessarily admit that a cognition having that very object has arisen. This is not established by the mere sentence alone, but rather from the comprehension of a qualified sentence; and its distinction lies precisely in its capacity to denote that specific meaning.

For it is by means of a sentence that conveys a specific sentence-meaning that the listener, having inferred the speaker’s intention regarding that subject, and then—by way of inferring the cognition whose object is that specific meaning—infer a particular object, and thus the elder listener proceeds to engage in activity toward that specific object; not otherwise. Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that a sentence possesses the capacity to convey a specific meaning. And since this [capacity] is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as residing precisely in the power of the individual parts (the words), it is proven that words denote their meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). If this is so, then because even sentences concerning accomplished facts (*siddhārtha*) produce the understanding of a specific meaning...
And because the words lack semantic capacity, the word-meanings serve as the cause [of the sentence meaning]. (19)

For even from sentences whose meanings are already established, such as "The king goes" and so forth, a cognition arises that has as its object a specific meaning—namely, the king's going and the like—and this [cognition] results from inferring the speaker's specific knowledge. And the inference of such knowledge is based on the composition of a specific sentence. Furthermore, the specificity of the sentence would consist in its capacity to convey that particular meaning.

Not otherwise. Therefore, it must be admitted that a sentence possesses the capacity to convey a qualified meaning. If it were argued that the inference of a cognition regarding that object need not necessarily be based on a sentence that conveys a related [meaning], because the attainment of a qualified inference follows simply from the specific collection of words that recall the particular meanings; [then we reply:]

For such is the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that it consists in the understanding of those word-meanings which are capable of mutual connection; and thus, even without the word-meanings themselves conveying the connected sense, since the inference of a specific sentence-meaning regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*) is possible through the inference of knowledge based solely on the particular arrangement of words, it is not established that the sentence-meaning is caused by the word-meanings. If this is so, then the same would apply to sentences whose meanings are effects (*kāryārtha*);
therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning would not establish the fact that the meaning is already connected (*anvitārthatā*).

Even in sentences such as "Bring the cow," it is possible to infer the specific meaning of the sentence through the prior inference of a qualified cognition, based merely on the words' capacity to denote the individual forms of their respective word-meanings; thus, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of related meanings) would not be established. For even without *anvitābhidhāna*, since the inference of a qualified cognition is possible through such a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that for those individual word-meanings whose relations are already known, the mere denotation of their individual forms [suffices]—[the theory is redundant]. Furthermore, even the individual form alone is not the denoted object, but rather only a specific word [denotes its form].

For it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a cognition whose object is precisely a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭārtha*), just as the capacity to denote (*vācakatva*) is grasped with respect to each word in relation to a specific meaning—such as, "the word *go* denotes that which possesses a dewlap and so forth," or "the word *aśva* denotes a horse. In the same way, the pervasion of that word with a cognition whose object is the meaning connected to it can be grasped [as follows]: "The arrangement of the word *go* by a reliable person (*āpta*) is preceded by a cognition of that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, as connected to another suitable and proximate meaning required by the context.
Consequently, even the claim that words denote the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of objects is not established.
Therefore, since [words] cannot denote that which is already possessed [of a relation], the Veda lacks authoritative validity.

For it is not possible for a Vedic sentence, being of non-human origin, to convey the meaning of the sentence by means of inferring the speaker’s knowledge; thus, it would lack authority. This might be argued: having observed the activity of the elder who is prompted [to act] immediately following the hearing of the word, one postulates that he possesses a cognition directed toward a specific object.

And since that [cognition] follows immediately upon the word, it is caused by nothing other than that; thus, the capacity of the word to denote its object is postulated. Subsequently, however, upon observing someone else’s composition of words that do not correspond to reality, one reflects: "How could the elder who is being prompted have arrived at a certain cognition of the object from a deviant sentence? and having thus deliberated, he determines as follows:

"Surely this speaker has been understood by him in this way; he does not employ words whose meanings are unconnected. Therefore, [the listener] concludes that 'surely this person has known the connection between these [words],' having ascertained the meaning preceded by an inference based on knowledge. [The opponent argues: "But one does not consider the previously apprehended denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) to be false; therefore, the denotative capacity exists. This is not sound.
For the power of a word is not inferred from an effect that is not produced by it.
Let there be an error regarding its being produced by that [connection]; and that error shall be removed. (22)

For the understanding of the elder (the person being prompted), which occurs immediately after the word, is not produced by the word itself such that it would lead one to postulate a causal capacity (śakti) in the word; rather, it is produced by the inferential mark (liṅga) consisting of the speaker’s cognition inferred from the word. Furthermore, an effect accomplished through one cause does not lead to the postulation of a capacity in something else, as this would result in over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

And although, because its non-production from that [cow] has not been ascertained and because it follows immediately after the word, one might through delusion apprehend that it is produced from the word—such that when the delusion regarding the word ceases, the delusion regarding the capacity caused by it will also necessarily cease, just like the cognition of fire produced by the smoke of a smoky buffalo—it is true that this [cognition], though uncontradicted in its own nature, nevertheless ceases precisely due to the sublation of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

Likewise, the assumption that sound possesses denotative power must be abandoned, because it is determined that the effect [of cognition] is not produced by it. Now, one might argue that even a sentence which merely restates an object already inferred could be capable of being denotative. That is not so, because there is no evidence for its being a restatement. For nothing is logically untenable except on the basis of its being a restatement, such that one would have to assume it. If it is argued that its status as a restatement follows from its denotative capacity, then this is a circular argument: denotative capacity depends on the restatement, and the restatement depends on the denotative capacity.

Therefore, denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is not established. If, for the sake of establishing the inference of a cognition whose object is a specific ultimate reality, one were to re-establish denotative capacity, that too would be untenable; for even without denotative capacity, it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a particular word by means of a particular cognition alone. Consequently, if the authority of worldly speech is accepted on the basis of its being an inference, then since words would lack denotative capacity, they would fail to convey meaning, and the Veda would consequently lack authority. Therefore, in order to establish its authority, [it must be admitted] even in the world...

The validity of words must be accepted as residing in their very nature as words. [Objection: Let it be that they lack validity; however, one should not postulate their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever from which the denotative capacity of a word could be postulated, since even in its absence, the comprehension of an object immediately following a word is possible in the world through inference alone, according to the reasoning already stated. [Reply: This would be so if the cognition of an object arose solely from hearing the speech of a trustworthy person (*āpta*). But the arising of cognitions is equal upon hearing the speech of both trustworthy and untrustworthy persons.
Furthermore, a cognition arising from the words of an untrustworthy person cannot be produced by means of a logical mark (liṅga). ||23||
Therefore, the power of the word must be postulated for the sake of establishing its production;
whereas those who maintain that cognition does not arise from the speech of an unreliable person [must likewise account for it]. (24)
The authoritative word is a logical mark (liṅga), while the refutation applies only to those [other means of knowledge];
such is the only difference between my words of the trustworthy and the untrustworthy. (25)
In that case, the validity of a cognition arising from the speech of one who is not authoritative is established;
however, that which arises from the speech of an authoritative person is seen to be [invalidated] by the defect of the speaker. (26)
Its validity is established because the cause—the speaker’s cognition—is possible;
since the arising of the cognition exists in both cases as well, there is no fault. ||27||

It is common knowledge that for those whose minds are undistracted and whose inner selves are tranquil, words uttered from any source whatsoever suddenly produce a consciousness directed toward an object, even without their having considered the specific excellence of the speaker’s intellect or whether he is trustworthy or untrustworthy. Since inference is not possible in such a case, the expressive power of words themselves must necessarily be postulated; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in our position.

However, for those who deny even this—which is established by all people—and instead assert that worldly speech is merely inferential, it follows that the Veda itself lacks authority. For it is impossible to conceive of a word’s denotative capacity (*abhidhāyakatva*) arising from a cognition of the sentence-meaning that has not been produced by that [word]; this is especially true regarding its capacity to denote what is already related (*anvitābhidhāyitva*), since the cognition of such a relation is unestablished. Indeed, there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the fact that a cognition of a related meaning arises in the elder listener immediately after hearing the word, by which the word’s having the related meaning as its object could be established.

If it is argued that inference is the means of valid cognition, that is not so, because its cause is not perceived. Furthermore, if it is claimed that activity serves as the inferential mark (liṅga), that is not the case, for such activity is inconclusive (anaikāntika). ||28||

It might be argued that the cognition of the related meaning by the elder who acts upon the instruction is understood through inference. That is not so, because no inferential mark (*liṅga*) for such an inference is perceived. But surely activity itself is the mark; for that activity is preceded by a specific comprehension, and thus it leads one to infer that comprehension. This is not so, because activity is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*); for according to your own view, activity occurs even in the case of one desiring silver when confronted with mother-of-pearl, due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between them.

Therefore, in the case of the sentence "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), since the four meanings—the nominal stem *go*, the accusative case-ending, the verbal root, and the injunctive suffix—are expressed merely in their own forms (*svarūpamātreṇa*), activity is established simply because there is no apprehension of non-connection (*ananvayāgraha*) even though the connection itself has not been explicitly expressed; thus, it is not possible to postulate that there is a cognition of the related meaning (*anvitapratīti*).

For how can one who, while directly perceiving the cognition arising with respect to the object standing before him as "this is silver," yet—due to the non-perception of the established causes [of such a cognition]—denies it, and instead imagines that the non-apprehension of difference (bhedāgrahaṇa) is the cause of purposeful activity even though it has not been observed elsewhere; and who, despite this specific postulation of the unobserved, understands that the sense organs and other factors, when accompanied by defects, produce erroneous knowledge, and thus postulates this [non-apprehension of difference]? How could he possibly do so?

Furthermore, by inferring from the activity of another—which is established even without grasping the distinction between the causes of that activity—through a non-conclusive [inference] accompanied by consciousness, one does not feel shame in postulating a capacity for the word, even if it has not been previously established elsewhere, as being the cause of that [consciousness].

If it is argued that practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on the non-apprehension of difference is subject to contradiction—just as the practical activity regarding silver in the case of mother-of-pearl is contradicted, whereas no such contradiction exists in cases such as "Bring the cow"—and therefore it is not based on non-apprehension; that is incorrect. For even practical activity based on non-apprehension, such as the activity regarding the unity of a flame or the activity regarding hot water, is seen to be non-contradictory. Likewise: "Seeing steam rising from a place where there is fire without smoke, one proceeds with the conviction that there is fire and is not frustrated. (29)

This is another example: suppose fire without smoke is situated in a certain place, and steam rises above it; someone, mistaking that steam for smoke and thinking "there is fire beneath this," exerts himself with the desire to obtain fire. Since he does not encounter a non-correspondence (failure) in his attainment of fire, the observation of non-correspondence in practical activity (*vyavahāra*)—even when that activity is based on non-apprehension—is therefore inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) as a reason for postulating the arising of a cognition of a connected object (*anvitajñāna*).

[The cognition] ought to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, because that [cognition] is not postulated, the fact that words possess a connected meaning (*anvitārthatva*) cannot be established; thus, the Veda would lack authority with respect to the sentence-meaning. Consequently, since the cognition of a connected meaning is unestablished—or even if it were established, since its existence could be accounted for solely through the inference of the speaker’s intention without recourse to the power of the word—even though it is produced by a sentence, it could just as well be brought about by the capacity of the word-meanings understood from the individual words, as in the case of sentences whose primary purpose is to state an already established fact (*siddhārtha*). Therefore, according to your own position, the capacity of words to denote a connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāyitva*) remains without proof.

Siddham. In our view, however, although it cannot be denied that words possess the capacity to denote related meanings (*anvitābhidhāyitva*) even in sentences concerning established facts (*siddhārtha*)—on the grounds such as the fact that words function according to their primary denotation (*śrutivṛttatva*)—because it is impossible for linguistic usage to be dependent on non-perception and because we do not accept [such sentences] as valid means of knowledge in the form of inference; nevertheless, they are refuted due to contradiction with observed reality (*dṛṣṭabādha*) and the complexity of postulation (*kalpanāgaurava*).

Furthermore, how is it that the assumption [of our view] involves such a burden? For you, who accept the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), must assume that words denote their own meanings as related to another meaning—which is understood from the words of the sentence possessing expectancy and compatibility—and since such a relation is possible even with supplied words like *sa-varaṇa* (with a covering), you might argue: "The capacity of word-meanings to relate is already established by their very nature; therefore, there is no burden of assuming a verbal power for us. To this, it is said: [the following verse follows]. [The verse: "The capacity of word-meanings to relate is established by their very nature. This means that the inherent power of word-meanings to enter into a relation is already established by their own nature; thus, we do not incur the burden of postulating a new verbal power (*śabda-śakti*). However, this is not so, because the capacity of word-meanings to relate is not established by their nature, but rather by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). If it were established by nature, then even when a sentence is heard where the speaker has no intention to convey a specific relation—such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*)—the meaning "bring the horse" (*aśvam ānaya*) would have to be understood. Therefore, the capacity to relate is not innate to the word-meanings. Consequently, the burden of assuming a verbal power remains ours alone. Thus, the claim that "the capacity of word-meanings to relate is established by their nature" is refuted. Furthermore, if the capacity to relate were established by nature, then even in cases where the speaker intends to convey a different meaning, the unintended meaning would still be understood. Therefore, the capacity to relate is not established by the nature of word-meanings. Hence, the burden of assuming a verbal power is indeed ours. This is the sense. Thus, the objection that "there is no burden of assuming a verbal power for us" is rejected. Therefore, the burden of assumption is equal for both sides. Consequently, the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*) is untenable. Thus, the theory of the denotation of the isolated meaning (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*) is established. This is the conclusion. Therefore, the burden of assumption is equal for both parties. Hence, the theory of the denotation of the related is not logical. Thus, the theory of the denotation of the isolated meaning is proven. This is the final point. Therefore, the burden of assumption is equal for both. In that case, by virtue of syntactic unity, only a restrictive rule (niyamamātra) is to be inferred.

The capacity of words to signify their respective meanings is indeed uncreated; it need not be postulated. However, the assumption of an intrinsic nature [for the word] and the imposition of restrictive rules is cumbersome. (31)

First, the assumption of a power (śakti) regarding the meaning and form of words is common to both positions. In the theory of the connection of what is already expressed (abhihitānvaya), the capacity of word-meanings to convey a connected meaning is already established; one need only assume a restriction based on syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), and that is the simpler option. On the other hand, in the alternative view, the capacity of words themselves to convey a connected meaning—which is entirely unestablished—must be assumed, and that is the more cumbersome position. Furthermore, the conformity with observed facts has already been demonstrated. As for the fact that, despite there being no difference in proximity, expectancy, and compatibility, only those meanings known through other means of knowledge serve as the cause for a restricted connection: [End of provided text]

It has been stated that in the case of words derived from [other] sounds, one does not observe the postulation of a triple capacity; this was refuted by the non-acceptance of mere proximity (*sannidhi*) as a constituent factor (*aṅga*). For proximity—consisting in the dependence on another word forming a single sentence with the word that expresses its own meaning—is a constituent factor for the cognition of word-meanings as invariably connected to one another; and since such proximity does not exist in the case of things known through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no cognition of a single, fixed sentential meaning therein.

And precisely because proximity (*sannidhi*)—which depends upon other words forming a single syntactical unit—is a necessary factor for the cognition of the related meaning of word-meanings, and not mere proximity alone, it follows that in cases where sentences such as those concerning the *Viśvajit* sacrifice are incomplete, one must postulate a word itself to provide the required object through verbal proximity. Thus, the fact that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has the word as its domain is established. Likewise, in the case of mantras and the like that are extended by analogy (*atideśa*), when the original words such as "Agni" are set aside due to the loss of their purpose, the modification (*ūha*) is accomplished by the mental insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of words such as "Sūrya" in acts like the offering (*nirvāpa*).

Otherwise, this [theory] would not hold; so let that matter rest for now. Although the extraordinary capacity (*apūrva-śakti*) must be postulated for both words and word-meanings alike, it is nevertheless more appropriate to postulate it for the word-meanings alone rather than for the words. For instance, in a case where there is a single word and a single word-meaning, according to the theory of "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), two capacities must be postulated for the word; whereas even under the theory of "relation of the denoted" (*abhihitānvaya*), there are likewise exactly two—namely, one for the word and one for the word-meaning. Thus, they are equal in this regard.

Even in cases where a single word has multiple meanings to be expressed—as with the word *akṣa*, which has three meanings such as "a die" and so forth—there is still the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (expression of related meanings), because one must postulate two powers for the word with respect to each meaning, resulting in six powers. In the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of related words), too, one must postulate one power for the word with respect to each meaning, resulting in three powers for the word; and since there are three word-meanings, there are likewise three powers for them, making the total exactly six. Thus, the two views are equal in this regard.

However, where many words are denoters of a single meaning—such as the words *pāṇi*, *kara*, and *hasta*—in that case, according to the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), there would be six powers due to the postulation of two powers for each word. But according to the theory of the relation of the expressed (*abhihitānvaya*), there are only four, because one power is postulated for each of the three words and one for the meaning; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). In this manner, the application of powers in cases of four, five, six, and so on, should be demonstrated.

One should infer that there is an addition of three in the case of four [words], an addition of four in the case of five, and an addition of five in the case of six. Furthermore, it has been stated that even though the postulation of *śakti* (potency) is equal [in both views], it is more logical that the meanings of the words themselves—not the words—are the cause of the sentence-meaning because of their immediate proximity. Therefore, the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what is expressed) alone is superior. And thus the author of the Sūtras, by stating "because the meaning is caused by that" (*arthasya tannimittatvāt*), clearly demonstrates that the sentence-meaning has its cause in the word-meanings.

For the author of the Bhāṣya also states that these words, having expressed their respective meanings, cease their operation; then, the word-meanings, now being denoted, cause the sentence-meaning to be understood. As for the explanation offered here—that a word expresses what is interrelated rather than expressing the interrelation itself, because the interrelation is understood from that which is interrelated—[that is incorrect].

The meaning of this is as follows: Just as an individual (*vyakti*), though perceived along with the form (*ākṛti*) expressed by the word, is said to be "comprehended through the form" because it is the object of the verbal cognition even while being within the range of the word's perception—since the cognition of the form is indeed the cause for the cognition of the individual—it is logical that the individual is not understood from the word alone, just as the form is not; for it is impossible to cognize the universal (*jāti*) in its isolation.

Indeed, this is the very nature of the form (ākṛti) that it cannot attain cognition without an individual instance (vyakti); for that [form] is the form of the individual, and there can be no cognition of a form devoid of its possessor. If such were the case, it would not even be a form. Therefore, the genus (jāti) is cognized only together with the individual instance; nevertheless, it is said that the cognition of the form is the cause of the cognition of the individual instance.

For what reason? Because a word, by its own inherent power, denotes the genus (*jāti*) alone; however, since it is impossible to convey that genus without the individual (*vyakti*), it conveys the individual as well. Therefore, the word’s capacity to convey the form (*ākṛti*) is innate, whereas its capacity to convey the individual is caused by that [conveyance of the form]. Thus, it is said that the cognition of the form is the cause of the cognition of the individual, but it does not mean that the form, first understood through the word, subsequently causes the understanding of the individual.

Likewise, since a word that expresses the related (*anvitābhidhāyin*) cannot convey what is related without [first conveying] the relation itself, the relation being understood is said to be "measured by" (i.e., delimited by) the word-meanings. And in the *Bhāṣya*, that which is related is expressed by the term "word-meaning" (*padārtha*), while the relation is expressed by the term "sentence-meaning" (*vākyārtha*);

the meaning is that word-meanings, being related, convey the sentence-meaning, and thus convey the relation. [The opponent suggests: "The capacity to convey the relation is based on the capacity to convey what is related"—this is the view of Yādava.
However, this interpretation of the text via such a laborious path does not shine.
For here, the status of word-meanings as the cause for the sentence-meaning has been clearly stated. (32)
If the theory that words denote [objects] as already connected is firmly established by reasoning, then the commentary on the text may proceed even by means of a strained method. (33)

When it has been established by reasoning that the individual word-meanings, expressed by their respective words, bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning, then this [objection] does not hold. (34)
And since the opponent has challenged the basis for the comprehension of the correlated [meaning], that very basis is stated by this commentary (bhāṣya). 35.

If, having accepted the logical connection, the opponent should point out a flaw in the basis [of that connection], then that basis, once challenged in the context of the syllogism, must be established in its true nature. (36)
But this is not the case; therefore, this explanation is not tenable.
As for what was said regarding "like an individual," that is incorrect from the perspective of the word itself. (37)
For us, the cognition of the individual is not [directly] from the word;
rather, it is the universal alone that is first understood from the word, which subsequently implies some particular individual. (38)

For a word denoting a universal (jāti) causes that very universal to be understood, and not the individual (vyakti), because it lacks the capacity for that; and because if an effect were to arise from what lacks the capacity, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Furthermore, since the apprehension of the universal could also arise from that which lacks the capacity [to denote the individual], [the individual need not be denoted]. If it is argued that the word also possesses the capacity with respect to the individual, then that individual too must be a denotation.

If, however, it is argued that where there is an inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), that is the denotable object (*abhidheya*), and since the universal (*jāti*) is such, while the power in the individual (*vyakti*) is based on its being the cause of denoting that [universal], therefore the individual is not said to be the denotable object—this is incorrect, because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*). If two powers of the word are postulated for those two objects, then by what means of knowledge is this internal distinction understood—that the power is inherent in the form (*ākṛti*) but based upon it in the individual?

Now, if it is argued that the word's power does not reside in the individual (vyakti) but only in the universal (jāti), and that while this [power] is perceived by the word alone, it is nevertheless said to be perceived along with the individual due to the very nature of things—that is not so, because there is no cause for the perception of the individual. Furthermore, it is impossible for the universal to be perceived together with one that is itself unperceived. How is it said that there is no cause for the perception of the individual? Because the word is not the cause, as it lacks the power [to denote the individual]. And because the universal is not yet established prior to its own perception, it cannot serve as the cause [of the individual's perception].

Therefore, one must admit that the prior cognition of the universal (jāti) is necessary. But [an objection may be raised]: since it cannot be cognized in isolation, and yet it is not cognized in isolation, there would be no cognition of the universal at all. Consequently, one must admit that the universal alone is what is cognized from the word.
Furthermore, a cognition of forms exists even when devoid of the actual form-possessing object;
for example, in the winter on the Himalayas, there is a perception of coldness through the sense of touch. (39)
Likewise, when a fragrant substance reaches the tip of the nose, no cognition arises regarding the substance itself; rather, it is the fragrance alone that arises [in consciousness]. (40)
Therefore, because it denotes the universal (jāti), the word should cause that [universal] alone to be understood;
once that has been cognized by means of the word, it subsequently causes the individual (vyakti) to be understood. ||41||

Or rather, let it be that even by means of a word denoting the genus alone, the individual (vyakti) is understood through the very fact of the [denotation] not being exhausted; thus, it does not necessitate the postulation of a separate verbal power (*śabda-śakti*). However, it is not so in this case, because without a separate power, the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) would be impossible. For the genus is indeed a different entity from the individual; it is therefore logical that when the genus is denoted, the individual does not enter into the process of denotation.

For the nature of a genus is not merely its possession of an individual (vyakti), such that by entering into the denotable [individual], the individual itself would also become denotable. Furthermore, since the nature of that which is related consists precisely in its possessing a relation, if that [related thing] were being denoted, the relation itself would necessarily enter into the denotation. Consequently, a separate expressive power (śakti) would have to be postulated even for that [relation]. Now, if it is argued that by the word "related" (anvita), the intrinsic form (svarūpa) of the word-meanings is indicated, and that it is possible to denote the relation without first denoting that [intrinsic form], then—[if this is so]—it is not the case...

The establishment of the cognition of concomitance (*anvaya*) is achieved through the word. For, unlike a universal (*jāti*), the essential nature of a word-meaning (*padārtha-svarūpa*) cannot be defined without its concomitance with an individual (*vyakti*); if it were so [definable], it would be conveyed by the word because that [concomitance] is not fully realized [otherwise]. Now, just as a universal is never perceived anywhere devoid of an individual, so too no word-meanings are ever observed anywhere devoid of connection with individuals; at the very least, all word-meanings everywhere possess concomitance even with the sense of existence (*asty-artha*).

"Even for that [relation], because it is established through non-finality alone, it does not possess the status of being denotable. True; however, while the mere connection (anvaya) is understood due to non-finality, its specific nature does not ascend to verbal cognition without denotation. Therefore, since there is a complexity in postulating a power (*śakti*) for the word to denote the related, the individual form (*svarūpa*) alone is the denotable object.

How then does the author of the Bhāṣya state that "the accusative case-ending, as it issues forth from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), is a qualifier of the meaning of the nominal stem," thereby asserting that the suffix (*pratyaya*) expresses [its meaning] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*)? Or, according to your own view, since all words express [their meanings] as already connected, how can that property be stated specifically of the suffix? Therefore, in accordance with the text, one must establish the distinction that other words denote their own mere forms (*svarūpamātra*), whereas the suffix expresses [its meaning] as already connected.

Alternatively, it is not by this [statement] that the suffix is said to express the relation (*anvaya*); rather, it is meant that while the suffix expresses its own meaning, that meaning is understood as already colored by the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) which was previously apprehended. In that regard, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is distinguished that—within the respective meanings of the base and the suffix, as well as in the aspect of their mutual coloring—it is precisely the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the base and the suffix that serves as the cause for the coloring by other word-meanings.

Just as it is analyzed how the apprehensive aspect (*grahaṇāṃśa*) is the cause of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and how—when one thing is perceived as qualified by the absence of another thing—the objective aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) falls within the domain of perception and other means of knowledge, while the non-existence aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) falls within the domain of non-existence; so too here, since the aspect of coloring (*anurāgāṃśa*) is established through cognition solely from the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the base and the suffix, the suffix does not denote that [coloring], but rather denotes its own meaning alone. And it has been said:
"When it is said that the base and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix..."
Even though it is designated by way of distinction, it is spoken of here according to its predominance.
"For the root *pac* (to cook) indeed expresses the cooking, and the suffix *aka* expresses the agent;
however, the agent as connected with the cooking is not denotable by either one [of them] alone."

However, suffixes expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) denote only a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). Indeed, no other denotable object for them can be established. For even in the case of "the priests wearing golden garlands" (*hiraṇyamālina ṛtvijaḥ*), the substrata (the priests) are themselves expressed by their own words; what else, then, could the possessive suffix denote other than the qualified entity? Therefore, it denotes only the qualified entity. Furthermore, as for other [words] which, like the case-ending (*vibhakti*), denote multiple meanings simultaneously—such as gender, number, and cause—they too are denoters of the related [meaning] (*anvitābhidhāyitva*). And all of this we shall explain in the *Aṅganirṇaya* itself.

But for other words, the denotable object is indeed their own individual meanings, whereas the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), consisting of those meanings as related to one another, is understood through the word-meanings (*padārtha*). For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the sentence-meaning is "indicative" (*lākṣaṇika*), because it is understood through a connection with the denoted meanings. Now, one might object: "Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is caused by inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); yet word-meanings are not inseparably concomitant with the specific sentence-meaning. How, then, can that [sentence-meaning] be indicated? It is not necessarily the case that indication is caused solely by inseparable concomitance; rather, the state of being part of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is also a cause in that regard.

For this very reason, even in the absence of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), there is justification for the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to that [sacrifice] in the case of "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), due to its syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). This syntactic unity is sometimes directly perceived, as in "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*). Sometimes it is to be inferred from context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors, as in the case of "one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" and "one sacrifices the *samidh* [fuel-sticks]"; here, a syntactic unity of the form "the procedure (*bhāvanā*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, accompanied by the *samidh*, must be performed" is postulated. The same should be understood in other cases as well.
Therefore, neither the sentence nor the individual words directly generate the cognition of the sentence-meaning; rather,
it is generated by the word-meanings expressed through the inherent forms of the words.
It is established that this [object] is perceived. ||42||
By Pārthasārathi Miśra, the determination regarding the theory of abhihitānvaya has been demonstrated according to tradition and according to his own insight, as set forth in the Vārttika. ||43||

Having observed the distinction between optional and obligatory rites made by the author of the Vārttika, the characteristic consisting in the completeness or deficiency of auxiliary elements is now set forth. (1)

Some indeed maintain that there is no difference whatsoever between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites, because in both cases all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) must be performed. By these partial theorists (*ekadeśin*), through the effortless presentation of weak arguments, the spread of this very view has been consolidated.
By refuting both [positions], the correct reasoning is demonstrated, by which the clear distinction between optional (kāmya) and obligatory (nitya) actions may be established. (2)
In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows:
"For eligibility everywhere depends upon application;
otherwise, the eligibility of Śūdras and others would be unavoidable. (3)

"Everywhere" means not only in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites, but also in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) ones. Only one who possesses the capacity for the synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of that collection of ritual limbs (*yajñāṅga-jāta*)—which has been established in a given rite through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and so forth, as well as through traditional law (*smṛti*), custom (*ācāra*), explicit injunction (*vacana*), designation by name (*nāmadheya*), and extended application based on indicative marks or purpose (*codanā-liṅga-nimitta-atideśa*)—[is entitled to perform it].

In this regard, it has been established in the *Tiryagadhikaraṇa* that there is a qualification [to perform the rite]. This is because the attainment of the fruit depends upon the totality [of its causes], and because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is such only when it is joined with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Furthermore, there must be an inclusion of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) in their combined state; otherwise, the contingency of the eightfold defects arising from optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) would follow. And since what is merely optional cannot be performed, how could there be the accomplishment of the performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*)? Moreover, if the fruit were attained even when only a few auxiliaries are included, then it would also apply to rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), as there would be no distinction between them.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in injunctions such as "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*), because the scriptural mention of a causal condition (*nimitta*) establishes that the rite must necessarily be performed when that condition exists, and because its non-performance would contradict that [injunction], one understands—by the force of that very [injunction]—that even one who is deficient in auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is still a means to the fruit, and thus it is performed in that manner? In the case of rites for specific desires (*kāmya*), however, since there is no such contradiction, performance occurs through the inclusion of all auxiliary parts. [Reply: This is not so. Even by virtue of a causal condition, the necessity of performance belongs only to the qualified person (*adhikārin*), and the qualified person is one endowed with all capacities, not anyone else.

If it were argued that, because the eligibility for the *sruva* ladles is understood from the indicative statement (*nimitavākya*), the collection of subsidiaries (*aṅgopasaṃhāra*) follows accordingly—such that whoever is capable of collecting as many as they can achieve the result with just those many—then, by the same logic, even in the case of a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya*), since eligibility is understood to belong to anyone merely desiring heaven, there would follow the consequence that one could perform it in exactly that manner [without all subsidiaries].

If the contraction of limbs were to occur by the force of a specific cause (*nimitta*), then even a *śūdra* who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), as well as those who have maintained the fires but lack knowledge (*vidyā*) and possess only the capacity to perform the constituent parts other than those [lacking], would be entitled [to the rite]. Therefore, the determination of entitlement (*adhikāra*) depends on the capacity for all constituent parts, because entitlement is contingent upon capacity, and because capacity is determined by what can be performed—which is itself established through the five chapters [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]. As it has been said: "When the task is known, there is entitlement."

By this, those who—having rejected the relationship of the signified and the signifier—propound the definition of "occasion" (*avasaralakṣaṇa*) as the definition of "qualification" (*adhikāralakṣaṇa*), are to be understood as refuted; for in both cases, there must be a collection of all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*). Some, however, maintain that being the object (*viṣayībhāva*) is preceded by being the instrument (*karaṇībhāva*);
they say that in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), there is completeness of the parts through that [instrumentality], whereas in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), it is the reverse.

It is established that the *apūrva* in the form of the task (*kārya*) is the primary meaning of the sentence; and since that [task] acquires its existence dependent upon human effort (*kṛti*), and since in such cases effort is nothing other than the exertion of a person, it requires a conscious agent as its performer. Furthermore, that person's status as a performer depends upon entitlement (*adhikāra*). For he who understands, "This is my duty; I am the master here," performs it, and no one else. Such a person is called "entitled" (*adhikṛta*). And in such cases, entitlement depends upon being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatā*).

For that action indeed becomes "one's own" when it accomplishes one's purpose; thus, by depending upon the purpose—thinking "this is my purpose"—there arises for a person the understanding of their entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the action that accomplishes it. And he who perceives the purpose as his own is the "one to be enjoined" (*niyojya*). Furthermore, an unprecedented purpose (*apūrvakārya*) is not an object of desire for anyone in the way that pleasure or the avoidance of pain is. Since the status of such a thing as a "purpose" is understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the entitlement to the action that accomplishes it would [already] exist [prior to the Vedic injunction].

Therefore, it must be established by the verbal testimony itself that "this is the task to be performed by this person. Thus, the task (kārya) is dependent upon the person to be enjoined (niyojya), and that person is characterized by qualifiers that are not themselves objects of attainment (anupādeya-viśeṣaṇa). Furthermore, that [task] is of two kinds, distinguished by the difference between the fruit (phala) and the cause (nimitta). Among these, since a fruit that has not yet arisen cannot serve as a qualifier by its own nature, it qualifies the person to be enjoined through the medium of the person's own desire for it.

And he is called one who desires the fruit who wishes to accomplish the fruit for himself; he understands that very action which is conducive to his own desire. (Now, if the apūrva were connected to the fruit as its producer, it would become a subordinate qualifier, and thus the established doctrine—that the *niyoga* alone is the primary meaning of the sentence—would fail. To this, he says: "Of the *niyoga*...")

The meaning is that even for the primary *niyoga*, in order to achieve its own establishment—namely, its connection with a *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined) characterized by a desire for a result—it must maintain and accept favorability toward that result. Favorability toward the result for the *niyojya* must be maintained by the primary *niyoga* as well, for the sake of its own establishment through its connection with the specific *niyojya*. And that [favorability] is a task to be accomplished through effort.

Since effort (*prayatna*) cannot be defined as something unconditioned, it requires a conditioner (*avacchedaka*). And that conditioner is generally a verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*), because only that possesses a relationship with the effort by its very nature. Indeed, no effort in the world is observed whose object is a verbal root-meaning such as "cooking" (*pāka*) that has not yet been attained. In some cases, however, by virtue of the word itself, a relationship between a substance and a deity (*dravya-devatā-sambandha*) becomes the conditioner, being connected to the effort brought about by the verbal root-meaning.

Thus, since the *kārya* (the "to-be-done") is delimited by the *kṛti* (the effort of volition), and since the *kṛti* is not cognized without a delimiter consisting of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) and so forth, the meaning of the verbal root and the like become the delimiters of the *kārya* through the mediation of the *kṛti*. And that which is the delimiter is called the "object" (*viṣaya*), for the object is indeed that which is connected [as a condition] to the cognition.

Furthermore, an effect (*kārya*) cannot be cognized as something unconditioned; therefore, that which conditions it becomes its object by being invariably concomitant with its cognition. And since that [object] is the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), and because an effect conforming to a desire cannot exist without an object, it is possible to apprehend it as a means to the desired end; thus, it becomes the object specifically in the form of a means (*upāya*).

And since that [obligation] is a means to an end for which assistance is produced by the performance of the entire collection of constituent parts (*aṅga*), if there is a transgression regarding the connection with any constituent part, the assistance generated by all the constituents will not be accomplished. Consequently, because it lacks the status of being a means, the object [of the injunction] ceases to exist; and since the subject (*viṣayin*)—the task to be performed—is no longer perceived, one would not perform the rite with its constituent parts deficient due to the force of that [perceived obligation]. However, this mode of operation is not possible in the case of a compulsory (*nitya*) rite. For in that case, there is no person enjoined who desires a fruit, such that they would fail to understand the task as something to be done because it were not a means to an end.
