However, one first understands the task (kārya) as delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha), which is qualified by the accomplished particularizing attributes; but once the task is understood as having an object, since a task cannot exist without an effort (kṛti), and since an effort is impossible without an instrument (karaṇa), it requires an instrument and thus perceives the nearby verbal root-meaning—which has become the object—as the instrument.

If it is asked, "How can the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which is indeed that which is brought about by human effort (*kṛti-nirvartya*), be the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to that [effort]?"—the answer is: because that [root-meaning], when delimited by that [effort], constitutes the very nature of that specific transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the effort; and such a thing is well-known in the world as being an instrument. For instance, although the axe is pervaded by the action characterized by the raising and lowering [of the hand] by the woodcutter, it is nevertheless the instrument with respect to that very action, because that action has as its fruit the splitting [of the wood]. Indeed, the raising and lowering [of the hand] directed toward a clod of earth does not result in the fruit of splitting.

Thus, although the efficient force (*kṛti*) is pervaded by the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), nevertheless, the status of that [efficient force] as being directed toward a specific *apūrva* depends upon its having that [verbal root] as its object; therefore, it is logical that the meaning of the verbal root functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, because the *apūrva* is the objective end (*uddeśya*), it possesses the nature of the task to be accomplished (*kāryatva*).

Thus, since the object—which has become eternal—is subsequently understood as having both the status of being the "thing to be done" (*karaṇatva*) and the accompaniment of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there is no absence of the object even when a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is omitted. Consequently, because the cognition of the "thing to be done" depends upon the object, and because that [cognition] does not perish when the object does not perish, the *niyoga* (the mandate) does not cease to produce an understanding of entitlement (*adhikāra*) toward the ritual action that is its means; by the force of that [understanding], it impels one to perform the rite even if it lacks a subsidiary. Thus it is established that the modified (*vaikṛta*) *niyoga* effects the performance of those subsidiaries which are distinct from those that have been substituted, prohibited, or whose purpose has been lost.

The distinction between optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites: This very matter, which appears auspicious at first glance, when examined with skill through the lens of subtle logic, turns out to be like brass. Why?
Because the fruit is remote, because there is no denotation of an *apūrva*, because its predominance is abandoned, and because its status as the object [of the injunction] is established. (Verse 5)

Because its own nature does not perish through the state of being equally primary, and because it lacks the status of being a motivator, as in the case of the Jāteṣṭi sacrifice, it follows by way of incidental application (prasaṅga). ||6||

For the fruit, which is conveyed by another word, is remote from the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), whereas the *apūrva* (transcendental result), which is conveyed by its own word, is proximate. In this regard, who that understands the relative strength of direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*) would assert that [the fruit] first connects with the *apūrva* as the means—having first connected with it through the remote [fruit], then related to the subsidiaries conveyed by other sentences that are even more remote—and only afterwards delimits the *apūrva* denoted by its own word by means of that [fruit] thus connected?

Although it is necessarily the case that the means to desire—which constitutes the object of the action and is the meaning of the verbal root—is a means to that [desire], nevertheless, it should not be defined first. Not...

For when a certain thing cannot be established without another, that [latter] thing must be understood only after first determining the former. Even when the primary thing has been understood, the thing that establishes it is indeed understood afterwards, just as the fire is understood from the smoke. Therefore, having first understood through the hearing of the word an *apūrva* whose object is merely the meaning of non-existence (*abhāva*), one subsequently understands its status as a means to the accomplishment [of the result]—since otherwise its being the objective of the "task" (*kārya*) which serves as the means to the fruit would be inexplicable—and for the sake of establishing that, the connection with the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is understood.

There is no loss of the object (*viṣaya*) when there is a deficiency in the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). For if, on the grounds that the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*) necessarily exists even in the final determination—which has a remote means of knowledge as its authority—one were to include it within the category of the object, then since that [status] would necessarily exist as its instrument (*karaṇa*) even in the case of what is eternal (*nitya*), and since that [instrument] belongs to that which is endowed with the auxiliaries, the object would likewise consist of that very thing; thus, in the absence of the auxiliaries, the loss of the object would follow as a logical consequence.

As for the one who says that it is not necessarily the case that what is the object of an injunction must be the instrument of its performance—because we observe that even the negative particle (*nañ*), which does not constitute an act of performance, can be the object of an injunction—he should be told: "Even that which is the object of an optional injunction (*kāmya-niyoga*) does not invariably possess the status of being the instrument of the fruit, since we observe that the connection between the substance and the deity, though not itself an act of performance, is the object in sentences such as those concerning the *Saurya* sacrifice."

If he should reply that even though the connection between the substance and the deity is not itself an act (*akaraṇabhūta*), it becomes the object (*viṣayatva*) in its very form as being invariably concomitant with that [act], then the discussion is the same. Therefore, just as in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), when the mere meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) has become the object, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are subsequently understood, so too it is in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*).

Once the status of the meaning of the verbal root as the object is established by direct statement (*śruti*), the subsequent connection with the fruit and so forth is understood from the syntactical context (*vākya*) and other means. (Verse 7)

Thus, there is first one remoteness characterized by the employment of another word, and another caused by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For instance, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not directly denote that heaven is the goal to be accomplished; rather, heaven’s status as the goal is understood through its connection with desire. Consequently, the fact that the sacrifice is the means to achieve heaven must be determined; this constitutes the remoteness.

And where the relationship between the substance and the deity is the object of the injunction (*niyoga*), since that [relationship] cannot be accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is untenable for it to be the object while not being an instrument; therefore, it must be stated as follows: the object of the injunction is the relationship between the substance and the deity, which is to be accomplished by means of the sacrifice that has become the instrument. And in the absence of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*), because the sacrifice that has become the instrument is absent, the relationship between the substance and the deity to be accomplished by it is also absent, resulting in the dissolution of the object.

Consequently, there is remoteness [of the object], because one must first infer a sacrifice through the relationship between the substance and the deity, then postulate that sacrifice’s status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*), and finally characterize the relationship between the substance and deity—which is to be accomplished by that sacrifice—as being the "object" (*viṣayatva*). Furthermore, in cases such as the Viśvajit sacrifice, where the person enjoined (*niyojya*) is one who desires a fruit [but no specific fruit is mentioned in the text], [the remoteness is even greater].

It is heard that there too, having postulated an agent (niyojya), having imagined the sacrifice’s status as an instrument (karaṇatva) in relation to it, and having determined the status of the object (viṣayatva) for such [an action], there is likewise remoteness [from the primary meaning]. Furthermore, regarding the postulation of the agent there, the cause is certainly not the mandate (niyoga), because that is not yet established. For that which is unestablished cannot serve as a basis for postulation. And here, the mandate is unestablished because the object has not been determined; for the cognition of an action without an object is impossible.

For sacrifice, having become an instrument (*karaṇībhūta*), is the object of the mandate (*niyoga*). And as long as the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*)—one who desires the fruit—is not yet conceptualized, the establishment of the sacrifice as an instrument cannot occur. Furthermore, the establishment of that [sacrifice] depends on the establishment of the person to be enjoined, and the establishment of the sacrifice as an instrument depends upon that; thus, a circular argument (*cakraka*) without foundation would result. Therefore, in that case, one first perceives the *apūrva* (transcendental result) as having as its object merely the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), and only thereafter does the conceptualization of the status of being the person to be enjoined and so forth occur. Consequently, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of performing the ritual according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*), which involves the non-elimination of the scope for the omission of auxiliary parts (*aṅgalopa*) and other such factors.

Furthermore, even though means such as Soma and others are heard within their own respective sentences, those who—without accepting them as objects in the form of what is to be accomplished (sādhya)—desire them to be objects in the form of means by the force of hearing a result, have displayed an extreme attachment to their own philosophical system. For what indeed is the distinction of the word for "result" (phala-pada) from other words? If it is argued that it is its dependence on [the action] for its establishment, we say no.

Because of contradiction. It might be argued as follows: "By the force of the connection between the person enjoined who desires the fruit and the sacrifice, since it is impossible for the sacrifice itself to be the means to that [fruit], an *apūrva* distinct from it must be established; and since that [sacrifice] is established as being conducive to it, the object [of the injunction] must necessarily be the means to that [fruit]. Thus, there is a distinction of the word denoting the fruit (*phalapada*) from other words. This is not so, because of contradiction.

Since it is not logically possible for a sacrifice that is momentary to be the means of accomplishing a result, one who desires the result does not understand [the injunction] as having that [sacrifice] as its object of action; rather, he understands the *apūrva* (unseen potency) which is the sacrifice serving as the means to the result. How could intelligent people assert such a mutually contradictory statement?

However, a certain person, considering himself clever and instructing [others] in the Prabhākara view, discharges this Brahma-missile: "The object of the verbal root-meaning—which serves as the instrument for the result—is not the objective domain [of the injunction]; rather, it is the 'thing-to-be-done' (kārya) of one who desires the result that must be understood as being inseparable from its causal totality (sāmagrī). And since this causal totality consists of the instrument and the procedure (itikartavyatā), the destruction of the procedure results in the dissolution of the objective domain."

Nor is it the case that the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not the object [of the injunction], for even when delimited by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there remains an expectancy due to the lack of full knowledge regarding its specific nature. Therefore, the mandate (*niyoga*) understood from its own word is subsequently delimited by the sacrifice; it is not the case that the sacrifice alone, conjoined with the fruit, serves as the delimiter. Otherwise, the very staff of Brahmā would swallow him, for even that [mandate] would lose its foundation because the fruit is too remote.

Indeed, it is not the case that the causal complex (sāmagrī), whose inseparable connection with the result is understood through other words, first connects itself with the result while remaining in its own place; likewise, the unseen potency (apūrva) also does not do so, as the remoteness from the result is equal for both. Enough of this. Now, another objection is raised against the well-established path: if the sacrifice, having become an instrument, were the object [of the mandate], then, since the mandate is defined by its object and cannot be defined independently of that object, the sacrifice’s status as a means to the result would have to be determined even prior to the comprehension of the mandate.

Once [the sacrifice] has been determined, one who desires the fruit is indeed capable of understanding the sacrifice as something to be performed (*kārya*) as the means to that [fruit]; thus, since the relationship with the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) is not untenable, there is no basis for postulating that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. denote an "effect" (*kārya*) distinct from the action. Consequently, your entire doctrine—the very essence of your philosophical treasury—concerning the denotation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), has become nothing more than a discarded topic of conversation.

Or, let the denotation [of the optative suffix] be established; however, its status as the primary element is not possible, because its object is the sentence-meaning which has become subordinate, just like the injunctions for the origin of the subsidiaries and the principal acts. For he who, even though the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are known to denote the primary action in the sentences containing the qualification (*adhikāra*), abandons their primacy in the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—since their objects are there applied to specific functions—and instead resorts to a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote a subordinate action, he...

How could one assume the expression of the primary action (*pradhānakārya*) in the injunctive statements (*adhikāravākya*), even though their capacity to express such a primary action is unknown elsewhere and they are instead employed for other objects? For by doing so, the primacy of the *apūrva* would be lost. Furthermore, it is indeed logical that the sacrifice, although not being the instrument (*karaṇa*), can be the object (*viṣaya*). Since the mandate (*niyoga*) is the means to the fruit, why should it not be logical that the sacrifice is its object by its very nature?

If it were argued: "It is true that the *apūrva* is the means for accomplishing the fruit; however, it is not within the scope of recollection in its own form. Rather, by that [recollection] which has the meaning of an existent (*bhāva*) as its object, the end is to be accomplished; and by that very activity (*kṛti*) which has that [existent] as its object, the fruit is also accomplished through the mediation of the *apūrva*."

Since a single *bhāvārtha* (verbal root-meaning) accomplishes both the *apūrva* and the fruit by means of that very same [activity] which has them as its object, it follows that the *bhāvārtha*—which has the *apūrva* as its object—is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the fruit; thus, there arises the contingency that the object itself possesses the status of an instrument. Furthermore, it is only by presupposing the *apūrva* as the instrument that the capacity of the sacrifice to be a means toward a fruit occurring at a later time can be conceived.

Granted that [the means] might not be possible when no door has been found; but why should it not be possible once a door has been found? What is this "door" found here? Is it some unprecedented (*apūrva*) distinct principle (*tattvāntara*)? If it were a distinct principle, then since the status of the sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) would be established by that alone, it would follow that the *apūrva* would be discarded like water poured from a vessel. Furthermore, the status of being a means to the fruit through the medium of the *apūrva* can only be determined once the nature of the means to the *apūrva* itself has been determined.

For that [instrument] is called its "door" (means) when, having been set in motion toward its own fruit, it is established as an intermediate means for the sake of accomplishing that [fruit]. This being the case, if one were to assert that what has become the instrument possesses the status of being the object (*viṣayatva*) of the mandate (*niyoga*), then there would result a logical circle: the status of being the object of the mandate would depend upon the status of being the instrument of the fruit; the status of being the instrument toward the mandate would depend upon that [status of being the object]; and the status of being the instrument of the fruit would depend upon that [status of being the instrument toward the mandate]. Furthermore, one who asserts that the object is destroyed when an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is omitted must be asked: does this destruction refer to that which is qualified by the auxiliaries, or to that which is merely characterized (*upalakṣita*) by them?

What follows from this? If [the injunction] were for the sacrifice as qualified by its subsidiaries, then it would follow that all the *prayāja* offerings and the *āgneya* sacrifices and so forth possess equal primacy, just as in the case of a qualification (*guṇa-adhikāra*). For just as when a *homa* qualified by curd is the means to the unseen potency (*apūrva*) for one desiring sensory power, there is equal primacy between the curd and the *homa*, and not a relationship of subordinate and principal—so too would it be here. On the other hand, if [the injunction applies to] the essential form of the sacrifice characterized by its subsidiaries, then since that form does not disappear even when the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is absent, there is no disappearance of the subject matter (*viṣaya-vilaya*) even when a subsidiary is omitted.

Furthermore, in this way, there would be neither the application of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *apūrva* nor the apprehension of the *apūrva* by them. For a mandate (*niyoga*) that is restricted by an injunction possessing a qualification (*sādhikāra-vidhi*), having grasped its own object as its purpose because it has no other objective to refer to, enjoins [the means] specifically as its own instruments—transcending their mere essential form—only with respect to those very things like rice-grains (*vrīhi*) which have been grasped as its own mediating means (*dvāra*). This is due to the connection with the subsidiaries.

If the *niyoga* (the mandate) were not apprehended prior to the absence of the object [of action], then all this would become like a toy for a child whose father has not yet been born. Alternatively, another explanation of the phrase "the fruit or the instrument would be the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*s) by virtue of their being non-motivators" is as follows: If the *bhāvārtha* (the verbal sense), which consists in the means to the fruit, were connected with the *niyoga*, then—by the principle that "that which is expressed as the purpose is the object"—the *apūrva* (transcendental result) resulting from the sacrifice together with its subsidiaries would, like the potsherd in the case of the scattering of husks, follow as being non-motivating.

Now, it is indeed accepted that in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the status of being "to be enjoined" (*vidheya*) is what motivates performance; for this very reason, the *śyena* sacrifice is considered non-beneficial (*anartha*) because it is not itself to be enjoined. Even if it were inferred [as a means] for the sake of establishing its own injunction, it still lacks the status of being "to be enjoined. That which prompts the performance of its own injunction for the sake of its own establishment is what is "to be enjoined," and not merely that which is a means to an injunction. In the case of optional rites, however, since the action is performed solely for the sake of the result, it also effects the injunction [of itself]; thus, it is not "to be enjoined."

Now, is it intended that the injunction is non-efficient (*aprayojaka*) with respect to the subsidiaries? For, if the injunction is accepted as having for its object the means to the fruit together with its subsidiaries, then—since such [an injunction] is itself prompted by the fruit—the injunction would also be the prompter of the subsidiaries, as they depend upon it. Regarding this, someone out of sheer audacity says: "Let there be no status of being enjoined (*vidheyatva*) for the subsidiaries; yet, this much does not entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others being prohibited."

Since both types of negation are impossible, for an action performed with a view toward some result is negated in two ways: either as extending up to the result, or as terminating merely in the means. For example, the tasting of wine for the sake of pleasure is prohibited precisely when it has arisen; [the prohibition is not that] "pleasure is not to be obtained by this," but rather "this pleasure to be achieved is not a proper act."

In some cases, mere instrumentality is negated; for example, one who is afflicted by disease and, seeking its alleviation, proceeds to act with the notion that something which does not actually help is the remedy, is dissuaded: "Do not do this; this is not the means for its alleviation. In that regard, a prohibition directed at the Agniṣomīya sacrifice—which culminates in a fruit—is not possible. For if it were stated that heaven—known by all people as an effect consisting of unsurpassed bliss—is not an effect, it would result in a contradiction with other means of valid cognition.

Nor is there a negation of its being a means [to an end], because that would contradict the scriptural statement. Therefore, it cannot be something to be prohibited. This argument is utterly trivial and does not even warrant a refutation. For instance, although the pleasure produced by drinking wine is known through other means of knowledge to be an effect (something to be done), it is declared by the word [of scripture] to be "not to be done" (akārya); likewise, the pleasure of heaven is also [declared to be such]. Indeed, other means of knowledge are explained as being incapable of immediate apprehension [in this context]. Therefore, even regarding the auxiliary parts (aṅgas) [of the sacrifice], the status of being "non-efficient" (aprayojakatva) is certainly undesirable.

And that [defect] would apply if the subject matter were qualified by the auxiliary (aṅga). He says: "True, if the subject matter were qualified by the auxiliary, there would be equal primacy and lack of causal efficiency. But it is not that which is qualified by it which is the subject matter; rather, that which has become the instrument (karaṇa) is the subject matter. And its existence as such would be lost upon the omission of an auxiliary; thus, when an auxiliary is omitted, it is said that 'the subject matter is dissolved,' but not because the auxiliary itself becomes the subject matter. Therefore, there is no fault."

This is not logical: if the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) does not exist when there is a deficiency of parts (*aṅga*), then even in the case of an obligatory rite (*nitya*), that which lacks parts would not possess the status of an instrument, and thus it would never be performed. If, however, in that case [the obligatory rite], the status of being an instrument belongs only to that which is endowed with as many parts as are obtained through the injunction (*vidhi*), then the same applies elsewhere as well: the status of being an instrument belongs only to that which is endowed with whatever number of parts are obtained through the injunction, because the inclusion of parts is restricted precisely to those parts grasped by the injunction. Thus, the status of being an instrument belongs only to that which is endowed with as many parts as are obtained through the injunction.

There is no disappearance of the subject matter when there is a deficiency of auxiliary parts (aṅga). Furthermore, since it is accepted that in the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice there is a combined qualification (*saṃvalitādhikāra*), only that which has become the instrument (*karaṇībhūta*) constitutes the subject matter; thus, performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*) would not be possible. Consequently, since it would be possible to state that the postponement (*utkarṣa*) is solely for the sake of completing the auxiliaries, the first section (*adhikaraṇa*)—which aims at breaking the inherent nature of the occasion (*nimitta*) due to conflict with the primary rite (*śeṣin*)—would be rendered purposeless. [Objection: But surely, in that case, the omission of auxiliaries must occur by the force of the hearing of the occasion (*nimitta*).

Even when the occasion (*nimitta*) has been heard, only that which is occasioned (*naimittika*) must be performed, and nothing else; furthermore, since an occasioned duty is a task whose object is the ritual action (*bhāvārtha*) that has become the instrument (*karaṇa*), how could there be the performance of something that is not such? Enough with this discussion regarding the object being the instrument.
For who, being wise, would himself take away all the wealth that is the essence of the treasury of every established doctrine and keep it as a conch-treasure in his own house? (8)

Therefore, in all cases—both the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*)—there must be a complete performance of all the constituent parts (*aṅga*). To this, it is replied: "The obligatory rite is performed according to one's capacity because of the scriptural mention of a specific occasion (*nimitta*); whereas the optional rite, in the absence of such [a restriction], is endowed with all its constituent parts. (9)

For here, in the injunction "one performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," life is understood to be the occasion (*nimitta*) for the oblation due to its connection with the word "as long as" (*yāvat*). And the nature of an occasion is such that, when it exists, the occasional rite (*naimitika*) must necessarily be performed. What does this "must necessarily be performed" mean? It means that [the rite] necessarily unites the performer with the intended fruit. That this very thing constitutes its status as a duty (*kāryatva*) has been demonstrated in the *Vidhiviveka*.

For this very reason, the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) is established as the purpose intended by all. For if the definition of the result were otherwise, then the scriptural teaching that all [obligatory acts] are means to a result would be contradicted. Now, one might ask: why is heaven not postulated as the intended result for all? It is because heaven is not sought by those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*); however, even they certainly desire the avoidance of transgression.

[Objection: How then could that [sacrifice] have heaven as its fruit, given that it is common to all [persons]? [Reply: But in that case, for the Viśvajit sacrifice as well, the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*) alone would be the fruit. Furthermore, if the rites for the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*) were mandatory (*nitya*), then rites such as the *viyūna* and others, which also aim at the destruction of sin, would likewise be mandatory; and consequently, they would have to be performed according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*). [Reply: It is said: First of all, it does not follow that the avoidance of transgression is the fruit of the Viśvajit, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

For demerit (*pratyavāya*) cannot be the result in its own nature, because it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Nor can it be the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [demerit], because that is already established by itself. Nor can it be the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of that [demerit], because suffering that has arisen perishes by itself. Therefore, the result must be conceived as the destruction of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause of demerit. Consequently, having determined the cause of demerit as delimited by demerit, its absence is the result.

The term *kalpayitavyam* (to be postulated) implies heaviness (*gaurava*). However, since happiness itself is what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is easily postulated; thus there is lightness (*lāghava*). Therefore, when a form of happiness is to be postulated as the goal, a distinction is stated: because heaven (*svarga*), consisting of an unrestricted form of happiness, is common to all people, it is superior to specific forms of happiness such as those derived from cattle, sons, and so forth.

Even those who, fearing the necessity of postulating a distinct injunction (*prayukti*), maintain that the qualification for [rites] like the *Kāmyeṣṭi* is not "desiring life" (*jīvan*) but rather "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), must also—setting aside the desire for the cessation of sin (*pratyavāya-nivṛtti*)—rely on this very same principle when postulating the qualification of "desiring heaven. For even in their own view, there exist certain prohibited acts that cause sin, as established by the conclusion of the *Śaṃyu-adhikaraṇa*. This is stated while provisionally accepting [their position]; however, there is no additional burden in taking "living" (*jīvana*) as the qualification for the entitlement (*adhikāra*).

Now, [the opponent might argue: "In the section concerning the *nimitta* (occasioning cause), the causative force of the injunction (*vidhi*) must be postulated; therefore, here too, the causative force of the injunction must be postulated by them. To this we reply: there is no difference, for here too they must postulate that the injunction is a means to a result (*phala-sādhanatva*). On the contrary, it is the causative force itself that is inherent to the injunction, while its lack of causative force is merely an exception (*apavāda*).

Furthermore, since the agency [of the performer] is understood through its inseparable connection with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and since that [agency] would be untenable for one who is not alive, his being alive is established; thus, only its status as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*) need be postulated. In contrast, in other cases, the very nature of the desire for the fruit, which is not understood from any other source, must be postulated. This constitutes a great difference. Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus, it has been stated that in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, heaven is the fruit, whereas in rites such as the *yāvajjīva* (lifelong) observances, the destruction of sin is the fruit because of their obligatory nature.

As for the claim that even the *viyūha* and other [meditations] are necessary because they have that [cessation of evil] as their fruit—that is not so. For it is said that the fruit of the necessary [meditations] is the destruction of evil, not that their necessity follows from having that as their fruit. What, then, is the distinction between these two?

This is the distinction: that which necessarily accomplishes its fruit is both *nitya* (obligatory) and *naimittika* (occasional); however, [rites] such as the *viyūna* do not necessarily accomplish their fruit, because there is no scriptural mention (*śabda*) of a specific occasion (*nimitta*). Let it be granted that the fruit is desired for all [such rites]; nevertheless, the necessity of accomplishing the fruit is the cause for the restriction of the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), and thus there is no contingency of performing them according to one’s capacity alone—this great lake of Nyāya is profound. He asks: "But how can there be a restriction of auxiliaries due to necessity?"

It is said: it is necessarily understood that when this [cause] exists, it produces this result. If it were not to produce it when there is a deficiency of its constituent parts (*aṅga*), its status as an indispensable means would be contradicted. [Objection: One must say that what is performed by an authorized person (*adhikārin*) necessarily produces the result; otherwise, even what is performed by a *śūdra* or others would produce it, as would performance at an improper time. Furthermore, since an authorized person is one capable of performing all the constituent parts, what is performed by someone of a different sort would not be a means to the result. [Reply: To this it is said: capability (*śakti*) is certainly not heard in scripture as a qualification of the authorized person.

That [capacity] is inferred because the instruction for performance would otherwise be inexplicable, given that such an instruction is impossible for one who lacks the capacity. In this regard, whatever is to be performed by the injunction of application (prayogavidhi), whether through direct Vedic statement (śruti) or implied meaning (artha), that capacity constitutes a qualification of the eligible person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa). And since that [capacity] brings about the performance of subsidiaries (aṅga) that do not conflict with the occasioning cause (nimitta) of its own sentence, it causes as many subsidiaries to be performed at any given time as can be performed then.

Nor does such a discrepancy arise from the inclusion or exclusion of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), because both are established through a single uniform mode of expression: "one should act according to one's capacity. And this is said regarding those auxiliary elements that are to be performed by virtue of the injunction of application (*prayoga-vidhi*); for that which is stated as "one should do" is appropriately qualified by "according to one's capacity."

However, those things which are established by their own nature or established by other injunctions and are relied upon—such as the acquisition of wealth and so forth in the world, and time, knowledge, and fire in the Veda—serve as qualifications for the eligible person (*adhikārin*) by their very essence, as in the case of "one who is connected with the new moon day, possesses wealth, possesses knowledge, and possesses fire. This is what is meant.

For indeed, an auxiliary (aṅga) is either adopted due to its connection with the injunction or abandoned in accordance with the occasion (nimitta); or, for the sake of favoring both, it is adopted for one who is capable and abandoned for one who is incapable—there is no other way. In that regard, favoring both is certainly superior if it is possible. And possibility exists in the case of those auxiliaries that are to be adopted, such as "one should prepare the rice-grains according to one's capacity" or "one should thresh them according to one's capacity. However, the essential nature of the Āhavanīya fire and so forth is not adopted by this injunction.

Although the fire is prescribed with respect to the *homa*, its specific form is not prescribed therein; for if it were enjoined that "one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should offer in the *āhavanīya* fire, while another may offer anywhere," then a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) would result. Nor is it possible to enjoin the offering as common to both by saying "having prepared the *āhavanīya* according to the rule, one should offer," because the preparation of the *āhavanīya* and other fires is itself enjoined here—both by implication and like the preparation of rice and other materials. Therefore, the mere performance of the *homa* would be required, regardless of the *āhavanīya*.

Alternatively, the oblation is performed in the *āhavanīya* fire with reference to one who possesses that fire; for if disregard were shown there, it would result in the total subversion of the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya*. Since the word "as long as life" (*yāvajjīva*) is fulfilled even by one's own lifetime, there is no absolute contradiction; thus, it is understood as: "One who possesses the fire, while living, should offer the oblation. By this, the [injunctions] concerning time, knowledge, and so forth, are explained.

Now, why is it that life is not likewise subsumed under other auxiliary factors (*aṅga*)? For even if subsumption were made on the basis of capacity—since one who possesses that capacity is "living"—there would be no absolute contradiction among them. In that case, some [element] would be set aside merely by way of conforming to the auxiliary factor (*aṅga*).

In considering whether the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are to be employed according to the specific occasion (*nimitta*), one finds that the auxiliaries are connected in such a way as not to conflict with the primary rite (*pradhāna*). However, in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*), since there is no conflict whatsoever with the statement regarding the occasion, the required auxiliaries are all to be included; thus, the performance must consist of the entire set of auxiliaries. In the case of an obligatory rite (*nitya*), however, by the aforementioned principle, while the selection of a Brahmin, fire, time, and ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) is abandoned, the other auxiliaries are to be included according to one's capacity. Thus, the distinction between the optional and the obligatory rites is established.

He said: This would be so if, immediately after the sign (*nimitta*), the signified (*naimittika*) were necessarily to arise; but that is not the case. For the word "sign" is a synonym for "cause," and causes do not necessarily possess their effects, since we observe a delay in the effect even when the cause is present, due to dependence upon auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). Thus it is said: the term "cause" applies to many entities of various kinds by making the production of an effect its basis, and it cannot transcend that [meaning].

Indeed, they do not call a man who has discarded his garland "garlanded. However, even when the lump of clay has not yet been fashioned [into a jar], the designation "cause of the jar" is applied; this is because it exists as a cause by way of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, life and so forth possess their causal status in the primary sense (*mukhya*) alone, and since such a cause is invariably concomitant with the effect, the necessity of the occasional rite (*naimitika*) is established. Therefore, the contraction of the limbs is indeed logical. For one for whom the occasional rite is fruitless, how could such a performance be accomplished? How much less so, then, according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*)? (10)

Why would there not be an expectation of a fruit for the task (*kārya*), since it is itself of the nature of a task? Even in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, heaven is not postulated due to an expectation of a fruit; rather, because a task is dependent upon an act of performance (*kṛti*), and because such performance depends—through the mediation of agency and entitlement—upon a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and because that [person] is not established as unqualified, there arises an expectation for its qualification. It is heaven that is postulated as that qualification, not as the fruit. And such [heaven], by the logic of the *Tādarthya-adhikaraṇa*, possesses the status of being the fruit.

It will be accomplished. However, in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), since the specific qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is already obtained through the occasion itself (*nimitta*), there is no establishment of a fruit by way of being a qualification for that [person]. Nor is it established as a fruit, because it is not required as such. For if the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) were the meaning of the sentence, there would be a requirement for an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*).

However, for one who holds the view that a ritual act (*naimittika-karma*) is fruitless because there is no requirement for a result—since the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is subordinate to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and possesses the nature of what is to be produced (*bhāvya*), constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)—in his opinion, even the performance of such a fruitless act cannot be established, let alone its performance according to one's capacity. If it is argued that engagement [in action] proceeds from the comprehension of what is to be done (*kārya*) and does not depend on a result, we say no; for without possessing a result, the very status of being "what is to be done" is impossible. For "what is to be done" is defined as that which has volitional effort (*kṛti*) as its primary element.

Furthermore, nothing other than pleasure and pain, or the means to avoid them, can be the primary object of purposeful action (*kṛti*). Now, one might object: "This inference cannot arise because it contradicts scripture; for scripture declares that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is the object to be accomplished (*kārya*). How, then, can it be refuted by inference?"

It is true that a scripture already in operation does indeed obstruct that [inference]; however, its very operation depends upon the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the word-meanings. Furthermore, that which is not pleasure, nor a means to it—such as the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*)—lacks the fitness to be the primary object with respect to volitional effort (*kṛti*). If one should think: "Since a single suffix expresses both the volitional effort and the action as its primary object, fitness is therefore not a cause in that case; whereas in instances where two words are first remembered as unrelated and subsequently expressed as related, there fitness is the cause"—that is not so, because it contradicts the theory of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*).

It is impossible to maintain that the two meanings—both of which are unfit for syntactic connection—are denotable as being connected by this very word; for such a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) itself would be inconceivable. Therefore, semantic inappropriateness (*ayogyatā*) prevents the syntactic connection between the meanings of two different words, but it also [prevents] the linguistic convention between the meanings of a single word. If it is argued that "there is no inappropriateness at the time of establishing the linguistic convention," we say no, because that consequence would apply to the other case as well. This might be so:

For in the section concerning desire (*kāma-adhikāra*), it is established that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is the denotable object; and since it is conducive to the fruit, the *apūrva* indeed possesses the fitness for being the primary object of the volitional effort (*kṛti*). That is not so; for if this were the case, a fruit would necessarily follow even in the case of a rite performed on a specific occasion (*naimittika*). For when, in the section concerning desire, the possession of a fruit is accepted as the means of fulfilling the status of being a task (*kāryatva*), then [that same logic] applies to the occasional rite as well.

By accepting that [the rite] is a task (*kārya*), one must also accept, as in the case of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), that it possesses fruitfulness (*phalavattva*) which brings about its fulfillment. In the absence of that [fruitfulness], just as there would be an absence of the status of being a person to be enjoined, the very nature of the task would dissolve; thus, neither performance nor performance according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*) is established. Let this matter rest for now. But surely: "The connection between a cause (*nimitta*) and a fruit (*phala*) is possible within a single sentence;
however, if there were a connection with two objects to be aimed at (*uddeśya*), the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would follow. (Verse 11)

For since it is impossible for two intended objects—the cause (*nimitta*) and the result (*phala*)—to be connected within a single sentence, and because a sentence is completed with respect to each intended object individually, it would be difficult to maintain that the result belongs to the sentence concerning the cause. To this it is replied:
"A syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) results from the connection of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) with both [the cause and the result].
There is no connection of the thing to be enjoined with the cause as an intended object (*uddeśya*). (12)

For when that which is to be enjoined (the *vidheya*) is connected with two objects of reference (*uddeśya*), a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs; but this is not the case here, because the action to be enjoined is connected with the result on one hand, and its necessity (*kartavyatā*) with the occasion (*nimitta*) on the other. And even so, there is no syntactical split, because [the two parts] remain mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣatvāt*).

For when it is stated, "When this exists, one should do that," there arises the expectation, "For what purpose? In that case, the result, being connected as "for this purpose," does not split the sentence; for it is two objects of the same class (*uddeśya*) that split a sentence, not those of different classes. For example, in the case of the two conditions, "he whose father and grandfather do not drink Soma," and the two results, "one who desires offspring" and "one who desires cattle"—therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

As for the fact that the venerable Maṇḍanācārya rejected the status of the cause (*nimitta*) as the objective (*uddeśyatva*) in order to avoid a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), that was intended with reference to its being the objective of that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), since the *Vārttika* repeatedly states that the cause possesses the status of the objective; enough of this excessive detail. Therefore, the distinction between the optional (*kāmya*) and the obligatory (*nitya*) rites is established. Thus, Pārthasārathi, relying on the opinion of the Teacher (*Ācārya*), has correctly demonstrated the distinction between the optional and the obligatory based on a small portion of reasoning. (13)
Thus ends the "Discrimination between the Obligatory and the Optional" in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* composed by the venerable Pārthasārathi Miśra, son of Yajñātma Sūri.
The nature, relationship, and means of proof of the auxiliary sciences (aṅga), along with their methods, which were stated correctly in the Vārttika, are here set forth in brief. (1)

We shall investigate, according to the Vārttika, all of this: the nature of the subsidiary (aṅga), its various types, its relationship with the primary (pradhāna), how that relationship exists, and what the evidence for it is, as well as how that evidence functions. In this regard, subsidiaries are declared to be of three kinds, based on whether their purpose is visible (dṛṣṭa), invisible (adṛṣṭa), or both;
among these, those with a visible purpose are of four types: genus (jāti), substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (kriyā). [Verse 2]
Action for the sake of the unseen is considered to be of two kinds, as is action for both purposes;
even in all actions for the sake of the seen, a restrictive unseen result (niyamādṛṣṭa) is admitted. (3)

The group of factors (*aṅga*) is threefold: those whose purpose is visible (*dṛṣṭārtha*), those whose purpose is invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and those whose purpose is both. Even among those with a visible purpose, they consist of genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*). Among these, genus and quality—as in "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) and "one purchases [the Soma] with a red [cow]" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*)—are enjoined as means for accomplishing an action; they attain the status of being subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) to that action through a visible assistance, namely by delimiting the substance that serves as its instrument. If it is asked, "But how can there be a means for accomplishing an action through the delimitation of a substance? it is replied:

Since it is the qualified [entity] that serves as the means for accomplishing the action, and since the cognition of that [qualified entity] is dependent upon its qualifiers, and since that which is not cognized cannot function as a means, genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*)—which serve as the means for the cognition of that [entity]—attain the status of being means for the action by way of that [entity]. However, the status of the quality as a means is considered to be figurative (*kalpyate*). Thus, while genus and quality have an indirect purpose, substance has a direct one. Furthermore, even actions such as threshing (*avaghāta*) have an indirect purpose, which they call "directly contributing" (*sannipatyopakāraka*).

However, the character of having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) belongs only to action (*kriyā*). That [action] is twofold: of the nature of a directly contributing auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka*), such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth; and of the nature of a remotely contributing auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. And those actions which are directly contributing auxiliaries and have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) assist the primary rite (*pradhāna*) accomplished by them by effecting the production, the acquisition, or the modification of their own factors (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. For example: kneading effects the production of the dough-ball; milking effects its acquisition; threshing effects the modification of the rice grains.

However, an *sannipāti* (concomitant) *saṃskāra* (refinement), while producing an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) for its own agent, becomes an auxiliary to the primary act. Thus, due to the different types of things to be accomplished—such as origination (*utpatti*) and so forth—the *sannipāti* is of four kinds. And that [refinement] performs origination and so forth, as appropriate, upon one of the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) and the rest.

For example: threshing [is related] to the object (*karman*); a vow to the agent (*kartṛ*); the sprinkling of the remains of the *prayāja* offering to the instrument (*karaṇa*); the sacrifice of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) to the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); "he plucks grass from the fire" (*agner tṛṇāny apacinoti*) to the point of departure (*apādāna*); and the bringing of curds to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, that which assists indirectly (*ārādupakāraka*) does not function through the medium of a *kāraka*, but rather through the medium of the *apūrva*; it assists the principal [action] by means of that [apūrva]. Furthermore, some action has both a visible and an invisible purpose, and it partakes of the designation expressed by the term for its substratum; as, for instance, the sacrifice of the animal-cake.

For that [act of offering] serves both purposes: by its aspect of renunciation (*tyāga*), it effects the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), and by its aspect of dedication (*uddeśa*), it effects the seen, namely the recollection of the deity. If it is argued that there should be only one purpose because the injunction (*codanā*) is a single unit—since the injunction is fulfilled by a single act, it is not logical for there to be two purposes—[we reply: No. Since the requirement for a purpose arises first from the fact that the act is directly perceived (*dṛṣṭatva*), the recollection of the deity is accepted first. Once that is accepted, a further requirement arises for one who does not see the utility of the aspect of renunciation in that [recollection]; and that requirement is satisfied only by the postulation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

Therefore, such a case serves both purposes. However, as for one who argues that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings serve both purposes—since the sacrifice itself lacks a directly perceived benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*), and since the two subsidiary pouring-mantras (*āsecanamantra*) cannot be applied to the sacrifice when it has not yet entered into its own domain of eligibility, and because that entry is impossible without an unseen merit (*apūrva*), they thus have an unseen purpose; yet, through their subsidiaries, they have a perceived purpose—one must say that for him, the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśayāga*) already possesses a perceived benefit prior to its connection with the subsidiaries.

If it were performed [merely for its visible purpose], it would not serve both purposes. Therefore, by the very reasoning already stated, it serves both purposes. And by this same reasoning, in all cases where there is a visible purpose, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) must be inferred. If, however, the visible purpose of threshing were merely the removal of the husk, then since that could be accomplished by other means as well, threshing would not necessarily be performed; in that case, the injunction for it would be contradicted.

Therefore, it is postulated that through threshing, rice grains permeated by the unseen (adṛṣṭa) are produced. Furthermore, although the unseen is produced by an action, when there is a requirement for the purpose of the restrictive rule (niyama), it is postulated as the fruit of that rule and is thus called the "unseen result of the restriction" (niyamādṛṣṭa). What, then, is this status of being an auxiliary (aṅgatva), and what is the authority (pramāṇa) for it?
This is stated: That by which the agent’s desired end is accomplished is called an auxiliary;
and the authority for this is the injunction (vidhi), conjoined with direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth. (Verse 4)

Being a means to what is desired (*samīhitasādhanatva*) is, first of all, the state of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*). That by which a person’s desire is accomplished—namely, that which becomes the object of the person’s activity prompted by that desire—is called an auxiliary to that desired end. And this alone is "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*). As it has been said: "For its being for the sake of another is distinguished by way of the aim (*uddeśa*). "Aim," "desire," "intention," and "will" are synonyms. Therefore, that which is a means to what is desired is denoted by the word "auxiliary" (*aṅga*), which is synonymous with "subordinate" (*śeṣa*), "quality" (*guṇa*), and so forth. And in this regard, the injunction (*vidhi*) is the authority (*pramāṇa*).

For that [injunction] consists in the instigation of volition, and it cannot instigate one toward anything other than the means for achieving a desired end; therefore, the injunction itself—lest its own nature be sublated—is the authority for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) by postulating the status of being a means to a desired end for its own object. But when the injunction is understood precisely as the state of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhanatva*), then subsidiarity is directly expressed by the word [of the injunction]; in every case, the word of the injunction alone makes known subsidiarity, whether through direct denotation (*śruti*) or through implication (*artha*).

How then [is it so]? The means of application (*viniyoga*) are *śruti* and the rest; application itself is simply "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*). If that [application] were derived solely from the injunction (*vidhi*), then it would not be logical for *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth to be the causes of that [application]. Therefore, it was said: "joined with *śruti*, *liṅga*, and the rest. For an injunction, while making known the general fact that the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is a means to the good (*śreyas*), requires something else to provide its specific details. It does not [provide them itself].

For indeed, without the scriptural mention of *vrīhi* and so forth, the purpose of the *vrīhi* and other grains for the mental realization (*bhāvanā*) of threshing and such acts would not be established; nor would the mantra for cutting the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) have its purpose in cutting without the indicative power (*liṅga*); nor would the sacrifice have its purpose directed toward heaven and so forth without the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "one desiring heaven"; nor would the *prayāja* offerings and others have their purpose in the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) without the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, for the sake of understanding the specific intended [object], there is first a dependence upon direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the meanings of verbal roots and nominal stems; indeed, it is their status as being enjoined that depends on *śruti* and the other means of proof. For an injunction (*vidhi*) makes known the subsidiary character (*aṅgatva*) of that which is enjoined, and not of anything else. Moreover, it does not directly enjoin anything apart from the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); rather, by taking that very [operation] as its qualified object, it enjoins its qualifiers as well by implication.

Even in a case where [an injunction] is already established in a general sense, an injunction perceived as having a specific object becomes restricted to that specific qualification by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not. And this status of being a qualification depends upon direct assertion (*śruti*) and so forth; for, by means of direct assertion characterized by expression within the same verbal suffix (*samānapratyaya-abhidhāna*), the number of the agent and other such factors become qualifications of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). By means of word-level direct assertion (*pada-śruti*), the meaning of the verbal root becomes a qualification; and for items expressed by other words, such as the animal (*paśu*) and so forth, as well as its number and gender, this status should be inferred from the direct assertion of the case-ending (*vibhakti-śruti*) and other such means.

Thus, by indicating the specific nature of the principal (śeṣin) and the specific nature of the subordinate (śeṣa), it makes known the status of being an auxiliary; the means of application (viniyoga)—such as direct assertion (śruti) and the rest—perform assistance to the injunction and are therefore called the causes of application. This is faultless. Among these, the direct assertion (śruti) is divided into three types: that which expresses the injunction (vidhi-vākya), that which effects the application (viniyoga-kṛt), and that which applies (viniyojikā).
The latter is further divided into three kinds based on the distinctions of identical words and so forth. ||5||

Among these, the enjoining [word] consists of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth; the denoting [word] is the direct mention (*śruti*) of "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth; and the applicatory [word] (*viniyojikā*) is threefold: single mention, a single word, and inflection (*vibhakti*). For that word from whose mere hearing a relationship is understood is the applicatory direct mention (*viniyoga-śruti*).

Thus, where there is a simultaneous denotation of multiple meanings by a single word—just as case endings denote gender, number, and grammatical relation simultaneously—there the denotation is of those meanings only as they are already mutually connected (*anvita*). This is because it is impossible for a single word to denote multiple unrelated meanings simultaneously without the operation of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from among identical forms), as is the case with the word *akṣa* denoting gambling pieces and so forth.

Otherwise, as in the case of the command "bring a cow," one who is instructed to "bring some individual [cow] that is capable" might bring any one of them, such as a plaything or the like, and would not hesitate; yet he does hesitate, wondering, "To what end was I employed? Therefore, there is the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*). Even in that case, by the force of cognition, the *kāraka* (case-role) is primary, while gender and number are secondary. Thus it has been said: "When the object (*karman*) and so forth are the meanings of the inflection, then singularity and so forth are qualifiers."

By this, those who maintain that number expressed by the case-ending becomes a qualifier of the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) through its implication by the injunction (*vidhi*) are refuted. Even if [the case-ending] were to express [the *kāraka*] and the [number] unconnectedly, the number would first connect with the *kāraka* itself—which is conveyed by the single word, which is primary, and which stands nearest—rather than with the nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*), which is remote and subordinate. The claim that "it is expressed as connected only with the nominal stem-meaning and not with the *kāraka*" belongs to those whose grasp of reality has been obscured by the darkness of their own sectarian tenets.

Mere faith is not authoritative, because there is no distinction in the cognition [of the object]. Just as when it is said "by means of a beast" (*paśunā*), a beast is understood to be the instrument (*karaṇa*), so too is "one instrument" (*ekam karaṇam*) indeed understood. Nor is it observed that a single denotative term, while connected with one meaning, does not denote another meaning; for it is accepted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the gerundive suffix (*kṛtya*) denote the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as delimited by the action. And how is the injunction implied? If you say "because it is for its sake," we say no.

Because it is impossible for the singular number—which functions as a qualifier with respect to either the nominal stem-meaning or the grammatical relation (kāraka)—to serve the purpose of an injunction while disregarding those [meanings]. Or, if such a possibility were admitted, then words like *kṣepiṣṭha* ("the swiftest") would also have to serve the purpose of an injunction; and to justify that, one would have to imagine them as qualifiers of Vāyu in his capacity as a deity. Consequently, Vāyu qualified by the attribute of being "swiftest" would be the deity, rather than the essential nature of Vāyu itself. Enough of this unworldly dispute.

Thus, in this way, number and the other [factors] are connected with the case-role (kāraka) by means of direct denotation (śruti), characterized by the employment of the single word "one" (eka). However, the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is connected by means of the word-hearing (pada-śruti). For the relationship between the meanings of the base and the suffix is understood from their mere hearing; it does not depend upon a reflection on the meanings as two separate words do. Therefore, even the word is subsumed under the category of direct denotation (śruti). Consequently, among the genus (jāti), gender (liṅga), and number (saṃkhyā), which are each connected to a single case-role, there is a mutual restriction according to the principle of the "tawny cow one-year-old" (aruṇaikahāyanī-nyāya).

The case-ending (*vibhakti*), as it were, indicates either the state of being an end (*sādhyatva*) or the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*), and thus serves as the cause for application (*viniyoga*). In this regard, the accusative case indicates the state of being an end, while the instrumental and other cases indicate the state of being a means. Therein, in the statement "one threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*), the accusative case, denoting the rice-grains as the ends to be accomplished, becomes the cause for the application of the act of threshing to them. How then is there no application of the oblation (*homa*) to the flour-particles (*saktu*)? Because they are not what is intended to be achieved. The rice-grains themselves are not directly intended by their own word;
rather, the rice-grains are intended as the means for accomplishing the *apūrva* (the unseen spiritual potency). (Verse 6)

For although the groats (*saktu*) are presented by the accusative case as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), they are discarded because they lack the quality of being desired (*samīhitatva*). Indeed, the accusative does not convey the state of being desired; rather, it expresses only the state of being something to be accomplished. Consequently, since the status of the groats as the primary object (*śeṣitva*) is impossible, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of the oblation (*homa*) turns back and requires another thing to be accomplished. However, in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), there is no such cause for turning back. To explain:

The efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of threshing, seeking its intended object (*bhāvya*), sets out to accept the rice grains (*vrīhi*) as its own object because they are presented by the accusative case as that which is to be accomplished; however, it hesitates because the rice grains themselves are not inherently desired for their own sake. In this regard, if their desirability could not be established in any way—as in the case of parched grain flour (*saktu*)—then the efficient force would turn back and seek another object to be accomplished. But it is possible for the rice grains to be desired insofar as they take the form of specific means for the production of the transcendental result (*apūrva*) under discussion. For instance, [the injunction] "one should sacrifice with rice grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).

Rice grains (*vrīhayaḥ*) are prescribed as the means for accomplishing the sacrifice; however, their direct status as the means of the sacrifice is not logical, because that position is precluded by the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is enjoined by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). Therefore, their status as a means is through being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sacrificial cake; thus, they are intended [as the object] in that very form, and in that same way they become the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*). And the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) is used for the purpose of indicating that [material cause]. In this manner, threshing (*avaghāta*) is established as being directly taught (*aupadeśika*) even in the case of barley (*yava*), since that specific form [of being the material cause of the cake] is no different in them either.

Thus, by means of the scriptural text (śruti) together with the context (prakaraṇa), there is the application (viniyoga) of threshing, because the indication of the means for the transcendental result (apūrva-sādhana-lakṣaṇā) is dependent upon that [context]. For it is thus that it attains syntactical unity (ekavākyatva) with the sentence regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices: "One threshes the rice-grains belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices. And those grains, being connected to that [sacrifice], being inseparable from their purpose, bring forth their own objective to be accomplished.

When that [purpose] has arisen, in order to accomplish the status of threshing as being for that purpose without abandoning its status as being for the sake of the rice (*vrīhi*), the word "rice" comes to have the meaning of a *lakṣaṇā* (indication) referring to the means of accomplishing that [purpose]. [Objection: But if this were the case, since the statement "he cuts the sacrificial grass" (*barhirlunāti*) would also form a single syntactical unit with the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the cutting would be enjoined for the sacrificial grass as a means of accomplishing those [sacrifices]; thus, the status of being for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary would not be established. [Reply: You have not correctly understood our position, O long-lived one.
For the rice, the sacrificial grass, and so forth, are not qualified by the New and Full Moon sacrifices as being for their sake.

Regarding the phrase "rice grains for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," this does not mean only those directly related to it; rather, even the subsidiaries (aṅgas) possess that relationship simply by virtue of being connected to it, because they too are contributive. And whatever purpose is served by those related elements—whether it be the primary apūrva or another apūrva—that which is enjoined there, such as the cutting and so forth, becomes an auxiliary (aṅga) to all of that when the rice, sacrificial grass (barhis), and other materials are indicated by their respective words as being the means to accomplish that purpose.

For this very reason, even though the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is qualified by the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice through its location, the girdle (*raśanā*) and its properties, which are enjoined for that post, belong not only to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the primary *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and its subsidiaries, but also to the subsidiary *savanīya* sacrifice accomplished by that same post. Consequently, the girdle and its properties are directly taught (*aupadeśika*) for its second encircling as well. If these properties were to apply to the subsidiaries of subsidiaries as well, then the rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and their properties would have to apply to the subsidiaries of the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice by direct injunction alone. This is not so.

Because of the absence of that [injunction]. For rice grains are not enjoined for the Vaimṛdha sacrifice; rather, when they are obtained there by means of the *codaka* (extended application), they are obtained simultaneously with the threshing itself. Thus, because they would be stated twice, an injunction is impossible. For this very reason, in the case of the *savanīya*, the specific instruction regarding the ropes and other items occurs only at the second encircling (*parivyāṇa*), and not elsewhere, due to the fault of being stated twice. Therefore, it is established that the application of threshing and other such acts is determined by direct statement (*śruti*) supported by context (*prakaraṇa*).

Therefore, in this case, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is assumed that the very word as heard has the purpose of indicating a specific meaning. However, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, it is the very form of the word itself that is assumed to be the factor effecting the application (*viniyojaka*). This much is the distinction; yet, dependence upon context remains the same in both instances.

However, in the case of an implement such as the *sruva* ladle, whose connection with the sacrifice is invariable, when it is enjoined as belonging to that [sacrifice]—such as its being made of *khadira* wood—even though the previously unestablished *apūrva* does not yet revolve in the mind during the inquiry into its purpose, that *apūrva* nevertheless comes to the heart by means of that very same invariable indicative mark (*liṅga*). Thus, even without the context (*prakaraṇa*), the application is established through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of its being a means to that [sacrifice].

Where duality does not exist, the characteristic of being a means (*sādhanalakṣaṇa*) is not possible; thus, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), when taken together with the context (*prakaraṇa*), is the cause for the application (*viniyoga*) of threshing. It might be argued: "The accusative case merely expresses that the rice grains (*vrīhi*) are the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); however, that they are to be accomplished by threshing arises solely from the sentence (*vākya*), which consists in the co-occurrence of those words. Therefore, how can the subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) of threshing to the rice grains be established by *śruti*? This is true, as you have said; nevertheless, the application is indeed by *śruti* alone. For application is, in fact, a relationship.

And that [relationship] consists of the nature of the means and the end between the desired and the undesired. In that regard, the accusative case, by establishing the status of the desired rice as the *sādhya* (the goal to be accomplished), implies the subordinate status (*śeṣatva*) of its counter-correlative; it then requires a sentence—consisting of the non-occurrence of other words—to obtain merely its specific qualification. Likewise, the instrumental case and others, having established the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*), imply the predominant status (*śeṣitva*) of their counter-correlative and require a sentence for the sake of its specific qualification. Therefore, in both cases, it is said that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) alone is the cause of application (*viniyoga*).

Furthermore, where the relationship of principal and subordinate (*śeṣi-śeṣa*) or the relationship of goal and means (*sādhya-sādhana*) is not explicitly stated, but must be inferred by considering the mere fitness for the status of principal and subordinate based on the juxtaposition (*samabhivyāhāra*) of two words—as in the case of "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*)—there the application (*viniyoga*) occurs through the sentence alone. For in that case, neither the status of being the goal nor the status of being the means is attributed to either the one desiring heaven or the sacrifice by any [other] word; rather, when the connection must be inferred from the juxtaposition of the two words, the primacy of the desirer and the subordinate status of the sacrifice are determined according to the principle: "But that which is not a means [is subordinate], because it exists for the sake of that [goal]. Thus he says:
How could one who already exists as a desirer of heaven be something yet to be brought into being?
For it is the agent of becoming who is yet to be brought into being, not the act of becoming itself within those things already existing.

For the agent of "coming into being"—which is another name for "arising"—is something yet to be accomplished (*bhāvya*); however, one who desires heaven has already arisen and cannot arise again, and thus would not be something yet to be accomplished. To this, it is replied: [The text continues: "But that [heaven] is indeed something yet to be accomplished. This is what is stated.

Even for the cooked rice, its status as the end to be attained (bhāvya) by one desiring heaven would be established through its own essential nature, just as it is for the sacrifice, the rice-grains, and so forth, when qualified by other factors such as dharma. ||8||

First, it is understood from the scriptural statement that for one desiring heaven (*svarga-kāma*), the efficient-force of sacrifice (*yāga-bhāvanā*) is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*). This status of being subordinate occurs in two ways: either if it accomplishes the desired end in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), or if it accomplishes some particular attribute (*dharma-bheda*) residing therein. In both cases, that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is the principal (*śeṣin*), as in the case of the *kratu* (sacrifice) with respect to the efficient-force of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. For the essential form of the sacrifice is not produced by the *prayāja* offerings; rather, it is their assistance (*upakāra*) alone that is accomplished. And yet, the *prayāja* offerings and so forth exist solely for the sake of the sacrifice.

We shall explain how they are connected. For instance, even though rice grains are already accomplished, they become the "bhāvya" (the object to be brought about) of the act of threshing; for there is no rule that only that which is to be produced in its own essential form can be a "bhāvya. This is because the status of being a "bhāvya" is possible even through a form endowed with other attributes.

In that regard, although it has been determined that subservience consists merely in being something to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), when there arises an expectation for a specific detail—namely, "by performing what kind of assistance does this [subordinate] become a subsidiary to this [principal]?"—the specific detail is postulated through functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). Among these possibilities, it is not possible for an existing person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) to be the object to be brought into being (*bhāvya*) by way of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The state of being an object to be brought about (*bhāvyatva*) exists only in the form of being distinguished by the result. For this very reason, the most eminent Mīmāṃsakas consider the term *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven) to be directed toward the result. Just as in the case of the statement, "One who has a staff recites the *praiṣa* formulas," when that which is qualified by the staff is enjoined as a subsidiary to the recitation, since the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is already established, the statement is possible as one intended to establish that the qualifying staff (*viśeṣaṇa*) is a subsidiary to the recitation.

Likewise, by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), once it is established through the very nature of the injunction that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the sacrifice has the human being as its purpose, it is understood by implication that the person's status as the "principal" (*śeṣin*) is not in their own essential form, but rather [as the recipient of a result]. Since no specific result is yet known, when the status of the "one desiring heaven" as the principal is stated, it refers specifically to the qualification called "heaven. Thus, the sacrifice is subordinate to the person by way of being a means to heaven. As they say: "Because a goal to be realized (*bhāvya*) is required, words expressing desire (*kāma-śabda*) are directed toward that; the predominance of the qualification is demonstrated in cases such as 'the man with a staff' (*daṇḍī*)."

This very point has been stated quite clearly by the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* in the first chapter [of the *Śābarabhāṣya*].
