Having raised the objection that there is no word denoting a result here, starting with the words "But surely heaven is not heard here," and having replied with the words "By this word *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven)," he then—anticipating the objection "But surely this refers to a particular person"—himself refutes the view that it refers to a person and the view that it refers to time. Furthermore, on the occasion of demonstrating the intention to express the number of the agent conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) as being merely a "condition" (*nimitta*), he makes this clear in the sixth book.

If it is argued that the author of the Sūtras himself stated that "one who desires a fruit is the *nimitta* (condition)," [we reply] that this was refuted by the statement "because [the rite] is obligatory (*nityatvāt*). Having thus concluded, on the basis of elimination, that this is indeed a connection with a fruit, [the author] asks: "But how can this [word] denote a fruit? He then presents two possible syntactical interpretations (*vacanavyakti*), showing that—just as in the case of "one who is dirty should bathe"—the person is construed as the subordinate element (*śeṣin*), such that "the sacrifice is taught for one who desires heaven. In that regard, it is precisely the intention to convey a specific benefit known as heaven [that is expressed].

It is stated at the end that [the result] will be accomplished. Even without that statement, the fact that it pertains to a person in general is understood from the verb itself; therefore, the purpose of the statement is to convey that "heaven arises from this sacrifice. Thus, wherever there is an absence of a case-ending that expresses the relationship between the means and the end, there the application is determined by the sentence.

However, where there is a case-ending expressing the state of being an object (*sādhyatva*) with respect to the principal (*śeṣin*), such as "the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn*), and a case-ending expressing the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) with respect to the subordinate (*śeṣa*), such as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajet*), there is application by direct statement (*śruti-viniyoga*). Even where, in either case, there is a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) expressing mere relationship—such as "for one desiring sensory power, [curd]" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*) with respect to the principal, or "of the sacrificer, the office" (*yajamānasya yājyā*) with respect to the subordinate—even there, that very genitive comes to denote a specific type of relationship through the consideration of suitability; thus, it is application by direct statement.

Even in cases where the dative case occurs with respect to the subordinate element (śeṣin), as in "the staff for Maitrāvaruṇa" (maitrāvaruṇāya daṇḍam), there too the very fact that the recipient—who is intended by means of the object—is to be accomplished is clearly heard in the scripture. However, when the dative is used in the sense of "being for the sake of that" (tādarthya), the application through direct scriptural statement (śruti) is even more evident, as in: "If one should be a drinker of Soma, for him one should offer this Śyāmāka pap to Soma-Indra; [and] the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are for all desires."

However, where there is a reversal of the case-endings (*śrutiviparyaya*), as for example in "on the previous day, on the new moon, [one prepares] the altar" (*pūrvedyur amāvāsyāyāṃ vedim*), where the locative case is used for the *śeṣin* (the principal), and in "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), where the accusative case is used for the *śeṣa* (the subordinate), there the status of being the end to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) must be conveyed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by that which expresses the means (*sādhana*), and the status of being the means (*sādhanatva*) must be conveyed by that which expresses the end. And since indication is everywhere caused by the sentence (*vākya*), this is called "application by sentence" (*vākyaviniyoga*). Thus, the application by direct statement (*śrutiviniyoga*) has been explained in detail.

He asks: "But how is it that a threefold application (*viniyoga*) of the scriptural statement (*śruti*) has been mentioned, when [the text] actually shows only a twofold application—namely, that of the word (*pada*) and that of the case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*)? There is no fault here, for the mention of the "word" (*padagrahaṇa*) is intended to include the "scriptural statement of identical expression" (*tulyābhidhāna-śruti*) as well. And thus: Because it is grasped by the factor of action (*kāraka*), the oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth have their purpose in the action;
since they are understood through the scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the factor of action, they override their status as qualifiers of the substance (*dravya*). (Verse 9)
Just as the oneness of the animal is understood through the direct statement of the word (*pada-śruti*),
so too [the mantra] is understood to be a subordinate element of the ritual action (*kriyā-aṅga*) by the more powerful direct statement of the common suffix (*samāna-pratyaya-śruti*). ||10||
In that regard, he demonstrates the scriptural mention of a common designation. Therefore, it is well said that there are three kinds of applicators.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Determination of the Auxiliary (Aṅga-nirṇaya), in the Nyāyaratnamālā.
The capacity inherent in all entities is designated as the "indicative mark" (liṅga).
But it was stated previously that a sentence is merely a collection of words.
The expectancy for the manner of performance is *prakriyā*, and it is of two kinds;
likewise, *krama* (order) is of two kinds, distinguished as textual proximity (*pāṭhasādeśya*) and performative proximity (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*). ||2||

Those learned in the Bhāṣya know that there are four types of designation— namely, the derivative, the conventional, the worldly, and the Vedic— and that these alone constitute the means of application.

In this regard, the application (*viniyoga*) of the *barhis* mantra to the specific act of cutting the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—which is a means for the unestablished result (*apūrva*)—is determined by its indicative power (*liṅga*) which depends upon the context (*prakaraṇa*). The applicatory power of indicative force (*liṅga*) operates only toward those subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) that have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), not toward those with an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Furthermore, even here, direct statement (*śruti*) requires the context (*prakaraṇa*) in order to establish the status of being an auxiliary to a specific means. Moreover, there is this further distinction: in this case, before the mantra is applied through indicative power, its connection to the sacrifice must already be required by some other means of knowledge.

In the absence of that [direct statement], the application by means of indicative power (*liṅga*) is not possible at all; this has been established in the section beginning with "from indicative power, order, and name" (*liṅgakramasamākhyānāt*). As for application by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), however, it was explained in detail on the occasion of the discussion of application by direct statement (*śruti*), for the sake of distinguishing it [from the latter]. Even among mantras, those words such as *savitṛ* which denote meanings not inherent [to the ritual act] have their application to acts such as the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) solely through syntactical connection. Application by means of context (*prakaraṇa*), on the other hand, pertains to the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and so forth. But what is context? It is the expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*).

Whose expectation for the "how-to" (itikartavyatā) is it? It belongs to the *bhāvanā* (productive activity). Because of its connection with the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) at the commencement of the action, it requires an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the sake of achieving that [object]. In this regard, by virtue of proximity, the meaning of the verbal root is connected [to the *bhāvanā*], such that "one should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice. From that, there arises the expectation for the "how" (*itikartavyatā*), namely, "How [is it to be done]? Therefore, the collection of subsidiary acts (*itikartavyatājāta*) which is connected to the *bhāvanā* for the sake of accomplishing the object to be brought about is said to be "prompted by the object" (*bhāvyaprayukta*). But not...

That which is to be brought into being (*bhāvya*) is capable of being connected with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). For it is not the case that the unprecedented (*apūrva*) is [the object] of "how [is it to be brought about]? rather, it is the case that [the injunction] is "one should bring into being" and "how [should it be brought about]? [Objection: But surely the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) has stated in various places that the fruit is the object to be brought into being—for instance, in the passages "one should bring heaven into being" and "the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is said to belong to the fruit"—and thus the entire collection of procedures, being prompted by the object to be brought into being, would be prompted by the fruit, not prompted by the *apūrva*. [Reply: It is said in response:

It is true that the result (*phala*) alone is primarily connected as that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*). However, because it occurs at a later time, it cannot be produced directly by a sacrifice (*yāga*) which perishes in a moment; therefore, it is established that this occurs through the medium of the *apūrva*. Thus, the meaning is: "Having produced the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice, one should bring about heaven. Nor does this much diminish the status of the sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇa*), for the author of the Bhāṣya himself stated in the first section of the seventh book (*saptamādhyāya*) that this is logically consistent, just as in the expression "the grains become cooked" (*tuṣapakvā bhavanti*).

And thus, since it is determined that when the *apūrva* is produced, the fruit is accomplished from that very [act], the necessity of the fruit’s production transfers to the *apūrva*. Consequently, it requires the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), [asking]: "How is this *apūrva* to be brought about by means of this sacrifice? In this regard, the *prayāja* offerings and other such elements are connected as the manner of performance (*itthambhāva*). Therefore, although they are prompted by the [ultimate] result, they find their final application in the intermediate result—the *apūrva* of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—just as the restriction of speech does. This we shall explain more clearly below.

Therefore, the *prayāja* offerings and others are connected through the production of a new transcendental result (*apūrvabhāvanā*). For the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja* requires something to be produced (*bhāvya*), and the *bhāvanā* of the fruit requires the manner of performance (*itthambhāva*); thus, by virtue of mutual expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, they form a single syntactical unit. The *bhāvanā* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, when endowed with the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja*, accomplishes the *apūrva*. Consequently, since the status of being a means belongs to that which is qualified [by subsidiaries], and this is possible only when the qualification produces an assistance, it is postulated that the qualification—the *prayāja*—functions as an auxiliary.

And even in that case, since its assistance can only occur by way of assisting the instrument (*karaṇa*), the assistance to the instrument is postulated later for the sake of fulfilling the purpose (*tādarthya*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which are understood to be auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). As it has been said: "The three parts, though taken up by a single productive activity, experience a state of mutual assistance and assisted-ness only afterwards."

In this way, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of both is indeed brought to rest. Now, it might be argued: "Since the *bhāvanā* of the *prayāja* requires an end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), and the *bhāvanā* of the fruit requires assistance for its instrument (*karaṇa*), the *prayāja-bhāvanā* must first connect with the assistance of the instrument due to the force of expectancy, rather than with the sacrifice itself by way of being for its sake (*tādarthya*). Therefore, *prakaraṇa* (context) is the authority for the relationship of assisted and assistant, but not for the state of being for the sake of that [sacrifice]. This is the talk of a fool; for expectancy itself is not an authority.

Verbal testimony (*śabda*), however, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only so far as there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This word is not independent; rather, it reaches its completion only in conjunction with another. In that case, if another [word] capable [of fulfilling the expectancy] is present nearby, then it enters into a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) with that very one. If, however, nothing is present nearby, then it completes itself by supplying (*adhyāhṛtya*) a suitable [word] and unifying with it. Thus, in this instance, although the injunction "he sacrifices the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) is expectant, no benefit to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*) is present nearby, because the word for it (*tat-śabda*) is not heard.

In that case, if the expectancy for syntactic unity with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—having been heard directly from scripture—were to be fulfilled [by something else], then there would be syntactic unity through a supplied benefit. However, according to the path already described, the fulfillment of the expectancy for syntactic unity with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* occurs for both [the *prayāja* and the main sacrifice]. Even though a benefit is required first, it has not been provided by anything whatsoever by which it might connect through syntactic unity with the *prayāja* injunction.

Thus, when the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the sentences concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *prayāja* offerings has been established through the relationship of subordinate and principal, the accomplishment of the required assistance follows thereafter. And it is said: "While the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices require assistance and the *prayāja* offerings and so forth require that which is to be assisted, the subservience (*tādarthyam*) [of the latter] to the former is understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) even while the assistance is still in an unaccomplished state. Since this would otherwise be impossible, the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇopakāra*) is postulated."

Therefore, in this case, it is merely the expectation of assistance (*upakārāpekṣāmātra*) that functions as the means of valid cognition for establishing that something exists for the sake of another (*tādarthya*); it is not the case that being a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*) or existing for the sake of another arises solely from the fact of providing assistance. For this very reason, those who know the *Tantra* say: "In the archetype (*prakṛti*), assistance is preceded by the ritual items (*padārtha*). Once the ritual items have been applied and the assistance has been postulated, the modification (*vikṛti*)—by virtue of its own requirement—first takes assistance itself as the applicatory factor (*viniyojaka*). And that [assistance] is of two kinds: the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) and the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

In this context, the *prakaraṇa* (context) of the *bhāvanā* of the fruit is the *mahāprakaraṇa* (great context). And that serves as the means of application (*viniyojaka*) for acts such as the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) in relation to the *prayāja* (fore-sacrifices) and so forth. For even the *bhāvanās* of the subsidiaries possess an expectancy regarding the "how" (*kathaṃbhāva-ākāṅkṣā*) for the sake of accomplishing the intermediate *apūrva*. Otherwise, the restriction of speech (*vāṅniyama*) would not be employed for the sake of the *apūrva* of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice. However, some say: "The so-called intermediate *prakaraṇa* cannot exist as a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*), because there is no corresponding object of proof (*prameya*)."

For cultivation (*bhāvanā*), having already established its relationship with that which is to be cultivated (*bhāvya*), requires the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*). In that regard, as long as the cultivation of a single subsidiary (*aṅga-bhāvanā*) remains dependent on a purpose, it becomes a subsidiary to the cultivation of the fruit (*phala-bhāvanā*) through the context (*prakaraṇa*); meanwhile, the other [subsidiary] is also connected by the primary cultivation itself. Thus, for all those things connected to the primary cultivation, a mutual relationship of principal and subsidiary (*anyonya-aṅgāṅgi-bhāva*) is impossible; therefore, there is no possibility of subsidiaries being applied by means of an intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*). However, since the "stepping forward" (*abhikramaṇa*) is enjoined among the *prayāja* offerings and so forth by direct syntactical statement (*vākya*) alone, it is their subsidiary not by virtue of an intermediate context. This is indeed stated in the *Vārttika*.
When the subsidiary nature of those [elements] situated in another context is known through the three means— direct statement and so forth—
it is further accepted by that very same indicative mark (liṅga).

This has not been heard before: for wherever something is enjoined by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth through the mere mention of a subsidiary (*aṅga*), there the requirement of "how-to-be" (*kathaṃbhāva*) regarding that subsidiary must necessarily be raised. And if, even further on, something is enjoined by the mention of that very subsidiary, then that requirement certainly persists.

Between those two connected members, whichever member is prescribed as unconnected does not possess an inherent expectancy for the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*), because it lacks the need for performance until its own expectancies have been fulfilled; therefore, that [expectancy] must necessarily be admitted as arising from another cause. Otherwise, the extension of application (*atideśa*) would be impossible in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such rites.

When, after enjoining some subsidiary (aṅga) by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth with reference to the *prayāja* offerings and others, and having in the middle enjoined something unconnected, one again enjoins a subsidiary at the end with reference to the *prayāja* offerings and others, then that unconnected subsidiary situated in the middle becomes a subsidiary of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth due to the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

For one who does not accept this, since the *upavīta* would be established as a subsidiary of the primary sacrifice through the stronger context (*prakaraṇa*) despite the proximity (*sannidhāna*)—because there is no interruption of the *sāmidhenī* verses by the *nivid* formulas—the demonstration of the interruption of the *sāmidhenīs* by the *nivid* formulas would be purposeless.

Now, it might be argued that because the single word *upavyayate* is heard, when there is a requirement for another element to achieve the expression of a connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*), the connected expression occurs with the *sāmidhenī* verses present nearby; however, in the absence of such proximity, since there is no other recourse, the connection is established with the primary action under discussion. This is incorrect.

Since that [relationship] is established between the meanings of the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) alone, for it is by means of the suffix that the primary apūrva is restated and the wearing of the sacred thread (upavyāna) is enjoined as its subordinate member; and since that [wearing] is a refinement of the agent, it enters into the sphere of the primary apūrva—just like the threshing of grain and so forth—and thus there is no need to look for another meaning in order to establish the denotation of the related meaning, as there are words of praise such as "nivīta is for men" and others by which the wearing of the sacred thread is expressed as already connected.

Therefore, there indeed arises for the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) themselves an expectancy regarding their specific mode of performance (*katham*); thus says the venerable author of the Commentary: "For there occurs a statement expressing an expectancy for a specific detail, such as 'one should recite the *sāmidhenī* verses—how so? And what is this principle that, even though they possess the nature of a task (*kārya*), those which are independent and do not produce a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) have no natural expectancy for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*), whereas those which are connected to a primary injunction (*sādhikāra*) do? For being a task (*kāryatva*) is the cause for that expectancy; [the distinction] is merely whether it is connected to a primary injunction (*sādhikāra*) or independent (*niradhikāra*).

Therefore, there is indeed a mere distinction; even a constituent part requires another constituent part. If this is so, how then is there no extension (*atideśa*) of the Soma-sacrifice rules to the *prayāja* offerings and others which are enjoined as unmanifest (*avyakta*), or how is there an extension of the *iṣṭi*-sacrifice rules to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites? Listen to this: for while there is no inherent requirement for things that lack a basis, a requirement arising from another cause cannot be denied.

In that regard, since the *prayāja* and other such elements are observed in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) is postulated; and when that exists, the establishment of extended application (*atideśa*) follows. However, in the case of the *prayāja*s and so forth, there is nothing that causes such a requirement to arise, and thus there is no extended application. To this, it is replied: Here, one must consider this alternative: is that very requirement for the procedure postulated by the same *prayāja* and other elements that cause the requirement to be conceived, or rather, is the requirement for the procedure postulated generally from the mere observation of those elements themselves?

If, first of all, the former alternative is accepted, then, since the animal dedicated for initiation (*daikṣapaśu*) lacks an inherent expectancy because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the very expectancy for the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) must be postulated upon seeing the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; thus, the investigation into the specific archetype (*prakṛti*) is not possible until its status as a modification (*vikṛti*) has been established.

When only the mere nature of the *kratū* is considered, there is no inquiry regarding the specific archetype due to the absence of expectancy. However, when its status as a modification is postulated by seeing the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no occasion for such an inquiry because the specific archetype has already been determined.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that in the section *na ca paśau ca liṅgadarśanāt*, by refuting the novelty (*apūrvatva*) of the animal sacrifice, its status as being "like the previous" (*pūrvavat*) is established through the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*), and that the inquiry here is merely whether some ritual properties (*dharma*) are extended from elsewhere or not. This is because the eighth book (*adhyāya*) deals with the topic of specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*). Moreover, that [general] discussion has not yet concluded, such that an inquiry into whether it is "like the previous" or "novel"—as in the case of the *darvihoma*—could be undertaken; therefore, only the specific extension is being considered.

And thus the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates precisely the deliberation regarding the extension of specific details: "In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*), or is it that of the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*)? Even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), having raised the objection as to how an indicative mark (*liṅga*) can be the means of bringing [the details] forward, he says, "Because of the similarity of the injunction" (*codanāsāmānyāt*). And this [reasoning] is possible only once the status of being a modification (*vikṛtitva*) has been established by way of general similarity, and not otherwise.

Now, if it is argued that, in order to avoid this fault, a mere expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is first postulated through the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), and subsequently an extension (*atideśa*) follows from the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānya*), then the same objection applies: since the expectancy would be postulated by the force of the teaching of the indicative mark called "stepping forward" (*abhikramaṇa*) in the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there would follow the application of the Soma-related ritual procedure (*saumika-vidhyanta*) due to its unmanifested nature (*avyaktatva*). Thus, the challenge remains equal.

This point must be resolved by us as follows: it is not the case that the *prayāja* offerings and others are "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). For that [sacrifice] is called unmanifest whose deity is not established by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a dative case ending, or the wording of a mantra. Since the deities of the *prayāja* offerings and others are connected through the wording of their respective mantras and so forth, they are not unmanifest. However, if something were considered unmanifest simply because its deity is not mentioned in its originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), then it would follow that even the *upāṃśuyāja* would be unmanifest.

For, having deliberated that "it should be so for him as it is for the deity," [the author] will state that Viṣṇu is the deity because of the mention in the *mantra* text: "Or it may be Viṣṇu, because of the recitation in the *hautra*. [Objection: In that case, even for the Jyotiṣṭoma, since the deity is denoted by the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the injunction "one draws the cup for Indra-Vāyu" (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*), there would be no lack of explicitness (*avyaktatva*). [Reply: The deity is not enjoined by the secondary derivative suffix with respect to the sacrifice; rather, it is enjoined with respect to the drawing of the cup (*grahaṇa*). Therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, due to impossibility as well, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the Soma-related rules to the *prayāja* offerings and the like.

For in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices together with their subsidiaries, it is prescribed that they begin on the previous day and be completed on the following day; and even there, the common elements (*tantra*) such as the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) and the washing of the hands (*hastāvanejana*) must be performed only on the following day, beginning at that time and concluding then. In that context, if the procedure of the Soma sacrifice—beginning with the *dakṣiṇīyā* and ending with the *udavasānīyā*—were extended (*atideśa*) to each of the [Darśapūrṇamāsa] subsidiaries such as the *prayāja*s individually, then while that [Soma procedure] was being performed for each one, there would be a displacement of the time of the primary sacrifice.

Nor is it possible for there to be a single performance (sakṛdanuṣṭhāna) by way of a common ritual application (tantra) or a consequential extension (prasaṅga). This is because of the difference in time and because there is no injunction for them to occur within the same ritual framework. For the *prayāja* offerings are performed before the principal sacrifice, while the *anuyāja* offerings are performed after it; furthermore, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are separated from those even further by the *sūktavākya* and other elements. Such being the case, a common ritual application does not exist, as it does not in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites of the *iṣṭi* ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*). Nor can one perform some auxiliary parts while omitting others according to one's capacity...

One cannot state that "one should perform the *cit*," because there is no specific knowledge of what that distinction is. Therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Soma sacrifice to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; consequently, a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) certainly exists. How then is it not accepted that the acts such as gambling (*videvana*) are subsidiary to the *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice? Because the requirement of the *abhiṣecanīya* is already satisfied by the fulfillment of its expectancy through the very duties obtained from the *codaka* (the general injunction), even prior to those [acts].

For the author of the Bhāṣya will state in the section on the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice that modifications (vikṛtis), which require the assistance of prescribed elements, first connect with the proximate subsidiary (aṅga) belonging to the archetype (prakṛti), even bypassing those [archetypal subsidiaries] already present. Thus, even for a modification whose application has been determined, its non-termination must be assumed due to the influence of the proximate subsidiary; and from that, the sequence (krama) arises. Furthermore, among the modifications, that which is recited within the midst of the archetypal subsidiaries—such as the Āmana-homa—is grasped by means of context (prakaraṇa).

In that case, it would follow that even the *videvana* and other such acts, which are performed during the time of the *Māhendra-stotra* in the midst of the primary constituent parts (*prakṛtāṅga*), would be subordinate to the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*). This is not so; for their origin does not occur there. Rather, these acts have originated elsewhere, and having attained the status of being constituent parts of the *Rājasūya* through context, they are merely brought down (*apakarṣa*) to the time of the *stotra*, as prescribed. Therefore, they do not possess the status of being constituent parts of the *Abhiṣecanīya*.

However, in the case of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) of the Rājasūya, the group of sacrifices beginning with the *Pavitra* and ending with the *Kṣatrasya Dhṛti* is presented as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) residing in its own sentence through the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application). Thus, whatever is an archetypal subsidiary (*prākṛta-aṅga*) of the *Pavitra* and whatever is an archetypal subsidiary of the *Kṣatrasya Dhṛti*, all that constitutes the archetypal subsidiary of the Rājasūya; and those acts situated in the middle of these, such as the gambling (*videvana*), fall within the scope of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, even if one accepts the existence of an intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*), there is no fault whatsoever.

Context (*prakaraṇa*) is of two kinds. And that [context] is solely the applicator (*viniyojaka*) of those things that serve as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakārin*) for the sake of the ritual action (*bhāvanā*), but not of substances and the like, nor of direct auxiliaries (*sannipātin*). For those, application occurs through *śruti* and the other means respectively; context, however, is merely an auxiliary. Even in the case of mantras, there is no grasping by context in their own form; rather, it is the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning produced by them—which is of the nature of an action—that is grasped, and even that only in conjunction with indicative power (*liṅga*). This has been demonstrated in the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) by the passage beginning, "But the verbal cognition of the sentence-meaning is one whose purpose is yet unfulfilled," and so forth.
However, for those who maintain that the effect (*kārya*) is something unprecedented (*apūrva*) and falls within the scope of the verbal injunction (*vākya*),
the status of the *prayāja* and other such rites as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *darśa* sacrifice cannot be established.

According to those who maintain that the *apūrva*—which is the primary object to be accomplished (*kāryabhūta*), denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, and which subordinates all other word-meanings—is what is conveyed by the sentence, in their view, the *prayāja* and other such rites would not be subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *darśa* and other sacrifices. Why? Because a primary action does not require connection with another primary action, by means of which a connection between the subsidiary *apūrva* and the primary *apūrva* could occur. (Verse 5)

According to the principle that "an effect does not exist for the sake of another," the *apūrva* of the *prayāja* offerings, being itself the primary element, does not require any further purpose. And since it is independent, it cannot be connected even with the proximate *apūrva* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). As for what has been said by someone here—that the sentences concerning the *prayāja* and other such rites, being recited in proximity to the *apūrva* of the qualified [main sacrifice], do not immediately convey a separate *apūrva* because they can be understood as mere restatements (*anuvāda*), just like the acts of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth—[that is incorrect].

However, [the words] present the very nature of the sacrifice as qualified by its own constituent factors (*kāraka*). And since that [sacrifice] does not terminate in anything else and is itself not an end-in-itself, it is fit for connection with an injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) which consists of a purpose; thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurring within the sentence of qualification denotes the meaning of the root as connected with those [factors] as subordinate members. Their status as subsidiaries is mediated through the assistance rendered to the instrument (*karaṇa*), and that [assistance] is produced by all the subsidiaries acting in concert. Since it is not possible for those [subsidiaries], which perish in a moment, to exist in their own form [simultaneously], there must be *apūrvas* (transcendental potencies) in the form of intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

Because it must necessarily be resorted to as a name (*nāmadheya*). That verbal suffix (*liṅ*) which was previously suspected of having the sense of a restatement (*anuvāda*), now—by virtue of being grasped by that which apprehends a distinct *apūrva* (unseen potency)—has its primacy sublated through its relation to the sacrifice whose purpose is the primary *apūrva*. Thus, it denotes [the action] solely as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of the qualification (*adhikāra*), and not as something primary in itself, because that would contradict the application of the subject matter. Having this very *apūrva* in mind, the Commentator stated: "And what is not enjoined cannot be a subordinate member. The meaning is that since actions devoid of an injunction are fragile, their status as subordinate members is impossible.

Now, if this is the case, there is also a commentary stating that "the human effort [involved] is merely a restatement (anuvāda)," regarding the recitation of the *jañjabhyamāna* mantra during the occasional (*naimittika*) rite of spitting. For in that instance, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) occurs solely through the mediation of the causal factor (*kāraka*), even without a separate transcendental result (*apūrva*); thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is indeed a restatement. Consequently, it is established that the *prayāja* offerings and others possess the status of auxiliaries. This entire system is pleasing only to those who are full of faith;
it cannot be acceptable to those who rely upon valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). ||6||
And thus,
when it is determined that the scripturally enjoined action is primary and its non-sublation is certain,
there can be no connection with another sentence in cases of either sublation or doubt. (7)
Because there is doubt regarding the existence of two sacrificers in the archetype, let this *pratipad* verse, "mā yuvaṃ hi stha," apply to the archetype. (8)

In injunctions such as "He who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Agnihotra," these suffixes (liṅ etc. have their capacity to denote an independent task (kārya) already known; they are not able to denote a task subserving something else in sentences such as those concerning the *samits* (the fuel-sticks). If it is argued that they denote [the task] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we say no, for there is no evidence for such secondary indication. If it is argued that the fact of having a subject already enjoined elsewhere serves as evidence, we say no, because a false application of the injunction is simply impossible. Indeed, it is not possible for the "grasper" (the verb) to take up [the action] by subverting the primary task understood from its own word.

If it is argued that, due to the suspicion of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), a new, unprecedented entity (*apūrvāntara*) is not immediately cognized, then this very point must first be examined: is it the case that by this [word] the very same *adhikārāpūrva* under discussion is denoted as the effect, or is it something else? In that regard, if one can conceive of its entry into the scope of that [original *apūrva*] by way of the causal factors (*kāraka*), then, by the force of recognition, one accepts the application of the object [of the word] just as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*).

But if, despite diligent searching, one does not perceive a door for entry into that domain [of the primary injunction], then—due to the sublation by recognition—one determines that there is indeed another primary injunction (*niyoga*) having the *samid*-sacrifice as its object. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of sublating the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). For the apprehending agent (*grāhaka*) grasps [an injunction] only after avoiding the sublation of a direct statement; it does not do so even when there is a suspicion of contradiction through such sublation. And in this case, first of all, a contradiction with the apprehending agent is suspected on account of the direct statement.

If the possibility of entering into the object exists, there is no contradiction between the Vedic text (*śruti*) and the apprehending factor (*grāhaka*); but if such possibility does not exist, then the apprehending factor would contradict the Vedic text, because that would entail the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor, when such a contradiction is suspected, can the apprehending factor be permitted to grasp [the primary sense]; let us take as an example the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, where the introductory verse (*pratipad*) "For you two are... (*yuvaṃ hi sthaḥ*), which is connected with two sacrificers, is not to be grasped [in its primary sense]. For even in that case, first of all, a doubt certainly arises.

Is it that somehow two sacrificers are possible within the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, and therefore there is no conflict between the direct statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), or rather, because such a possibility does not exist, there is a conflict? This being the case, if—in the passage "He offers the *samidh* oblations"—because the conflict is uncertain due to the suspicion that the principal apūrva might be intended, the connection remains with the archetype; and if, that being so, it is said that the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix) resorts to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the force of that very [connection], then, because the conflict with the direct statement is uncertain due to the suspicion that two sacrificers might be possible...

If the *pratipad* [lunar day] were actually grasped, then by its very force, it would follow that the hearing of the word "two" (*dvitva*) functions as an indication (*lakṣaṇaka*) or is intended to refer to the wife (*patnī*). If you argue that a contradiction is certain there and not merely a suspicion, how so?

In that case, the commencement of this section [of the treatise] is justified. For once a matter has been determined by logic, further deliberation is no longer possible; even when doubt exists, the resolution of conflict occurs later, as in the case of the *samit* sacrifice following the *pratipad* sacrifice. If it be thought that there was no initial doubt regarding the *samit* and other offerings, but rather—due to proximity—the misconception arose that "this belongs to the original *apūrva* (unseen potency)," and consequently, because there was no conflict, they were accepted by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), [we reply: [This is not so. Even in the case of the *samit* and others, there is indeed an initial doubt. How? Because the word "then" (*tarhi*) is used, which implies a sequence of time. Furthermore, since the *apūrva* of the original sacrifice is already established, the question arises: "Is this [new offering] also for that same *apūrva*, or is it for another? Therefore, the doubt is certainly present at the outset. Consequently, the conflict is resolved later, and thus the commencement of this section is appropriate. As for the statement that "because of proximity, there is the misconception that this belongs to the original *apūrva*," this is incorrect. Why? Because proximity does not override the force of the direct injunction (*śruti*). If proximity were more powerful than the direct injunction, then in the case of the sentence "He offers the *āghāra* oblation with ghee" (*ghṛtena juhoty āghāram*), the *āghāra* would belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices due to proximity, and the mention of "ghee" would be redundant. But such is not the case. Therefore, proximity is not stronger than the direct injunction. Thus, the doubt remains: "Is this for the *apūrva* of the original sacrifice, or for another? Hence, the commencement of the section is valid. As for the claim that "there is no doubt regarding the *samit* and others," this is refuted by the very fact that the word "then" is employed. Furthermore, the doubt is not merely about whether it belongs to the original *apūrva* or another; rather, the doubt is whether it belongs to the *apūrva* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* or to the *apūrva* of the *agnihotra*. This is because the *agnihotra* is also mentioned in proximity. Therefore, the commencement of the section is correct. As for the argument that "the doubt is not about belonging to the original *apūrva* or another, but rather that due to proximity there is the misconception that it belongs to the original *apūrva*," and that "because there is no conflict, there is acceptance by the grasper"—this too is incorrect. Why? Because even if there were no conflict, the doubt would still persist. If there were no doubt, there would be no need for the subsequent discussion of conflict. Since the doubt exists, the discussion of conflict is necessary. Therefore, the commencement of the section is valid. Since the doubt exists, the discussion of conflict is required. Therefore, the commencement of the section is justified. Why? Because even if there were no conflict, the doubt would persist. If there were no doubt, there would be no reason for the subsequent discussion of conflict. Since the doubt exists, the discussion of conflict must take place. Therefore, the commencement of the section is appropriate. Nevertheless, that [initial understanding] is set aside by the subsequent perception of contradiction; just as when the inclusion of a word within the context has been determined by the logic of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), its subservience to that purpose is set aside upon the appearance of a contradiction with direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) according to the logic of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Furthermore, if another *niyoga* (injunction) were understood [from the subordinate acts] just as it is from threshing (*avaghāta*) and the like, then why would one not accept that the words *yajati* and so forth occurring in the sentences concerning the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries—just like the words *avahanti* and so forth occurring in their respective sentences—denote their own meanings as connected to the primary *apūrva*? For this is the reasoning there: if these [subordinate acts] were to denote their own meanings as connected to the primary *apūrva*, then, since they would be understood at the very moment of their origin as being directed toward something else [the primary], they could not have another *niyoga* as their object.

Because a connection with two distinct effects is untenable; for it is impossible to understand a single entity as being simultaneously connected to two separate effects. Furthermore, this can be asserted only when another injunction (*niyoga*) has been perceived, not when it has not been perceived. Therefore, if another injunction has not been apprehended, then—in the absence of any contradiction—the word *yajati* occurring in the *samit* passage would denote its own meaning as connected to the primary apūrva, just like the word *avahanti* and others.

Now, if it is first apprehended, then—given the contradiction with direct scriptural statement (śruti)—the apprehension by the "grasper" (grāhaka) is untenable; thus, this is like a rope with nooses at both ends. Alternatively, if another unprecedented result (apūrva) is not first apprehended, then even though the capacity of the [root] *yaj* itself to denote its own meaning as connected to the primary unprecedented result is understood, it is later sublated by the apprehension of a different injunction; consequently, the apprehension by the "grasper" is also sublated due to the contradiction with direct scriptural statement. Therefore, in no way whatsoever is the status of the *prayāja* offerings and the like as subsidiaries possible.

Furthermore, although it was stated—referring specifically to the prohibition against speaking untruth—that "even that which is not prescribed does not become a subsidiary (*aṅga*)," the assertion that this concerns a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding auxiliaries that provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) was made solely by considering the context of the recitation of the *jañjabhyamāna-mantra*, which pertains to direct application (*sannipāti*). Otherwise, how could the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) have stated, in the passage "In the case of its abandonment, [there are] the ritual acts," that the human effort is a restatement with reference specifically to that which provides remote assistance? Therefore, it cannot be explained in such a manner.

How, then, should this be explained? It should be explained thus: the statement of the injunction has the intention of enjoining the application (*viniyoga*), while the other has the intention of enjoining the performance (*prayoga*). For without an injunction, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) for the *samid* offerings and so forth would not be established, just as in the case of the *soma* and other elements. Just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma," although there is no separate injunction for the *soma* apart from the injunction for the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), its status is enjoined by the primary injunction itself since it is applied by the instrumental case ending.

If it is argued that, in the same way, once the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are applied to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no need for a separate injunction because the injunction of the qualified primary sacrifice itself establishes the injunction of its qualifiers—the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—then [the reply is: True, a qualified injunction does indeed imply its qualifiers; however, the status of being a qualifier does not exist without [an independent basis].

It is established through injunction (*vidhi*). If it is argued that it is established by context (*prakaraṇa*), we say no, because that very context itself is dependent upon injunction. For the meaning of context is the application of one thing that has a requirement to another thing that has a requirement; however, subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) devoid of an injunction have no need for a purpose (*prayojana*), since the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is satisfied by obtaining the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) presented within the same word as its object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*). An injunction-impelled activity, however, is not satisfied by that alone; therefore, it does have a need for a purpose.

And since that [connection] exists, the status of the *prayāja* and other rites as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is established through their application (*viniyoga*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, for the sake of establishing their subsidiary status, there must indeed be an injunction regarding the *samit* and other rites. Thus, since the performance of those rites—which have become subsidiaries—is accomplished by the very injunction of the qualified primary sacrifice, the injunction regarding the subsidiaries in that respect is called a restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, both [the injunction and the restatement] are logically consistent; everything is thus clarified. That very context (*prakaraṇa*) is the means of application for the *prayāja* and other rites.

Order (*krama*), however, is characterized by spatial proximity (*sāmānadeśya*); it is of two kinds: proximity of recitation (*pāṭhasādeśya*) and proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhānasādeśya*). First, regarding the former: where the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*) are recited in the same location, as in the case of the *dabdhi*-mantra and the *upāṃśuyāja*. Regarding the latter: where the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) have a common performance, as in the case of the *daikṣa* animal sacrifice and the ritual duties pertaining to the animal (*paśudharma*). By both types of proximity, there occurs the application (*viniyoga*) of the *dabdhi*-mantra and the animal-ritual duties respectively to the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

*Samākhyā* (name) is a derivative designation (*yaugikī saṃjñā*), and it is both worldly and Vedic; for example, "the *hotṛ*-cup" (*hotṛcamasa*) and "the office of the *adhvaryu*" (*ādhvaryava*). By means of this, there is an application (*viniyoga*) of the *hotṛ* to the drinking from the cup and of the *adhvaryu* to the performance of his ritual duties. As for the one who considers the operation of an injunction (*vidhivyāpāra*), namely the naming of the material (*upādānābhidhāna*), to be a seventh means of proof (*pramāṇa*) regarding application—that view is answered by the impossibility of such an object of cognition (*prameyāsaṃbhavāt*). Furthermore, as for what is said—that the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth performed thereby is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—[that too is explained by the aforementioned means].

That too is incorrect, because the application is made by the Veda itself to that which has the form of a means to the *apūrva*. For this alone is the state of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) having the form of a means to that [apūrva]: namely, that through which there is subordination to the apūrva. Even so, how is it said to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)? The grains of rice (*vrīhayaḥ*) possess the status of being a means to the apūrva through the channel of the sacrifice, beginning with the rice-grains, the flour, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth.

The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) enjoined with reference to such [substances] becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to everything situated in the relationship of door and doorkeeper (*dvāra-dvāribhāva*). Furthermore, how is it that the sprinkling and so forth have their purpose directed toward the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) through "appropriation" (*upādāna*)? If it is held that the subservience to the mandate (*niyoga*) is understood for the sprinkling and so forth simply by being grasped by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), that [subservience] is not possible through the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatā*); rather, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), its subservience is accomplished solely through the status of assisting the instrument. Thus, the mandate itself is apprehended as connected to that [instrument].

By postulating that [the *prayāja*s] assist the instrument (*karaṇa*), one implies their subservience to that instrument. If this is so, then this very thing is simply *prakaraṇa* (context) stated under a different name. For even in your view, its nature is precisely this: in order to avoid the contradiction of the *apūrva* being subservient to the *prayāja*s—which have been brought about by the grasping of the "grasper" (*grāhaka*)—one must postulate [their utility] through the door of assisting the instrument, since direct instrumentality is impossible for them. If it is argued that the nature of the assistance itself is what belongs to the context (*prākaraṇika*), whereas the fact that the *prayāja*s produce that assistance is merely based on the direct statement (*aupādānika*), [we reply:]...

In that case, the application (*viniyoga*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would be based on context (*prakaraṇa*). For the application through context is not established merely by the production of an assistance (*upakāra*) postulated by the context. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), whether those performed in close proximity (*sannipātin*) or those taught as independent injunctions (*anārabhyādhīta*), would have their application determined by context simply because they produce such assistance. Therefore, the status of being a subsidiary for acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is indeed based on context. Now, it might be argued: "Context applies what is unconnected [to another rule], whereas sprinkling is already connected [by a direct statement]. This is not a fault.

Even for those [subsidiaries] that are directly connected, there is a dependence on a means (*dvāra*), because the postulation of a means—which serves as the instrument of assistance—occurs precisely as it does in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others. Thus, although there is no difference in the nature of the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa-śarīra*), the rule is merely conventional: that for connected items, the *upādāna* (the act of taking up) provides the means, whereas for unconnected items, it is the *prakaraṇa* (context). Furthermore, it has already been discussed previously that even in the case of the singularity of the animal and so forth, the application (*viniyoga*) occurs through direct statement (*śruti*) itself, and that the connection of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices with their results occurs through syntactical connection (*vākya*) and other means. Therefore, the authorities regarding subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) are exactly those that have been stated.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Determination of the Auxiliary (Aṅga-nirṇaya), in the Nyāyaratnamālā.

In this manner, once the three requirements have been presented by means of direct statement (śruti) and so forth, the productive urge (bhāvanā)—which is now fit for performance—is enjoined; that is to say, it is made to be performed. For the very nature of an injunction (vidhi) consists in its being a prompter to action. If it is argued: "Once the fruit is understood, the performance is established through that [fruit] alone, so there is no need for an injunction," we reply: No, because activity cannot occur merely by understanding [the act] as a means [to a desired end].

For it is understood only that sacrifice is the means to the result; however, since no specific distinction is perceived—whether the action's capacity to produce the result is like that of a cloud filled with rainwater which dispels the heat of one whose body is scorched by the midday sun during the summer season (which is created by fate), or whether it is like a water-station or food provided by another, or produced by oneself—one would not engage in the act.

Since an injunction (*vidhi*) has the nature of impelling, it brings about the result for the agent alone; thus, it becomes the prompter of performance (*anuṣṭhāpaka*). Furthermore, since a qualified performance is impossible without the performance of its qualifying attributes, the injunction also becomes, by implication, the prompter of those attributes as well. In that regard, the manner in which it prompts whom is considered in the fourth [book]. Therein—

First, regarding the portion consisting of the fruit (*phalāṃśa*), since the person engages in it spontaneously, an injunction (*vidhi*) does not cause its performance. How, then, is it said that both [the means and the end] are indicated (*lakṣyamāṇatva*)? It is stated that even the portion consisting of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhyāṃśa*) possesses the character of being defined by an injunction (*codanālakṣaṇatva*), just like the portion consisting of the means (*sādhanāṃśa*). This is not a fault. For its "character" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is to be known through an injunction (*codanāprameya*). In this regard, although the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites are understood through other means of knowledge, their status as the means of accomplishing the fruit is established by the authority of the injunction; thus, they possess that character.

In this way, since the fact that the fruit is also to be accomplished through that [action] is not understood from anything else, it is understood solely from the injunction; thus, that too possesses the characteristic of being enjoined. Nor does it follow from this much alone that it lacks the status of being enjoined, for an injunction is not merely the making known of what was previously unknown.

By what means could the fruit (phala) be something to be enjoined (vidheya) by virtue of being its object? Rather, it is the instigation of one who has not previously engaged [in action] that constitutes an injunction; thus, that wherein a person who was previously inactive is set in motion by the force of an injunction is what is enjoined. Now, with regard to the fruit, mental engagement (pravṛtti) has already arisen even upon the comprehension that it is to be accomplished by the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; however, the engagement there remains merely at that level. For bodily and vocal activities do not actually reach the fruit. But when its status as a means (sādhana) is known in reality, one who was previously inactive indeed engages [in action].

Therefore, that [result] is not something to be enjoined as a fruit. Likewise, even the subsidiaries such as the bringing of curds (*dadhyānayana*) are performed solely for the sake of the *āmikṣā* and so forth, and not for the sake of the *vājina* and so forth. Furthermore, a substance intended for disposal (*pratipatti*) does not cause its own performance; for the performance of the principal (*śeṣin*) is not for the sake of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*), but rather the performance of the subsidiary is for the sake of the principal. Even in the case of the principal, where there is an application elsewhere of a means already employed for another purpose—as in the case of the cake-plate (*puroḍāśakapāla*) being used for the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*)—since it serves as a means only because it has been employed by another, it lacks independent causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*).

For what purpose, then, is it established that the sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings is a disposal (*pratipatti*)? Because even the remaining *prayāja* remnants are employed solely for that [purpose], there is no possibility of their being employed by the act of sprinkling itself.

It is true that even though it is a remnant (*śeṣa*), the remnant of the *prayāja* does not cause the production of the substance; rather, it would be the cause for the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Consequently, in the Vājapeya sacrifice, one would have to produce another vessel to hold the *prayāja* remnant for the purpose of sprinkling the omenta (*vapā*) of the Prājāpatya offerings. To prevent this, the status of the *prayāja* remnant as something to be disposed of (*pratipādya*) is established. Now, one might object: disposal (*pratipatti*) also necessitates holding [the substance], because otherwise a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result, and such a deficiency is improper.

For this very reason, the production of common vessels (*sādhāraṇapātra*) is performed in the *sattra* sacrifice; for it serves this purpose: if the performance begins with the vessels of any one sacrificer, and subsequently, while those vessels have been employed, that sacrificer should happen to be negligent, then the prescribed disposal (*pratipatti*) of the vessels during the ritual act of the *paridhāna* would be omitted, and consequently, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would arise.

If the disposal (*pratipatti*) were not the purpose for retaining [the remnant], then, disregarding the disposal, the performance could take place using the vessels of any single [priest]. Therefore, since the disposal of the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings is accomplished by the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), retaining it serves no purpose. However, if the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) are primary, then the retention would indeed be appropriate for the sake of ensuring the integrity of the omenta of the *prājāpatya* animals; thus, the statement regarding its being a disposal is logical.

If the inquiry into what is a motivator (*prayojaka*) and what is not a motivator (*aprayojaka*) belongs to the fourth book (*adhyāya*), how is it then that matters such as whether something is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); whether it is an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*) or not; the existence or non-existence of *apūrva*; the distinction between injunctions of rule (*niyamavidhi*) and injunctions of result (*phalavidhi*); whether something is a commendatory passage (*arthavāda*) or possesses a fruit (*phalavat*); whether it is for the sake of time (*kālārtha*); whether it pertains to auxiliaries or the primary rite (*pradhāna*); and whether rites are equal primaries or possess the status of quality and primary—these are all investigated? It is precisely for the sake of establishing what is a motivator and what is not a motivator. For instance, if the *godohana* vessel and the like are for the sake of the sacrifice, they are motivated by the injunction of the sacrifice; otherwise, they would not be.

Likewise, if the oneness and other such qualities were intended for the sacrifice, they would be prompted by that [sacrifice]. In the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, since there exists a distinct transcendental result (*apūrva*), it is the portion consisting of renunciation (*tyāga*) that prompts that *apūrva*. If this were so, then even upon the destruction of the sacrificial material (*havis*), another material would have to be produced and the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice performed for the sake of accomplishing the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). This is not the case. Although the new sacrifice is prompted by the *apūrva*, the sacrifice itself is not the prompter of the substance. Because the substance is only a single part [of the whole], there is no fault.

Thus, since there is equality or inequality regarding the purpose (*artha*), the status of being a motivator (*prayojaka*) or non-motivator was determined previously through an investigation into the relationship between the primary (*śeṣin*) and the subsidiary (*śeṣa*). For this very reason it was stated: "The subject matter of the third [book] has been traversed"; therefore, the determination of the meaning of the definition follows directly thereafter. Furthermore, the fact that items smeared with *soma* are to be disposed of (*pratipādya*) was mentioned in the context of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*). Likewise, since the agent, place, time, quality, substance, and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) that serve a visible purpose are already established by their own nature, no injunction (*vidhāna*) for them is possible; even if they were intended to exclude other places and so forth, [no injunction would be required].

It might be argued that this must be a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), as no other type of injunction (*vidhi*) is possible, and therefore it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). To this we reply: there is indeed another type of injunction called *niyama*, which consists in the fulfillment of what is only optionally obtained. Therefore, it is an injunction. Furthermore, this exposition of the *niyamavidhi* also applies by way of restriction to the injunctions for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices.

This is for the purpose of establishing that [the injunction] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the *samādhi*. Likewise, if passages such as "hearing the verses of the sinless" were merely explanatory (*arthavāda*), then qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood would not be motivated by the injunction of the sacrifice; however, this is not the case if they are injunctions of results (*phalavidhi*). In the case of sacrifices like the *Viśvajit*, if there were no result, it would be difficult for the injunction to function as a motivator at all; but when there is a result, that motivatory power exists.

Then follows the investigation into the specific distinctions regarding the results [of the rites], prior to the consideration of the relationship between the subsidiaries (aṅga) and their purposes. Likewise, having considered the principal rite (aṅgin), in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," if the [text] were intent upon the relationship between the subsidiary and its purpose, then the Sautrāmaṇī and other rites would be prompted by the injunction of the principal rite. If, however, it were for the sake of [specifying] time, then the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) would not be the prompters of the Soma sacrifice. Similarly, after stating that the *jāteṣṭi* (birth-rite) sets aside the immediate sequence following the occasion because of conflict with the primary rite (*śeṣin*), it is stated that it is prompted by the time of purification (*śauca*).

Furthermore, the presentation of the fruit as accruing to the son is by way of being a corroborative argument (*upodghāta*). For if it were the fruit of the son, there would be a contradiction with the primary purpose (*śeṣin*), whereas such a contradiction cannot be maintained if it is the fruit of the father. Therefore, it has been stated that even for those [subsidiaries] that have become auxiliary members (*aṅga*), such as the Sautrāmaṇī, there is an occasioning force (*prayojakatva*) for their own specific time. Likewise, if the Anumati offerings and so forth, as well as the acts of gambling (*videvana*) and so forth, were equally primary (*samaprādhānya*), then the fruit itself would be the occasioning factor for all of them. However, in the case of the relationship between subsidiary and primary (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), those elements which lack an independent person to be enjoined (*aniyojya*) are prompted by the sacrifice (*kratu*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the primary rites (*pradhāna*), the injunction (*vidhi*) alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*), and not the fruit (*phala*); how then can it be said, like the view of a partial scholar (*ekadeśin*), that in the primary rites the fruit is the motivator, while in the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) the injunction is? [Reply: We do not say at all that the injunction is not the motivator in the primary rites; rather, we are conducting an investigation into a specific type of motivation (*prayukti-viśeṣa*). Just as the injunction for the performance of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, although it is the motivator for the bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*), is said to be motivated by the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), because it is that which motivates it.

Just as [in the previous case] it was determined that the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) is the motivator and not the *vājina* (whey), so too here the question is whether the fruit is the motivator of the gambling (*videvana*) and other acts, or whether it is the sacrifice (*kratu*). This is precisely the meaning: are they employed for the sake of accomplishing the fruit, or for the sake of accomplishing the benefit to the sacrifice? In this same way, in the subsequent discussion regarding the status of the gambling and other acts as subsidiaries (*śeṣa*), the investigation is conducted specifically concerning their particular motivation.

Likewise, because the *dadhi-graha* (curd-offering) is obligatory (*nitya*), it is prompted by the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices as something permanent; however, because the *vaiśvānara* and others are occasional (*naimittika*), they are not prompted as something permanent. Because the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) is not a subordinate part (*anaṅga*), it is not prompted by the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. Similarly, the *svaru* (wooden chip) and the two *raśanā* (ropes) are prompted by the animal sacrifice and the sacrificial post (*paśu-yūpa*).

Thus, having considered what constitutes an instigator (*prayojaka*) and what does not, since there must necessarily be a sequence among the many subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and primary rites (*pradhāna*)—all of which are enjoined by a single performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) and performed by a single agent—the specific details of that sequence are considered in the fifth book. Now, one might object: this investigation into sequence should not even be undertaken, because sequence is not something to be enjoined and thus lacks the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*). Furthermore, if a non-subordinate element is omitted, the primary rite remains free from defect (*avaiguṇya*). But how is it that sequence is not to be enjoined? To this it is replied: "Being itself unenjoined in its own nature, it is not a qualifier of that which is enjoined; and being devoid of denotative power, it is disregarded by the apprehending [agent]. (Verse 1)
Devoid of the status of being a constituent part of an injunction and excluded from the scope of injunctive implication, by what manner does sequence (krama) arise as something to be enjoined? 2.

First of all, sequence cannot be enjoined in its own form, because it is not something that can be performed; for a sequence, being independent, cannot be carried out like a substance or other such elements. If it is argued that this is not so—just as substances and the like, though not inherently performable, fall within the scope of an injunction by virtue of qualifying a performable action, so too shall it be for sequence—that is not correct, because it does not qualify something that is itself enjoined. For it is appropriate that substances and the like be enjoined since they serve as qualifiers of the performable action which is the object of the injunction; however, sequence is not...

Likewise, because it is a qualification of a composite whole (*saṃghāta*) and because that [composite] is not something to be enjoined. For it is not the composite that is enjoined; rather, it is the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*) that are enjoined, and these are not the substrata of sequence. Indeed, sequence is not possible in each single [element]; therefore, it is not something to be enjoined. If it is argued that it is "like number" (*saṃkhyāvat*), we say no, because number serves as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). In this regard, one might think: just as in the injunction "He offers eleven *prayāja* oblations," number—though residing in a composite—is enjoined, so too should sequence be. That is not so, because number is merely an indicator.

For in that case, the number eleven is not being enjoined; rather, repetitions characterized by that number are enjoined, and since these are of the nature of action, it is indeed proper that they be enjoined. Therefore, the author of the Vivaraṇa maintains that all sequence—whether belonging to the third book (the Tārtīya) or the fifth book (the Pāñcamika)—is not subject to injunction.

The author of the *Nibandhana*, however, says: "Let it be that the third-order sequence (*tārtīyaka-krama*) and numbers such as eleven can be grasped because they are possible to denote; thus, since they serve the purpose of an injunction (*vidhy-aidamarthya*), they possess the status of being enjoined (*vidheya*) by virtue of being performed as implied by the injunction. But this is not possible for the fifth-order sequence (*pāñcamika-krama*). For there is no denotation whatsoever for it, and that which is not denoted cannot be grasped by a grasper."

The "seizing by the grasper" (*grāhakagraha*) is defined as the expression of a connection—by way of the relationship between purpose and that which serves the purpose—with those [subsidiary elements] mentioned in proximity to an injunction that possesses authority and consists of a purpose, even though they themselves are not purposes. Such a seizing by the grasper is not possible for that [injunction] alone; and for that which is not so seized, there is no evidence for its being for the sake of the injunction (*vidhyaidamarthyam*); and for that which lacks such a purpose, the injunction does not necessitate performance; and for that whose performance is not necessitated, there is no possibility of being an object of injunction (*vidheyatva*).

As they have said: "That which is undertaken for the sake of accomplishing something else is the thing to be enjoined. But how is it that there is no expression of sequence? For the suffix *ktvā* expresses anteriority in time, as in "the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati... However, the suffix *ktvā* is not an expresser of anteriority because of its deviation in cases such as "having opened his mouth, he sleeps," where the sequence of time is absent; rather, the meaning of *ktvā* is simply the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), since this is never absent. How then is anteriority understood in the case of "he ate and [then] went"? [It is understood through the context.]

It is said: for the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed after that very verbal root which is employed first among two roots expressing actions having the same agent; thus, since the sequence of performance is understood from the hearing of the *ktvā* suffix—wherein the meaning is understood according to the order of employment and the performance follows the understanding of that meaning—the sequence of performance is perceived. However, while there might still be a suspicion regarding the expression of priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) in the case of [the suffix] *śas*, such a suspicion is utterly remote in the case of [suffixes like] *artha* and so forth.

Therefore, since sequence is not an auxiliary factor because it cannot be denoted [by words], there is no deficiency even when it is omitted; thus, the inquiry into sequence is purposeless. To this, they reply: "Even though sequence is not an auxiliary factor, it is certainly not to be disregarded, because in its absence, the specific performance [of the rite] would not be established."

It is true that the sequence is indeed a non-essential factor (*anaṅga*); nevertheless, an investigation into sequence should not be commenced [as a separate topic], because even though it is a non-essential factor, it is worthy of respect. For the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*) is understood as being accomplished by a specific performance embraced by a particular sequence known through direct revelation (*śruti*) and other means. Therefore, although the injunction regarding performance does not necessitate the actual execution of the sequence, it certainly necessitates a specific performance, and since that specific performance cannot be established without a particular sequence, that sequence is respected. Thus, the definition of sequence (*kramalakṣaṇa*) ought to be commenced. However, this is not accepted, due to contradiction with both reasoning and the texts.
Even though it is not of a nature to be performed, [it is so designated] by virtue of being a qualification of that [action]. ||3||
How is it that the sequence does not become subordinate?
Even though this [sequence] is devoid of denotation, it somehow enters the intellect. (4)

Endowed with expectancy and compatibility, like one performing the ancestral sacrifice (śrāddha) and other rites, the apprehender proceeds toward the apprehension; for this is the cause even in other cases as well. (5)
The suffix -tva- is heard [in the word *pūrva*] to express priority in time through both traditional usage (*smṛti*) and grammatical application (*prayoga*).
Thus, it indicates that sequence is a characteristic of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). ||6||
There would be neither Sūtra nor Bhāṣya; therefore, this is not seen [as a valid position]. ||7||

We agree that sequence cannot be enjoined in its own essential nature; however, it is impossible to deny its status as something to be enjoined when it functions as a specific aspect of the application of what is enjoined.

Time is enjoined as an adjunct to the performance [of rituals], and sequence is exactly like that. As for the objection that it is a qualifier of a collection (*saṃghāta*): a collection is not understood to be the locus of sequence, for one does not say "a collection by means of sequence"; rather, one says "the ritual objects (*padārtha*) are performed in sequence. As for the claim that sequence is not perceived in each individual [element]: this is not a fault, because, like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it resides in two things together, and is thus understood in that way.

Alternatively, this [sequence] does not reside in a composite entity consisting of two things. Rather, it exists in each individual thing as something possessing a counter-correlative, just like length and so forth. For sequence is priority and posteriority; it is not that both possess priority nor that both possess posteriority. Instead, the priority of one is understood in relation to the other, and the posteriority of the other is understood in relation to that first. Therefore, in every respect, it does not reside in a composite whole, but rather resides in the individual entities. And since it resides in the entities, it is enjoined by the very injunction of those entities themselves, just like the curd and other such items.
