As for the claim that "because it is not denoted, there is no apprehension of this [injunction] by the apprehender," that too is incorrect. What is the use of denotation here? For it is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatva*)—and not denotation—that characterize the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*); let us not abandon denotation, since in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, there is indeed the denotation of the injunction as related to the person to be impelled (*niyojya*).

Since the specific sequence required by the injunction of performance—which casts various word-meanings upon a single agent—is already presented by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and other indicators, and since it is also suitable, why should the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurring in the principal sentence wait for a bribe, like a base man, in order to express its own meaning as connected with that sequence?

Furthermore, even in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, which have other designations, they are not denoted by their own specific terms as being connected to the primary *apūrva*; rather, it is the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurring within the primary sentence that denotes its own meaning as connected to that [primary]. Your view is that the term's own expression is applicable merely to bring them into proximity; and since proximity exists even without such a direct denotation, the sequence is indeed established, and thus it falls within the scope of the "grasper" (*grāhaka*).

Just as in the *pitṛyajña* and the *viśvajit*, where the agent (*kartṛ*)—though not explicitly mentioned—is nonetheless an auxiliary element (*aṅga*), so too will it be for the sequence (*krama*). Furthermore, the reason "because it is not explicitly mentioned" (*anabhihita*) is not universally applicable (*avyāpaka*). This is because in such passages as "the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati," the prior time is already expressed by the suffix *-ktvā*. As for the claim that "prior time is not the meaning [of the suffix] because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*)," that is not correct; for a word does not cease to have a meaning simply because that meaning occurs in other contexts.

Let it not be that the word *agni*, when used in the sense of "fire," lacks that meaning simply because it is also applied to a young boy (*māṇavaka*). Nor let it be that [the requirement of] having the same agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) is not part of the meaning [of the suffix *ktvā*], because it is applied even where there are different agents—as in "having heard the lineage of Yadu, a man is liberated from all sins"—and because it is applied even to the mere root-meaning when preceded by the particles *alam* or *khalu*. It might be argued: "We do not say that something is not the word-meaning because of deviation; rather, the established rule is that the word-meaning is that which cannot be obtained otherwise."

And the same applies to the requirement of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). For it is not possible for that [agent], being unexpressed, to be understood from any other source; however, the comprehension of priority in time is also established through the rule of usage (*prayoganiyama*). This is because in common usage, the suffix *ktvā* is employed after a verbal root that expresses an action with a common agent when it is used prior [to the second action]. Therefore, since the comprehension of priority in time is established even otherwise, it does not constitute the meaning of the word. This is not correct, because there is no such restriction on usage.

For there is indeed common usage in the world such as "he goes having eaten," and it occurs many times in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and other texts, such as: "O Jātavedas, cutting out his heart, [the Maruts] extinguished him with water by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma)."

There are many such examples, such as: "Having honored [the guest], he turned back," and "Having killed the deer," and so forth. Therefore, there is no restriction regarding usage; rather, since it cannot be obtained from any other source, it is established that the state of being prior in time (*pūrvakālatva*) is what is denoted by the suffix *ktvā*. Thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not universally applicable (*avyāpakatva*). Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras clearly indicates its status as an injunction by stating, "The sequence is characterized by direct Vedic statement" (*śrutilakṣaṇam ānupūrvyam*). The author of the Bhāṣya also proclaims the status of sequence as something to be enjoined in various places, saying, "He enjoins the order of initiation," and "That sequence is enjoined," and so on.

Therefore, it is not tenable—either logically or according to the text—that the sequence is not subject to injunction. For there is no reason why sequence should be called non-injunctive, given that it possesses the status of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) like number; for its purposefulness is established by the fact that it is grasped by the apprehender [of the action], and its status as a means to accomplish the assistance of the instrument is determined through its inclusion via the door of delimiting the performance, as indicated by the verbal suffix (*liṅga*). Furthermore: "And how could sequence have the character of being defined by a Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*)?
For its own nature is not cognizable by that [injunction], nor are its status as the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or the means (*sādhana*). (Verse 8)
The gender alone [is not the cause], because, as with number, the gender is not invariably determined;
for if that were the case, then substance and so forth would likewise be [the cause]. (9)

How, then, can such an order—which is not enjoined and is not something to be performed—be characterized by injunction (*codanā*)? For its essential nature is not cognizable through injunction, because, like the *apūrva*, it is cognizable through other means of knowledge. Nor is it the means to the *apūrva* like curds and so forth, because that is not admitted. Nor does an injunction inform us that it is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), as is the case with the qualification [of the sacrificer]; thus, it is not characterized by injunction. And that which is not so characterized does not deserve investigation; therefore, the section on the characteristics of order (*krama-lakṣaṇa*) would be unnecessary to commence.

In this regard, it might be argued that just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," the number—though not itself the object of the injunction—is nonetheless included within the scope of the Vedic mandate (*codanā*) as a qualifier for the action that is the object of the injunction; likewise, sequence (*krama*) also, by way of qualifying the specific performance enjoined by the ritual injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*), would be characterized by the Vedic mandate.

This is not the essence [of the matter], because the number is not determined by the object [it qualifies]. For a number, by presenting distinct actions suitable for its own inherence, serves as an indicator; however, sequence in no way presents a particular performance. Indeed, while one can specify that "when these actions have been performed, the number two is achieved," it is impossible to determine that "when this performance has been carried out, this sequence is achieved."

Even though in certain specific applications a particular sequence may be established, nevertheless, prior to the performance, it cannot be determined that "this is the sequence for this [rite], but not for that. In such a case, the only conclusion that follows is: "It must be performed according to this sequence. Consequently, since the action qualified by a specific sequence is what is enjoined, to claim that there is no injunction is mere idle talk. This being so, even if...

If it is argued that sequence is not something to be enjoined, then in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) and the like, one could likewise maintain that what is enjoined is only the sacrifice to be accomplished by means of Soma, and not the Soma itself; for Soma would merely be an indicator of a particular sacrifice. Furthermore, since that [Soma] too would be non-enjoined as it serves only to indicate a specific form (*ākṛti*), nothing remains to be enjoined other than the performance of action (*kṛti*). Thus, you have very well established your point.

Furthermore, since it is improper to treat something as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) when it can function as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), the injunction of the sacrifice is the same even regarding its sequence, except for those who forget their own established doctrine (*svasamaya*). Moreover, by asserting that "the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is delimited by a performance grasped through a specific sequence," you would be disregarding the fact that the determination of sequence occurs after the injunction of performance, since you claim that one considers the sequence of those [acts] already performed. Furthermore:

What has been determined as the object to be enjoined in the statement "of the Adhvaryu" and so forth? The agent would be established through the general rule (*codaka*); if he were not so established, he would not be established even by this statement. (10)

If the sequence were not prescribed, what then would be the scope of the injunction, "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati..."? Since initiation is already established for all of them by the general rule (codaka) due to their status as sacrificers, and the Adhvaryu as the performer is also established by that same rule, if the sequence were not prescribed, this sentence would be devoid of any subject matter. On this point, they say: "Even in the injunction regarding the Adhvaryu, it is indeed a restrictive rule (niyama). This is its meaning:

For in the *sattra* sacrifice, since those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the office of the priest is prescribed for the sacrificers themselves; thus, the [separate] priests are excluded. All the priestly functions must be performed by the sacrificers alone. In that case, there is no authoritative basis for the rule that whatever one person performs as the *ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu) should be designated as "Adhvaryu," and that he alone must perform all other *ādhvaryava* duties as well.

And thus, since the agency of all [officiants] would prevail everywhere without restriction, the statement "the Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati," serves to restrict the Adhvaryu as the agent for the initiation of the one designated as Gṛhapati. This, however, is incorrect. For if the specific agent for the initiation is not obtained through the *codaka* (the general transfer rule), then it cannot be obtained even by this explicit statement, because the meaning of the words occurring therein remains unknown.

All terms such as *adhvaryu* and the like apply to all persons; in that case, which person is designated as the *adhvaryu*, and for whom—among those designated as *gṛhapati*—is the performance of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) prescribed? Or rather, who are excluded? For indeed, all persons can be denoted by the word *adhvaryu*, and this being so, it is not possible to restrict the agent to a specific individual by means of this [term]. This might be argued:

It is merely this much that is enjoined: "one initiates the four [officiants], beginning with the householder (gṛhapati)"; and because he performs the initiation which is the duty of the Adhvaryu, he is designated by that term [Adhvaryu]. This might be some kind of desperate grasp at a straw (*kāśakuśāvalambana*) even so, if it were possible to definitively identify the Brahman and the others; but since they cannot be definitively identified, it must be stated: "which one among them initiates?"

Thus, when there is a requirement for a fixed rule regarding the officiating priests (pratisthātṛ) who are subject to restriction—such as the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin and others—that very rule which is observed in the archetype (prakṛti) must be accepted; for while some form of restriction may be possible, total lack of restriction (avyavasthā) is untenable. In the archetype, however, the restriction is established by the name (samākhyā) itself.

For a name (*samākhyā*) is not itself the enjoiner of a restriction regarding the agent; rather, the injunctive word of performance (*prayogavacana*), while enjoining the performance of many objects by many [agents], requires a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) and thus relies upon a restriction understood in some way through the name. This being the case, the injunctive word for the performance of the *satra* sacrifice, also depending on that [name], enjoins here as well those ritual items (*padārtha*) which were performed by a single agent in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as having a single agent. Therefore, because it is already established by implication, the Adhvaryu priest need not be specifically enjoined in the initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Now, even if there were no fixed rule [regarding the agent], it would still be untenable for the word *adhvaryu* to denote a specific person; thus, in either case, an injunction regarding the agent is impossible. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the sequence itself is what is enjoined. Consequently, since the performance (*prayoga*) is enjoined as qualified by the specific sequence known from the Śruti and other sources, it is established that the sequence is both enjoined and a subsidiary element (*aṅga*). And as it is said: "Sequence is indeed a subsidiary, being based on the single injunction of performance."

Now, is it said that "the sequence is indeed to be enjoined by the injunction of performance"? How can there be an injunction by the injunction of performance for that which has not been assigned [by other means]? There is no fault here, because this [sequence] is also assigned by direct statement (*śruti*) and the other criteria. Just as ritual items (*padārtha*) assigned by direct statement, indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, are enjoined by the injunction of performance, so too is the sequence assigned by direct statement and the others. However, this is the distinction: while other factors are adjuncts to the essential nature of the action (*karmasvarūpa-anubandha*), sequence is an adjunct to the performance (*prayogānubandha*), like place (*deśa*) and so forth.

Indeed, there is no rule that everything must be applied solely by means of the third [chapter's] criteria; rather, those [criteria] apply to the purposefulness (*idamarthya*) of the constituent parts (*padārtha*), whereas for the purposefulness of the sequence (*krama*), the criteria such as direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth belong specifically to the fifth [chapter]. It is not at all untenable that these [latter criteria] can also be shown to be included within the third chapter. Among them, the first is the sequence of direct statement (*śruti-krama*), where the verbal expression is intended to convey either the sequence itself or something qualified by it.

For example: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the sacrificer, should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; the first consumption is that of the one who utters *vaṣaṭ*. This is the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), which is determined by the force of the purpose, as in the case of cooking and the oblation (*homa*). That sequence among ritual acts which is relied upon—whether situated in an injunctive sentence or in a mantra—is the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the *āgneya* sacrifices. However, [regarding] those acts performed together...

When the performance of combined (sannipātin) elements must be carried out by way of repetition, the very same sequence applies to the second and subsequent repetitions as well, due to the injunction regarding the performance (prayogavacana). However, when there is an injunction that all items—whose locations were understood to be distinct in the archetype (prakṛti)—must be performed at the location of one of them in the ectype (vikṛti), the sequence adopted with the adventitious (āgantuka) items is such that it does not subvert the position established for each item in the archetype; this is the "sequence by sections" (kāṇḍakrama).

Just as in the Sādyaska sacrifice, when the animal victims are slaughtered together in place of the *savanīya* offerings, the immediate sequence following the *āśvina* cup is not sublated; so too, the "order of the principal" (*mukhyakrama*), which is the order of the primary acts, is adopted even for the subsidiaries in order to avoid sublating the unity of the subsidiary and the principal as understood from the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*). For example, in the case of the two rites dedicated to the female and male deities prescribed by the single sentence "There are two [deities] belonging to Sarasvatī," although their performance is understood through the order of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, the very order of the principals prevails even regarding the subsidiaries.

Although all orders of sequence (*krama*) are subject to the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), it is stated that "the two orders—the primary (*mukhya*) and the sequential (*prāvṛtika*)—are governed by the motive force (*prayojaka*)," because their authority is also based on the concomitance (*sāhitya*) understood through the injunction of performance. In the case of a conflict among direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), the primary (*mukhya*), and the sequential (*prāvṛti*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding. This applies even to textual order (*pāṭha*).

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is weaker than the order of the Brāhmaṇa texts. Furthermore, because it relies on the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the order based on the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance) is weaker in the case of modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). In that regard, the weakness of the order of recitation compared to direct statement (*śruti*) and purpose (*artha*) was declared in the section concerning the sublation of order (*kramabādha-adhikaraṇa*). However, no contradiction between direct statement and purpose is possible, because the motivating factor (*prayojaka*) is conceived exactly according to the direct statement. For if it were heard [in the scripture] as "having offered, one should cook," then, having postulated a visible purpose for the cooking, one might offer with any substance whatsoever.

Likewise, even regarding the textual reading, the weakness of that which pertains to the Brāhmaṇa compared to that which pertains to the Mantra has been stated in the rule *mantratastu prakṛtau tu svaśabdatvāt*. Even more so than that, the weakness of the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*) [compared to the order of mention] has been stated in the rule *avadānābhighāraṇāsādaneṣu*. Furthermore, the weakness of that which relies on the general injunction (*codaka*) compared to that which relies on the specific performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*) has been stated in the rule *tadvacanātu vikṛtau yathāpradhānaṃ syāt*.

Thus, the performance qualified by a specific order—delivered by the means of knowledge such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the rest, which are distinguished by their relative strength—is enjoined by the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*). [Objection: But was not the operation of the injunction of performance itself already considered in the fourth [book]? Since it is the very same here as well, how can there be a difference in definition (*lakṣaṇabheda*)? [Reply: True, in both cases it is indeed an investigation into the injunction of performance; however, there the investigation concerned the specific nature of that which is to be performed, namely, "Which subsidiaries are the prompter for what purpose? whereas here the investigation concerns the specific nature of the performance itself, namely, "What kind of performance, characterized by what order, does it enjoin? Thus, there is a difference in definition.
Thus, when the group of effects has been defined by means of these five characteristics, it is investigated in the sixth chapter who is qualified for this [path]. (11)

For when that which is to be performed has been determined, it is possible to determine one's capacity; once that capacity is determined, the cognition of entitlement (adhikāra), which depends upon it, follows. (12)

For as long as that which is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) is not understood, its capacity [to produce a result] cannot be understood; and by means of that capacity, the determination of entitlement (*adhikāra*) is established. Thus, the five chapters that expound what is to be performed serve as the cause for the investigation of entitlement. Nor does this causal status belong to a single chapter alone; for it is appropriate that even a collection of them—provided it presents a single unified purpose—should stand in such a relation toward another collection, just as the first six chapters stand toward the latter six. Even a single chapter, being a composite of various methods (*naya*), is treated as a unity precisely because it is subsumed under a single purpose.

Since even this group of five chapters establishes what is to be performed, it is logical that they constitute a single unit which serves as the basis for qualification (*adhikāra*). Among these, first of all, the existence of qualification is established by way of an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*), for only when that exists can the inquiry "To whom does this [injunction] belong? arise, and not otherwise.

In this regard, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) expressed in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*); thus, setting aside the heaven—which is presented by another word as a qualification of the person—it takes as its object to be brought about the meaning of the verbal root itself, which is brought forward by the direct statement (*śruti*) characterized by being expressed in the same word, and which is not subordinate to anything else.

One accepts [the injunction] because the sentence of the Śruti is more powerful; the meaning of the sentence is that "one should perform the sacrifice by means of substances such as heaven. Furthermore, the word "desire" (*kāma*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since for one performing the ritual action, a desire necessarily arises for its accomplishment through those means. Thus, having stated that there is no qualification (*adhikāra*) at all—because the sacrifice is primary due to the sublation of the sentence by both *Śruti* and *Liṅga*, and therefore no fruit is accomplished by this [word "desire"]—the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is then stated on the strength of the injunctive *Śruti*.

For the injunction (*vidhi*), being more closely connected to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) than to the meaning of the verbal root expressed by the same word, first restricts that [activity] toward a human goal; this is because its very nature is that of an instigation (*pravartanā*), and it is impossible to incite a person toward an operation whose fruit is not a human goal. Therefore, precisely through its connection with the injunction whose nature is instigation, when a productive result in the form of something desired is required, only its specific qualification is understood from the sentence. Once that is understood, the meaning of the verbal root expressed by the same word is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its proximity, while substances and so forth are accepted as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus he says:

If the connection with the prompted productive urge (bhāvanā) occurs first, prior to the integration of the constituent parts, then those elements being connected subsequently would not possess the status of being the object to be enjoined. ||13||
Now, meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) complete in all its parts is the domain of the prescribed rule;
therefore, an action devoid of the rule would not yield the fruit of human endeavor. ||14||

If, first of all, the bare *bhāvanā* (efficient force) were enjoined prior to its connection with the three factors (*aṃśatraya*), then—even though those factors would subsequently connect with the *bhāvanā* as subordinate elements dependent on the injunction of the qualified *bhāvanā*—the *bhāvanā* itself would not possess the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), because it has already been touched by the injunction in its bare form. On the other hand, if the *bhāvanā* does not connect with the injunction prior to its connection with the three factors, then, being devoid of an injunction, it would—due to proximity—take the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as its end (*bhāvya*), and thus the status of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as the end would not be established.
This is not so;
for the connection between the injunction and the *bhāvanā* is first understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
But because of their unfitness, they do not find liberation at that time. ||15||
And through its connection with the injunction, it is understood in this very way:
that this cultivation (bhāvanā) must be completed by such constituent parts as would enable it to obtain a connection with the injunction;
thus it becomes [understood].
The human goal is that which is to be accomplished, and the constituent parts are that which are to be enjoined. ||17||

First of all, the relationship between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), which are conveyed by a single word, is expressed through direct audition (*śruti*). However, at that stage, because the productive urge alone cannot be performed, the connection, though apprehended, is not yet fully realized. Even while that [connection] remains unrealized, the person, upon its apprehension, determines at that very moment: "This [productive urge] must indeed be connected with an injunction. Thereafter, it must be completed by such constituent parts (*aṃśa*) as it possesses when it enters into connection with the injunction.

Furthermore, that which does not have a human goal as its fruit cannot be connected with [the efficient force]; therefore, concluding that it must have a human goal as its fruit, and seeking its specific qualification, one bypasses the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) situated in the same word—since that lacks the status of a human goal—and looks toward what is expressed by another word. Therein, because the specific qualification is understood through words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) connects with it. And being thus connected, while still requiring an instrument (*karaṇa*), it—by virtue of proximity—takes up the meaning of the verbal root presented in the same word, according to the principle of the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

He accepts [the action] as the instrument (*karaṇa*); then, when there is an expectation regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*), he grasps the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) understood through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means as the mode of procedure (*itthaṃbhāva*). Thereafter, the *bhāvanā*, qualified by all its constituent parts, is enjoined. Thus, because the connection with the injunction is perceived at the very outset, it is established that the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the objective to be accomplished (*bhāvya*). Furthermore, even though the connection with the injunction is already perceived, since the fulfillment of each part occurs only after the relationship between the parts has been established, the status of the parts themselves as being enjoined (*vidheya*) is also established. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. [Objection: But how can the injunction (*vidhi*) be fourfold, given the distinctions such as the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) and so forth?
In this way, you yourself have proclaimed that there is only the single injunction of application (prayogavidhi). ||18||

By asserting that the injunction follows after the three requirements have been presented by means of scripture and other factors, it is effectively stated that the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) alone is the sole injunction. And they describe that [injunction] as being of four kinds:
one is called the injunction of origination (*utpattividhi*), which is investigated in the second [book];
another is the injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*), which is investigated in the third [book]. (19)
In the fourth and fifth [chapters], there is the consideration of the rules for application;
whereas the rule concerning qualification is another, which falls within the scope of the sixth chapter and those following. (20)

"Therefore, the designation of them as a single entity is untenable. It is replied: "Because the triad beginning with origination is understood through its connection with the injunction, and because they possess the status of an agent by their very nature, the fourfold character of the injunction is maintained. (21)

When an injunction (*vidhi*), whose essential nature is to set in motion what has not yet been set in motion, aims at the nature of the action (*karma*) for the sake of establishing that [action], then—by virtue of the very comprehension of its connection with the injunction—one postulates that the action which is its object is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, its status as a producer is established. And by that very [status], the fact that the action which is its object is a means to a result, or that it provides assistance to something possessing a result, is postulated; this constitutes its character as an applicator (*viniyojaka*).

Furthermore, since a person’s entitlement (*adhikāra*)—that is, ownership—is established in relation to an action that accomplishes a result, this entitlement is also indeed an object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the injunction (*vidhi*). And it is logical that [the injunction] is the motivator (*prayojaka*) by its very nature; thus, because there are four types of objects of knowledge, there is a fourfold division of the injunction. For the word "injunction" denotes an essence consisting solely of the impelling force (*pravartaka*), and it is through the impossibility of its connection [otherwise] that the other three are postulated; thus, the fourfold division of the objects of knowledge is established. But the fourfold division is not [intrinsic] to the nature [of the injunction] itself. As it has been said:
"The third [type of injunction] is called 'prescriptive' (*vidhātrī*), for the performance [of the rite] is dependent upon it."
And among these four, in some cases one is intended to be expressed;
in some cases one, two, three, or even all four. (22)

The statement "one performs the *agnihotra*" has the purpose of enjoining the origin (*utpatti*) alone; the statement "he conquers with the *samidh* [fuel-sticks]" has the purpose of enjoining both the origin and the application (*viniyoga*), because without an injunction, application through the context (*prakaraṇa*) would not be established—as was already explained previously. The statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*" has the purpose of enjoining the application (*viniyoga*), the qualification (*adhikāra*), and the performance (*prayoga*), since its origin is already established by the rule "one should sacrifice with *soma*. The statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" has the purpose of enjoining all four [origin, application, qualification, and performance].

Since not even a single [instance] is established from another source, it has already been stated how the *śruti* and other means of application are established as the applicators of an injunction, even though the injunction itself is the applicator. Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus, when it is determined by the force of the injunction that the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), and when there is a requirement for its specific nature, then heaven (*svarga*) and the like—whose primacy is understood through their connection with desire (*kāma*)—become the ends to be accomplished, even though they are subordinate to the person; they do not, as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), function merely as means.
For even in the prima facie view, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not refer solely to the person.

Rather, it is intended to establish that the substance called "heaven" is a means for accomplishing an action. But how is it determined by both the proponent and the opponent that the word expressing the person (the agent) has that [action] as its primary purpose? It is said:

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) considers it thus: By the very capacity of the action (*kriyā*), a person (*puruṣa*) is already established as being subordinate (*aguṇabhūta*). In that context, the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) does not designate a specific person—just as the word "king" (*rājan*) or words like "rice" (*vrīhi*) designate a specific substance—because one who is desirous of heaven at one time may well cease to be so at another. Furthermore, if it were taken as an indication of time (*kālopalakṣaṇa*), the same fault would apply. Therefore, there can be no [injunction] for a person qualified by the desire for heaven.

There is a connection by way of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatvena anvayaḥ*). Here, there would be a connection by way of being a subordinate element. In that case, because the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) is already established, the [injunction] pertains to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇaparatva*), as in the case of "one whose turban is red" (*lohitoṣṇīṣādi*). Even in that instance, if the desire for heaven were taught as a subordinate element, it would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). For no visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) is possible for the desire for heaven in relation to the ritual action. Furthermore, there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*) for the injunction if it were to teach the desire qualified by heaven as a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

However, since heaven—which consists of material substance—is seen to have a visible purpose as being accomplished through ritual action (*karman*), and because there is parsimony in enjoining its mere status as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), this is indeed an instruction regarding a substance. The suffix *aṇ*, denoting the agent, along with the verb *kāmayati* (desires), is a restatement (*anuvāda*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that by the force of the injunction itself, it is understood that the activity—the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—has the person as its ultimate purpose; for no prudent person engages in an action that does not serve their own interest. And its subservience to that [purpose] arises from its being a means to accomplish the assistance required by that [person].

Since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is understood to have human purpose (*puruṣārthatva*) through that very injunction by means of accomplishing the required assistance, and since there remains a requirement for a specific kind of assistance, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—functioning as a designation of a specific person whose connection was previously established by the aforementioned logic as being otherwise inexplicable—expresses the status of that person as the beneficiary (*śeṣin*) who requires a specific fruit; thus, it aims at conveying the specific assistance known as "heaven," which serves as its qualifier.

Therefore, in both positions, the word *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven) does not refer to the person, but rather to heaven; the dispute concerns only the status of subordinate (*guṇa*) and primary (*pradhāna*). For this very reason it has been said: "Is heaven subordinate and the ritual action primary, or is the ritual action subordinate and heaven primary?"

Regarding the phrase "by way of being primary": is the connection of the one desiring the fruit [now] by way of being the principal (*śeṣin*)? Certainly. If so, how then is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "desire" (*kāma*) and words such as "king" in passages like "A king desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," where the word "king" and others express the subordinate (*śeṣa*)? It is said: because both refer to the agent (*kartṛ*). For, just as in the case of the king, the benefit to the one desiring the fruit occurs by way of being the agent; this is for the purpose of [establishing] the sense that "one who is dirty must bathe" or "one who is hungry must eat."

For when the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is clearly expressed by the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), yet the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣitva*) belongs only to the *malina* and so forth, why is it that the status of being a subordinate does not belong to the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) and others, whose agency is to be inferred from their association with the fruit? Indeed, the connection with agency is not an obstacle to the status of being a subordinate; for it has already been shown in the case of the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings and so on that it is possible for all the factors of action (*kāraka*) to possess the status of being a subordinate.

If this is so, how then is the distinction established that the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) is the "residual case of the principal" (*śeṣivibhakti*), while the third and subsequent case-endings are "residual case-endings" (*śeṣavibhakti*)? It is said: the distinction is justified by the demonstration of the relationship between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*). For the second case-ending demonstrates the state of being the goal (*sādhyabhāva*), and the state of being the goal is possible only for that which is the principal (*śeṣitva*); therefore, it is entirely appropriate that the understanding of this [principal status] arises from the second case-ending which expresses it.

The third case endings (*tṛtīyā*) and others, however, are said to be the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for that [status of being a subordinate] because they denote a state of being a subordinate (*śeṣabhāva*) through their proximity to being a means (*sādhanatva*). But where the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*) belongs precisely to the absence of the means established by those [case endings], there the status of being the goal (*sādhyatva*), although not expressed by words, must be inferred; thus the distinction is established. Therefore, while the person desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājyakāma*)—who is connected with the agency (*kartṛtva*)—has the status of the principal, the king (*rājan*), on the other hand, has only the status of a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) because his connection with the substance and the action conforms to the principle of being a means (*sādhanatva*).

Even that connection as a "person to be impelled" (niyojya) which is desired for one who desires the fruit, when analyzed, turns out to be precisely the aforementioned connection as the "principal" (śeṣin). Otherwise, there would be no distinction from the [mere] connection as an agent (kartṛtva). For it is thus:
the so-called "person to be impelled" is he who understands the task (kārya) as his own; and that "belongingness" of the task consists in its being dependent upon his volition. (23)
That which is pervaded by a person's intention is indeed that which has that person as its agent;
and the states of being an agent and being subject to an injunction are brought about by the relationship of the subordinate and the principal. (24)

Even for one who holds the view that the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*) establishes the connection [of the agent] as being the performer (*kartṛtva*) with respect to one desiring heaven, while the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) establishes the connection as being the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*), such a person is likewise unable to state a distinction in the connection apart from the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*). To explain: he who understands "this is my duty" is the person to be enjoined; therefore, by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it must be established that "this is the duty of one desiring heaven. The meaning is that it is to be pervaded by the activity of one desiring heaven.

For it is true that one understands, "This task is mine," and whatever is pervaded by the performance of an action belongs to that agent alone, just as in the case of the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*). Therefore, because the King and the one desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) are connected [to the rite] through their status as agents, this distinction must be justified as follows: while the one desiring self-sovereignty possesses the status of the *niyojya* (the person to be directed), the King possesses the status of the agent. Furthermore, even within the status of being an agent, the one desiring self-sovereignty holds the status of the *śeṣin* (the principal), whereas the King holds the status of the *śeṣa* (the subordinate).

Now, is it not the case that the status of being an *niyojya* (one who is to be impelled) is due to being a cognizer (*boddhṛ*), and not due to being a subordinate (*śeṣin*)? What, then, does the word "desiring" (*kāma*) signify? It signifies that the person desiring [a result] is the cognizer with respect to the task delimited by its object—namely, that the task delimited by the sacrifice has the person desiring heaven as its cognizer.

If this were so, since there would be no connection with the object to be accomplished for one who possesses desire apart from the status of being an agent of cognition, he would understand only that specific meaning expressed by the word "one should sacrifice" (yajeta)—namely, "this is a task"—but not "this is my task. This is because there is no relation whatsoever between the self, which is denoted by the word "mine," and the mandate (niyoga). Consequently, there would be a state of non-eligibility for the mandate. For one who merely understands "this is a task" is not an eligible person (niyojya); rather, it is one who understands "this is my task. And thus, purposeful activity (pravṛtti) would not be established.

For no one engages in action merely because something is "to be done" (kārya); rather, [one acts] thinking, "This is my task. Furthermore, a word that indicates the person to be enjoined (niyojya) would be useless; for even without such a word, a person who desires heaven (svargakāma), being already proficient in the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), certainly understands it. In that case, there would be a restriction (parisaṃkhyā): namely, that only one proficient in the meaning would understand, and no other. But such a restriction is impossible, because even when such a restriction is attempted, the understanding of those who are proficient cannot be prevented.

Furthermore, in the case of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) and similar rites, since all [participants] possess the status of being enjoined—characterized by the capacity to understand—their [status as] enjoined would not require further verbal supplementation (*adhyāhāra*). Therefore, it must be stated that one who desires the status of being enjoined—characterized by the understanding "this is my duty"—must necessarily be made to comprehend it through a statement precisely in this form: "this is his duty. And thus, there follows the consequence of its connection solely through the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*).

If it were argued: "True, this is indeed the connection; nevertheless, there is no confusion between the status of being an agent and the status of being enjoined, because the objects (*viṣaya*) differ. For the status of being an agent..."
[The opponent claims: "In the case of both the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) and the injunction (*niyoga*), there is the state of being the person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*).

This is incorrect; for apart from the verbal root-meaning, no other *kārya* (task/obligation) is established even today, since it [the *kārya*] exists only when the state of being the person to be enjoined is present. (25)

For it is precisely this relationship with the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled), established within this very context, that serves as the basis for postulating the denotation of an action distinct from the [mere] act. Therefore, since that [relationship] is not established prior [to the understanding of the sentence], one cannot claim that there is no confusion [of roles] due to a difference in the object [of the injunction]. Furthermore, because such a relationship is absent in common worldly usage—even when the vocative case is present in sentences such as "Devadatta, bring the cow"—Devadatta and others would not possess the status of a *niyojya*. Consequently, it must be stated that being a *niyojya* is simply the state of being subordinate (*śeṣitva*) toward the task to be accomplished, or else it is the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). As for the one who says: "It is true that the agent and the *niyojya* are distinct by way of the distinction between the subordinate and the superior..."
However, that distinction exists with respect to the act of creation; in the effect, both possess the status of being qualities. ||26||

Although there is indeed a distinction between the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and the status of being a person to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*) precisely because of the difference between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), nevertheless, the person to be enjoined does not possess the status of being the principal (*śeṣitā*) with respect to the injunction (*niyoga*), since that [injunction] is the primary element in all cases. As it has been said: "Who would not accept that when the injunction is accomplished, everything else is subordinate to it? What, then, is the status of being the person to be enjoined? It is the status of being the principal with respect to the effort (*kṛti*).

And with respect to that [kārya], being subordinate (śeṣatva) means being the agent (kartṛtva). Therefore, even though one understands the task (kārya) as being pervaded by an activity (kṛti) for one's own sake, one is called "the person to be impelled" (niyojya); however, the task itself is not for one's own sake. Thus, what is the meaning of the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"? It means: the task, delimited by the sacrifice, is pervaded by an activity for the sake of one who desires heaven. Consequently, since both the agent and the person to be impelled are subordinate to the task, there is no confusion regarding their relationship of subordinate and principal (śeṣa-śeṣibhāva) with respect to the activity. But he too troubles himself in vain; for instance: since activity is subordinate to the task, it does not attain the status of being subordinate to anything else.
Since the effect is a subordinate part of this [knowledge], this [result] would occur through that [effect] as its medium. ||27||

Indeed, an effort (*kṛti*) understood through verbal expression alone cannot be subordinate to the person (*puruṣa-śeṣatva*), as it is subordinate to the injunction (*niyoga*). For that which is for one purpose cannot logically serve another purpose. However, if that effect (*kārya*) were subordinate to the person, then by means of it, the effort—as well as the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—would become subordinate to the person through its subordination to the *apūrva*, just as the factors of action (*kāraka*) are subordinate to the *apūrva* by means of their subordination to the sacrifice; but this would not be the case otherwise.

[Objection: Even if the mandate (*niyoga*) is not subordinate to the person, since the fruit is subordinate to it, and since that [fruit] too is pervaded by the effort (*kṛti*) in the same way, the effort will become subordinate to the person through that [fruit]. What then is the status of occasional rites (*naimitika*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*)? For in those cases there is no other fruit through which the effort could become subordinate to the person. Yet even there, there is an enjoined agent (*niyojya*) who possesses the occasion (*nimitta*) or who is engaged in the prohibited action; how could he understand the task (*kārya*) as being pervaded by an effort for his own sake?

Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that even an action (*kārya*) in the form of an injunction (*niyoga*) possesses the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*). And this is logical; for no one can understand "this is my duty" (*mamedaṃ kāryam*) unless it serves their own interest. If this were not so, then even the result (*phala*) would not be established as a human goal, for its understanding is likewise precisely of the nature: "this is my duty. Therefore, even against one's will, one must state the following distinction: with respect to the action itself, the person possesses the status of being the principal (*śeṣitva*), the status of being the one to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*), the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*), and the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*).

Thus, it is incorrect to say that the vocative case-ending serves as the authority for a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). This is because in commands such as "O Agnīdh, spread the fires," the Agnīdh and others lack the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣin*) with respect to the action (*kṛti*); and one who is not subordinate cannot be a person to be enjoined. An objection is raised:
"In the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), which consists of what is to be done (*kārya*), there would be the status of being a person to be enjoined by virtue of being subordinate.
But when [the injunction] has the nature of an instigator (*pravartaka*), the person to be instigated (*pravartya*) possesses the status of being a person to be enjoined. (Verse 28)

For your established doctrine is that an injunction (*vidhi*) is essentially rooted in an internal volition (*saṃkalpa*) of the form "I shall do this," which has the nature of impelling (*pravartanā*). And that [impulsion], like a productive operation (*bhāvanā*), requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) as well as an agent to be impelled (*pravartya*), who is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). In this regard, does the word "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) provide the object to be brought about required by the productive operation, or rather the person to be enjoined required by the injunction? It cannot be both, for that would result in a contradiction of forms (*vairūpya*), since one or the other would necessarily be established through the other.

For in a ritual action whose fruit is heaven, it is not possible for one who does not desire that [heaven] to be the *niyojya* (the person to be enjoined); thus, the establishment of the *niyojya* depends upon the fruit. And since it is impossible for one who desires heaven to be the *niyojya* in a ritual action whose fruit is something else, the fruit is established as the qualification of the *niyojya*. Therefore, because the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) denotes a person, it is proper that it refers specifically to the *niyojya*. It is replied: True, the *niyojya* is required by the injunction (*vidhi*); however, at that time, he cannot be definitively determined. But the fruit possesses the capacity [to be so determined]. (29)

Prior to the determination of the group [of auxiliaries], it is not possible to determine [the qualified person]. For the status of being a *niyojya* (the one to be enjoined) does not belong to one who merely desires a fruit; rather, it belongs to one who possesses the capacity for performance (*anuṣṭhāna-śakti-yukta*). And that capacity is defined in dependence upon the comprehension of what is to be performed. Furthermore, the action to be performed is precisely that which is joined with both the auxiliaries and the primary rite; and just as the injunction regarding that action occurs only after the connection of the three factors [object, means, and result] has taken place, and not first—because it would otherwise be impossible—so too is the *niyojya*. However, the fruit can be understood even before the connection with the other factors; therefore, this [injunction] is directed toward that [fruit]. And once it is understood...

Once that constituent part has been determined, the injunction—enjoining a person who desires its fruit and is capable of its performance—directs him toward the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as qualified by all its attributes. And it has been said: "In the *bhāvanā* consisting of both the subsidiary and the primary elements, there is a simultaneous injunction of the person. Furthermore, even when there is a connection with the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the word expressing desire does not have the person as its primary referent; rather, it has the specific fruit as its primary referent.

For it is understood from the injunction itself that there is indeed someone here to be enjoined to an activity, and he is the subordinate (śeṣin) of that fit activity; for no one can be enjoined to an activity that does not serve his own purpose. He alone is the subordinate who desires to enjoy a specific result to be brought about by that activity. When this is understood, yet the specific result remains unknown, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) must necessarily refer to that very [result].

In this regard, when considering whether [the Vedic statement] is intent upon its own meaning by expressing the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) as the primary object, or rather [expresses it] as the subordinate element (*śeṣin*), the latter—namely, the demonstration of the status of being a subordinate element, which is capable of being understood—is the superior [interpretation], rather than abandoning that intent which has the person to be enjoined as its object because such a person is impossible to ascertain. For while the status of being a subordinate element is indeed qualified by the capacity [to perform the act], that capacity is useful for the performance [of the ritual] and not useful for the status of being a subordinate element; since the status of being a subordinate element belongs only to the performer, those who lack the capacity have no entitlement, just as a non-king has no entitlement to the Rājasūya sacrifice.

For in that case, kingship does not fall within the scope of the qualification (*adhikāra*); likewise, because power (*śakti*) also does not enter into the nature of the qualification as its subordinate element (*śeṣitva*), it is possible to determine its status as the subordinate element even prior to the determination of the agent. Thus, the connection of the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is solely by way of being the subordinate element. And since that [connection] is intended for the cognition of a specific result, the person’s qualification (*adhikāra*) regarding the ritual action—which is the means to that [result]—is established through the connection of heaven and so forth as the result. Therefore, the determination of its specific details must now be undertaken.

In that regard, since the primary injunction (pradhānavākya) indicates the eligibility of all [performers] without distinction, the application of the auxiliary rites (aṅga) follows that [primary injunction]; thus, "whosoever is able to perform it, he shall do it. For example: when it is determined that the cutting (avadāna) applies to liquids, solidified substances, and meat, the rule "he cuts with the sruva-spoon" refers specifically to liquids by virtue of its own capacity (sāmarthya). ||30||

Thus, when it is understood that all [beings] possess the qualification [to perform sacrifices] through the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the injunctions regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) come to have a capable object; therefore, it is argued that even animals and plants possess this qualification. To this, it is replied: because the connection with the auxiliaries is understood as being constant (*nityavat*), there would be the consequence of subverting them if they were merely occasional (*pākṣikatva*); thus, only that which is accompanied by the auxiliaries is the means to the fruit, not anything else. [Objection: But since the auxiliaries serve a single purpose, there might be an option (*vikalpa*) between them—just as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*)—such that the primary rite (*pradhāna*), even when joined with only one or another auxiliary, would be a means to the fruit.

Do not speak thus. For it is not merely the state of having a single purpose (*ekārthatva*) that is the reason for optionality (*vikalpa*); rather, it is the fact of being independent [yet] accomplishing a single benefit. Furthermore, there is no single purpose for the *samit* and other [fuel-sticks], because the injunctions regarding the *samit* and others—being mutually independent—each postulate a distinct intermediate apūrva known as a "benefit. As the author of the Bhāṣya has said: "And that which is performed through connection with the *samit* is not [the same as] that which is performed through connection with the *tanūnapāt*."

But is it not the case that there is a single benefit through all the constituent parts (*aṃśa*), and yet there is no independence (*nairapekṣya*) among them? For if the *samits* and other subsidiaries were enjoined as means for a benefit already established beforehand, then—since they would all be understood as means to that [benefit] independently of one another—there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between them. But this is not so; for it has already been explained that when the subsidiaries are connected to the primary rite, the benefit is only postulated subsequently, based merely on their being for the sake of that primary.

Therefore, for the purpose of avoiding conceptual constructions corrupted by the eight defects, because the cultivation of the principal [meditation] is enjoined as distinguished by its constituent parts taken together, all [the factors] possess the status of being means to the fruit simultaneously, by virtue of accomplishing a single benefit, just like the Āgneya and other [sacrifices].

In the case of the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, it is understood that where there is a single purpose, there is no independence; and where there is independence, there is no single purpose. Thus, the possibility of an option (*vikalpa*) does not arise. However, in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), since both serve as the material for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and thus have a single function, they are understood through two separate scriptural injunctions to be independent of one another; hence, an option between them is appropriate. Therefore, because the entire ritual—including its subsidiaries—is the means to the result, only one who is capable of performing it possesses the entitlement (*adhikāra*).

As for the claim that since all persons are understood to have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the principal injunction (*pradhānavākya*), the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) must therefore pertain to those who are capable, in accordance with that [principal injunction]—that is incorrect, because there is no contradiction. For it is not certain by the principal injunction that all persons have the entitlement; rather, this is understood only in a general sense. In that case, in the absence of a specific means of knowledge (*viśeṣapramāṇa*), the entitlement would belong to all. However, due to the requirement of the subsidiaries, a specific [entitlement] is understood, and thus it does not belong to all.

However, it has been demonstrated in the *Yathāśakti-nirṇaya* that where there is a contradiction with the principal injunction (*pradhānavākya*) regarding a conditional qualification (*naimittikādhikāra*), the inclusion of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) occurs according to one's capacity. Therefore, animals, birds, and the like; Śūdras; those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*); and those whose physical deficiencies cannot be remedied, lack qualification for the Rājasūya and similar sacrifices. Furthermore, since the cutting of portions (*avadāna*) for liquids and other substances is prescribed there in a specific form, there is no restriction based on the nature of the substance itself. Consequently, the application of auxiliary elements is not described as being contrary to the qualification.
Just as there is a description of the qualification according to the application of the constituent parts. ||31||
Thus ends the third chapter of the Nyāyaratnamālā.

Thus, the manner of connection with the directly enjoined (aupadeśika) auxiliary elements, along with its authoritative basis, pertaining to the first six chapters, has been demonstrated. Now, the method of connection with the extended (ātideśika) auxiliary elements, which is to be expounded by the latter six chapters, is being stated. For the class of verbal expressions is twofold: that consisting of direct injunction (upadeśa) and that consisting of extension (atideśa). "This should be done in this way" is an injunction; "This should be done like that" is an extension.

In that regard, the specific extension (*atideśa*) of those [details] belonging to sacrifices such as the *aindrāgna*—which do not have their own prescribed rules—is considered in the seventh chapter and following. Therein, the *prayāja*s and other elements recited in the section on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and similar rites obtain a connection with all sacrifices through direct injunction (*upadeśa*). How so?

For the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) assists the instrument (*karaṇa*) and thus deserves to be connected with that very [instrument]. Moreover, that [instrument] being enjoined as a fruit cannot be joined with the *itikartavyatā*, because it would result in a contradiction of form (*vairūpya*). Therefore, once the sacrifice has been enjoined in relation to the fruit, the ritual duties (*dharmas*) are enjoined by means of an inferred sentence (*anumita-vākya*) which restates (*anūdya*) the sacrifice; consequently, they become enjoined for all sacrifices without distinction.

[Objection: But surely, since the sacrifice under discussion is restated by means of a sentence inferred from its mention within the context (*prakaraṇa*), how can it be considered "pāriplava" (applicable to all)? [Response: This is not a fault, because even from the mention within the context, one must postulate a verbal root *yaji* (to sacrifice) itself as the restater of the primary act; and by that [root], through its own inherent power, there is a restatement of all sacrifices. Even when one postulates [the injunction] as "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," since it is impossible to intend a qualification for that which is being pointed out as the subject, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the ritual properties (*dharma*) apply to all [sacrifices].

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the meaning of the suffix is indeed *bhāvanā* (productive activity), which is enjoined as qualified by the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And its distinction from other verbal forms and so forth has been established through its nature as having an apūrva (transcendental result) as its concomitant. In that case, when one *bhāvanā* qualified by a specific procedure is being enjoined, how could there be the attainment of another? The *bhāvanā* being enjoined itself is connected with the three factors in a manner that does not violate its uniformity.

Once that specific [injunction]—namely, "one should do this in this manner by means of this"—has been enjoined, the mutual relationship between the constituent parts follows thereafter, according to the principle of the *aruṇa-ekahāyanī* (the red one-year-old cow). As it has been said:
"The three parts, though grasped together by a single productive urge (*bhāvanā*), subsequently experience a state of mutual assistance as the assisted and the assister."

Although the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) assists only the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is nevertheless not directly connected with that [instrument]; for it is not the case that "the sacrifice is thus," but rather "one should act in this manner. Therefore, because of its connection with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the collection of subsidiaries is prompted by a specific *apūrva* whose form is the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), and is thus not promiscuous (*pāriplava*). Even if it were prompted by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), since it is enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice under discussion (*prakṛta-yāga*), it would not be promiscuous.

Although a term may have a general meaning, it functions in a specific sense by virtue of its governing context; therefore, even under the view that [the ritual details] are prompted by the sacrifice (*yajiprayuktatva*), there is no universal promiscuity (*pāriplavatva*). And so the Commentator will state in the first section of the ninth book: "Are the ritual properties restricted to each respective context, or do they all apply everywhere? This is established whether [the properties] are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) or prompted by the sacrifice. If this is so, why then has the prompting by the *apūrva* been established here?

Even though [the ritual acts] are employed for the sake of the sacrifice (*yajña*), they can indeed be established as being restricted by their respective specificities, because they are employed for those particular [ends]. However, when one intends to speak of the subsequent [result], the connection with the *apūrva*-bhāvanā (the creative force of the unseen) is stated; thus there is no fault. It is reasonable that the collection of ritual properties (*dharmajāta*) connected with the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) is "employed for the sake of the object to be produced. But as for the object to be produced itself, they would not say that it is the *apūrva* which produces heaven (*svarga*). For, as the author of the Bhāṣya states in various places, it is the *bhāvanā* that is said to belong to the fruit.

In the section concerning the "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*), [the author] demonstrates that the inquiry concerns the specific nature of the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*)—namely, whether it is the sacrifice or the desire—and shows that in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the desire itself is the end to be achieved. Furthermore, in the section concerning the Viśvajit sacrifice (*viśvajidadhikaraṇa*), he states that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not assert that the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is what must be performed; for by saying, "Indeed, that [unseen potency] is understood only when there is a state of being the agent with respect to a fruit," he demonstrates that the postulation of the unseen potency occurs subsequent to the determination of the fruit as the end to be achieved.

Even in the Siddhānta, while demonstrating the requirement for a specific fruit (*phalaviśeṣa*), it is not the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself that is enjoined as something to be performed (*kartavya*). Rather, at that time, there arises an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*) as to what else is to be produced by that operation; thus [the author] says: "How, then, is the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the sacrifice (*yaji*) heard here? [It is said: 'One should effect something else by means of the aggregate of sacrifices known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa'—it is that *apūrva* which is enjoined as the thing to be performed, not the sacrifice. Therefore, this must be explained. Why was it explained by the Bhāṣyakāra himself?

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that in this sentence, 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' the fruit is heard of, and therefore that [fruit] must be what is to be performed? Having raised this, the following is offered as a reply: "True, it is heard of, but it is not produced by the sacrifice; for when the sacrifice has perished, that [fruit] comes into being. However, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is produced by it; therefore, it is not the [fruit] whose performance is enjoined. The meaning of this is as follows: the sacrifice does not directly accomplish the fruit because it is perishable; rather, it does so through the medium of the *apūrva*.

Because of the determination that "the fruit will arise only when that unprecedented [result] has been produced," that [sacrifice] must be performed for the sake of its accomplishment; thus, the collection of subsidiaries is prompted by the future [fruit]. Just as the restraint of speech [leads to] an intermediate result, it culminates in an intermediate *apūrva*. This very point is further clarified by means of an objection: since the manifest subordination of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) to the fruit cannot occur through multiple repetitions, it is understood to be mediated by the *apūrva*.

By this, the commentary on the first part of the ninth [chapter] is also explained: the requirement for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not felt toward the meaning of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), as in "how is it to be done? rather than "of what kind is the sacrifice (*yajis*)? Therefore, that which is to be accomplished is connected with the procedure, and that is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). By stating "it is to be accomplished," [the author] shows that the meaning of the suffix is an activity directed toward an end (*bhāvya*) and conjoined with an injunction.

Therefore, "that which is to be done" (kartavyam) means that for the sake of the result (*bhāvya*) of that operation, there is a requirement for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance); this is the meaning. And since that [result] is the *apūrva*—because the status of being the *bhāvya* (the end to be produced) cannot belong directly to the fruit [of the action], it is transferred to the *apūrva*—therefore, that alone is said to be the direct *bhāvya*. Consequently, in the *Viśvajit* section, when the necessity of performing another [action] through an operation is stated, the question "of what [is it the result]? arises as a requirement; thus, the [implicit] ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is not tenable.

For when the specific object to be brought about (bhāvya), called the "unprecedented" (apūrva), is denoted by its own word itself, then no expectancy would arise as to what the state of being the object to be brought about belongs to, such that there would be an elliptical supply (adhyāhāra) of that specific object. But when the operation directed toward the object to be brought about is accompanied by an injunction—namely, "it must be done"—then an elliptical supply arises, necessitated by the requirement for a specific object to be brought about. This is the case elsewhere as well.

Whether it is said that the sacrifice is to be performed or that the desire is to be performed, the point is not that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is to be performed; rather, by stating "But surely the fruit must be what is to be performed," that very [point] is established. It is not the case that the word-meaning of the term *bhāvya* (that which is to be brought about) refers to the *apūrva*. Therefore, for those who prattle that the author of the Bhāṣya stated that the *apūrva* is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) due to a failure to consider such arguments as these, mere indifference is the only appropriate response.

But for what purpose is the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) accepted for a new, inferential future result (*bhāvyabhāva*), while abandoning a perceptually apprehended future result? This too has been addressed by the Commentator himself, who raised the objection: "In the case of the fruit, the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the sacrifice (*yajati*) is perceptible, whereas the *apūrva* is inferential," and then [replied] that even though it is perceptible...

It is understood that because [the result] cannot arise otherwise, it occurs through a mediated process (*praṇālika*). And by this much, there is no loss of the status of sacrifice as an instrument (*karaṇa*) established by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). For even that which brings about a result through a mediated process is an instrument; for example, "they cook with cow-dung" or "they become cooked from husks. By this, the objection is refuted. How is it refuted by this? It is said:

Although the relationship between the sacrifice and its fruit is directly perceived, it cannot occur immediately for that which is momentary; therefore, it is resorted to through the mediation of an inferred *apūrva*. Once the *apūrva* is inferred, there is no distinction whatsoever between the fruit and the *apūrva*, since both are understood to be the "thing-to-be-attained" (*bhāvya*). Furthermore, because the means [to the fruit] is not yet known, there is no reason here why the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) should bypass the *apūrva*—which is the immediate thing-to-be-attained—and proceed instead toward the fruit.

By this, the application of the properties of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*), and the milk offerings (*sānnāyya*), as well as the rules of speech-restraint (*vāṅniyama*) and so forth, to their respective intermediate apūrvas has been explained. Therefore, it is established that because they are connected to the bhāvanā of the intermediate apūrva, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are fixed and not promiscuous (*pāriplava*). Consequently, for sacrifices such as the Aindrāgna for which no properties have been taught, the properties are established through extension (*atideśa*); it is for the purpose of proving this that the seventh book (*adhyāya*) and those following must be commenced.

In that regard, in the seventh [chapter], the entire extended application (atideśa), including its exceptions, is to be established by means of direct scriptural statement and by name; furthermore, the extended application based on inference is also treated in general terms. However, its specific details are considered in the eighth [chapter].

In the ninth [book], however, having established that the primary status of the ritual action—which is to be accomplished by the tenth book and those following—is applicable to the ritual elements extended [from the archetype], an investigation into specific applications known as *ūha* (adaptation) is undertaken. Although the word *ūha* generally denotes mere reasoning (*tarka*), in this treatise it refers specifically to that reasoning concerning the modification of ritual elements that were understood in one way [in the archetype] but must be applied otherwise [in the ectype]. Furthermore, although in this context only the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) is being considered—namely, whether the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is prompted by the acts of threshing and grinding in the archetype, or rather prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*).

Is the number three employed because it is enjoined by the *pravovājīya* hymn, or because it is employed as the first [number]? Do the words *savitṛ* and so forth denote what is inherently present [in the sacrifice], or not? Is the word *yajñapati* (lord of the sacrifice) used for its own sake or for the sake of another? Is the recitation of the mantra prompted by the essential nature of Agni, or is it prompted by a specific deity?

Similarly, even in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), regarding other items such as wild rice (*nīvāra*), the insertion of nails (*nakha-āvapana*), the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), and the eating of honey (*madhu-aśana*), their application through the fivefold method consists solely in the instruction that they take the place of the functions of the original (*prākṛta*) rice and so forth; nevertheless, its proper connection is immediately after the eighth [book]. For, when considering the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone, no desire to know the specific application arises, due to the absence of a cause for it.

When, however, the ritual details (dharmas) have been extended by analogy (atideśa) to a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the question arises: "How are these to be applied here? Furthermore, as a means to that end, there arises the desire to know: "For what purpose were these employed in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti)? Therefore, the investigation into the original injunction (upadeśa) also results in a specific application regarding those things extended by analogy; thus, it is commenced immediately after the section on specific extension (viśeṣātideśa). As an introductory supplement to this, the principle that [the details] are prompted by the transcendental result (apūrva) is recalled, having been established in the first section of the seventh book (Adhyāya).

Alternatively, this very point is established here: it has been stated that the determination of the *dharma* is consistent even when [the rites] are prompted by specific sacrifices (*yajiviśeṣa*). As for *ūha* (modification), however, since it cannot exist without being prompted by the *apūrva*, its being prompted by the *apūrva* in this context has been asserted. Or rather, while in that [previous] case [it concerned] the indirectly contributing factors (*ārādupakārin*), here the prompting by that [apūrva] is predicated of the directly contributing factors (*sannipātin*). In that [previous] case, however, the reference to the directly contributing factors was merely for the purpose of refuting an objection.

In that [previous section], it was merely a sign (nimitta), whereas here the *prayojaka* (the motivating factor) has been investigated; thus, there is no tautology. Furthermore, the subordination of ritual items (*padārtha*) based on their utility (*upakāra*), which is to be established in the tenth book and its subsequent sections, must be relied upon for the sake of accomplishing modification (*ūha*). Otherwise, that would be impossible. For when ritual items are connected to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) without regard for their utility—just as they were in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*)—then their performance would have to occur exactly as they stood, just as in that model. But when, as in the case of...

Since assistance was rendered in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and subsequently in the ectype (*vikṛti*), the benefit is first established; and since such an assistance is known to arise from those very constituent elements (*padārtha*), their extension (*atideśa*) occurs later for the sake of accomplishing that [assistance].
