In that case, since one must reciprocate exactly as one has been assisted, even when there is a modification (*vikṛti*), the remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) serve as means for producing an unseen assistance toward the arising of the supreme *apūrva*. Likewise, the directly-contributing auxiliaries (*sannipātinaḥ*), whether they produce a visible or invisible effect upon their own substrate, serve as means for the arising *apūrva* by way of generating the capacity for the sacrifice. Even the mantras provide assistance by way of manifesting the deity and so forth; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [assistance], the modification (*ūha*) of directly-contributing elements—namely mantras, *sāmans*, and purificatory rites—is established.

For it is not the case that the sprinkling performed upon the rice grains does not accomplish the archetypal auxiliary benefit for the *naivāra* sacrificial cake; thus, it must be modified (*ūhitavya*). The same should be understood regarding the transfer of *sāmans* to other *ṛks*.

Even in the case of mantras, when there is a modification (*vikṛti*) involving a different deity or a different substance, it is not possible for them to provide assistance as they do in the original form (*prakṛti*) while remaining unmodified. Therefore, *ūha* (adaptation) is established as an eightfold application, consisting of the alteration of each of the nominal stem, gender, and number individually, or of two of them together, or of all three collectively; or alternatively, it consists of the repetition of those very elements as they stand. It should be understood that since the priority of the ritual action (*kārya*) must be taken into account even in that *ūha*, the discussion has been commenced here in the middle [of the treatise] as being common to both *ūha* and *bādha* (sublation).

In the tenth [chapter], the extent of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) is considered by way of sublation (*bādha*) and augmentation (*abhyuccaya*). But how is the sublation of that which is obtained through scriptural injunction determined? We shall explain this as it is. First, for the sake of establishing that, the following is considered: is the collection of archetypal subsidiaries (*prākṛta-aṅga-jāta`) transferred to the modification (*vikṛti*) in its own form alone, disregarding the benefit (*upakāra*), such that one asks, "How should one perform the *saurya* sacrifice?"

The method by which the Āgneya sacrifice accomplishes its own purpose is extended [by analogy] to the Saurya sacrifice; consequently, as a means to that end, the intermediate apūrvas produced by the prayāja offerings and so forth, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) produced by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), and the seen (dṛṣṭa) produced by genus, substance, quality, threshing (avaghāta), and so forth—interwoven with the restrictive unseen (niyamādṛṣṭa)—are extended. Then, the constituent elements (padārtha) that serve as the means to those [apūrvas] are extended, along with the verbal injunctions that serve as the means for the cognition of those very same elements.

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the entire collection of subsidiary parts (*aṅga-kalāpa*) constitutes the remainder of the scriptural injunction for the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well; therefore, when all those parts are enjoined, one may assume—just as in the archetype—a visible or invisible purpose according to the circumstances. Thus, there is no sublation (*bādha*). Even if there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the scriptural texts themselves, nevertheless it is the constituent elements (*padārtha*) that are extended, not the benefit (*upakāra*); because in the archetype the benefit is preceded by the constituent elements, its cognition in the ectype is likewise preceded by them.

In this regard, it is not logical that the assistance provided by the subsequently performed [elements] should be extended by bypassing the elements already performed first. Therefore, since the extension (atideśa) applies to the elements themselves—regardless of their specific functions—it is argued that there is no sublation (bādha), because one can assume here the visible and invisible purposes for those extended elements.
To this, it is replied: "There must be an extension of the *manner* (prakāra), because it was required previously;
therefore, [the application occurs] through the sequence of the intermediate functions, the subsidiary parts, and the verbal injunctions. (Verse 1)

Although in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the assistance [rendered by the subsidiaries] is preceded solely by the scriptural items (*śāstrapadārtha*), nevertheless, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) at the stage of extension (*atideśa*), even though there is no difference in the fact that all scriptural items, entities, and functions are already established, the requirement for "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*) first accepts the very mode of the modified ritual's productive operation (*bhāvanā*). For it is not the scriptures or the entities themselves that are required in their own form, but rather the archetypal mode; that alone is first accepted, and it is extended as qualified by the intermediate functions which are themselves qualified by the entities.

It brings about the qualifications by implication; therefore, for the sake of establishing those [qualifications], there are intermediate acts, and for their sake, the subsidiaries, and from those, the scriptures. Although the word-meanings understood first must be considered in that very same way, nevertheless, because they are not required [at that stage], one disregards the word-meanings and considers only the manner [of performance]. Thus, when the word-meanings are obtained by implication—such as the exclusion of rice (*vrīhi*) in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice where it is directly heard, and the resulting exclusion of threshing (*avaghāta*) which is dependent upon it—the transfer (*atideśa*) applies only to that benefit (*upakāra*) which is endowed with qualifications other than those [excluded ones].

Some [authorities] state that there is a connection of the primary auxiliary (upakāra) with the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) through direct instruction (upadeśa), just like the case of the assistant (niyojya) in the Pitṛyajña. ||2||

An *upadeśa* (direct instruction) is indeed a textual composition (*grantha-sandarbha*), and it presents the meaning of an injunction (*vidhy-artha*) as something to be accomplished (*kāryatayā*) in connection with other matters. That [injunction] is indeed *aupadeśika* (derived from direct instruction). Furthermore, that which is inferred by one who does not find completion [in the text] is also indeed *aupadeśika*, as in the case of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. And just as there is an auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the ectype (*vikṛti*), the benefit postulated by the meaning of the injunction possesses the character of being *aupadeśika*; thus says someone. That is not correct. For, due to the difference in the auxiliaries (*upakāraka-bheda*), there would be a cognition of a specific benefit.
Expectancy indeed exists even prior [to the cognition of the sentence]; that same [expectancy] is equally present in the meanings of the words as well. (3)

The establishment of a specific excellence in assistance depends upon the specific objects that provide that assistance; such a specific form of assistance cannot be determined when those objects have not yet been ascertained. For initially, there is established merely the requirement that "there must be some specific excellence in assistance," and this is exactly the same regarding the objects themselves, since the requirement arises that there must be distinct objects that generate that assistance.

Now, it might be argued that an injunction (*vidhi*) is not capable of implying specific ritual details (*padārtha*) by itself; rather, it requires the presentation of the distinctions among ritual elements such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and giving (*dāna*) through other sentences or by means of extension (*atideśa*). However, it implies the "assistance" (*upakāra*) specifically. For this alone constitutes its specific implication: namely, that there exists some kind of assistance. Indeed, this [assistance] is not defined in the manner of a ritual detail—such as "this is it"—but is rather postulated from the injunction itself as being based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*).

Nevertheless, how can a specific benefit (*upakāra-viśeṣa*) belonging to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) be considered directly taught (*aupadeśika*)? For indeed, without the general rule (*codaka*), an injunction is not capable of implying it. True; nevertheless, although [the archetype] is capable of postulating any specific benefit, it adopts that which belongs to the archetype due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Therefore, even in the case of a specific implication of an injunction, there is merely a restriction (*niyama*) [of that specific benefit] derived from the general rule.

Here [the opponent] says: But if this were so, since it would be possible for threshing and the like—which have visible purposes—as well as substances, qualities, and so forth, to be implied by the injunction itself without restriction, and since the injunction of extension (*atideśa*) would only yield a restriction, it would follow that even rice (*vrīhi*) and other such items would be connected to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) solely through direct instruction (*upadeśa*). Alternatively, if it is defined that whatever substance or the like is directly implied by the injunction is not "taught by direct instruction" (*aupadeśika*), then in that case, the fact that the Viśvajit sacrifice is a means to the fruit of heaven would not be "taught by direct instruction."

This is because [the application] is constructed by the relationship with a specific enjoined person (niyojya) as conceived by the injunction. Therefore, there is no instruction regarding the benefit (upakāra); rather, when co-present with the ritual elements (padārtha), the extension (atideśa) of the benefit itself is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For extension is indeed the state of being like that (tadvadbhāva). Thus, the distinction is this: that which is obtained either directly or through a mediated process is "extended" (ātideśika), whereas that which is established solely by the textual arrangement, independently of that [extension], through direct statement (śruti) or meaning (artha), is "original" (āpadeśika).

As for what is also said—that even though an auxiliary (*upakāra*) taught for one [element] may be extended (*atideśa*) to another, it thus possesses the status of being "extended," and therefore, because both direct teaching (*upadeśa*) and extension (*atideśa*) can occur simultaneously in a single instance, these two are not distinct means of knowledge (*śabdapramāṇa*) that stand in opposition; and for this very reason, there are not two sets of six based on teaching and extension—but rather, they are associated with the function of teaching (*upadeśakārya*), and "function" (*kārya*) here is a designation for the assistance produced by the word-meanings, not for the mandate (*niyoga*).

For this very reason, the implication of an injunction (*vidhyākṣepa*), which is designated as "appropriation" (*upādāna*), was considered in the first six chapters (*pūrva-ṣaṭka*), because the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*) and the others are implied by the injunction. However, matters such as the "framework and insertion" (*tantrāvāpa*) were investigated in the latter six chapters (*uttara-ṣaṭka*), since they concern the determination of assistance (*upakāra*) even in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Otherwise, [if these were not so determined], they would merely fall within the scope of extended application (*atideśa*).

The investigation into whether the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries are to be performed for the *āgneya* and other sacrifices by way of a single performance (*tantra*) or by repetition (*āvṛtti*), and so forth, would not be relevant here; therefore, the two groups of six [topics] do not rely upon direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*), but rather rely upon the functions of direct instruction. That too is refuted because, according to the reasoning already stated, it is impossible for the assistance (*upakāra*) to be based on direct instruction. For indeed, only direct instruction and extended application are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the two groups of six depend upon them; such being the case, how could there be an investigation into *tantra*, *āvāpa*, and so forth, regarding matters that are the objects of direct instruction?

Otherwise, how could there be an investigation—based on the names and designations of the seventh and eighth [books], and by means of non-injunctions and indicative marks—concerning the *upakāra* (auxiliary benefit), which is to be known through direct instruction? For we say that such an investigation would be incidental (*cāturthikī*), as it falls within the scope of what is implied by the injunction, for the purpose of establishing the attainment of the constituent elements (*padārtha*). Indeed, if the *upakāra* were not established, it would be impossible to describe the attainment of the constituent elements by virtue of it. Therefore, that investigation is an *upoddhāta* (introductory or preparatory discussion).

"Like the refutation of the state of being *pāriplava*": even in our own position, the discussion regarding *tantra*, *āvāpa*, and so forth is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). For, once the determination of the number of constituent elements (*padārtha*) has been established in the tenth book, the occasions for *tantra* and *āvāpa*—which consist in the measurement of the performance (*prayoga*)—are considered in connection with the topic of measurement (*parimāṇa*). And since these apply equally to both the prescribed (*upadiṣṭa*) and the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) constituent elements, the application of *tantra* and the rest must indeed begin only after both have been dealt with.

Although an initiation [of the discussion] might be possible even near the fourth and fifth [books], since they consist of an investigation into specific types of application (*prayoga-viśeṣa*), nevertheless, an initiation here is also possible because this [sixth book] consists of an investigation into measure (*parimāṇa*). Since the objection is no different, an initiation must likewise take place here; for according to your own view, since the seventh and eighth books—consisting of investigations into both [measure and application]—have as their objects of knowledge the categories of "effect" (*kārya*) and "substance" (*padārtha*) taught [in the first book], they would be included within either of the two groups following the fourth [book]; therefore, one of them must necessarily be commenced.

The commencement of the subsequent group of eight [auxiliaries] is due to a specific truth; likewise for us as well, there is no fault regarding the beginning of the *tantra* and so forth. Furthermore, the acceptance of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) after the attainment of the assistance (*upakāra*) is also useless, because the constituent elements are attained by implication through the very attainment of the specific assistance. Moreover, in this case, the specific rules (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) are not postulated subsequent to the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*). This is because, following the rule concerning the assistance common to all constituent elements, rules for specific constituent elements cannot possibly exist.

Thus it is established that when things are obtained through their effects, there is a sublation in the absence of those effects. Consequently, the objection that "it is not proper for there to be a sublation of what is obtained by a scriptural statement" is refuted; for a scriptural statement itself brings about the constituent parts (padārthas) by means of their effects, and in the absence of those [effects], its power as a bringer-about is contradicted. Such is the nature of the scriptural statement: "Just as the Āgneya sacrifice is assisted, so too is the Saurya. What is that by which assistance must be rendered? It is the intermediate effect (avāntara-kārya), such as the *samidh* offerings and so forth.

That too must be produced by those very same materials, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), exactly according to their original nature. Thus, having understood the general application, one subsequently examines the constituent elements in their own form, considering: "How has this assisted? How has that assisted? In that context, having observed that threshing (*avaghāta*) provides assistance through its visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaprayojana*) in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), and because such a state is impossible in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, one concludes that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the previously arisen general knowledge.

Thus, even in the case of a substitute (pratyāmnāna), when ritual items are obtained through their functions, the function of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—namely, the placing of the oblation—is first established. While there is a requirement for its means of accomplishment, before the *kuśa* grass can be obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), the *śara* grass is prescribed by a direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavākya*) for that very purpose; therefore, there is a sublation of the *kuśa*. Similarly, in the case of a prohibition, there is a displacement (*utkālana*) of the general form of the *codaka* from its specific object, as in: "One should not choose a *ṛṣi* lineage."

Therefore, having excluded those auxiliary elements whose purpose is lost, those that have been replaced, and those that are prohibited, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is established as applying only to the remaining auxiliaries; thus, the sublation (*bādha*) is proven.

Some declare that even for acts such as *han* (striking), though their purpose is lost in cases like the *kṛṣṇala* gold pieces, they still possess the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣatā*), even if there is no actual performance. ||4||
This is for the purpose of establishing that [the sublated cognition] has been sublated; otherwise, it would not be established.
For if the attainment [of the object] were being prevented, it would be like the case of direct Vedic statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and so forth. ||5||

For the established position is that the third [type of sublation] is indeed "sublation of what has not been obtained" (*aprāptabādha*). In that case, if the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) itself were not accepted for those elements whose purpose is lost, then since there would be no prior application (*prāpti*) of the *han* (striking) and other such acts, the terminology of "sublation of what has been obtained" (*prāptabādha*) would be inappropriate; it would instead be merely a "sublation of what has not been obtained," like the cases of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth. Therefore, by means of the *codaka*, the entire collection of archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries is indeed brought forward; however, while this application remains, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains and similar instances, because there is an absence of purpose for the *han* and other acts, there occurs a sublation characterized by non-performance.

Likewise, in the case of the injunction "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara*," there is a sublation characterized by that very [definition], because the *darbha* grass—whose status as an auxiliary member is understood through the *codaka* (transfer rule) and remains unsublated—is not included within the performance injunction (*prayogavacana*), which is satisfied by the directly perceived *śara* grass. Similarly, in the case of "one should not choose a *ṛṣi*-descendant (*anārṣeya*)," since the prohibition itself is included within the performance injunction, the choosing—which, though previously established, is now impossible—is simply not performed.

Therefore, since the *codaka* (the extended injunction) cannot be prevented from anything at all, it is said that even though everything is brought forward by it, it is nonetheless set aside because it lacks inclusion within the *prayogavidhi* (the injunction of performance). And this is logical; for there is no separate *codaka* for each individual constituent element (*padārtha*) such that one might be obtained while another is excluded. Indeed, in the "Sūtra on Assistance" (*upakāra-sūtra*), the entire collection of jewels that are the archetypal elements (*prākṛta-padārtha*) is strung together; thus, when that [collection] is drawn forth, everything is drawn forth, and if it is not drawn forth, nothing at all is. As it has been said:

"But that [omission] is due to the attainment [of the rule] through explicit statement, because the purpose of the injunction is complete in its entirety. Now, is this commentary merely the rambling of a madman, suggesting that there is no statement of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) for those elements whose purpose has been lost? And [is it not also said]: "Therefore, the *codaka* does not enjoin that which has lost its original (*prākṛta*) purpose"? Likewise, [is it not said]: "Sublation (*bādha*) is when a certain cognition in the form 'this is thus' is rendered false by another cause"? We say: No.

Falsehood, first of all, consists in the intention behind the performance [of an action], for the falsity of all cognitions arises precisely from a discrepancy with empirical practice (*vyavahāra*), and not from a lack of correspondence with reality (*ayāthārthya*). For it has been stated that a cognition which is non-correspondent with reality is impossible. Regarding the claim that "whatever is perception does not err, and what errs is not perception," this is because in cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, it was declared to be a case of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*). If you say, "In that case, let it be a non-apprehension just like that," we say no; for the causes of apprehension are present.

It is indeed logical that the eyes and other sense organs, because they function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), cannot grasp silver that is not present; therefore, non-apprehension [of such silver] occurs. In this case, however, since the cause for apprehension—namely, the water—is present, non-apprehension is impossible. How then does sublation (*bādha*) occur? It was stated that it is due to a discrepancy in practical activity (*vyavahāra-visaṃvāda*). But we see that this very point is not tenable. For practical activity based on non-apprehension would only be reversed when the apprehension [of the true object] dispels that non-apprehension. To this, it is replied:

Only the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is understood through the *codaka* (the extended injunction), but performance does not follow from that alone. Since that [performance] is caused by the inclusion [of elements] within the ritual procedure (*prayoga-vidhi*), and because that [procedure] does not include those things whose purpose has been sublated, there indeed occurs here too a discrepancy between the theoretical understanding and actual practice.
Otherwise, even knowledge would not arise here from the *codaka*.

That [cognition] would be produced by a defective cause, whereas the person who enjoins it (the *codaka*) here is not defective. Even for those who hold the view that a cognition which has arisen with an unreal object, such as the water of a mirage, is rendered false by another cognition that reveals the true nature of the object—those [who hold this view] are likewise unable to declare that the cognition of the attainment of an entity produced by that [injunction] is false on account of the non-existence of the object and so forth, because the cognition produced by the [injunction] arises from a non-defective source while the cognition of the mirage arises from a defective cause.
In this context, "sublation" (*bādha*) consists merely in the non-performance [of the action], even though the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are present.

Therefore, since there is an absence of the performance of that result even for those items obtained through the *codaka*, it is explained by way of the result that there is no *codaka* statement, nor does the *codaka* enjoin anything. To this we reply:
How can there be a connection of the ritual elements (*padārtha*) with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by means of the *codaka*?
Does it occur independently of any purpose, or rather by means of that [purpose]? (8)

Having postulated a purpose for those [elements] that are independent when combined, why would there be an application in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or a sublation in the modified form (*vikṛti*)? ||9||
There would be a sublation of the locus if such a connection were possible;
but if the attainment occurs through the mediation of the effect, how could it occur when that [effect] is omitted? (10)

For one who maintains that there is a sublation consisting in the non-performance of those very auxiliaries whose status as auxiliaries is established by the *codaka* (the general transfer rule) and remains unsublated, he must be asked about this option: does the attainment of the status of an auxiliary for the *hansa*-grains and so forth in the case of the *kṛṣṇala*-grains occur through the *codaka* independently of the original purpose, or rather by means of that [original purpose]? And if he should say that the connection with the modification occurs independently of that [purpose], one should reply to him as follows:

That being the case, since the status of [the *hṛdaya* and other organs] as subsidiaries is understood through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), one would have to postulate a purpose—whether visible or invisible—for their suitability; thus, because they would be employed in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) such as the *kṛṣṇala* offering just as in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the establishment of "sublation" (*bādha*) characterized by non-performance would not occur. Furthermore, the sublation of the instruments (*karaṇa-bādha*) in the tenth book and elsewhere would result in the absurdity of applying them independently of their specific functions.

If, in order to avoid this objection, he should resort to the second position and say, "The subsidiaries are obtained only by way of their effects (*kārya*), not independently," then one should reply to him: "In that case, the application of the act of *kṛṣṇala*-grains (pounding) is not possible, because of the absence of a medium (*dvāra*). For how can it be said that something enters through a particular medium when no such medium exists for it in that context?"

Indeed, pieces of wood do not produce combustion by virtue of their wetness; rather, they are able to attain the status of being a means for the accomplishment of boiled rice through that [combustion] as an intermediary. In that case, the statement that "the act of threshing is an auxiliary to the *kṛṣṇala*-sacrifice" would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) because it enjoins an impossible purpose by way of a natural intermediary. Regarding this, it may be argued: "The benefit produced by all the auxiliaries is first indicated;
thereafter, there is the extended application (*atideśana*) of the auxiliaries through their intermediate functions. (Verse 11)

We do not say that the extension of the meaning of the word is independent of the effect; rather, the assistance produced by all the subsidiaries is extended first. However, immediately after that, there is no extension of the intermediate effects, but rather of the subsidiaries themselves, and that assistance indeed exists even in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains.

Since the ritual items (*padārtha*) are extended [to the modified sacrifice] precisely as means for accomplishing that [result], there is no non-attainment [of them]. Thus, when the status of the items as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) toward the *apūrva* is understood by way of their contribution (*upakāra*), and it is recognized that their capacity to produce that contribution follows the very same procedure known in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no occasion to postulate a different procedure. Furthermore, since it is not possible for the act of threshing (*avaghātaka*) to produce that [contribution] in this [modified sacrifice] in such a manner, it is not performed. Therefore, both attainment and performance are logically established. Consequently, the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) remains intact, as it does not admit the attainment of items independently of their contribution.
This too does not avoid the previously mentioned objection;
for when the status of being a remainder is perceived, it is independent of its function as a means [to another purpose]. ||12||

Resorting to another mode of assistance for the archetypal sacrifice, it would, in our view, become a cause for the initial [sacrifice], just like an auxiliary belonging to a previously unestablished rite. (13)

Although the extension (*atideśa*) of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is indeed preceded by the assistance [to the primary], nevertheless, since the status of being a subsidiary is understood as independent of intermediate effects, and because that [status] cannot be established without a means for accomplishing the assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*), and because that [assistance] cannot be accomplished through the method known from the archetype (*prakṛti*), the performance of subsidiaries such as *avaghāta* (threshing) and *āmanahoma* (the *āmanah* oblation)— which are like the *apūrva*s— would have to be undertaken by postulating their status as instruments of the sacrifice through some other mode.

Furthermore, you maintain that entities are related even with respect to the benefit they produce; yet those entities do not have their connection to the benefit established first. For there is no word denoting a benefit that could express a benefit as already connected to the meanings of the words. Nor do the words denoting the entities themselves exist in a modified form that could express the entities as connected to the benefit.

Therefore, since the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) itself is expressed by its own word as being connected to the purpose of the ritual elements, the performance of the rite must take place after having postulated it as the means to achieve that [purpose]. And thus:

Even though intermediate effects are obtained from the assistance [rendered by the subsidiaries] and from those [effects] the constituent elements (padārthas) are reached, nevertheless, because they are not directly expressed by words (*aśabda*) and thus lack mutual connection, their relation to the purpose is established only through the *apūrva*; therefore, even for those whose means are lost, the performance must indeed take place by way of postulating that [the *apūrva*]. If it is argued that the status of being a means to the assistance is not necessarily inherent in the subsidiaries, and therefore one should not postulate their being means to the assistance—[we reply: how then is the assistance postulated in the archetype (*prakṛti*)? Because it is required.

For the primary act (pradhāna) indeed has a requirement for assistance; therefore, in the archetype (prakṛti), the capacity of the subsidiary elements (śeṣas) to produce that assistance is postulated. However, in the ectype (vikṛti), since the primary act’s lack of expectancy is satisfied by the very assistance produced by the collection of subsidiaries whose purposes are not lost, there is no postulation of an assisting capacity for those [subsidiaries] whose purposes are lost. This is not sound.

For if even those things that provide no assistance were considered auxiliary members (*aṅga*), then the postulation of their being generators [of the transcendental result]—which is based on their dependence on the primary rite—would be untenable. Indeed, in the case of modified rites (*vikṛti*) which have already obtained the archetypal assistance, there is an absence of such dependence; consequently, for new elements (*apūrva*) such as the *āmana-homa* and others, there would be no basis for postulating them as generators [of the result], and thus, due to their lack of assistance, their performance would not be established—just as in the case of the *avaghāta* (threshing) and so forth. If it is argued that their performance is required out of fear that the scriptural injunctions would otherwise be rendered meaningless (*vacanānarthakya*), yet the extended application (*codaka*) is not meaningless since its purpose is fulfilled by other auxiliary members, [we reply: no. For even in the presence of other auxiliaries, the *codaka* would still be subject to the same fault of meaninglessness regarding those specific new elements. Thus, the performance of those [new elements] would not be established. Therefore, the postulation of their being generators of the result is not tenable. Consequently, the view that the *apūrva* is produced from the primary sacrifice itself is the correct one. This is because the archetypal procedure (*prakṛti*) is indeed established through the *codaka*, and the archetypal auxiliaries are understood to be present in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) by virtue of that very *codaka*. Hence, the archetypal auxiliaries are not repeated in the modified rite. Furthermore, if the archetypal auxiliaries were not included in the modified rite, then the *codaka* would be meaningless with respect to them, and the modified rite would fail to obtain the archetypal assistance. Therefore, the archetypal auxiliaries are not repeated in the modified rite. As for the new elements (*apūrva*) such as the *āmana-homa*, they are not included in the modified rite because they are not mentioned in the archetype. Since they are not mentioned in the archetype, they cannot be brought over to the modified rite by the *codaka*. Thus, the performance of those [new elements] is not established. Therefore, the archetypal auxiliaries

To say that it [the *tva*-affix] is [the indicator] is incorrect, because here too there would be purposelessness (*ānarthakya*). For it is not intended that the application of the word-meaning follows merely from the attainment of an assistance common to all word-meanings; rather, since the injunction of word-meanings is desired precisely through the scripture itself, and since those [meanings] lack a generic form, there must be an extension (*atideśa*) for each one individually. Consequently, even in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*), if the scripture were not followed, it would be purposeless. Therefore, there is no other recourse but either its non-extension or its performance.

Let it be useless as you wish; however, one cannot postulate that a meaning is not understood merely on that account, for there is no evidence here that it produces any benefit. [Objection: But surely the very impossibility of its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is the proof, since something that provides no benefit cannot be an auxiliary. [Reply: Alas! Because of the statement "it should be like the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*), another mode of providing benefit is not possible. Therefore, if you say that there is non-performance [of the act], that has already been answered: the scriptural authority enjoining the threshing as an auxiliary "like the archetype" would apply to the *kṛṣṇala* grains.

Furthermore, if it is argued that since the application [of the original rule] is not sublated, why should there be a performance of the *kuśa* grasses whose purpose is not lost, on the grounds of substitution (*pratyāmnāna*)? No; for even by that [substitution], the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is not destroyed. Therefore, since the status of being auxiliaries is unsublated for both the *kuśa* and the *śara* grasses, their performance would occur as an option (*vikalpa*) because they serve the same purpose, not through sublation. But how can there be an option between the direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and the extended application (*atideśa*), which possess unequal strength? Or rather, should it be said that the extended application is sublated by the direct injunction? If you say "yes," then the *kuśa* grasses do not have the status of being auxiliaries, because the authority for them—the extended application—has been sublated.

Now, there is neither sublation (*bādha*) of the extended application (*atideśa*), nor is there an option (*vikalpa*). What then? Is it a combination (*samuccaya*)? That too is not the case, because they serve the same purpose (*aikārthya*). If so, why was it stated that there is non-performance due to the ritual injunction (*prayoga-vacana*) not encompassing [the two]? We reply that that very statement is incorrect, because there is no sublation of their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*). Indeed, what difference is there between *kuśa* grass and *śara* reeds, both of which are auxiliaries and means of accomplishing the benefit (*upakāra*), such that a person of poor character would have an attachment for the injunction regarding the *śara* reeds alone, as if in the second instance?

This is the distinction: for the *śruti* texts, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the authority, whereas for the others, it is inference (*anumāna*). This distinction is not valid, because even by means of direct perception, inference remains uncontradicted. For when there is a conflict between two authorities, one becomes false due to the sublation of its object of cognition (*prameya*) by the stronger one; however, when the object of cognition is not sublated, since both serve equally as the means to accomplish the purpose, the performance of the rite is identical, as the cause for the action is undifferentiated. Indeed, an injunction (*vidhi*), being itself that which is to be accomplished, implies the performance of the means, and the status of being a means belongs to both.

Since there is no difference in the status of the *kuśa* and *śara* grasses as subsidiaries, and since both are equally possible as means [of fulfillment], there is no distinction regarding the requirement for their performance. Therefore, because both are performed, there is no sublation (*bādha*) characterized by non-performance. Similarly, in the case of the rule "one should not choose an *ārṣeya*," having accepted the alternative of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) itself was relied upon by the *codaka* (the extended injunction) to avoid that [prohibition]. If it is argued that the exclusion mentioned there pertains to the general form of the independent injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), which is instructional in nature, and not to the *atideśa* (extended application).

How then is the mention of "a portion" [of the rite] to be understood? If you say it is to be disregarded because it contradicts logic, alas! What a great delusion you have resorted to, in that you attribute falsehood to your own ignorance. For it has already been stated that when there is no sublation of the general application (*aṅgatva*), there is no distinction whatsoever between what is taught directly (*upadiṣṭa*) and what is extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*). Furthermore, even if the two objects of cognition (*prameya*) are not set aside, if the performance or non-performance of an action were to occur based on the distinction that "this is cognized by a stronger means of knowledge" and "that is cognized by a weaker means of knowledge," then...

One who perceives fire from afar, yet infers it from a nearby object, would abandon that which has been inferred and run toward the distant one if he desired to cook. Similarly, regarding the general injunction "one performs the *yeyajāmahe* in sacrifices," because the specific prohibition "one does not perform the *yeyajāmahe* in *anuyāja*s" is more powerful than the rule prescribing the word (the *yeyajāmahe*), just as the scriptural rule regarding the *āhavanīya* fire overrides others, it can be asserted that the *yeyajāmahe* is not performed in the *anuyāja*s even when the prohibition exists; thus, the demonstration of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is useless.

Therefore, as long as the application [of a rule] remains uncontradicted, non-performance is in no way possible; thus, it is the very application that must be sublated. As for the objection that this being so, the designation of "sublation of the applied" (*prāptabādha*) is untenable because there would be no distinction between the third [book on conflict] and the tenth [book on sublation], we reply:
"The restriction of a general rule by means of a specific object and so forth, whereby its established form is curtailed, is what is called 'sublation of the applied' (*prāptabādha*). (Verse 14)

But when the conceptualization of the scripture that is to be conceptualized is itself sublated by the very act of conceptualization—due to the swift removal of the fruit by means of the established [truth] which cuts off the root—they cite that as an instance of "sublation by what was not yet reached" (aprāptabādha). ||15||

Where the application of a rule already established by scripture—which approaches a particular case through a general door—is set aside by a specific injunction such as a *yāga* sacrifice or the like, there is "sublation of what has been obtained" (*prāptabādha*). This occurs, for example, in the sublation of archetypal (*prakṛta*) versus modified (*vaikṛta*), general versus particular, obligatory versus occasional, rites for the sake of the sacrifice versus rites for the sake of the person, earlier versus later, the few versus the many, the unoccupied versus the occupied, and the subsidiary versus the principal, as well as in the sublation of their respective properties. [The sublation] of the archetypal...

For ritual elements (*dharma*) are not obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) by the injunctive text (*codaka*) through their own specific forms as "this must be done" or "that must be done. How then? Just as the primary sacrifice (*prakṛti*) accomplishes its purpose, so too does the modified sacrifice. And such a state can be achieved only when those very constituent parts are connected in that same manner, and not otherwise. Their attainment is understood without distinction through the general form of their capacity to accomplish that purpose.

This cognition, having arisen without distinction, is later rendered erroneous upon the occasion of determining the specific nature of those objects, through the consideration that [the killing] and so forth cannot possibly function as a means [to the desired end]. However, this does not entail the invalidity of the scripture, for it merely postulates the exclusion of specific objects [as its domain].

For, due to the non-perception of specific distinctions, the scripture appears to have everything as its object because of the observation of mere generalities; its lack of authority arises from the false assumption that it encompasses all particular objects. Indeed, through the non-perception of specific distinctions and the observation of mere generalities, the scripture is mistakenly understood to have everything as its domain.

Upon seeing this, it is considered that this [particular rule] is not the domain of that [general rule], for the scripture has another domain altogether; rather, due to the fault of considering only the general aspect, it was erroneously determined to have this as its domain. Therefore, through the loss of purpose (*arthalopa*), substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), there is a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of the *codaka* (the rule of extension). Similarly, the general scripture enjoining the *āhavanīya* fire is restricted to other types of oblations by a specific scripture enjoining the [*padahomāḥ*] foot-oblations. This applies to the case of the number fifteen (*pāñcadaśya*).

The number seventeen, which is occasional (*naimittika*) and pertains specifically to the Vaiśya, excludes from its scope other castes that are otherwise subject to the permanent (*nitya*) and non-specifically prescribed rule. Furthermore, that number seventeen, being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), excludes from its scope those Vaiśyas other than those desiring stability (*pratiṣṭhākāma*), who are instead subject to the recitation of twenty-one verses for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Moreover, there is no relationship of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) here, because both rules are equally general in their respective domains.

For the recitation of twenty-one verses is common to all three classes for one desiring stability, while the rule of seventeen verses is common to both those desiring stability and those not desiring it—specifically Vaiśyas. However, when a Vaiśya desiring stability encounters both [recitations], there is a sublation of the latter (the seventeen-verse recitation), which serves the purpose of the sacrifice and has a different kind of result, by the former (the twenty-one-verse recitation), which serves the purpose of the person and possesses a more proximate fruit. Likewise, even in the case of sequence, regarding the simultaneous interruption (*upaccheda*) of the *codaka* and the *pratihartr*, since there is no distinction between general and particular, their mutual sublation occurs solely by virtue of their sequence.

In this regard, the meaning of the treatise is as follows: for a sacrifice characterized by a subsequent interruption of the Udgātṛ and a preceding interruption of the Pratihartṛ, the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*). This should be understood to apply likewise in the case of an interruption of the Udgātṛ alone. Similarly, in the *Pañcaśarātra* sacrifice, on the first day named *Āgniṣṭut*, when the rules of the one-day (*ekāha*) *Āgniṣṭut* have been reached, the *Subrahmaṇyā* formula belonging to Agni is obtained; however, for the remaining fourteen days, the formula belongs to Indra. Since the purpose can be achieved even with a minor deficiency, the former is set aside.

Therefore, the name *agniṣṭut* refers to the extension (*atideśa*) of [elements] other than the *subrahmaṇyā* addressed to Agni. Likewise, because the rule "whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya*, they perform that in a low voice" and the rule "one should recite for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* with as much voice as one desires" prescribe a different tone for the principal rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, this [low-voice rule] has a different scope. Nor is it a general rule, because the word "whatever" (*yaktiṃcit*) denotes a specific element within the context.

Thus, there is sublation here on the basis of the distinction between that which has scope and that which lacks scope. Similarly, the low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*) prescribed as a subordinate element of the *yajus* by the rule "the *yajus* is low-voiced" is sublated in the case of *nigadas*, because it contradicts the primary purpose of making oneself understood by another. Consequently, the injunction for low-voicedness regarding *yajus* formulas applies to those *yajus* other than the *nigadas*.

Likewise, regarding the rule "He who is to sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal (*paśu*), or Soma [should do so] on the new moon day or the full moon day," since the new or full moon day is prescribed for the *iṣṭis*, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice, it follows that when one adopts a course of a single initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, it is impossible to coincide with the lunar festival (*parvan*) for both the *sutyā* (pressing) and the *dīkṣaṇīyā* (initiation offering). Since one of the two must be set aside, the lunar festival is set aside for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in order to avoid a deficiency in the primary rite. Therefore, the prescription of the lunar festival for the *iṣṭis* applies to cases where there is no conflict with the time of the primary rite.

Thus, for one who is intent upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in every respect, its cessation is brought about by swiftly removing its object through cutting away the root of that construction. In this regard, there is sublation of what has not yet been attained, as in the case of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth. For there is no scriptural injunction stating "one should worship Indra with the *aindrī* [verse]," such that the attainment of the *aindrī* verse could be sublated by the rule "one should worship the Gārhapatya fire with the *aindrī*. Indeed, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone is not inherently authoritative; rather, the Vedic statement (*śruti*) inferred from it is the authority here. Even in the inference of that [Vedic statement], the indicative mark alone is not the authority, but rather—

That [inference] which requires the expectation of a mantra for its authority in the postulation of a Vedic text is cut down by direct perception—namely, the Vedic text itself—which, through its mandatory application elsewhere, precludes it. (16)

By that direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), which—having deprived the mantra of its application by assigning it to the worship of the Gārhapatya fire through the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra that was previously in need of completion (*sākāṅkṣa*)—renders the mantra free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkurvat*), the very expectancy that constitutes the root of the assumption [of a *śruti*] is removed; thus, the *śruti* whose existence depends upon that [expectancy] is unable to re-emerge. In this same way, "sublation of what has not been obtained" (*aprāptabādha*) is to be understood in other cases as well. This is established.

For nothing that has been obtained by it is sublated, nor is there the possibility of sublation of what was not obtained; why? Because it is only as previously stated that it is logical. As for the argument that the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), which applies in its entirety, ought not to exclude anything—

Its very nature consists of truth alone; however, that nature is obstructed by a powerful cause, just as a general rule is set aside by a specific rule. It should be understood that even the objection—that because it is obtained through explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*), it excludes [the application of] the *codaka* (transfer rule) due to the completeness of its purpose—is refuted on the grounds of its very nature, which limits its scope to only certain instances. Furthermore, although in this case there is no falsity due to a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*), [it is nonetheless sublated].

Although the knowledge of the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) can be indicated [by a defect], it is nevertheless indicated by another cognition that sublates it (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). For both have been stated as indicators: "That cognition whose instrument is defective, and that wherein there is a cognition of falsity—that is an incorrect cognition. Among these, in the case of Vedic cognitions, since a defect in the instrument is impossible, only the sublatting cognition serves as the indicator, not the knowledge of a defect in the instrument. And it has been said:

"As for the second indicator mentioned—the cognition of a defect in the cause—that was not presented [as applicable] because it pertains to worldly matters and is not possible in the case of the Veda. But how can false knowledge be produced by a non-defective instrument? For false knowledge is certainly not produced by that which is sublated; rather, it is produced once it has already arisen.

It makes known that which is false as being real; its origin, however, is solely due to a defect in the cause. That is indeed true. For here too, a defect in the cause certainly exists; even though no inherent defect whatsoever exists in this Veda, which is not of human origin, nevertheless, because the cognizer’s intellect is generally distracted and because of the failure to discern exceptions due to fallacious arguments (*nyāyābhāsa*), a false cognition arises as it spreads forth.

Therefore, it is for this very reason that the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra is purposeful for the sake of correctly determining the principles of logic; nor can this [subject] be determined prior to the occurrence of a sublation (bādhaka), as if by pressing a finger [against the eye], which is why it has been stated that falsity (mithyātva) is to be characterized solely by the presence of a sublation—thus all is explained. Consequently, it is established that when a cognition determined as "this is thus" is declared false due to some other cause, there is no scriptural injunction (codaka-vacana) regarding those things whose objects have vanished.

Because of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "The *codaka* does not enjoin that which has lost its natural purpose," and because of the Sūtra passage "But it would be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣaḥ*)," there is a displacement of the *codaka* from those subsidiary elements whose purpose is lost, which are replaced, or which are prohibited. Thus, in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* grains and so forth, acts such as *han* (striking) are not subsidiary parts; likewise is the action [in general]. However, the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction arises from the restriction itself, not from the essential nature of the act. ||17||

In this regard, it might be argued: "Even if the act of threshing (*hanti*) does not serve a visible purpose in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, why should it not still be applied for the sake of accomplishing the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule? That is not so; because its performance is impossible there. For it is postulated that rice grains produced specifically by threshing accomplish the *apūrva*; however, such a thing is not possible here. Furthermore, because [the rule] lacks a motivating factor (*aprayojakatva*).

For the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) of threshing is not the motivator; rather, once the essential form [of the action] has been established by its visible purpose, it is merely the restriction itself that is motivated by that [visible purpose]. Therefore, although grinding is not prohibited in the case of *caru* offerings—since even what is ground does not destroy their nature as *caru*—nevertheless, because there is no visible purpose [for it], the essential form of grinding is not established, and since the application of the restriction depends upon that [establishment of the form], the restriction is not carried out. Furthermore, even if a purpose existed, the restriction would be set aside in the case of *caru* and other such offerings, just as the sacrificial cake-pan (*puroḍāśakapāla*) is set aside, due to the absence of a motivating factor.

By this, the sublation of the original restriction regarding the material substance—namely rice and barley—in the case of the *citriṣṭi* sacrifice performed with rice-grains is explained. For it is thus:
when the employment of the original material has been established, a restriction is here enjoined;
however, only worldly (cultivated) rice-grains are to be taken as the material, not [wild] rice. (Verse 18)

For there is no scriptural injunction stating that one should sacrifice with rice as the oblation in the archetype (*prakṛti*), such that by extension (*atideśa*) the rice-grains would also consist of that [essence]. Regarding the sacrifice, it is heard in scripture that "one should sacrifice with rice," whereby rice functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). And an instrument is that which falls within the scope of the agent's activity. As they say:
"An instrument is indeed everywhere the object of the agent's activity."

Therefore, one should sacrifice by taking up rice grains (*vrīhi*). And their status as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) is possible in the sacrifice—which is already established by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) and restricted to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—by way of being its material cause (*prakṛti*). Thus, the meaning of the scripture is: "Having taken up rice grains and having prepared the oblation (*havis*) with them, one should sacrifice. In this context, having restated "having prepared the oblation and sacrificed," only the phrase "with rice grains" is enjoined. This being the case, the identity of the oblation with that [rice] is merely implied (*ārthika*), not directly stated by the text (*śrauta*). And it is not so in the case of the rice-grains themselves.

For it is not the case that there, by means of the primary material (*prakṛti*), the attainment of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—which would then be restricted by the rule "with rice"—is established; because it is possible to sacrifice by taking only those grains of rice already established in the world. If it is asked: "But even in the archetype (*prakṛti*), since it is possible to perform the sacrifice by taking only a worldly cake (*puroḍāśa*), how is it that the attainment of the sacrificial oblation through the primary material is established? To this it is said: "The oblation known as the *puroḍāśa* is indeed intended to be accomplished by cooking (*śrapaṇa*);
its being cooked by the performer himself is what is enjoined. (Verse 19)

For the sacrificial offering (havis) in the form of a cake (puroḍāśa) cannot be accomplished without baking; therefore, the question arises whether it should be taken from a worldly source or produced by oneself through the procurement of its constituent materials. Although an absence of restriction might appear to follow from the originative injunction—"one should sacrifice with an eight-potherd [cake]"—since this is compatible with either alternative, nevertheless, because of the statement "he bakes on potsherds," one does not take what has been baked by another. Thus, its being performed by oneself alone is what is to be enjoined, while everything else is established by the force of the originative injunction itself.

The skull-bowls are established by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is also [established] by implication (*sāmarthya*), because there is no status as a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśatva*) for that which has not been cooked; thus, words such as *puroḍāśa* and *caru* denote a specific substance that has been cooked. Therefore, in this case, the fact of being performed by oneself (*svayaṃkartṛkatā*) alone is what is to be enjoined. As the venerable Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) has said:

Because of the statement, "One cooks in skull-pots," one does not take what has been cooked by another; by the force of that [statement], the taking of the original material (*prakṛti*) follows. For otherwise, it would not be possible to cook it oneself. When the taking of the original substance is thus established, there arises an expectation as to what state and what form the substance to be taken should have. In response to this expectation, the word *vrīhi*—which denotes a specific genus (*jāti*) together with its husks—restricts the choice, thereby excluding the states of flour and rice, as well as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and other such substitutes.

If, however, one were to prepare the sacrificial offering (havis) by taking the raw material (prakṛti) according to this very treatise, and it were further enjoined that "this [offering] is to be made with rice," then there would be prolixity (gaurava). Moreover, the injunction "he cooks it on potsherds" (kapāleṣu śrapayati) would become purposeless if another way were possible; and that is improper. Therefore, wherever there is cooking, there its agency belongs to the performer himself; and wherever that [agency] exists, there the acquisition of the raw material is obtained; and wherever that [acquisition] exists, there is the restriction to rice.

In the case of rice grains (*taṇḍula*), however, because the purpose of cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is lost, it is excluded. When that [cooking] is excluded, how could there be the attainment of the requirement for self-performance (*svayaṃkartṛkatva*) therein? How much less the taking of the original material (*prakṛtyupādāna*), and how much less the restriction to *vrīhi* rice? Thus, the restriction to *vrīhi* is not possible in those [rice grains]. [Objection: But surely, due to the capacity of the threshing (*avaghāta*), there would be the taking of the original material even in the case of rice grains. [Reply: No, he says.

For it cannot be said that, on the basis of the injunction "one threshes the rice," the threshing is prescribed with reference to the rice for the purpose of establishing that the act must be performed by oneself—since this is not already established—and thereby the use of the primary substance (the rice) is secured. Nor does such an act necessarily follow as it does in the case of cooking (*śrapaṇa*), such that one could enjoin self-performance as a restatement of it, saying: "One should thresh oneself and not take what has been threshed by another," because the removal of the husk (*vituṣīkaraṇa*) can also be achieved by means of scratching with the nails or plucking.

By this, grinding (*peṣaṇa*) is explained. For that too is not established by rule; for even by means of threshing (*avaghāta*), the rice grains, once softened, become powdered. Thus, the sequence is as follows: first, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is enjoined; then, when its material is required in any way whatsoever, it is produced by taking the primary substance (*prakṛti*) due to the injunction regarding cooking; then, when there is a requirement for a specific primary substance, by the rule "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), the immediate exclusion of other primary substances such as flour (*piṣṭa*) [is established].

By excluding rice that is separated by being ground, and by further excluding wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like which are more remote, *vrīhi* rice is prescribed. Then, when there arises the requirement of how the oblation (*havis*) is to be produced from those [grains], the injunctions for threshing, grinding, and so forth are established. However, since the purpose is lost once the rice grains are obtained, cooking ceases; consequently, there is a sequential cessation of the taking up of the raw material (*prakṛti*) from which they are derived, as well as the rules regarding *vrīhi* and the acts of threshing and so on. Thus, it is established by worldly practice that any kind of grain may be used, provided it excludes inferior types such as *avaraka*. This applies even in cases where there is no sacrificial cake (*apuroḍāśa*).

In cases such as boiled rice (*caru*), fermented grain (*dhānā*), groats (*mantha*), parched grains (*lāja*), and barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared by means of cooking (*śrapaṇa*), the restriction regarding *vrīhi* rice and the preparatory rites such as threshing (*avaghāta*) certainly apply. This subtle "jewel of logic" can be discerned only by those whose mental eye has been refined through familiarity with the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārtika*, and not by those of superficial vision. Regarding this, the authors of the *Vārtika* sing these two verses: "If, due to the loss of purpose, the cooking is dispensed with in the case of rice grains, how can there be self-performance of that cooking which has been dispensed with?"
"How could the material cause (upādāna) of primordial nature (prakṛti) be dependent on that [the Lord] in the interim?
How could there be a restriction regarding rice under His control, and how could it be so in His absence?"

Thus, in the tenth [book], it was considered whether the *āmana-homa* and other such rites—which, being devoid of the transfer of their modified function (*vaikṛta-kārya-āpatti*) due to the sublation of the archetypal elements by the loss of purpose (*artha-lopa*) and so forth—are to be performed as supplementary additions (*abhyudaya*) or not.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of the Auxiliary Factors (*aṅganirṇaya*), in the *Śrīnyāyaratnamālā*. 4.

In the eleventh [book], however, the extent of the application (*prayoga*) is considered by way of *tantra* (common procedure) and *āvāpa* (insertion). *Tantra* refers to the performance of common subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and so forth, such as the *prayāja*s and others in the case of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices. Therein, first of all, it is established that the fruit of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices is common (*tantra*). The question is: is this fruit—the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—common to the *āgneya* and others, or is it distinct for each? That is to say, do they serve as means to the fruit independently of one another, or collectively?

Regarding the refutation of the view that the word *kāma* refers to the person (*puruṣa*) and so forth, which was carried out here by the author of the Bhāṣya: although it was not explicitly formulated as a sūtra, it should be understood that it was treated as an introductory supplement (*upoddhāta*) to the discussion of the sūtras, just like the *pratipadādhikaraṇa*, which serves as an introductory supplement to the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*. As for the view that [the word] refers to the occasion (*nimitta*) because the Vedic text mentions the person in its performance, this was already refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself in the context of the relevant section; here, the author of the Bhāṣya has merely recalled it.

Furthermore, this refutation of the view that the person (*puruṣa*) is the primary referent [of the Vedic injunction] is also an introductory argument (*upodghāta*) for the section concerning "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*); therefore, we have already demonstrated it there by means of a prospective examination (*anāgatapratyavekṣaṇa*). Moreover, the view that the injunction refers to a causal motive (*nimitta*) is untenable because such a motive is not required. Since a result is indeed required, it is logical that the result itself is what is established by this [injunction].
Those who maintain that the word "desire" (*kāma*) in the commentary establishes the person as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*) are refuted by this very [argument]. (Verse 1)

Those who maintain that because an action is independent of its fruit, it is the *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) who is expected by the action and is expressed by words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*), for them there is a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*, which is intent on refuting the view that [the Veda] has man as its ultimate purpose. For by this [argument], the status of [the word] as denoting the agent alone is not being refuted; rather, it is only the status of having man as its ultimate purpose that is refuted by the passage beginning with "this is the speaker of man," and so forth. Furthermore, if [the suffix] were taken as referring to the cause (*nimitta*), then—since there would be no sublation of the direct Vedic text (*śruti*)—there would be a sublation of the grammatical gender (*liṅga*). Otherwise, there would be a sublation of the direct Vedic text itself. (Verse 2)

And if the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) were intended primarily to denote the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), then—since the person qualified by the desire for heaven would be the one to be enjoined just as a person qualified by a house fire or similar affliction is—the desire for heaven would be a mere occasion (*nimitta*) for action, exactly like those other conditions, and it would not be established that heaven is the fruit (*phala*). This might be argued: it is indeed reasonable that things such as a house fire, being already accomplished, [should serve as occasions].

As for the claim that [heaven] becomes the *nimitta* (the causal occasion), since heaven is not yet accomplished, it cannot serve as a *nimitta*; therefore, it must be a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) precisely by way of being the fruit. That is not correct. For that which is unaccomplished cannot logically function as a qualification for a person to be enjoined who is already established; indeed, in the absence of a qualification, the establishment of a person to be enjoined characterized by that qualification is not possible.

Furthermore, how can an injunction (*niyoga*) be established by that which is unestablished? One who accepts its establishment must necessarily admit that the desire for the result is its qualification. And since that [desire] is already established, it is indeed capable of defining the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) solely by way of being a causal occasion (*nimitta*), just as in the case of "one who desires another's wife may perform penance. This being so, the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as expressing an action to be performed, which is understood by everyone in the world, remains uncontradicted. If it is argued that this contradicts the very nature of desire, we say no.

Because of the superior force of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). In this regard, it might be argued: although the connection with desires (*kāma*) as a causal occasion (*nimitta*) is possible, nevertheless, it is more appropriate to accept them as qualifications by way of being the fruit (*phala*), so as not to entail the subversion of the inherent nature of desire. For desires, by their very nature, have that which is desired as their primary object; and if they were merely causal occasions, that primacy would be lost. Therefore, it is proper that they be the fruit. That is not so, because direct scriptural statement is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*). For the inherent nature of desire is indeed an indicative mark.

In this regard, if it were intended to signify a condition (*nimitta*), there would be a sublation of the direct statement (*śruti*); however, if it were intended to signify a result (*phala*), there would be a sublation of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*). For that suffix is understood in common usage as denoting an action in the form of a task (*kārya*); thus, having been derived from that [usage], if it were to signify a result, it would have to be led to a different meaning. Therefore, when there is a doubt—whether one should accept the sense of a result by sublating the direct statement in favor of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), or whether one should accept the sense of a condition by sublating the indicative mark in accordance with the direct statement—it is logical to favor the direct statement.

For if [the action] were directed toward the fruit, since that fruit occurs at a later time, it would be impossible for an action—which is momentary—to be its direct means. Nor can an action’s status as a means to the fruit be established through an intermediate apūrva (unseen potency), as is the case with an action that is a means to the *paramāpūrva* (ultimate unseen potency) via the *utpattyapūrva* (origination-unseen potency). This is because an *apūrva* that does not inhere in the action and does not exist at the same time cannot logically constitute the power (*śakti*) or the operation (*vyāpāra*) of that action; for it is only power and operation that effect the realization of an action’s status as a means to a fruit.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for one thing to be the means of accomplishing another through an intermediary—for example, as wood is the means for fire through the intermediary of burning—or for experience to be the means for the maturation of memory through the intermediary of a latent impression (saṃskāra); thus, action would be ineffective as a means.

However, [the opponent argues that] there must be a means to the means (sādhanasādhana), for indeed, one who desires a fruit cannot directly engage in the means itself; just as one desiring rice cannot perceive plowing as the thing to be done (*kārya*). Thus, by this independent procedure—which contradicts worldly experience—it would have to be assumed that the Vedic optative suffix (*liṅ*) abandons its well-known worldly denotation of an action as a "thing to be done" and instead denotes an extraordinary "thing to be done" called *apūrva*. Since this entails a contradiction with the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), it is superior to interpret the suffix as having the sense of a "condition" (*nimitta*).

But if this were the case, there would be the fault of complexity (*gaurava*), since one would have to postulate that the injunction (*vidhi*) possesses the status of an instigator (*prayojaka*). This is not a fault; for it is logical to postulate that [the injunction] has that status by accepting its nature as a cause (*nimitta*) in order to favor the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Nor is this particularly difficult to postulate, since the fact that an effect is instigated by its own means is established by common worldly experience in a general sense—just as smoke’s connection with fire and the visibility of form are established.

Therefore, just like a specific effect (*kāryaviśeṣa*), even when something previously unknown is being cognized, its status as the motivator (*prayojakatva*) is recognized only as something already known—such as its connection with fire—and not as some entirely new thing that must be postulated. If it is argued that although it is known in a general sense, it must be postulated as unknown in this particular instance, this should not be said by one who forgets the established rule that inference has for its object only what is already known. Moreover, this much [postulation] must necessarily be made regarding the fruit even in the case of rites performed for a specific desire (*kāmādhikāra*).

Indeed, it is not established in common worldly experience that a specific result, such as heaven, serves as the motivator for the performance of rites like the Jyotiṣṭoma. Nor is it established in common experience that a result—which is distinct from the action itself—serves as a motivator in a specific capacity, such that its existence would need to be postulated. Furthermore, even the result does not motivate by virtue of being a "result," but rather by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*kārya*); and since this status of being "to be accomplished" is no different for an action that lacks the form of a result, there is no additional complexity. Moreover, because the result is dependent upon the injunction, one must consider only that much [the injunction itself].
Even in the context of desire, there is no application [of the means], just as there is none regarding the subsidiary parts of a ritual.

For if, as in the case of an occasional mandate (*naimittika-adhikāra*), the injunction (*vidhi*) were not the motivator even in the case of a mandate for one who desires a result (*kāma-adhikāra*), then it might be possible to say that one should not assume its status as a motivator and instead postulate it merely as a mandate for one who desires a result. But this is not the case; for in a mandate for one who desires a result, the injunction itself impels the performance of the means and the performance of the subsidiaries, just as in other cases, and not the fruit. This is because the fruit, occurring at a later time, is to be accomplished solely through the meaning of the injunction existing at that [present] time, and thus depends only upon the fulfillment of that [injunction].

For that [result] is not accomplished directly by the action such that it would cause one to perform it; rather, it is logical that the injunction, being itself accomplished by that [action], causes its performance. If it is argued that the result, like the injunction, is also the motivator precisely through the medium [of the action], we say no, because the medium is impossible.

It might further be argued: "Just as the originative apūrva (utpattyapūrva), though being the direct object to be accomplished by an injunction, is not the motivator because it is not itself something to be performed—since the originative apūrva is not a task to be done, but rather the supreme apūrva (paramāpūrva) brought about by it—and since that which is not a task to be done is not a motivator; therefore, it is the supreme apūrva alone that, through an intermediary, is the motivator of the constituent acts—so too, in the context of rites for specific desires (kāmādhikāra), the fruit also impels the means through the medium of the apūrva. But this is not so, because an intermediary is impossible.

For if the supreme apūrva (paramāpūrva), like the origination-apūrva (utpattyapūrva), were incapable of being an independent motivator, then it would likewise become a mere means to the fruit which is the motivator. But since it is itself the primary effect, is not proximate to the fruit, and is perceived first, why should it wait for motivation by the fruit, which is remote and perceived last? For the status of the fruit as that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) arises from its connection with the person to be enjoined (niyojya) as qualified by the obligation (niyoga) understood [by him]; thus, its being perceived last is entirely logical.

But surely, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), since that which serves as the instrument for the fruit is the object, when it is determined that the fruit—which is independent of being accomplished by the fruit itself—is to be accomplished by the ritual act, the host of defects such as the abandonment of the primacy of what is designated as the *apūrva* has already been demonstrated. Therefore, the mandate (*niyoga*) itself, by virtue of its own capacity for instigation and because it is not mediated [by anything else], [is the primary object].

The intermediate apūrvas (utpattyapūrvas) must serve as the means for the ritual action that brings about the fruit, because they are not themselves prompted by that [fruit]. For the intermediate apūrvas, being in themselves of a non-action nature, become actions only when prompted as means for the accomplishment of the supreme apūrva; thus it is logical that they become the means for the supreme apūrva, which is the prompter of the ritual action. First, the supreme apūrva is what is to be accomplished, and since it cannot be achieved without the intermediate apūrvas, those too must be performed.

And since those [results] have their accomplishment dependent upon action (*karman*), it follows that action must also be performed; it is by this sequence that the injunction (*vidhi*) becomes the instigator of the performance of the means for the *apūrva*. Nor is the necessity of performing the *apūrva* dependent on the necessity of performing the result, because the *apūrva* itself is what is to be accomplished (*kārya*). And how could it be said that "whatever is not the motivator of one thing can yet be the motivator of another through that medium"? Thus it is established that even in the context of optional rites (*kāmādhikāra*), the motivator is the injunction alone; there is no difference in the conceptualization of motivation between occasional rites (*naimittika*) and optional rites. On the contrary:
