In the section concerning desire (kāma), there would be three additional features: its unprecedented nature, its being a means to a fruit, and the fact that the sacrifice is the means to that [fruit];
however, its status as the motivator (prayojakatva) remains the same.

Regarding the postulation of the impelling force (*prayukti*), it remains the same in both views: whether the apūrva is in both [the sacrifice and the result] or in both [the result and the apūrva], the apūrva is equally unestablished. However, the distinction is this: in the case of a rite for a specific desire (*kāmādhikāra*), one must postulate that the apūrva—which has an as-yet-unestablished form—is the means to the result, and that the sacrifice is the means to that apūrva. Even if, however, there is no postulation of an impelling force in the case of a rite for a specific desire, nevertheless, the nature of the apūrva as the subject (*dharmin*) and its status as the means to the result, as well as the sacrifice's status as the means to that [apūrva], must be postulated. But in the case of a rite contingent upon a specific occasion (*naimittika*): [There is a difference between] the action-form of the task (*kārya*) and the established entity as the subject (*dharmin*).
There would be mere causality; it is better that it be occasional (naimittika). ||5||

Furthermore, because it would involve abandoning what is established by worldly consensus, there remains indeed a contradiction with the Vedic scripture (*śruti*). Therefore, since there is no contradiction with scripture and because of the parsimony of postulation (*kalpanālāghava*), it is more appropriate that [the act] is occasional (*naimittika*) rather than being a matter of desire (*kāmādhikāra*). But how can there be occasionality for that which lacks words such as "when" (*yat*)? We do not say that the occasionality is directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śrauta*). Rather, just as in the case of the *jañjabhyamāna* (one who yawns), since the person qualified by desire is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the occasionality of the desire is inferred by implication. Moreover, the status of being denoted by the word "when" does not belong to the occasion;
therefore, its status as the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) is established, and in this context, that is established from another source.

For the word "ya" (who/which) expresses merely the state of being the person to be enjoined (*uddeśyatva*), not the state of being a cause (*nimittatva*). Since the connection [of the injunction] is with one who possesses a house fire or the like by virtue of being the person to be enjoined as qualified by an attribute that is not itself to be performed (*anupādeya-viśeṣaṇa*), it is said that the burning, which serves as that attribute, possesses a causal status (*nimittatva*) by implication. And since even for one who desires a result (*phala-kāma*) the person to be enjoined is equally the subject of the injunction (*uddiṣṭa*), the desire for that result is likewise indistinguishable [from the attribute]; thus, its status as a cause is logical.

Furthermore, there are many instances where words such as "if" (*yat*) are heard—for example, in passages such as, "He who desires offspring, he who desires cattle, if he should desire that Parjanya be rainy," and so forth; yet, even in these cases, there is no difference in the fact that they have the status of being contingent conditions (*nimitta*). Now, one might object: the obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*), such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), cannot possibly be contingent; for if they were performed as a rule, then the injunctions regarding contingent conditions would be rendered purposeless.

Now, if there were performance [of the rite] only when the occasion (nimitta) exists by virtue of that [desire], then the injunction for lifelong performance would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, it is argued that the qualification based on desire alone is logical. To this, we reply: "No. For if the sentence were common to both positions, then its meaningfulness might be accepted in this [latter] position; however, here, by means of a collection of arguments such as the non-sublation of direct Vedic statement (śruti), it is determined that the sentence has the occasion alone as its primary purport.

If, that being so, one or the other becomes purposeless, let it be; for what is called "purposelessness" is not included within the category of scriptural authority (*śruti-pramāṇa*). That which is understood to have a purpose retains its purposefulness, while for that which is understood to be entirely purposeless, that very [absence of purpose] is preferable. Alternatively, let there be a repetition of the performance, as in the case of the *Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*, for the sake of purposefulness; however, it is not possible to assume a different meaning [for the text].

Alternatively, the lifelong repetition of the very performance that is occasioned [by a specific event] is enjoined by the *yāvajjīva* (lifelong) statement through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For that [repetition] is worldly; whereas the assumption of a different meaning for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurs only here [in the Vedic context]. Therefore, it is not logical that this belongs to the category of optional rites (*kāmya-adhikāra*).

Or rather, let us adopt the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, which is supported by the *Sūtra* and the *Bhāṣya*: the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) delimited by the sacrifice and other elements, being accompanied by an injunction and requiring a desired end to be accomplished, accepts heaven and so forth as the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) by means of the sentence, and not as the occasioning condition (*nimitta*), because that [condition] is not required [for the accomplishment of the action].

For in that case, the instrumentality of the sacrifice and so forth becomes possible through the mediation of an imagined *apūrva*, just as firewood, pulling, and so forth serve as means for cooking rice through the mediation of burning and digging; or just as the group of six sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya* serves as a means to the ultimate *apūrva* through the mediation of the originating *apūrva*; or just as threatening and so forth serve as a means to the hundred-fold torments. Thus, everything remains well-established.

[However,] in the case of the *Saurya* and other such rites, it would follow that desire (*kāmanā*) is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), for no scriptural statement therein suffers from meaninglessness. (7)

Or, let it be that in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other such rites, because of the existence of the scriptural injunction "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva), they have the status of having a fruit as their purpose; but in the case of rites such as the Saurya sacrifice, where there is no scriptural injunction regarding their being obligatory (nityatva), why should one accept that they have the status of having a fruit as their purpose merely for the sake of avoiding the charge of meaninglessness? Or rather, the intention is this:
it has been determined that even in the case of the Darśa and others, the apūrva is what is to be expressed [by the verb].
Do not abandon the embrace of desire even when it has taken refuge elsewhere.

In order to avoid the futility of the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong [observances], once it is determined that in passages such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" the word *kāma* (desire) has the purpose of denoting a fruit, it follows that for one who desires [that fruit], the comprehension of an obligation (*kārya*) cannot arise with respect to something that is not a means to that end. Furthermore, since a ritual action (*karman*), being momentary and transitory, cannot possibly be a means to that [endless] result, it is understood that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes a stable obligation distinct from the action itself. This being understood, the same applies to the optative suffix in the case of the Saurya and other rites—whether it refers to the action or to something distinct from it.

"Because there is no partiality [toward one over the other], and in order not to destroy the inherent nature of desire, it is logical that [the word] has only the fruit as its primary meaning. We say: "No.

Even a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of denotation does not sublate an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in this way; however, a direct scriptural statement consisting of the same word-form (*samānapada-rūpā śruti*) is indeed a sublater of even this [indicative mark]. (9)

Although the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) denotes a general "task" (*kārya*) common to both because it is used in common worldly practice for actions (*kriyā*) and because it is used in Vedic injunctions such as those concerning the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for the sake of the "unseen potency" (*apūrva*), there is no contradiction in its denotation even when that task is a specific one distinct from an action; nevertheless, when that general category requires a specific instance, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*)—which is introduced by the same word through the direct denotative power (*śruti*) characterized by co-referentiality—is connected as the specific instance, and thus [the suffix does not denote anything else].

It can be prevented by the force of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), whose nature is desire, which serves as a qualifier for the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) supplied by another word. For the suffix, even as it is being uttered, expresses its own meaning—a general obligation—already colored by the meaning of the verbal root. As it has been said: "The accusative case-ending, being uttered after a nominal stem, declares that the meaning of the nominal stem is the qualifier. Therefore, although there is no difference in the mode of expression, the optative suffix is set aside precisely because of the contradiction with the direct hearing of the word (*pada-śruti*). Regarding this, the Prābhākaras mock [the opponent], for they believe:
"If the *apūrva* (unseen potency) were the expressed meaning, then the action would be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*)."
Because of the fault of having multiple meanings, there can be no denotation of both [meanings] simultaneously. (10)

For when it is maintained that the *apūrva*—which is distinct from the action and is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers—is expressed because it is mentioned in grammatical coordination with the person enjoined who desires a fruit, then it is not easy to maintain that the action itself is also its denotation; for it is improper for a single word to have multiple denotations, and because the cognition of the action can be accounted for through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Indeed, since the status of the *apūrva* as the object to be accomplished is invariably concomitant with the status of the action as the object to be accomplished, once this is understood through the word, it brings the action to mind [by implication]; thus, there is no possibility of the action being the primary denotation.

Furthermore, since there is no ground for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of [rites] such as the *saurya* sacrifice, that [result] is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as something entirely unprecedented (*apūrva*). Therefore, it is not logical to abandon the inherent nature of desire and admit that [the optative] has the status of a conditional cause (*nimitta*). This, however, is merely their own conceit; those who follow authoritative means of knowledge do not believe it. For it is said: "It is improper for a word to have multiple meanings due to the fault of having multiple potencies (*śakti*).
Since both [meanings] are established by a single [potency], the one that is actually perceived is what is to be denoted. (11)

In cases such as "Lolika, bring the cow," they do not consider the optative suffix (*liṅ*) to function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), but rather through its primary sense alone. In that regard, if it were the case that when the action to be performed (*kārya*) is denoted by the primary sense, the postulation of a further power would result—and only then would figurative status be accepted—this is not so; for the primary sense is established in both instances by the single power of denoting the mere fact of being to-be-done (*kāryamātra*).

Indeed, having multiple meanings is undesirable because it entails the fault of postulating multiple powers, whereas having multiple forms is not inherently defective, as seen in the various types of *apūrvas*: those pertaining to obligatory, optional, archetypal, modified, and prohibitive rites.

That is its denotability. Therefore, just as those [entities] possess that denotability because they are grasped by a single common characteristic, namely their status as effects (*kāryatva*), so too will the poor action (*kriyā*) possess that denotability through its connection with it. He says: "Not by a single power; for when the nature of the action is presented by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it is precisely its qualification in the form of 'to-be-done-ness' (*kartavyatā') that must be conveyed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*)."

However, since the *apūrva* has not been attained by anything else, its very nature must be denoted as qualified by the state of being something to be accomplished (*kartavyatā*) by means of the suffix *liṭ*; thus, neither of the two aforementioned modes is possible. If it denotes the qualified [entity], then it would denote the *apūrva* itself and not the action; if, on the other hand, it denotes the qualifier, then it would denote the action itself and not the *apūrva*. This is not so.

This word denotes a qualified entity; when it is directed toward an action, since the essential nature [of that entity] is already established by the verbal root itself, it becomes directed toward the qualifier. For example, in the injunction "the staff-bearer recites the directions" (*daṇḍī praiṣānanvāha*), although the word *daṇḍin* denotes a qualified entity, it is directed toward the qualifier without resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Likewise, even a word expressing an effect, when employed in reference to an action, does not thereby involve figurative indication; thus, in both cases, the meaning is primary. As for the one who says...

But if this were the case, then even in the context of desire (*kāma*), only the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) as presented by the same word would be the denotable object; thus, the fact that the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is understood as the denotable object would imply that the action itself is taken figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) for the sake of establishing that [denotation]. To this, he should be instructed as follows: "Alas! Have you not heard the saying: 'For one who eats stones, even dry chickpea cakes become easy to eat'? For [the agent] understands the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—even though it is understood as expressing a specific task in the form of an action—as being connected to the person to be impelled (*niyojya*)."

Since it leads to the unprecedented (*apūrva*) by first leading to the general, how could it not be capable of leading to the unprecedented which expresses the general? Therefore, although the optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses the general state of being an obligation (*kartavyatā*), where there is the status of being enjoined for one who desires a fruit, it denotes the unprecedented by the force of that [desire]; elsewhere, however, it denotes the action because it is presented in the same word. Consequently, just as the optative word, despite expressing the general, denotes the various unprecedented results through its connection with them, why is this not also accepted for the action? If it is argued that this is due to the difference in the nature of the obligation (*kartavyatā*) regarding those [unprecedented results], we say no, because such a difference does not exist. In this regard, it might be thought that the status of being the object of the verbal suffix (*kṛt*) is what constitutes the goal.

The "state of being to be done" (*kartavyatā*) is the indicator for what is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*); and since all *apūrva*s are endowed with that [state], it is logical that they are denoted by them. However, the "state of being to be done" of an action consists in its being pervaded by an effort directed toward the attainment of a result; because there is no difference in this nature, [the *apūrva*s] are denoted. Even though in worldly cases such as bringing a cow, a state of being to be done is not understood independently, nevertheless, in the Veda, the same kind of state of being to be done will belong to sacrifices such as the *saurya*.

For the optative suffix (*liṅ*), when uttered in syntactic proximity with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), denotes that very [sacrifice] as being of such a nature [as something to be performed]. If it is argued that such a state of "being to be done" (*kartavyatā*) has never before been understood in the case of a worldly action, we reply: No; for what has been understood in the case of the mandate (*niyoga*) by virtue of which it is accepted? If it is argued that although not understood from the world, its such state of being to be done is understood from the Veda itself, then the same applies to the action as well.

But surely, how can even scripture establish the duty to perform an action that is of the nature of suffering, when it is contradicted by direct perception? Or [how can this be said of] the self of the injunction (*niyoga*), which consists of devotion to the Blessed One and has bliss as its sole essence, since its status as a duty would not be contradicted by other means of knowledge? Even that [injunction], being accomplished through the expenditure of much wealth and effort, is merely a form of suffering and cannot serve as the intended object of a conscious agent's activity.

Just as its status as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*) arises from the eternal and independent Vedic injunction (*āmnāya*), so too will it be for ritual action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, since a mandate (*niyoga*)—being distinct from the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain—is not established as something to be accomplished independently, like an action, this is untenable. For volitional effort (*kṛti*), which consists of the exertion of consciousness, must have as its object only that which is preceded by desire; and since desire has as its object only pleasure or the avoidance of pain, volitional effort likewise has that very same object.

Therefore, it is not tenable that the unprecedented (*apūrva*) possesses primacy, as has been explained in the *Śaktinirṇaya*. Furthermore, you cannot maintain that the "to-be-done-ness" (*kartavyatā*) of an action consists in its being pervaded by an activity directed toward another purpose; for this would entail a contradiction with your own position. For in common worldly usage, once it is understood that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. denote the action as the object to be performed, there is no exclusion of the specific form of the action itself. In the Veda, however, it is your view that—due to the co-occurrence with words expressing desire (*kāma*)—one understands that these suffixes extend only as far as the unprecedented (*apūrva*).

Regarding the view [of the opponent]: if it is understood that an action, characterized by a "duty-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) consisting in its being pervaded by the performance of a primary purpose other than itself, exists for the sake of that [other purpose], then—alas!—even in the case of the Veda, since one must merely postulate that it culminates in the *apūrva* without abandoning that very form [of being for the sake of another], the intended primacy of the *apūrva* would be contradicted.

For the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is indeed an obstacle only to a specific [meaning] in the form of an action, but not to its being subordinate to something else; therefore, since both worldly and Vedic [linguistic usage] express the function of being subordinate to another, there is no multiplicity of meaning. On the contrary, it is precisely from the co-occurrence with the term "one who desires heaven" that this very [subordination] is understood. One who maintains that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others denote an independent action (*svatantrakārya*) must be asked: "What is your proof for this?"

If he should say that "because of its co-utterance with the person enjoined who desires the fruit, a task (kārya) distinct from the action is established as not being subordinate to anything else," one should reply to him: "No, because that would prove the opposite. For the co-utterance with the word expressing desire (*kāma*) is indeed an authority for denoting a task that is subordinate to something else, not for its independence.

For he, desiring heaven, is capable of understanding that the action is subordinate to it by virtue of its being desired; for this reason, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are accepted as denoting an *apūrva* (unseen potency) conducive to that [heaven], rather than denoting an action unfit to be a means to it. How then can there be an acceptance of primacy that contradicts one's own authority? [Objection: But even if something is conducive to the result in actual fact, it need not be denoted as such by the word.

Is it because of this that [the apūrva] must be denoted as the primary element? Certainly not, for there is not even a grain of evidence for its primacy. Furthermore, precisely because of its connection with the word denoting the person to be impelled (niyojya), it must be denoted in such a way that one who desires the fruit understands the nature of the task as "this is my task," just like the apūrva of the subsidiary rites (aṅga).

For how can one who asserts that the *apūrva* pertaining to the *prayāja* and other such subsidiaries—being incapable of becoming independent because its scope is already assigned (*viniyukta*)—is denoted by its own word (the verbal root) only as a subordinate element through *lakṣaṇā*, despite that word having the capacity to denote the primary action as determined by the *adhikāra* injunction; how can such a person [maintain this] elsewhere than in the case of the *kāma-adhikāra* injunctions, where there is a capacity to denote a primary action previously unknown, and instead, a capacity to denote an action understood from common worldly usage to be subordinate?

Furthermore, because of the co-utterance with words denoting desire (*kāma*), and because the denotation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is necessarily established by the authority [of the Veda], the *apūrva*—whose primary status has been set aside [by the verbal suffix] through its being the object of the instrument (*liṅ*) and likewise through its being the object of application—is denoted as the primary factor itself, without contradicting the world, one's own means of knowledge, or its own scope. Thus speaking, he would not be laughable. Since in both cases the capacity to denote an action as a subordinate factor is established by the very same [suffix], there is no figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) nature of the action.
This is because, according to the world and one's own means of knowledge, it has as its object that which is for the sake of the fruit.
The apūrva has no other purpose, nor is it primary for any reason whatsoever. ||12||

This is the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*). By this, it is shown that even in the case of a contingent injunction (*naimitikādhikāra*), because one follows the understanding established in the context of the optional injunction (*kāmādhikāra*), it is another matter—the *apūrva*—that is denoted; and for the sake of establishing that, a fruit must necessarily be postulated, just as there is a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Furthermore: "Even though the *niyoga* (the mandate) is primary and the action (*karman*) is subordinate, the denotation belongs only to the general [form], through the abandonment of the two specific [features]. (13)

Although the nature of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) regarding the *niyoga* (the mandate) is of one kind because it is the primary object intended by the agent's effort, while the nature of what is to be done regarding the action is of another kind because it is subordinate as being pervaded by the effort directed toward something else, nevertheless—the word *liṅ* (the optative suffix), when applied to both, must have as its denotation a universal "task-ness" (*kāryatva-sāmānya*) that conforms to all instances, just as the word "cow" (*go*), despite its application to individuals such as "Khaṇḍā," abandons the distinction between predominance and subordination and denotes "cowness" (*gotva*) by grasping the commonality underlying all specific individuals like Khaṇḍā.

Since it is logical for a word employed in multiple instances to have its primary (mukhya) sense everywhere, it is improper to resort to secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); this very point was observed by the venerable author of the Bhāṣya in the *Kapiñjalādhikaraṇa*. By this, the theory that words such as "cow" denote their own meaning only as connected to an action (*kāryānvita*) is refuted—given that they are used in such cases as "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*) where they are connected to an action, and in such cases as "there are fruits on the riverbank" (*nadītīre phalāni santi*) where they are connected to an established fact (*siddhārtha*)—because these words denote their own meaning as connected merely to an object that is desired, proximate, and capable, a feature common to both types of usage.
If, however, this were not tolerated— that the denotation of words should fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition— then the Veda would lack the status of a valid authority.

For if, even though a word is employed in multiple instances and a universal (*sāmānya*) inhering in all of them exists, one were to refuse to accept that it denotes this [universal] and instead—on the grounds that it denotes a particular (*viśeṣa*) as understood at the time of its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)—were to accept that its function elsewhere is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇikī*), then, because words are employed in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) based on an object already ascended into the speaker’s mind (whether by means of a valid cognition or a semblance thereof), the denotable object (*abhidheya*) of all words would be precisely of that kind [i.e., a mental construct]. Consequently, since such a thing is impossible in the case of the Veda, which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), the Veda would lack the capacity for communication.

Otherwise, the Veda would necessarily be forced to be of human origin, and thus its authority would be lost. Similarly, in the case of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), it has been established—within the context of the "section on desire" (*kāmādhikāra*), which is accepted as the locus for linguistic usage—that it denotes an *apūrva* (unseen potency) that is conducive to the fruit for the person to be enjoined who desires that fruit. Consequently, because it denotes such an *apūrva* in accordance with its established usage even in the contexts of occasional rites (*naimittika*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*), one must likewise assume a fruit and a person to be enjoined who desires that fruit; thus, in all cases, there would be an "authority based on a fruit," just as in the case of the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice.

Therefore, since the authority of the Veda is not obstructed even in the case of established facts (*siddhārtha*), the attempt to reject the authority of such passages as "Brahman is bliss" results in nothing but nihilism; enough of this. Consequently, there is no figurative nature (*lākṣaṇikatva*) in the action. Thus, in the *saurya* and other sacrifices, because the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—which denotes the general category of what-is-to-be-done (*kārya*)—refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) through the direct statement of its inclusion in the same word (*samānapadopādāna-śruti*), the desire for a result (*kāmanā*) must, in your own view, serve merely as a causal condition (*nimittatva*) so as not to subvert that [denotation].

Therefore, since an action conjoined with an injunction necessarily requires a fruit, the word *kāma* (desire) refers exclusively to that [fruit] and not to a causal occasion (*nimitta*), because it is not observed [as such]. This alone is the reason for refuting its status as a causal occasion; the mention of its being "eternal" (*nityatva*) is merely an incidental corroboration. Furthermore, it has already been established that even a transitory action can be a means to a fruit by way of an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of the *apūrva*. There are indeed many examples of this, such as the *kāṣṭhāgneya* and *avagoraṇa* rites; one need not weary the mind over this specific point.
Nor should a non-worldly (alaukika) denotable object be postulated. On this point, there are these summary verses:
The Vedic revelation would be upheld if there were reliance on [the injunction] as the cause;
for it is the very indicative mark (liṅga) of the nature of desire that is contradicted [otherwise]. (15)
If the Vedic text were dependent upon the result [of worldly experience], it would abandon its well-known meaning and resort to something non-worldly; therefore, it would be contradicted. ||16||
But as for the assumption of an application of an injunction based on a causal sign (nimitta), that applies equally whether the result is dependent [on the person] or upon that [sign]. ||17||
There exists an unprecedented form which is the means for that fruit; and therein, sacrifice is the means—these three are your constituent parts, therefore meditate upon them. (18)
Now, the postulation of the application [of the word] pertains only to the cause, not to the result;
nevertheless, that [postulation of the application] is better, because otherwise three things would have to be postulated. (19)
If it is asked, "How then can there be a causal condition (nimitatā) without the words 'yat' and so forth? [the answer is:
For one who desires a result, [the condition] exists by necessity, but it is not a causal condition because of the Vedic revelation (śruti). ||20||
But how could that which is heard as eternal become something contingent?
For it would follow that some part of the word of those two [the Veda and the Smṛti] would be rendered meaningless. (21)
Let it be useless, for the establishment of valid cognition does not depend upon a purpose;
alternatively, the postulation of different applications may arise from a specific cause. ||22||
The contingency of [the word] being merely indicative arises only where there is no scriptural statement of eternality;
since both contingencies would apply, the scriptural statement is not capable of subverting the indicative mark. ||23||
Therefore, if it is argued that [the sacrifice] is indeed a fruit by virtue of its essential nature as a mark (liṅga), that is not so;
for the direct scriptural mention of the word (pada-śruti) sublates the mark consisting of the very form of the desire.
Moreover, the verbal suffix expresses only the unprecedented [result] (apūrva), not even the action;
for it would express both only as persisting through their performance. (25)

Just as the universal "cowness" (gotva) is the cause of the cognition of a cow, so too the hearing of the optative suffix (liṅ) expresses merely the fact of being an effect with respect to both the action and the injunction. ||26||

Therefore, because of the support of scripture and because it involves only a slight assumption, this [interpretation] would be merely a figurative designation; however, this [following verse] is its refutation. ||27||
An action requires a result, for it is only when capable of being enjoined that it functions;
therefore, that [result] alone is apprehended, while the status of being a cause is disregarded. (28)
If it is asked how an action can be the means of accomplishing a result while being fragile, [the answer is:
it is so because of its connection with intermediate actions; by its own nature, however, it would not be [a means]. (29)
Just as memory arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā) by means of a valid cognition, so too does the softening [of food] occur through fuel by virtue of intermediate processes. (30)
Just as the arising of torments such as being struck by a hundred lashes occurs through acts like threatening and so forth, even though the nature of that action is itself transitory. (31)
Due to the influence of intermediate actions, there may be a rule regarding the primary action;
likewise, that result will not come to pass—why, then, is the mind distressed in this matter? (32)

Thus, since the result is the primary objective, it is now considered whether that result belongs to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices collectively (*tantra*) or individually (*bheda*). The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) of the *āgneya* and others require an object to be produced (*bhāvya*) while remaining mutually independent, they are connected in that very manner [individually]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: when the *āgneya* and other sacrifices are enjoined with reference to a single result, their collective nature—understood from the fact that they are denoted by a single word—is intended to be expressed. Furthermore, since all of them attain a state of non-dependency through a single result, the result belongs collectively (*tantra*) to all of them.

Then, since the limbs [of the sacrifice] are enjoined as means for accomplishing the benefit of the rite by means of sentences that are themselves independent, one might suspect that they possess that status as means independently, just as the *saurya*, *āryamaṇa*, and other such offerings serve as means for attaining spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth. To this it is replied: there is no application of these [limbs] by means of a sentence; rather, once they are presented by their own respective sentences merely in their essential form, their application occurs through the context (*prakaraṇa*). And since that [contextual application] functions non-simultaneously, all of them are applied together. How, then, is it with the injunctions of the subsidiary parts?

The claim that [the injunctive suffix] has the nature of being solely a motivator (*prayojaka*) is incorrect. However, when it is accepted that the injunction (*vidhi*)—namely, the very fact of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*)—is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, even then, in order to avoid the eight faults of an option (*vikalpa*), all [subsidiaries] such as the *prayāja* offerings—which have already been assigned their respective roles by individual injunctions supported by the context (*prakaraṇa*) merely through their subordination to the sacrifice—are [all simultaneously enjoined] by a single primary injunction that prescribes a *bhāvanā* qualified by all [subsidiaries].

Because simultaneous performance is understood, and because the assistance of all [auxiliaries] is conceived together by means of the distinction between their intermediate functions directed toward that [final] purpose, the combination (*samuccaya*) of all is established, just as in the case of firewood and other factors that are auxiliary to cooking. For it has already been demonstrated that the injunction of ritual items does not occur with reference to the benefit [they provide], since that benefit is not yet established prior to those items. However, where a single function is understood through another means of knowledge—as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*)—or where there is a plurality of performance-injunctions despite a single purpose—as in the case of the *udbhid* and *citrayāga* sacrifices both intended for the sake of cattle—there, option (*vikalpa*) prevails.

Now, if only the injunction of the primary rite (*pradhāna-vidhi*) is the motivator for performance, and not the injunctions for the subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*), then what is the purpose of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding them, such as "this armor of the sacrifice is being made"? For it is an established principle that these serve to strengthen the motivating power of the injunction; if they were not motivators, what function would their strengthening serve? It is said in reply: Since the primary injunction itself enjoins the primary rite as qualified by all its subsidiaries, all explanatory passages are auxiliary (*śeṣa*) by way of praising those subsidiaries. Thus, there is no fault.

This is not so. For the status of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) arises through their being syntactically connected as a single sentence with an injunction; however, since it is impossible for explanatory passages situated within sentences concerning subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to form a single sentence with the primary injunction, it follows that they cannot be subordinate to it. This is not a fault. For the primary injunction, being incapable of encompassing the qualified object as a whole, necessarily transfers its force to the qualifications, which are the subsidiaries. Thus, it is logical that the explanatory passages situated therein complete the sense by forming a single sentence with the injunction located there.

Or, for example, by the statement "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," the power of the injunction regarding the specific act of seizing [the animal] is transferred by implication to Vāyu, who serves as the qualifier; thus, it acts as an auxiliary. However, there is this distinction: in that case, the application of Vāyu is established by the direct sentence (*vākya*), whereas that of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*). Yet, this much does not constitute any difference in terms of the lack of connection with the *arthavāda*. Thus, it is proven that even the auxiliary members function collectively.

Therefore, when many principal rites (*pradhāna*) share the same time, place, and agent, their auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are performed once for all; this is *tantra* (common performance), as in the case of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices. However, where there is a difference regarding even one of these factors—as in the case of the two sets of three [offerings] where there is a difference in time; or in the *Varuṇapraghāsa* rites where there is a difference in place between the offering to the Maruts and the others; or in that very context where there is a difference in agent for those performed on the western fire—there is an insertion (*āvāpa*) of the auxiliaries, as in the injunction: "Having offered to Agni Pavamāna, one should offer to Agni Pāvaka and Śuci upon the same sacrificial grass (*barhis*). Such is the nature of *tantra* and *āvāpa* in ritual application.

When the extent [of performance] has been considered, that very extent is examined in the twelfth [book] by way of *prasaṅga* (incidental application). Although there is no difference in the extent of the performance itself, the Commentator has stated the distinction between those factors that motivate *tantra* (common performance) and *prasaṅga*:
"That which is common is *tantra*; but that which does not motivate when for the sake of another is *aprayojaka*.
In this very way would *prasaṅga* occur, provided that one's own injunction exists."

That which is performed for multiple purposes is a *tantra*; that which, though performed for another purpose, becomes the means (*sādhana*) or the object of presentation (*pratipādya*) for something else, is *anuniṣpanna*. In such cases, there is no requirement (*aprayojakatva*). For example: the sacrificial cake-pan (*puroḍāśakapāla*) for the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*); the footstep (*pada*) for the anointing with dice (*akṣāñjana*); the whey (*vājina*) for the whey-sacrifice (*vājinayāga*); and the dung and blood for the discarding (*nirāsana*). In these instances, even though [the primary purpose] is not present...

However, since items such as the *kapāla* (potsherds) cannot be employed for the purpose of scattering the husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) and so forth, they lack *prayojakatva* (the status of being a motivator). On the other hand, where both [rites] have their subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) applied independently of one another, yet the fulfillment of the benefit (*upakāra*) for the second rite is achieved by those very subsidiaries performed for the sake of the first, then even if that [second rite] is not capable of being a motivator, its omission occurs; just as the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake offering), because the benefit is fulfilled by the *prayāja* and other rites performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice, is applied by extended injunction (*atideśa*) for its own sake without regard for its connection to the animal sacrifice.

In that case, there is *prasaṅga*, because [the sacrifice] does not cause the *prayāja* and other rites to be performed separately. And here, when they cannot be obtained for another purpose, they themselves become the motivators (*prayojaka*).

For this very reason, the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, which are absent in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), are caused to be performed by means of the *paśupuroḍāśa*. [The opponent] says: If the *prayāja* and other rites, having been performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice, benefit the *paśupuroḍāśa* but are not performed for its sake, how then can they be its subsidiary (*aṅga*)? For it is intended that being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*) constitutes being a subsidiary.
And its being for that purpose is due to the mention [of it], not because of benefit; nor is there any such benefit here. ||33||

That for whose sake something is performed is for that purpose, and it alone is called an "auxiliary" (aṅga), not merely that which is helpful. Now, since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are not performed with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) as their objective, how can they be its auxiliaries? [Objection: If this were the case, then the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*) would also be an auxiliary of the animal sacrifice.

Although the nature of the potsherds (*kapāla*) is indeed employed for the sake of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), they are nevertheless utilized for the purpose of scattering the husks (*tuṣopavāpa*); thus, it is correct that they possess the status of being "subordinate" (*śeṣa*), characterized by being the object of an activity directed toward another [purpose]. However, the *prayāja* offerings and the like are not, in any way whatsoever, objects of a person’s activity directed toward the animal-sacrifice cake; therefore, their status as subordinate to that cake is impossible. It is said in reply: There is no status of subordination (*śeṣatā*) of the *prayājas* with respect to the cake.
Rather, their status as its subsidiary (*aṅga*) is understood through their suitability (*yogyatva*) for it. (Verse 35)

Just as even when a fire does not actually burn, it is still designated as "burning," so too, even though the *prayāja* and other such rites are not performed for the sake of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), they can indeed be designated as its subsidiaries by virtue of their suitability (*yogyatā*). Furthermore, because another [subsidiary] is already established, it does not necessitate performance; thus, even in the case of those things that are subsidiaries to something else, the conventional usage of "subsidiarity" occurs by virtue of suitability. Others, however, maintain that suitability itself is what constitutes subsidiarity.

Therefore, they describe the fact that even in the case of the *puroḍāśa* cake, the primary status of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth indeed exists. Let it be so; in any case, the conventional usage of "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*) is established, and thus everything is consistent. This is the summary of the meaning: first, the *bhāvanā* is denoted by its own word; and although its connection with the injunction through a common designation is perceived, it is not immediately finalized due to a lack of semantic fitness.

This state is called the "procedure of the injunction" (*vidhiprakrama*). From this procedure of the injunction, it is understood that the injunction must be fulfilled with such components as it requires to be complete. Consequently, when there arises the expectation of what its result (*bhāvya*) should be, one bypasses the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—even though it is expressed by the same word—as it is unsuitable, and instead accepts [the result] such as heaven (*svarga*), which is expressed by another word. This has been explained in the first section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādye*).

In the absence of that [directly expressed result], it is supplied from an explanatory passage (arthavāda), and in its absence, it is supplied by ellipsis (adhyāhāra); this has been established in the *Rātrisatra-adhikaraṇa* and the *Viśvajit-adhikaraṇa*. Therefore, when there is a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) expressed within the same word is connected as the instrument; such is the meaning of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, since the status of being an instrument for a result that occurs at a later time is not possible for a momentary act directly, there arises a requirement for a stable medium. Since the [theories of] refinement of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*) and the propitiation of a deity (*devatārādhana*) have been refuted in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* and in the section concerning the beginning of the action (*karmārambha-bhāvyatva*), and since those cannot serve as the medium, one must resort to the *apūrva*. Thus, by supplying the word "that" (*tat*), [the injunction is understood as]: "Having produced the *apūrva* by means of sacrifice, one should bring about heaven. In this way, the sacrifice—endowed with the *apūrva* as its intermediate operation—is like wood and the like possessed of a flame, which brings about cooking.

Once it has been stated in the section on the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) that [the sacrifice] is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the fruit, the question arises: "How is this *apūrva* to be performed? Thus, a further expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) arises, just as [the expectancy for fuel etc. arises] for the sake of producing a flame. Therein, the collection of subsidiaries (*aṅga-jāta*)—consisting of genus, substance, quality, action, and sequence—is accepted as the "manner of performance" (*itthambhāva*), being offered through their respective means: by the sixfold direct injunction (*upadeśa*), the threefold extended application (*atideśa*), tradition (*smṛti*), custom (*ācāra*), and the literal sense of the Vedic texts (*śruti-artha*), and so forth, just like [the acceptance of] dryness and other such qualities.

For this very reason, the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) is prompted by the fruit; thus, when the transcendental result (*apūrva*) has been postulated, and even when the intermediate *apūrva* has not yet been postulated—as in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites—the primary *apūrva* is employed toward the fruit. Therefore, just like the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, it is prompted by the ultimate *apūrva*; indeed, the primary sacrifice is prompted by the fruit itself. However, as for the subsidiary (*aṅga*), it is [prompted] when the *apūrva* has been postulated.

It should be understood that, as a subsidiary to that [principal action], the *avāntarāpūrva* (intermediate apūrva) is enjoined as a subsidiary to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others—just like the restriction of speech (*avāṅ-niyama*)—and is therefore prompted by the intermediate apūrva, not by the ultimate apūrva (*paramāpūrva*). Consequently, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*), the performance of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all its specific attributes must be undertaken by one seeking the fruit, provided they are capable of performing all the subsidiaries; this performance is accompanied by the sequence established through direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), and so forth, and is determined in its extent by the principles of *prayojakatva* (prompting), *aprayojakatva* (non-prompting), *tantra* (common performance), *āvāpa* (insertion), *prasaṅga* (extension), and their respective exceptions.

However, regarding obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, the injunction prescribes them even for a person who is unable to perform some of the constituent parts (*aṅga*). All of this is summarized in the Vārttika by the passage beginning with "The word denoting the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) causes those [factors] to be remembered, as in common worldly usage," and so on:
"Therefore, even though it has already begun its form, the injunction awaits until the productive operation has attained its fitness, being independent of anything else."
It should be understood that this is what has been shown by the preceding [verse].
"The illustrious Yajñātmananda, renowned throughout the three worlds, having received the sacred learning from him alone, became famous as Pārthasārathi. (36)

Having plunged into the turbulent ocean of Mīmāṃsā—which is difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom due to the sequence of their objections—the wise one has fashioned this garland using the jewels of logic (nyāyaratna) esteemed by his respected teachers. (37)
Salutations to Jaimini, who, having crossed over by means of the lamps of logic, shines as if with blazing fires. ||38||
Thus ends the "Determination of the Auxiliary" (*Aṅganirṇaya*) in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*, the work of Pārthasārathi Miśra, son of the venerable teacher Yajñātman.

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence."
